title: Nested Data Structures
text:
Modules
This workshop is built around a single, uncomfortable idea: your data is never really about your data. Every dataset you collect is a partial, imperfect snapshot of a broader process — almost always structured, layered, and nested in ways standard analysis ignores.
The workshop is written for researchers in judgment and decision making — studying consumer choice, financial behavior, risky decision making, and policy response — who work with both observational panel data and randomized experiments.
The field of nested data analysis is fundamentally about recovering the data-generating process (DGP) from these snapshots. The models here don’t just fit your data better — they get closer to the truth about the process that produced it.
The unifying question throughout is: What assumption is standard regression making here, and what happens when it’s wrong?

title: Nested Data Structures
text:
How to Use This Workshop
Each section pairs conceptual explanation with R tutorials and — wherever possible — both an experimental example and a secondary/observational data example. All code is shown using the toggle button at the top right of each page.
This workshop assumes you are comfortable with basic regression and have used R before. No prior exposure to multilevel modeling is assumed.

title: Nested Data Structures
text:
Key Premise

Science combines observable data with assumptions to infer latent or general processes. Research errors frequently stem from unexamined assumptions about the structure of that data. The goal of nested data models is not just to “control for clustering” — it is to recapture the data-generating process.

The models here are tools for thinking. Understanding their assumptions — and when those assumptions fail — is the heart of this workshop.

title: Module 0: All Data is Nested
text:
The Central Claim
Before we learn any specific model, we need to confront a claim that sounds provocative but is actually quite mundane once you sit with it:
Not “some data.” Not “longitudinal data” or “hierarchical organizational data.” All of it.

title: Module 0: All Data is Nested
text:
All data is nested.



Two Examples That Look Different But Are Not
Example 1 — An incentivized risky-choice experiment. You recruit 200 participants. Each participant makes one incentivized choice between a safe option and a risky gamble. The gamble descriptions are sampled from a larger set of 60 possible risky problems — each with different probabilities and payoffs — so each participant sees a different gamble. At first glance this looks flat: 200 rows, one per person, one response each.
But consider the structure underneath. Each participant is a particular person sampled from a population of possible decision-makers, carrying their own stable risk preferences, their own financial situation, their own affective state on the day of the study. Each gamble is a particular stimulus sampled from a population of possible risky problems, with its own expected value, variance, and framing properties. The 200 observed choices are not 200 independent draws from a single distribution. They are 200 snapshots of a process with at least two levels: the gamble level and the person level.
Example 2 — A household spending panel. You observe 200 households making monthly spending decisions over 18 months — 3,600 rows total. Each month’s decision is nested within the household’s financial cycle: income shocks, recurring obligations, seasonal patterns, and the trajectory of decisions that came before. Each household has a characteristic spending level, a characteristic level of volatility, and a characteristic sensitivity to price changes.
The inferential structure is identical to Example 1. Each row belongs to a higher-level unit (a person, a household) that shapes it. Rows within the same unit are more alike than rows from different units. Standard regression, which assumes all rows are independent, is wrong in the same way in both cases.


Same Logic, Different Field
The nesting logic appears everywhere in JDM research, often under different names:

Daily diary studies ask participants to record a risky or impulsive decision each day for two weeks. Each day’s entry is nested within the person — and the person’s mood, financial situation, and recent decision history shape each entry.
Consumer panels track the same households purchasing across product categories over months or years. Each transaction is nested within the customer, whose stable price sensitivity and brand loyalty show up in every row.
Repeated risky-choice experiments present each participant with dozens of gamble pairs. Each response is nested within both the participant (risk preferences) and the gamble (payoff structure and framing). Both sources of variance are real and both need to be in the model.
Customers nested within product messages occur whenever a firm sends different information treatments to different customers, or whenever participants in an experiment each see multiple product descriptions. The message is a level of the data — not just a condition label.

The question is not whether nesting exists — it almost always does — but which higher-level process each row belongs to and which level matters for your claim.


Why Does This Matter?
Because ignoring nesting produces three kinds of errors: standard errors that are too small (inflated Type I error), estimands that conflate within-person and between-person effects, and causal language that is not supported by the design. The rest of the workshop is about diagnosing and fixing these errors.






NoteThe Three-Step Lens



Use this lens whenever you encounter a new dataset.
DGP: People make decisions in contexts, under constraints, shaped by stable preferences and shifting circumstances. The data-generating process is layered: stable person-level traits, varying situation-level features, and moment-to-moment noise all contribute to each observed response.
Observable pattern: Repeated or clustered rows are correlated. The same person’s choices look more alike than different people’s choices. The same gamble elicits more similar responses than different gambles. These patterns are not noise — they are information about the DGP.
Model implication: Flat regression treats all rows as independent, which assigns all of the between-cluster similarity to the residual. This is almost always wrong. It produces standard errors that are too small, coefficients that mix levels, and inference that is not trustworthy.

title: Module 0: All Data is Nested
text:
What This Module Covers
This module lays the conceptual groundwork for everything that follows.
Part 1: The DGP Perspective — What process generated this data, and what levels does that process have? We develop intuition for what a data-generating process is, why it is almost always nested, and what it means to “recapture the DGP.”
Part 2: Types of Nested Structures — Which of the four main nesting structures does my data fit, and what does each assume? Pure hierarchies, crossed structures, panel data, and longitudinal data each arise from a different relationship between observations, people, and contexts.
Part 3: Measuring Non-Independence — How much of my variance lives at the group level? Is the independence assumption badly violated? The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) and design effects are the core diagnostic tools. We show how even modest ICCs produce dramatic distortions in inference.
Part 4: Data Structure and Format — How should my dataset be structured to make the nesting visible and the analysis correct? Long format, identifying variables, and reading a dataset to see its level structure immediately.






NoteSame Observables, Different Stories



Consider two researchers who collect the same dataset: household monthly spending measured for 18 months, with an average positive correlation of 0.42 within households.
Researcher A says: “Spending is persistent — households have stable spending habits, and month-to-month fluctuations are minor noise around a stable level.”
Researcher B says: “The correlation is driven entirely by time-invariant income — richer households spend more every month, so their rows look similar. Within a household, spending fluctuates unpredictably around that income-constrained mean.”
Both researchers see the same 0.42 correlation. Both are working from the same data. But they have opposite models of what drives it — one says stable habits (a within-person process), the other says fixed income (a between-person characteristic).
The observable pattern does not tell you which story is true. Only design choices — within-person centering, instruments for income shocks, experimental manipulation of budget constraints — can discriminate between them. This is the central challenge of working with nested data: the same correlation structure can arise from genuinely different DGPs, and your model choice embeds an assumption about which DGP you believe.
Throughout this workshop, whenever you learn a new model or assumption, ask: What else could produce the same observable pattern? What design or data would discriminate?








TipReviewer Challenge: Which Level is Generating This Pattern?



When presenting results from nested data, expect a sharp reviewer to ask:

“Is the effect you are claiming a within-person change, a between-person difference, or both mixed together?”
“Which level of the nesting structure could be driving this result instead of the level your theory is about?”
“If the ICCs are low, does that mean clustering is irrelevant — or does it mean the penalty is large because cluster sizes are large?”
“Could the ‘treatment effect’ you estimate be entirely driven by which group or context someone was in, rather than the treatment itself?”

These are not hostile questions. They are the natural consequences of working with data that has structure. The models in this workshop teach you to answer them before the reviewer has to ask.








TipObservational and Experimental JDM: The Same Nesting Logic










Observational JDM version
Experimental JDM version




Consumer spending panel: each purchase nested within customer history and market context
Risky choice experiment: each response nested within participant and gamble stimulus


Household finance longitudinal study: monthly decisions nested within household trajectories
WTP elicitation across framing conditions: each response nested within person and message


Policy rollout across regional markets: consumer outcomes nested within policy regime and region
Multi-site framing experiment: responses nested within participant, stimulus, and site



The modeling tools differ in detail but share the same logical foundation: every row belongs to a higher-level process, and ignoring that process produces wrong inference.

title: Module 0: All Data is Nested
text:
A Note on Prerequisites
This workshop assumes you understand basic linear regression: what a slope and intercept mean, how to fit a model in R, what a residual is. You do not need to have any prior exposure to multilevel modeling, mixed-effects models, or hierarchical linear models. If you have heard these terms and found them confusing, that is fine — we start from scratch.
Throughout this workshop, every major concept is illustrated twice — once with observational JDM data (consumer panels, financial diaries, policy rollouts) and once with experimental JDM data (framing studies, risky-choice tasks, multi-site field experiments). The goal is that readers from both traditions recognize their own work in the examples.
Module 0 gives you the vocabulary to recognize structure. Module 1 gives you the model families that represent it — from random intercepts to crossed effects to growth curves. The two modules together answer the question: what kind of data do I have, and what model does it require?

title: The DGP Perspective
text: The Data-Generating Process

title: The DGP Perspective
text:
Your Data is a Photograph
Imagine you want to understand how rivers move. You walk up to a river and take a photograph. The photograph captures the river’s position at exactly that moment — the precise shape of the water, the location of each ripple, the exact color of the surface.
Now: how much can you learn about the river from one photograph?
You can learn something. You can see that it flows roughly north, that the banks are wide, that the water looks fast. But you cannot see the seasonal floods, the drought periods, the long-term shift of the channel, or the way the current varies across different cross-sections. One photograph freezes a moment in an ongoing process.
Your dataset is that photograph. The process that generated your data — the underlying mechanisms, the population of people, the range of contexts, the flow of time — is the river. Your job as a researcher is to infer as much as possible about the river from your one photograph. The models in this workshop are tools for doing that inference more honestly.

title: The DGP Perspective
text:
What is a Data-Generating Process?
A data-generating process (DGP) is the full set of mechanisms that produce your data. It includes:

The population of units you are sampling (people, firms, countries, neurons)
The population of contexts, stimuli, or conditions under which observations occur
The temporal process by which things change and unfold
The relationships between variables — what causes what, and how strongly

Your dataset is one realization of this process. A different sample, a different week, a different set of stimuli, would have given you different numbers — but from the same underlying process.
The question that motivates nested data analysis is: what does this realization tell us about the process?

title: The DGP Perspective
section: Why the DGP is Almost Always Nested
text:
Why the DGP is Almost Always Nested
Think about the last study you ran or analyzed. Ask yourself: where did the observations come from?

People are sampled from populations that have subgroups, histories, cultures, and contexts. A sample of Dutch students in 2024 is not the same as a sample of American workers in 1990, even if both studies measure “risk preference.”
Time points are sampled from a continuous process. A mood rating collected at 9am on a Tuesday is part of a longer trajectory of mood for that person, and is nested within their week, month, and life stage.
Stimuli or items — the vignettes, products, words, or images you use — are sampled from a much larger space of possible stimuli. Your findings will generalize to the extent that your stimuli are representative.
Context — the lab, the country, the platform, the season — introduces systematic variance that your model needs to account for.

In every case, observations are not independent draws from a flat distribution. They cluster. People who share a classroom share a teacher. Employees at the same firm share a manager, a culture, and an incentive structure. Responses to the same survey item at different times are correlated because the person has not changed that much between measurements.
The independence assumption — that each observation is an independent draw, unrelated to all others — is almost never literally true. It is, at best, an approximation. And it is an approximation that can go badly wrong.

title: The DGP Perspective
text:
A Simple Demonstration
Let’s make this concrete. Suppose we study whether exposure to a weekly financial disclosure (showing expected returns) predicts willingness to invest. We collect 8 weeks of data from 30 households: 240 observations total.


Code
# Simulate: 30 households, 8 weeks each
# Each household has a stable investment willingness (random intercept)
# and their own sensitivity to disclosure exposure (random slope)
n_people <- 30
n_weeks  <- 8

person_intercepts <- rnorm(n_people, mean = 50, sd = 10)
person_slopes     <- rnorm(n_people, mean = 4,  sd = 2.5)

df <- expand_grid(
  person = 1:n_people,
  week   = 1:n_weeks
) |>
  mutate(
    disclosure_exposure = rnorm(n(), mean = 5, sd = 2),    # how much of the disclosure each HH read
    wtp_invest  = person_intercepts[person] +
                  person_slopes[person] * (disclosure_exposure - 5) +
                  rnorm(n(), 0, 6)
  )

# Plot: pooled view (ignoring nesting) vs. within-person view
p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = disclosure_exposure, y = wtp_invest)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e63946", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title   = "Pooled (ignoring nesting)",
    x       = "Disclosure exposure (0–10)",
    y       = "Willingness to invest (0–100)",
    caption = "Each dot is one household-week"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = disclosure_exposure, y = wtp_invest, group = person)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = factor(person)), alpha = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title   = "Within-household (respecting nesting)",
    x       = "Disclosure exposure (0–10)",
    y       = "Willingness to invest (0–100)",
    caption = "Each line is one household's 8-week trajectory"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  scale_color_viridis_d()

library(patchwork)
p1 + p2









The left panel treats all 240 observations as independent. It shows an upward slope — but it blurs together two very different sources of variation:

Between-household difference: households that are generally more financially confident also tend to engage more with disclosures and have higher baseline investment willingness. The positive slope in the pooled view partly reflects this selection.
Within-household effect: on weeks when a given household reads more of the disclosure, their investment willingness is higher. This is the causal question the researcher actually wants to answer.

These are distinct phenomena. The right panel begins to separate them — each household’s trajectory shows the within-household exposure–willingness relationship. The pooled view conflates both.
The DGP here has two levels: a stable household-level layer (baseline investment preferences, financial literacy) and a week-level layer (deviation from that baseline in response to varying disclosure exposure). Ignoring this structure produces an estimate that mixes the causal question (disclosure effect within households) with the selection question (which households engage more overall).






NoteWhy Repeated Choices Are Not Simply More Sample Size



A common intuition: “I have 30 participants each making 8 choices — that’s 240 data points. More data means more power.”
This is only true if the 240 choices are 240 independent pieces of evidence. They are not. Within each household, the 8 choices share the household’s stable risk preferences, income level, and financial context. Those shared influences inflate the similarity among the household’s rows.
The effective sample size is not 240 — it is somewhere between 30 (fully redundant observations within households) and 240 (fully independent observations). The exact number depends on the ICC: how much of the variance in investment willingness is at the household level versus the week level.
If the ICC is 0.30 and each household has 8 observations, the design effect is approximately \(1 + (8-1) \times 0.30 = 3.1\). Your 240 observations behave like roughly \(240 / 3.1 \approx 77\) independent observations. Adding more participants builds real precision; adding more weeks from the same households builds less.


The data-generating process has clear structure, and ignoring that structure does not just make estimates less precise — it can make them wrong.

title: The DGP Perspective
text:
The Three Questions
Every dataset you encounter deserves three questions before you run a single model:






ImportantThree DGP Questions



1. What is the sampling unit? What are the rows in your dataset? People? Days? Observations? Products? Multiple types nested inside each other?
2. What are the higher levels? Are your sampling units grouped into something larger? People within countries? Days within people? Patients within therapists? Even if you did not design the study this way, the DGP probably has this structure.
3. What assumption does my model make about the relationship between levels? Standard regression assumes levels do not exist — every row is independent. Is that reasonable? Can you quantify how wrong it is?


These questions are not rhetorical. Answering them is the first step of every analysis in this workshop.

title: The DGP Perspective
section: The DGP Frame vs. the “Fix My Standard Errors” Frame
text:
The DGP Frame vs. the “Fix My Standard Errors” Frame
There is a narrow and a broad way to motivate multilevel models.
The narrow frame says: clustered data violates the independence assumption, which inflates Type I error rates. You need multilevel models to get correct standard errors.
This is true and important. But it is a surprisingly weak reason to care about these models. It frames them as a statistical correction — something you do defensively to avoid getting dinged in review.
The broad frame says: your data has structure that reflects real processes. The variance at the person level is not nuisance to be corrected — it is scientifically interesting. How much does baseline mood vary across people? How much does the sleep-mood relationship vary? Who benefits most from sleep? These are not questions about standard errors. They are questions about the heterogeneity of human experience.
The models in this workshop answer both frames. But the broad frame is the more interesting one, and it is the one that will make you a better researcher.

title: Types of Nested Structures
text: Types of Nested Structures

title: Types of Nested Structures
text:
A Taxonomy of Nesting
Nesting takes several forms in social science data. Getting them confused leads to misspecified models and wrong answers. This section maps out the main types, shows what they look like in a dataset, and explains how the DGP perspective helps you identify which structure you have.
The key distinction is between pure hierarchies (units nested strictly within higher-level units) and crossed structures (units belonging to multiple grouping factors simultaneously). Real data often combines both.

title: Types of Nested Structures
text:
Pure Hierarchy: One Nesting Level
The simplest nested structure: lower-level units are grouped into higher-level units, and each lower-level unit belongs to exactly one group.
Example: Consumers nested within retail stores.

Hundreds of consumers, each shopping at one of several stores
A consumer’s purchase amount depends partly on their own spending habits and partly on the store environment (location, product mix, ambient cues)
Purchases within the same store are more similar to each other than to purchases from other stores

Think of a rectangle divided into colored columns — each column is a store, and each dot within a column is a consumer. The columns (stores) explain part of why purchases cluster.


Code
# Simulate a two-level structure
n_stores             <- 6
n_consumers_per_store <- 8

store_effects <- rnorm(n_stores, 0, 15)

df_stores <- expand_grid(
  store      = 1:n_stores,
  consumer   = 1:n_consumers_per_store
) |>
  mutate(
    consumer_id     = row_number(),
    store_effect    = store_effects[store],
    purchase_amount = 85 + store_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 8),
    store           = factor(store, labels = paste("Store", 1:n_stores))
  )

ggplot(df_stores, aes(x = store, y = purchase_amount, color = store)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5,
               color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title    = "Consumers nested within retail stores",
    subtitle = "Black bars = store means; dots = individual consumers",
    x = "Store", y = "Purchase Amount ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









Notice that purchase amounts cluster within stores. Some stores attract higher-spending consumers due to location, product mix, or ambient cues. Purchases within the same store are more similar to each other than to purchases from other stores. A model that ignores stores treats these 48 observations as 48 independent data points. They are not — they are 6 groups of 8.
Data format: One row per consumer visit. You need a consumer ID and a store ID.

title: Types of Nested Structures
text:
Three Levels: Nesting Within Nesting
The hierarchy can extend further. Consumers are nested within stores, which are nested within retail chains or geographic regions.
Example: Purchase occasions nested within customers nested within banking platforms.
Three nested boxes: the outer box is the platform, within it are customers, and within each customer are multiple occasions.
Each level adds a new source of systematic variance:

Occasions differ from each other within a customer (day of week, mood, context)
Customers differ in their baseline spending and financial habits
Banks and platforms differ in the population they serve, fees, and product mix



Code
n_banks                 <- 3
n_customers_per_bank    <- 4
n_occasions_per_customer <- 5

bank_effects     <- rnorm(n_banks, 0, 8)
customer_effects <- rnorm(n_banks * n_customers_per_bank, 0, 5)

df_three <- expand_grid(
  bank     = 1:n_banks,
  customer = 1:n_customers_per_bank,
  occasion = 1:n_occasions_per_customer
) |>
  mutate(
    customer_id       = (bank - 1) * n_customers_per_bank + customer,
    bank_eff          = bank_effects[bank],
    customer_eff      = customer_effects[customer_id],
    transaction_amount = 150 + bank_eff + customer_eff + rnorm(n(), 0, 4),
    bank_label        = paste("Platform", bank),
    customer_label    = paste0("C", customer_id)
  )

ggplot(df_three, aes(x = customer_label, y = transaction_amount,
                      color = bank_label)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 18,
               size = 4, color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ bank_label, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    title  = "Three-level structure: Occasions within Customers within Platforms",
    x      = "Customer",
    y      = "Transaction Amount ($)",
    color  = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









The key diagnostic question for three-level data: how much variance lives at each level? Later, the ICC will give us a principled answer.

title: Types of Nested Structures
text:
Panel Data: Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal
Panel data combines the cross-sectional and time-series structures. You observe multiple units (people, firms, households) at multiple time points.
Example: Monthly spending by 50 households measured over 24 months.


Code
n_households <- 50
n_months     <- 24

household_baseline <- rnorm(n_households, 1000, 200)

df_panel <- expand_grid(
  household = 1:n_households,
  month     = 1:n_months
) |>
  mutate(
    baseline   = household_baseline[household],
    spending   = baseline + 20 * (month - 12.5) / 12 + rnorm(n(), 0, 80),
    time_trend = month
  )

# Show 6 households
sample_hh <- sample(1:n_households, 6)

ggplot(df_panel |> filter(household %in% sample_hh),
       aes(x = month, y = spending, color = factor(household))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title    = "Panel data: 6 households over 24 months",
    subtitle = "Each line is one household's spending trajectory",
    x        = "Month",
    y        = "Monthly Spending ($)",
    color    = "Household"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









Panel data has two sources of nesting simultaneously: 1. Observations are nested within households (same household at different times) 2. Observations might also be nested within time periods (all households in month 1 face the same economic conditions)
This means you potentially need fixed or random effects for both dimensions — a crossed structure, not a pure hierarchy.

title: Types of Nested Structures
text:
Crossed Random Effects
In a crossed structure, observations belong to multiple grouping factors that are not nested within each other.
Example from JDM research: Participants evaluate product messages in a pricing study.
In a JDM experiment, 40 participants each evaluate 80 product messages. Each message is a pricing or promotional offer sampled from a larger population. The outcome is willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars.
A grid: rows are participants, columns are messages. Every cell is one WTP judgment. No row is nested inside any column — they cross.

Each observation belongs to one participant AND one message
Participants are not nested within messages, and messages are not nested within participants
Both participant differences (baseline WTP, income, brand affinity) and message differences (quality of framing, scarcity cues) contribute to WTP



Code
# Small illustration: 4 participants × 4 messages
crossed_df <- expand_grid(
  participant = paste("P", 1:4),
  message     = paste("M", 1:4)
) |>
  mutate(wtp = 50 + rnorm(16, 0, 15))

ggplot(crossed_df, aes(x = message, y = participant, fill = wtp)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(wtp)), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#deebf7", high = "#08519c") +
  labs(
    title    = "Crossed structure: each participant evaluates each message",
    subtitle = "Cell = WTP for that participant-message combination",
    x        = "Message",
    y        = "Participant",
    fill     = "WTP ($)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









The key point: participant 1’s WTP for message 3 is not in the same “group” as participant 2’s WTP for message 3. Both observations share a message, but not a participant. This crossed structure requires a different model than a pure hierarchy.
Now a full simulation showing the consequences of getting this wrong:


Code
n_participants <- 40
n_messages     <- 80

participant_effects <- rnorm(n_participants, 0, 12)   # people differ in baseline WTP
message_effects     <- rnorm(n_messages, 0, 8)        # messages differ in baseline WTP
message_quality     <- runif(n_messages, 1, 10)       # message quality predictor

df_msgs <- expand_grid(participant = 1:n_participants, message = 1:n_messages) |>
  mutate(
    participant_eff = participant_effects[participant],
    message_eff     = message_effects[message],
    quality         = message_quality[message],
    wtp             = 50 + 4 * quality + participant_eff + message_eff + rnorm(n(), 0, 10),
    participant     = factor(participant),
    message         = factor(message)
  )




Code
# Without message random effects (wrong)
model_no_msgs <- lmer(wtp ~ quality + (1 | participant),
                      data = df_msgs)

# With crossed random effects (correct)
model_crossed <- lmer(wtp ~ quality + (1 | participant) + (1 | message),
                      data = df_msgs)




Code
wrong_se   <- broom.mixed::tidy(model_no_msgs)[2, "std.error"][[1]]
correct_se <- broom.mixed::tidy(model_crossed)[2, "std.error"][[1]]

tibble(
  Model          = c("Without message RE", "With message RE (crossed)"),
  Quality_SE     = c(wrong_se, correct_se)
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "SE of message quality effect: ignoring vs. modeling message-level variance")



SE of message quality effect: ignoring vs. modeling message-level variance


Model
Quality_SE




Without message RE
0.083


With message RE (crossed)
0.332





Some participants have higher baseline WTP due to income, brand affinity, or general deal-seeking tendencies. Some messages are more compelling due to framing quality, scarcity cues, or discount depth. Both sources of variance must be modeled — ignoring message-level variance deflates the standard error on the quality effect, producing anti-conservative inference.

title: Types of Nested Structures
text:
Repeated Measures and Longitudinal Data
Repeated measures means the same unit is measured multiple times — on the same variable, under different conditions, at different time points, or both.
The critical distinction:

Repeated measures (experimental): Each person experiences multiple conditions. The conditions are fixed (e.g., gain frame vs. loss frame). The person is the random unit.
Longitudinal data: Each person is measured at multiple time points, and time is part of the model. Change over time is the phenomenon of interest.

Both are cases of observations nested within persons. But they ask different questions. Repeated-measures experiments ask: “does the framing condition affect the outcome?” Longitudinal models ask: “how does the outcome change over time, and does it change differently for different people?”


Code
# Repeated measures: gain vs. loss framing
df_rm <- tibble(
  person    = rep(1:20, each = 2),
  condition = rep(c("loss_frame", "gain_frame"), 20),
  purchase_intention = 55 + ifelse(condition == "gain_frame", 8, 0) +
                       rnorm(40, 0, 20)
)

p_rm <- ggplot(df_rm, aes(x = condition, y = purchase_intention,
                           group = person, color = factor(person))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Repeated measures: 2 framing conditions per person",
       x = NULL, y = "Purchase Intention (0-100)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Longitudinal
df_long <- tibble(
  person = rep(1:10, each = 5),
  time   = rep(1:5, 10),
  score  = rep(rnorm(10, 50, 8), each = 5) +
           rep(rnorm(10, 2, 1), each = 5) * (rep(1:5, 10) - 3) +
           rnorm(50, 0, 3)
)

p_long <- ggplot(df_long, aes(x = time, y = score,
                               group = person, color = factor(person))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Longitudinal:\n5 time points per person",
       x = "Time", y = "Score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

library(patchwork)
p_rm + p_long

title: Types of Nested Structures
section: A Map of Common Data Structures
text:
A Map of Common Data Structures









Structure
Example
Nesting
DGP implication




Pure hierarchy
Consumers within retail stores
Strict: each unit in one group
Between-group variance is real


Three-level
Purchase occasions within customers within platforms
Nested levels
Variance at each level


Panel
Households across months (panel)
Cross-sectional + time
Unit effects and time effects


Crossed
Participants × product messages
Each unit in multiple groups
Two sources of random variance


Repeated measures
Person × framing condition
Each person measured in each condition
Within-person correlation


Longitudinal
Person measured over time
Observations in person
Individual trajectories



The single most common mistake is treating one of these as another. The second most common mistake is failing to ask the question at all.






TipPractical Exercise



Look at the last dataset you analyzed. Ask:

What is the row in this dataset?
Can I draw a diagram of what contains what?
Are there two dimensions of grouping (e.g., people AND stimuli) that are crossed rather than nested?
What does a standard regression assume about the structure I just identified?

title: Measuring Non-Independence
text: Measuring Non-Independence

title: Measuring Non-Independence
text:
Why We Need a Number
Nested structure is not binary — it is not just “present” or “absent.” Nesting can be strong (observations within a group are nearly identical) or weak (observations within a group are barely more similar than observations from different groups). The strength of nesting determines how badly standard analysis fails.
We need a number that quantifies this strength. That number is the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC).

title: Measuring Non-Independence
text:
The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient
The ICC answers a deceptively simple question:

Of all the variance in my outcome, what fraction is due to group membership?

If you pick two observations at random from the same group, how correlated will they be? That correlation is the ICC.
\[
\text{ICC} = \frac{\sigma^2_{\text{between}}}{\sigma^2_{\text{between}} + \sigma^2_{\text{within}}}
\]
where \(\sigma^2_{\text{between}}\) is the variance in group means, and \(\sigma^2_{\text{within}}\) is the variance of individual observations around their group mean.






NoteInterpreting ICC Values




ICC ≈ 0: Knowing which group an observation is in tells you almost nothing. Group membership barely predicts the outcome. Nesting is present but weak.
ICC ≈ 0.05–0.15: Typical for many psychological studies. Modest clustering. Looks small but has real consequences for inference.
ICC ≈ 0.20–0.40: Strong clustering. Common in organizational data (employees within firms), educational data (students within schools), or within-person repeated measures.
ICC ≈ 1.0: All variance is between groups. Observations within a group are identical. Knowing the group tells you everything.



Let’s see three cases:


Code
# Generate data with three different levels of ICC
make_grouped_data <- function(icc, n_groups = 10, n_per_group = 20) {
  sigma_between <- sqrt(icc)
  sigma_within  <- sqrt(1 - icc)

  group_means <- rnorm(n_groups, 0, sigma_between)

  expand_grid(group = 1:n_groups, obs = 1:n_per_group) |>
    mutate(
      y   = group_means[group] + rnorm(n(), 0, sigma_within),
      icc_label = paste0("ICC = ", icc)
    )
}

df_icc <- bind_rows(
  make_grouped_data(0.02),
  make_grouped_data(0.20),
  make_grouped_data(0.60)
)

ggplot(df_icc, aes(x = factor(group), y = y, color = factor(group))) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5,
               color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ icc_label, ncol = 3) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(
    title    = "Same data, different ICCs",
    subtitle = "Black bars = group means; dots = individual observations",
    x        = "Group",
    y        = "Outcome"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









When ICC = 0.02, the group means barely differ — the groups look almost interchangeable. When ICC = 0.60, the group means dominate: knowing which group you are in tells you most of what you need to know about someone’s score.

title: Measuring Non-Independence
section: How to Compute the ICC in R
text:
How to Compute the ICC in R
The ICC comes directly from a null (intercept-only) multilevel model — one with no predictors, just a random intercept for the grouping variable. The model partitions total variance into between-group and within-group components.


Code
# Simulate a dataset: households nested within bank branches
# (each branch has a different financial coaching culture and local economic environment)
n_branches    <- 30
n_per_branch  <- 15

branch_effects <- rnorm(n_branches, 50, 6)   # between-branch variance in savings behavior

df_branches <- expand_grid(
  branch    = 1:n_branches,
  household = 1:n_per_branch
) |>
  mutate(
    monthly_savings = branch_effects[branch] + rnorm(n(), 0, 8)  # within-branch variance
  )

# Fit the null model: only branch random intercept, no predictors
null_model <- lmer(monthly_savings ~ 1 + (1 | branch), data = df_branches)
summary(null_model)

Code
# Extract variance components
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(null_model))
var_between <- vc$vcov[1]   # branch-level variance (shared branch environment)
var_within  <- vc$vcov[2]   # household-level residual variance

icc_value <- var_between / (var_between + var_within)
cat("ICC =", round(icc_value, 3))


ICC = 0.245


Code
cat("\nThis means", round(icc_value * 100, 1), "% of the variance in monthly savings")



This means 24.5 % of the variance in monthly savings


Code
cat("\nis explained simply by which branch the household belongs to.\n")



is explained simply by which branch the household belongs to.


The performance package provides a cleaner interface:


Code
library(performance)
icc(null_model)

The ICC here reflects how much the branch environment — local economic conditions, coaching culture, program availability — shapes savings behavior beyond household-level characteristics. A branch ICC of 0.20 would mean that simply knowing which branch a household belongs to explains 20% of the variance in their savings outcomes.

title: Measuring Non-Independence
section: Why Even a Small ICC Is a Big Problem
text:
Why Even a Small ICC Is a Big Problem






WarningCritical Reviewer Challenge: Small ICC Does Not Mean Clustering is Irrelevant



A common mistake: researchers see a small ICC (say, 0.05) and conclude the clustering penalty is negligible. This is wrong when cluster sizes are large. The relevant quantity is the design effect, which multiplies the ICC by the cluster size.
With 50 transactions per household and an ICC of 0.05: \[\text{DEFF} = 1 + (50 - 1) \times 0.05 = 1 + 2.45 = 3.45\]
Your nominal 500 transaction-level observations act like only \(500 / 3.45 \approx 145\) independent observations — a 3.5× penalty from an ICC that many researchers would dismiss as “small.”


The reason is the design effect (DEFF): a multiplier that tells you how much your effective sample size shrinks due to clustering.
\[\text{DEFF} = 1 + (n_{\text{cluster}} - 1) \times \text{ICC}\]


Code
deff_df <- expand_grid(
  icc          = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30),
  cluster_size = c(5, 10, 20, 50)
) |>
  mutate(
    deff        = 1 + (cluster_size - 1) * icc,
    effective_n = 1000 / deff,
    label       = paste0("n = ", cluster_size)
  )

ggplot(deff_df, aes(x = icc, y = deff, color = factor(cluster_size),
                     linetype = factor(cluster_size))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Cluster size") +
  scale_linetype_discrete(name = "Cluster size") +
  labs(
    title    = "Design effect as a function of ICC and cluster size",
    subtitle = "DEFF = 1 means no clustering penalty; DEFF = 5 means your 1000 obs act like 200",
    x        = "ICC",
    y        = "Design Effect (DEFF)",
    caption  = "DEFF = 1 + (cluster_size - 1) × ICC"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









JDM example: Suppose you have 300 consumers in 15 bank branches of 20 consumers each, and the ICC for monthly savings on your outcome is 0.10 — a value common in branch-level financial data:
\[\text{DEFF} = 1 + (20 - 1) \times 0.10 = 1 + 1.9 = 2.9\]
Your 300 observations act like only \(300 / 2.9 \approx 103\) independent observations. You have nearly three times less statistical power than the raw sample size suggests. If you treat 300 clustered observations as 300 independent ones, your standard errors are too small, your p-values are too small, and your confidence intervals are too narrow.


Code
# Simulate Type I error inflation from ignoring clustering
simulate_inflation <- function(icc, n_groups = 20, n_per_group = 10, n_sims = 2000) {
  sigma_between <- sqrt(icc)
  sigma_within  <- sqrt(1 - icc)

  p_values <- replicate(n_sims, {
    group_effects <- rnorm(n_groups, 0, sigma_between)
    y <- rep(group_effects, each = n_per_group) +
         rnorm(n_groups * n_per_group, 0, sigma_within)
    x <- rnorm(n_groups * n_per_group)
    t.test(y[x > 0], y[x <= 0])$p.value
  })

  mean(p_values < 0.05)
}

icc_grid <- c(0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30)
type1_rates <- sapply(icc_grid, simulate_inflation)

tibble(ICC = icc_grid, `False Positive Rate` = type1_rates) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Type I error rate when ignoring clustering (nominal alpha = 0.05)")



Type I error rate when ignoring clustering (nominal alpha = 0.05)


ICC
False Positive Rate




0.00
0.052


0.05
0.054


0.10
0.053


0.20
0.052


0.30
0.060





When ICC = 0, ignoring clustering is fine — you get the expected 5% false positive rate. But as ICC grows, so does your false positive rate. At ICC = 0.20, you are rejecting the null hypothesis incorrectly nearly twice as often as you should be.

title: Measuring Non-Independence
text:
Assumptions of the ICC
The ICC is not just a number — it embodies assumptions. Checking those assumptions is part of using it correctly.






WarningAssumption 1: Groups are exchangeable



The ICC assumes that groups are drawn from a common population, and that the relationship between observations within a group reflects a common process. If your groups are wildly different in kind — not just in degree — the ICC may not characterize the nesting correctly.
How to check: Look at group means and within-group variances. Are any groups wildly different from the rest? Could the nesting structure be non-stationary (e.g., the within-group correlation is strong in some groups, absent in others)?








WarningAssumption 2: The grouping variable captures the relevant nesting



A single ICC assumes there is one meaningful level of nesting. If data is actually three-level (observations in therapists in clinics), a single ICC from a two-level model will be misspecified.
How to check: Fit null models at each level and compute ICCs for each. Compare the variance components.








WarningAssumption 3: The ICC is stable across groups



A standard ICC treats within-group variance as homogeneous across groups. In reality, some groups may be much more variable than others (heteroskedasticity at level 2).
How to check: Plot within-group standard deviations against group means. A strong relationship suggests heteroskedasticity.




Code
# Check: is within-group variance stable across bank branches?
df_branches |>
  group_by(branch) |>
  summarise(
    group_mean = mean(monthly_savings),
    group_sd   = sd(monthly_savings),
    n          = n()
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_mean, y = group_sd)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "#e63946") +
  labs(
    title    = "Within-branch SD vs. branch mean savings",
    subtitle = "A strong relationship suggests heteroskedastic nesting",
    x        = "Branch Mean (Monthly Savings)",
    y        = "Within-Branch SD"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









In this simulated dataset, there is no strong relationship — within-branch variance is roughly constant across branches. That is reassuring, but not always the case in real data. A common violation: wealthier branches tend to have higher and more variable savings behavior, because high-income households have more discretionary slack.

title: Measuring Non-Independence
section: ICC in Experimental Research: Two Sources of Non-Independence
text:
ICC in Experimental Research: Two Sources of Non-Independence
The ICC applies equally to experimental designs — but the sources of non-independence are different, and there are typically two of them at once.
In a within-subjects experiment, each participant responds to multiple stimuli or conditions. Two responses from the same participant will be more similar than responses from different participants: this is the participant-level ICC. Two responses to the same stimulus (rated by different participants) will also be more similar than responses to different stimuli: this is the stimulus-level ICC.






NoteTwo ICCs in a Crossed JDM Design



Consider a willingness-to-pay study: 60 consumers each evaluate 20 financial products (savings accounts, insurance plans, investment funds). The outcome (WTP in euros) has clustering at two levels simultaneously:

Participant ICC: Consumers differ in how generous or cautious they are overall. A high-WTP consumer’s responses across products are more similar to each other than to a different consumer’s responses.
Product ICC: Some products attract systematically higher WTP regardless of who evaluates them — because of perceived quality, brand, or framing. Responses to the same product across participants share variance.

Ignoring either ICC inflates the Type I error rate for any focal comparison (e.g., whether a transparent fee disclosure increases WTP). This is why Module 1 Part 6 introduces crossed random effects: (1 | participant) + (1 | product) models both ICCs simultaneously, and the design-effect penalty compounds across both levels.
# Crossed design: two ICCs
null_crossed <- lmer(wtp ~ 1 + (1 | participant) + (1 | product), data = df_wtp)
icc(null_crossed)  # returns ICCs for both grouping levels
In typical consumer valuation studies, product ICCs of 0.10–0.25 are common — meaning that 10–25% of the variance in WTP is attributable to which product was being evaluated, not to who evaluated it. Ignoring this inflates false positives for any framing manipulation applied at the product level.

title: Measuring Non-Independence
section: The ICC as a Scientific Finding
text:
The ICC as a Scientific Finding
Throughout this workshop, we treat the ICC primarily as a diagnostic tool — something you check before deciding what model to use. But it is also a finding in its own right.
JDM examples where the ICC is itself substantively informative:

If the ICC for risky-choice acceptance across gamble items is 0.18, that means 18% of the variance in choice behavior is explained simply by which gamble was presented — payoff structure and framing matter a great deal, beyond individual risk preferences.
If the ICC for monthly savings across bank branches is 0.22, that means 22% of the variance in household savings is explained by which branch the household belongs to — local program access, advisor quality, and community effects account for nearly a quarter of the variation.
If the ICC for willingness to pay across participants in a repeated valuation task is 0.45, that means the dominant source of variance is stable individual differences in preferences, not trial-to-trial variation.

Each of these ICCs tells you something substantive about the DGP — not just about which model to use.
The decomposition of variance across levels is one of the most underutilized findings in social science research. Report it alongside your treatment effects.

title: Data Structure and Format
text: Data Structure and Format

title: Data Structure and Format
text:
The Shape of Nested Data
Before fitting any model, you need your data in the right shape. Nested data analysis requires long format: one row per observation at the lowest level of the hierarchy, with identifier variables that track higher-level units.
This sounds simple. In practice, it trips up a surprising number of researchers.

title: Data Structure and Format
text:
Long Format vs. Wide Format
Most people who have worked with repeated measures data in SPSS or Excel have encountered data in wide format: one row per person, with multiple columns for each time point or condition.


Code

title: Data Structure and Format
section: Converting Wide to Long in R

title: Data Structure and Format
text:
The Essential Identifier Variables
Every nested dataset needs at least two types of identifier variables:

Level-2 identifier: A unique code for each higher-level unit (household, branch, customer, country). This is what tells the model which observations belong together.
Level-1 identifier or index: A variable that distinguishes observations within the same level-2 unit (week number, transaction, product evaluated).

In three-level data, you need identifiers at all three levels.






ImportantChecklist: Preparing Nested Data



Before fitting any model, verify:

One row per level-1 observation (not one row per person, unless you have only cross-sectional nesting)
A unique, clean level-2 ID (numeric or factor, no missing values, consistent coding)
A level-1 index within each level-2 unit (day number, trial number, condition)
Level-2 variables appear on every row for that unit (age, sex, and other person-level variables are repeated across all a person’s rows)
No structural missingness (if some observations are genuinely missing vs. structurally absent, treat them differently)

section: A Note on Balanced vs. Unbalanced Data
text:
A Note on Balanced vs. Unbalanced Data
Balanced data means every level-2 unit has the same number of level-1 observations. All 6 households have exactly 5 weeks of spending data. All 20 bank branches have exactly 15 customer records.
Unbalanced data means the number of observations varies across level-2 units. Some households completed the full 5-week spending diary; others dropped out after 2 weeks. Some branches have 10 customers in the dataset; others have 28.
Standard ANOVA-based approaches for repeated measures struggle with unbalanced data — they were designed for balanced designs. Mixed-effects models handle unbalanced data gracefully, because they use the information available for each unit without requiring complete cases.

title: Data Structure and Format
text:
Looking Ahead
With the conceptual foundations in place — DGP thinking, types of nesting, ICC, and data format — we are ready to start fitting models. Module 1 builds the core toolkit: fixed effects, random intercepts, and random slopes. At each step, we will be explicit about what assumption the model is making and what happens when that assumption is wrong.

title: Module 1: The Mixed-Effects Framework
text: Module 1: The Mixed-Effects Framework

title: Module 1: The Mixed-Effects Framework
text:
The Toolkit
Module 0 established that your data is almost always nested and that ignoring nesting inflates Type I error, shrinks effective sample sizes, and obscures the true data-generating process. Now we build the tools to do something about it.
The mixed-effects model is the central workhorse of nested data analysis. It is called “mixed” because it combines two types of effects:

Fixed effects — parameters that apply to the entire population. The average relationship between sleep and mood. The overall effect of a treatment.
Random effects — parameters that vary across units (people, firms, classrooms) and are treated as drawn from a distribution rather than estimated individually.

This combination lets the model do something powerful: borrow strength across units. A student who was absent for half the year still contributes information about their classroom. A person who completed only 2 days of a diary still informs estimates of the group average. The model uses all available information, weighted by how much each unit tells us.

title: Module 1: The Mixed-Effects Framework
text:
How This Module is Organized
The module builds in steps, each adding one layer of complexity while being explicit about what assumption is being made and what assumption is being relaxed.
Part 1: Fixed Effects introduces the fixed-effects estimator — the simplest approach to handling nesting. It is easy to understand and makes strong assumptions. We examine each assumption carefully and show when it fails.
Part 2: Random Intercepts introduces the random-intercept mixed model: the most common multilevel model in psychology. We show how it differs from fixed effects, what it assumes, and how to check those assumptions.
Part 3: Random Slopes adds the most important extension: allowing the relationship between a predictor and outcome to vary across units. We discuss when this matters and when it does not.
Part 4: Fixed vs. Random — When to Use Which addresses one of the most frequently asked questions in applied multilevel analysis. The answer involves the scientific question, the data structure, and several testable assumptions.
Part 5: Three-Level Structures extends the framework to three levels of nesting and introduces the challenge of variance decomposition across levels.
Part 6: Crossed Random Effects covers the case where observations belong to multiple grouping factors simultaneously — the structure that arises naturally in most psychological experiments.

title: Module 1: The Mixed-Effects Framework

The rightmost column is intentional. Every model in this module corrects a dependence problem — observations that are not independent. None of them, on their own, solve an identification problem — the question of whether your predictor is truly exogenous. That distinction is the heart of Module 3.

title: Module 1: The Mixed-Effects Framework
text:
Core Assumptions
Every model in this module makes assumptions. We will state them explicitly at each step. For now, here is the set of assumptions that span the entire module:






ImportantAssumptions of the Mixed-Effects Framework




Linearity: The relationship between predictors and the outcome is linear (at each level)
Normality of random effects: The random effects are drawn from a normal distribution
Normality of residuals: Level-1 residuals are normally distributed
Homoskedasticity: The variance of residuals is constant across units and predictor values
Independence of residuals: Level-1 residuals are independent after conditioning on the random effects
Independence of random effects from predictors: (for random effects models) The random effects are uncorrelated with the fixed-effect predictors

Not all of these apply to all models. Fixed-effects models, for instance, do not require Assumption 6. Understanding which assumptions apply to which model — and how to check each one — is the goal of this module.

title: Fixed Effects Models
text: Fixed Effects Models

title: Fixed Effects Models
text:
Two Settings, One Problem
Fixed effects models are usually introduced in the context of panel data — the same firms tracked over multiple years, the same countries tracked across decades. But the exact same logic applies whenever observations are nested within units, regardless of whether time is involved.
Consider two studies:
Study A (Longitudinal): You track 30 households across 8 monthly waves in a financial coaching program. Each month, you record how many pages of the financial disclosure document they reviewed and how much they saved. Households differ in underlying financial literacy: more literate households engage more with disclosure and save more regardless of engagement. The disclosure effect is confounded with literacy.
Study B (Experimental): You run a within-subjects experiment. Each of 80 participants evaluates 12 product descriptions — 6 under a “scarcity” framing (“only 3 left!”) and 6 under a neutral framing. Each participant sees both conditions.
Both studies share the same fundamental structure: multiple observations nested within the same unit (household, participant). But the problem each creates is different.
In Study A, financially literate households read more disclosure and save more — so the disclosure engagement effect is confounded with literacy. Ignoring nesting produces a biased estimate.
In Study B, condition is randomly assigned, so individual persuadability does not systematically correlate with the scarcity condition. The problem is not bias — it is dependence: ratings from the same participant are not independent observations. A pooled regression treats each rating as an independent draw and underestimates uncertainty. Standard errors are too small, confidence intervals too narrow, and Type I error rates are inflated.
Fixed effects address both problems by absorbing all stable person-level characteristics — eliminating the literacy confound in Study A and recovering correct within-person standard errors in Study B.

title: Fixed Effects Models
text:
The Model
Let \(Y_{ij}\) be the outcome for observation \(i\) within unit \(j\) (month \(i\) for household \(j\); rating \(i\) by participant \(j\)). The fixed-effects model is:
\[
\underbrace{Y_{ij}}_{\text{outcome}} = \underbrace{\alpha_j}_{\substack{\text{unit fixed} \\ \text{effect}}} + \underbrace{\beta_1}_{\substack{\text{within-unit} \\ \text{slope}}} \underbrace{X_{ij}}_{\substack{\text{within-unit} \\ \text{predictor}}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_{ij}}_{\substack{\text{residual}}}
\]
The \(\alpha_j\) is a separate intercept for every unit — a dummy variable for household \(j\), or a dummy variable for participant \(j\). It absorbs everything that is constant within that unit: the household’s financial literacy, the participant’s baseline persuadability.
The slope \(\beta_1\) is estimated purely from within-unit variation: how does \(Y\) change when \(X\) changes within the same unit?

The Within-Demeaning Transformation
An equivalent way to see what FE does is through demeaning. Let \(\bar{Y}_j = \frac{1}{n_j}\sum_i Y_{ij}\) be the unit mean. Subtracting the unit mean from every observation:
\[
\underbrace{(Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_j)}_{\substack{\text{outcome} \\ \text{demeaned}}} = \beta_1 \underbrace{(X_{ij} - \bar{X}_j)}_{\substack{\text{predictor} \\ \text{demeaned}}} + \underbrace{(\varepsilon_{ij} - \bar{\varepsilon}_j)}_{\substack{\text{residual} \\ \text{demeaned}}}
\]
After demeaning, every trace of between-unit variation is gone. The \(\alpha_j\) terms vanish completely — they cancel out when you subtract the unit mean from both sides. What remains is the pure within-unit relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\).
In the household study: we are comparing each month’s disclosure engagement to that household’s own average — controlling for the household’s literacy, income, and every other stable characteristic.
In the experiment: we are comparing each participant’s rating under scarcity to their own average rating — which is precisely what within-subjects experimental designs intend.

title: Fixed Effects Models
text:
Two Examples: Longitudinal and Experimental

Example 1: Households (Longitudinal Panel)


Code
# --- STUDY A: Households tracked over 8 monthly waves ---
n_households <- 30
n_months     <- 8

# The confound: financially literate households engage more AND save more
hh_literacy  <- rnorm(n_households, 50, 10)
hh_intercept <- hh_literacy * 0.5 + rnorm(n_households, 0, 5)

df_households <- expand_grid(
  household = 1:n_households,
  month     = 1:n_months
) |>
  mutate(
    hh_literacy    = hh_literacy[household],
    hh_intercept   = hh_intercept[household],
    # Disclosure engagement: partly driven by literacy, partly random month-to-month
    disclosure     = hh_literacy[household] * 0.3 + rnorm(n(), 0, 8),
    # True WITHIN-household effect = 0.4 (pages reviewed → percentage points saved)
    # Literacy also raises savings directly — this is the confound
    monthly_savings = 15 + 0.4 * disclosure + hh_intercept + rnorm(n(), 0, 10),
    household_f     = factor(household)
  )

# Naive pooled regression
naive_hh <- lm(monthly_savings ~ disclosure, data = df_households)
broom::tidy(naive_hh) |>
  filter(term == "disclosure") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "Pooled OLS: estimated effect of disclosure (confounded by literacy)")

Example 2: Within-Subjects Experiment

# --- STUDY B: Ratings nested within participants ---
n_participants <- 80
n_ratings      <- 12   # 6 scarcity, 6 neutral

# Nesting: participants differ in baseline persuadability; condition is randomly assigned within person
persuadability <- rnorm(n_participants, 50, 10)

df_exp <- expand_grid(
  participant = 1:n_participants,
  rating_num  = 1:n_ratings
) |>
  mutate(
    condition    = rep(c("scarcity", "neutral"), n_ratings / 2)[rating_num],
    scarcity_bin = as.integer(condition == "scarcity"),
    # True WITHIN-person effect of scarcity = 4 points
    # But persuadability (a person-level trait) also drives ratings
    purchase_intent = persuadability[participant] + 4 * scarcity_bin +
                      rnorm(n(), 0, 8),
    participant_f   = factor(participant)
  )

# Naive pooled regression: mixes within-person and between-person variation
naive_exp <- lm(purchase_intent ~ scarcity_bin, data = df_exp)
broom::tidy(naive_exp) |>
  filter(term == "scarcity_bin") |>

title: Fixed Effects Models
text:
How Fixed Effects Solve This
Fixed effects recover the within-unit slope by including a dummy for every unit. In the household study that is 30 household dummies. In the experiment it is 80 participant dummies. Each dummy absorbs everything that is constant within that unit.


Code
# Study A: FE via lm with household dummies
fe_hh  <- lm(monthly_savings ~ disclosure + household_f, data = df_households)

# Study B: FE via lm with participant dummies (equivalent)
fe_exp <- lm(purchase_intent ~ scarcity_bin + participant_f, data = df_exp)




Code
# Compare naive vs. FE for both studies
bind_rows(
  broom::tidy(naive_hh)  |> filter(term == "disclosure") |>
    mutate(study = "Study A", model = "Pooled OLS",    term = "Predictor"),
  broom::tidy(fe_hh)     |> filter(term == "disclosure") |>

  broom::tidy(naive_exp) |> filter(term == "scarcity_bin") |>

) |>

Both uses are valid. The experimental use is often overlooked — but within-subjects ANOVA is, mathematically, a fixed-effects model.

title: Fixed Effects Models
section: The Assumptions of Fixed Effects Models
text:
The Assumptions of Fixed Effects Models
Each assumption is framed for both a longitudinal/observational setting and an experimental/repeated-measures setting.






WarningAssumption 1: Strict Exogeneity



The equation implication: For the within-demeaned estimator to be unbiased, we require:
\[E[\varepsilon_{ij} \mid X_{i1}, X_{i2}, \ldots, X_{in_j}, \alpha_j] = 0\]
In words: the residuals must be uncorrelated with the predictor at every observation point — past, present, and future — after conditioning on the fixed effect.
In longitudinal data: This fails if the outcome feeds back into the predictor. If a household’s rising savings rate causes it to engage more with the disclosure document in the next month (they feel good about progress and want to read more), then disclosure at \(t+1\) is correlated with the savings residual at \(t\). This is reverse causation — and it violates strict exogeneity.
It also fails with anticipation effects: if households know the disclosure program starts in month 3, they may begin saving more in month 2 in anticipation — causing the month-2 savings residual to be correlated with the future predictor.
In experiments: Strict exogeneity is typically satisfied by design — random assignment ensures that condition is not caused by the outcome. But it can fail in carryover designs where the treatment in one block affects the outcome in a later block (order effects, fatigue, contrast effects). Counterbalancing and washout periods address this.









How to check: In longitudinal data, plot residuals against future values of the predictor. In experiments, check for order effects by including trial number as a covariate.








WarningAssumption 2: No Time-Varying (or Trial-Varying) Confounds



What it means: Fixed effects only remove stable unit-level confounds. If a confound changes across observations within the same unit, the fixed effect cannot absorb it.
\[\alpha_j = \text{constant over all } i \text{ within unit } j\]
If the unit’s “true level” shifts — a household moves to a wealthier neighbourhood mid-study; a participant becomes fatigued midway through a session — the single \(\alpha_j\) is no longer a valid representation.
In longitudinal data: Any policy, economic shock, or personal event that co-occurs with your predictor is a time-varying confound. Example: if households that read more disclosure also simultaneously switch to automatic savings transfers that month, the savings effect is confounded with the automatic-transfer adoption — not with any stable characteristic, but with a time-varying behaviour.
In experiments: Practice effects, fatigue, and demand characteristics that change systematically across trials. If participants become better at evaluating products as the experiment progresses (learning), and if scarcity items happen to appear later in the session, this is a trial-varying confound.
How to check: Include trial order or time as a covariate. Check whether substantive estimates change when you control for order.








WarningAssumption 3: Sufficient Within-Unit Variation



What it means: Fixed effects can only estimate \(\beta_1\) from within-unit variation. If the predictor barely changes within units, the estimator is imprecise:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_j \sum_i (X_{ij} - \bar{X}_j)(Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_j)}{\sum_j \sum_i (X_{ij} - \bar{X}_j)^2}\]
The denominator — total within-unit variation in \(X\) — appears in the denominator of the variance of \(\hat\beta_1\). Small within-unit variation → large standard errors.
In longitudinal data: A predictor like household income barely changes within a household from month to month. FE is poorly suited to estimating the effect of stable characteristics. Disclosure engagement varies monthly — but only because households differ in their timing. If most households read the same pages every month, within-household variation in disclosure is small.
In experiments: This is usually not an issue because condition is deliberately manipulated. But if the manipulation is very subtle (a framing tweak that most participants barely notice), the effective treatment variation is low.


Code
# Study A: how much within-household variation does disclosure have?
df_households |>
  group_by(household) |>
  summarise(within_sd = sd(disclosure)) |>
  summarise(
    mean_within_sd  = mean(within_sd),
    total_sd        = sd(df_households$disclosure),
    within_fraction = mean(within_sd) / sd(df_households$disclosure)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "Study A: fraction of disclosure variance that is within-household")



Study A: fraction of disclosure variance that is within-household


mean_within_sd
total_sd
within_fraction




7.713

WarningAssumption 4: Fixed Effects Are Stable (One Intercept Per Unit)



What it means: The model assigns each unit exactly one intercept \(\alpha_j\). This assumes the unit’s baseline is constant across all its observations:
\[Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \beta_1 X_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}\]
In longitudinal data: If a household’s financial situation changes dramatically mid-study — a job loss, inheritance, or major purchase — the single \(\alpha_j\) no longer represents either period accurately. The early-period and late-period intercepts differ, but the model conflates them.
In experiments: If a participant’s attention or mood changes substantially mid-session (and this change is not modeled), the stable-intercept assumption is violated. Attention checks and session-split analyses help detect this.
How to check: For longitudinal data, split the sample at the midpoint and compare unit intercepts across periods. For experiments, split trials into first-half and second-half blocks and test whether the effect estimate shifts.








WarningAssumption 5: Homoskedasticity and Independence of Residuals Within Units



What it means: After conditioning on fixed effects, residuals \(\varepsilon_{ij}\) are assumed to be independent and identically distributed:
\[\varepsilon_{ij} \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\ \sigma^2_\varepsilon)\]
Two components: (1) constant variance across units and observations (homoskedasticity), and (2) no correlation between residuals of the same unit across observations (independence).
In longitudinal data: Serial correlation is nearly universal. A household’s savings rate this month partly predicts next month’s — so residuals at \(t\) and \(t+1\) are correlated. Heteroskedasticity also appears if variance changes over time (e.g., households become more variable in later stages of the program).
In experiments: Autocorrelation is less severe for blocked designs (participants evaluate each product once), but can appear in trial-level data with carryover.
What to do: Use cluster-robust standard errors, which are valid even under heteroskedasticity and within-unit correlation.


Code
fe_lm_hh <- lm(monthly_savings ~ disclosure + household_f, data = df_households)
df_households <- df_households |> mutate(fe_resid = residuals(fe_lm_hh))

ggplot(df_households, aes(x = disclosure, y = fe_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "#e63946", se = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title    = "Study A: FE residuals vs. disclosure engagement",
    subtitle = "No pattern expected if strict exogeneity holds",
    x = "Disclosure pages read", y = "FE Residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

title: Fixed Effects Models
text:
What Fixed Effects Cannot Do
Fixed effects are powerful but have important limits that apply equally in both settings:

They cannot estimate unit-level predictors. In Study A, you cannot estimate the effect of household income tier (constant within household). In Study B, you cannot estimate the effect of participant financial literacy (constant within participant). All between-unit variation is absorbed by the \(\alpha_j\) terms.
They discard between-unit information. If the between-unit relationship is scientifically interesting — whether more disclosure-engaged households differ from less engaged ones — FE discards that comparison. This is the price of controlling for all stable unit-level confounds.
They assume a common slope. The model estimates one \(\beta_1\) for everyone. If the effect of disclosure on savings differs across households (some are very responsive, others not at all), FE averages over this heterogeneity. Random slopes (Part 3) address this.
They are not well suited to purely between-subjects designs. If every participant sees only one condition (between-subjects), there is no within-person variation in the predictor — FE collapses entirely to OLS. The fixed-effects logic requires that the predictor varies within units.








NoteWhat Fixed Effects Can and Cannot Say



What you can say after a fixed-effects analysis:

Within-unit variation in X is associated with within-unit variation in Y, after removing all stable unit-level differences.
Time-invariant confounders (financial literacy, stable personality, household income tier) are not driving this result.
The estimate is not inflated by the kind of between-unit sorting that makes observational comparisons suspect.

What you cannot say:

That the relationship is causal — time-varying confounders (a household simultaneously adopting automatic savings and reading more disclosure) still bias the estimate.
That the between-unit relationship is the same — FE explicitly throws away between-unit variation and cannot speak to it.
That your standard errors are correct if residuals within a unit are correlated over time — cluster your SEs at the unit level.

Fixed effects are a powerful first step toward causal identification. They are not the last step.








TipReviewer Challenge: Three Questions for Fixed-Effects Results



Challenge 1 — “What is the time-varying confound?” A sharp reviewer will ask what event or process could have changed at the same time as your predictor, within the same household or participant. For the disclosure study: did households that read more disclosure also receive more coaching calls that month? Did they happen to receive a bonus? Fixed effects do not solve time-varying confounding — they only remove stable differences. Be ready with a list of the time-varying confounds you checked and ruled out.
Challenge 2 — “Is the within-unit variation sufficient to identify this?” If disclosure engagement varies very little within households over 8 months (most households read the same amount every month), the FE estimate is identified from almost no variation. Very small within-unit variation → very wide standard errors → you are essentially running an underpowered analysis even if the total N looks large. Report the within-unit SD of your key predictor.
Challenge 3 — “Are the fixed effects really stable?” If a policy change, economic shock, or personal event shifted households’ baseline savings behavior mid-study, the single \(\alpha_j\) is misspecified. A reviewer familiar with panel econometrics will ask whether you tested for structural breaks in the unit intercepts — for instance, by including time-period interactions or running the analysis separately on early and late waves.
