title: Random Intercepts
text: Random Intercepts

title: Random Intercepts
text:
Beyond Absorbing Unit Differences
Fixed effects remove between-unit variation by absorbing it into dummy variables. That works, but it destroys information:

You can no longer estimate the effect of unit-level predictors (household income tier, participant trait anxiety)
You cannot make predictions for new units not in your sample
You learn nothing about how much units differ from each other — the variance itself is scientifically informative

Random intercepts take a different view. Instead of asking “what is the specific intercept of unit \(j\)?”, the model asks “what is the distribution of intercepts across all units in the population?” It treats unit-level deviations as draws from a probability distribution rather than as fixed constants to be estimated.
This single shift — from “estimate each intercept” to “estimate the distribution of intercepts” — has wide-reaching consequences for inference, prediction, and interpretation.

title: Random Intercepts
section: The Model in Two Equivalent Forms
text:
The Model in Two Equivalent Forms

Two-Level Notation
Random intercept models are most naturally described in two levels.
Level 1 describes variation within units (within the same household across months; within the same participant across stimuli):
\[\underbrace{Y_{ij}}_{\substack{\text{outcome for} \\ \text{obs } i \text{ in} \\ \text{unit } j}} = \underbrace{\beta_{0j}}_{\substack{\text{unit-specific} \\ \text{intercept}}} + \underbrace{\beta_1}_{\substack{\text{slope}\\ \text{(fixed)}}} \underbrace{X_{ij}}_{\substack{\text{predictor}}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_{ij}}_{\substack{\text{within-unit} \\ \text{residual}}}\]
Level 2 describes variation between units — it models where each unit’s intercept comes from:
\[\underbrace{\beta_{0j}}_{\substack{\text{unit-specific} \\ \text{intercept}}} = \underbrace{\gamma_{00}}_{\substack{\text{grand mean} \\ \text{intercept}}} + \underbrace{u_{0j}}_{\substack{\text{unit deviation} \\ \text{from grand mean}}}\]
where \(u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_u)\) — the unit deviations are assumed normally distributed with mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2_u\).


Combined (Single-Equation) Form
Substituting Level 2 into Level 1:
\[\underbrace{Y_{ij}}_{\text{outcome}} = \underbrace{\gamma_{00}}_{\substack{\text{grand mean} \\ \text{(fixed)}}} + \underbrace{u_{0j}}_{\substack{\text{unit random} \\ \text{intercept}}} + \underbrace{\beta_1 X_{ij}}_{\substack{\text{slope}\\ \text{(fixed)}}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_{ij}}_{\substack{\text{within-unit} \\ \text{residual}}}\]









Component
Symbol
Type
What it captures




Grand mean
\(\gamma_{00}\)
Fixed
Average baseline across all units


Slope
\(\beta_1\)
Fixed
Average within-unit effect of \(X\)


Unit deviation
\(u_{0j}\)
Random
How much unit \(j\) departs from \(\gamma_{00}\)


Residual
\(\varepsilon_{ij}\)
Random
Leftover within-unit variation



The model estimates three variance parameters: \(\sigma^2_u\) (between-unit variance), \(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\) (within-unit residual variance), and their ratio defines the ICC.


Comparing to Fixed Effects
The FE model was:
\[Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \beta_1 X_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}\]
where \(\alpha_j\) was estimated as a separate free parameter for each unit.
The random-intercept model replaces the free \(\alpha_j\) with \(\gamma_{00} + u_{0j}\), imposing the constraint that unit deviations are drawn from a normal distribution. This constraint enables partial pooling (shrinkage) and allows between-unit inference — but it comes with the critical assumption (independence of random effects from predictors) that the FE model does not require.

title: Random Intercepts
text:
Two Examples: Longitudinal and Experimental

Example 1: Household Savings and Financial Disclosure (Longitudinal)
30 households each complete a monthly financial diary for 7 months. We want to know: within a household, does reading more of the financial disclosure document predict higher savings that month?


Code
n_households <- 30
n_months     <- 7

# Stable household-level baseline savings (between-household differences)
hh_baseline <- rnorm(n_households, mean = 25, sd = 8)

df_diary <- expand_grid(
  household = 1:n_households,
  month     = 1:n_months
) |>
  mutate(
    disclosure = rnorm(n(), mean = 6, sd = 2),       # pages read (varies month-to-month)
    # True within-household effect: 2 pct-points of savings per page read
    savings    = hh_baseline[household] + 2 * (disclosure - 6) + rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    household  = factor(household)
  )

# Fit random intercept model
model_ri_diary <- lmer(savings ~ disclosure + (1 | household), data = df_diary)
summary(model_ri_diary)

title: Random Intercepts
section: The Assumptions of Random Intercept Models
text:
The Assumptions of Random Intercept Models






WarningAssumption 1: Normality of Random Effects



Plain-language meaning: The household (or participant) deviations from the grand mean are assumed to form a bell-shaped distribution — not a two-humped distribution, not a skewed one, not a collection of discrete clusters.
What the model assumes away: That units might fall into distinct subgroups (high-savers vs. low-savers as distinct types) rather than lying along a smooth continuum.
JDM example (observational): If financial literacy creates two discrete groups of households — those enrolled in an advice program (high baseline savers) and those not (low baseline savers) — the distribution of \(u_{0j}\) will be bimodal, not normal. The model will estimate a single Gaussian that fits neither group well.
Experimental analog: If participant emotionality is bimodal (high-empathy vs. low-empathy types), or if you have two demographically distinct participant pools (students vs. workers), the normality assumption may be violated.
Skeptical reviewer objection: “Your random intercepts assume a single normal distribution of baseline savings. But you recruited from two income tiers — your random effects probably have two peaks. What does your distribution look like?”
Observable warning sign: A bimodal or heavily skewed Q-Q plot of BLUP estimates.
What to check:


Code
re_vals <- ranef(model_ri_diary)$household[, 1]

p_hist <- tibble(re = re_vals) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = re)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#deebf7", color = "#1e3a5f", bins = 10) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Random intercepts: histogram",
       x = expression(hat(u)[0*j]), y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_qq <- tibble(re = re_vals) |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = re)) +
  stat_qq(color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Random intercepts: Q-Q plot",
       subtitle = "Points off the line = non-normality",
       x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_hist + p_qq









What claim survives even if violated: The fixed-effect estimate \(\hat\beta_1\) (the within-unit slope) is reasonably robust to mild non-normality of \(u_{0j}\), especially with large \(n\) (> 50 units). The random effect variance estimate \(\hat\sigma_u^2\) is more sensitive.








WarningAssumption 2: Independence of Random Effects from Predictors — The Critical Assumption



Plain-language meaning: Households with higher baseline savings (\(u_{0j} > 0\)) should not systematically read more (or less) of the disclosure document. The random intercepts must be uncorrelated with the predictor.
What the model assumes away: Any tendency for higher-baseline units to have systematically higher (or lower) predictor values. If wealthier households both save more by default and read disclosure more because they are more financially engaged, then \(u_{0j}\) and \(X_{ij}\) are positively correlated — and the random-effects estimator is biased upward.
JDM example (observational): In the financial diary study: if households with stable high savings (large \(u_{0j}\)) tend to be precisely the households that engage most with disclosure (high average \(\bar{X}_j\)), the random-effects model will attribute some of the between-household sorting to the within-household slope. The fixed-effects model would remove this bias; the random-effects model does not.
Experimental analog: When stimuli are randomly assigned, this assumption is satisfied by design for the treatment variable. In the WTP study, anchor framing is randomly assigned across offers, so participant baseline WTP cannot systematically predict which framing condition they see. Randomisation is what makes experiments safe for random effects.
Skeptical reviewer objection: “Your random-effects estimate of the disclosure slope is larger than a within-demeaned fixed-effects estimate. That gap is the signature of correlated random effects. Have you run a Hausman test?”
Observable warning sign: The RE estimate for the predictor is noticeably larger than the FE estimate. This gap — called the “Hausman discrepancy” — is the classic diagnostic.


Code
# Hausman-style comparison: RE estimate vs. FE estimate
df_diary_panel <- df_diary |>
  mutate(hh_id = as.integer(household), month_id = month)
df_pdata <- pdata.frame(df_diary_panel, index = c("hh_id", "month_id"))

fe_plm <- plm(savings ~ disclosure, data = df_pdata, model = "within")
re_plm <- plm(savings ~ disclosure, data = df_pdata, model = "random")

cat("Fixed effects estimate:", round(coef(fe_plm)["disclosure"], 3), "\n")


Fixed effects estimate: 1.955 


Code
cat("Random effects estimate:", round(coef(re_plm)["disclosure"], 3), "\n")


Random effects estimate: 1.952 


Code
cat("\nHausman test:\n")



Hausman test:


Code
print(phtest(fe_plm, re_plm))



    Hausman Test

data:  savings ~ disclosure
chisq = 0.017224, df = 1, p-value = 0.8956
alternative hypothesis: one model is inconsistent


The independence diagram. The key diagnostic is whether household-level averages of the predictor (\(\bar{X}_j\)) are correlated with the random intercepts (\(\hat{u}_{0j}\)):


Code
# Is the random intercept correlated with the household's mean disclosure?
hh_means <- df_diary |>
  group_by(household) |>
  summarise(mean_disclosure = mean(disclosure), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(re_estimate = ranef(model_ri_diary)$household[, 1])

ggplot(hh_means, aes(x = mean_disclosure, y = re_estimate)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e63946", se = TRUE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(
    title    = "RE independence check: random intercept vs. household mean predictor",
    subtitle = "A non-flat slope here = RE ⊥ X is violated — use fixed effects or cluster-mean centering",
    x        = "Household mean disclosure engagement",
    y        = expression("Random intercept " * hat(u)[0*j])
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









When this plot shows a strong positive slope, the random intercept and the predictor are correlated — the RE estimator is biased. In that case, use fixed effects (Part 1) or cluster-mean centering (Module 2).
What claim survives: If the Hausman test is non-significant (FE and RE estimates agree), the RE estimates are unbiased and more efficient than FE estimates. The claim “controlling for stable household characteristics, each additional page of disclosure is associated with X points higher savings” stands.








WarningAssumption 3: Normality and Homoskedasticity of Level-1 Residuals



Plain-language meaning: After accounting for household baselines and the disclosure slope, the leftover month-to-month variation in savings is drawn from a normal distribution with the same spread for every household.
What the model assumes away: That some households are inherently more volatile than others (heteroskedasticity), or that the residuals follow a skewed or heavy-tailed distribution.
JDM example: Households with high income volatility (self-employed, commission-based earners) will have much larger month-to-month savings swings than salaried households. Their residual variance is larger — producing a funnel shape in the residuals-vs-fitted plot.
Experimental analog: Some offers may produce more disagreement across participants (ambiguous pricing conditions → higher SD). This shows up as condition-specific heteroskedasticity.
What to check: A residuals vs. fitted values plot. A funnel shape means variance increases with the fitted value (heteroskedasticity). A curve means the relationship is nonlinear.


Code
df_diary <- df_diary |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(model_ri_diary), resid = residuals(model_ri_diary))

p_rv <- ggplot(df_diary, aes(x = fitted, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "#e63946", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs. Fitted",
       subtitle = "Funnel = heteroskedasticity; curve = nonlinearity",
       x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_qq2 <- ggplot(df_diary, aes(sample = resid)) +
  stat_qq(color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#e63946") +
  labs(title = "Q-Q: Level-1 residuals",
       x = "Theoretical", y = "Sample") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_rv + p_qq2









What claim survives: With large samples (≥ 100 observations), the fixed-effect estimates are reasonably robust to moderate heteroskedasticity. Use robust standard errors (cluster-robust at the household level) if heteroskedasticity is detected.








WarningAssumption 4: Independence of Level-1 Residuals Within Units



Plain-language meaning: After conditioning on the household random intercept and the disclosure slope, the leftover month-to-month fluctuations are assumed to be independent of each other. Last month’s unexpectedly high savings does not predict this month’s savings beyond what the model accounts for.
What the model assumes away: Temporal autocorrelation in the residuals. The random intercept absorbs the stable between-month baseline difference, but it cannot capture temporal autocorrelation in the within-household fluctuations — the part that comes from spending habits, mood, or financial events carrying over from one month to the next.
JDM example: A household that had an unexpectedly low-savings month (car repair) may continue saving less the next month (still recovering). The random intercept captures their stable low-savings baseline, but not the temporary carryover from the shock. This produces positive lag-1 autocorrelation in residuals.
Experimental analog: This assumption is more defensible in experiments because stimuli are presented in random order and participants are asked to evaluate each one independently. However, contrast effects (rating relative to the previous offer) can induce trial-to-trial correlation.
What to check: Compute lag-1 autocorrelation of residuals within each unit:


Code
acf_df <- df_diary |>
  group_by(household) |>
  arrange(month) |>
  summarise(lag1 = cor(head(resid, -1), tail(resid, -1)),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(acf_df, aes(x = lag1)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#1e3a5f", color = "white", bins = 15) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e63946") +
  labs(
    title    = "Lag-1 autocorrelation of residuals, by household",
    subtitle = "Distribution centered near 0 = independence assumption roughly met",
    x        = "Lag-1 autocorrelation",
    y        = "Number of households"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









If the distribution is substantially right-shifted (most values positive), residuals are serially correlated and you need to model the autocorrelation explicitly — see Module 4 (Autoregressive Structures).
What claim survives: Serial correlation inflates the precision of the fixed-effect estimate (standard errors are too small). The point estimate itself is still unbiased. Adding an AR(1) residual structure or cluster-robust standard errors corrects the inference.

title: Random Intercepts
section: Partial Pooling: What Random Intercepts Do Uniquely
text:
Partial Pooling: What Random Intercepts Do Uniquely
Neither pooled OLS nor fixed effects can do what random intercepts do: borrow strength across units to produce better estimates for units with little data.

Pooled OLS: forces all units to have the same intercept (complete pooling)
Fixed effects: estimates each unit’s intercept independently (no pooling)
Random intercepts: shrinks each unit’s estimate toward the grand mean, weighted by how much information that unit contributes (partial pooling)

The combined equation makes this explicit. The random-intercept estimate for unit \(j\) is a weighted average:
\[\hat\beta_{0j} = \underbrace{\lambda_j \bar{Y}_j}_{\substack{\text{unit's own}\\ \text{mean} \times \text{reliability}}} + \underbrace{(1 - \lambda_j) \gamma_{00}}_{\substack{\text{grand mean} \times\\ \text{(1 - reliability)}}}\]
where \(\lambda_j = \frac{\sigma^2_u}{\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_\varepsilon / n_j}\) is the reliability of unit \(j\)’s estimate. Units with many observations (\(n_j\) large) or high ICC (\(\sigma^2_u\) large relative to \(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\)) get reliability close to 1 — their own data dominates. Units with few observations get reliability close to 0 — the grand mean dominates.


Code
unit_means <- df_diary |>
  group_by(household) |>
  summarise(unpooled = mean(savings), n_obs = n(), .groups = "drop")

re_ests <- tibble(
  household        = rownames(ranef(model_ri_diary)$household),
  random_intercept = ranef(model_ri_diary)$household[, 1]
) |>
  mutate(
    grand_mean = fixef(model_ri_diary)["(Intercept)"],
    pooled_re  = grand_mean + random_intercept
  )

comparison <- left_join(
  unit_means |> mutate(household = as.character(household)),
  re_ests, by = "household"
)

ggplot(comparison, aes(x = unpooled, y = pooled_re)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(comparison$pooled_re),
             color = "#e63946", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = min(comparison$unpooled) + 0.5,
           y = mean(comparison$pooled_re) + 1.5,
           label = "Grand mean", color = "#e63946", size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "Partial pooling: unpooled means vs. random-intercept estimates",
    subtitle = "Estimates are pulled toward the grand mean (red) — that is shrinkage",
    x        = "Unpooled household mean savings (no pooling)",
    y        = "Random-intercept estimate (partial pooling)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









Points fall below the diagonal for high units and above it for low units — every estimate is pulled toward the grand mean. This is not a flaw; it is the model being appropriately uncertain about extreme values based on limited within-unit data.






TipReviewer Challenge: Three Questions About Your Random Intercepts



Challenge 1 — “Why random effects rather than fixed effects?” The key difference is Assumption 2 (RE ⊥ X). If households that are better savers also engage more with disclosure — a plausible self-selection story — the random-effects estimate is upwardly biased. A Hausman test can diagnose this, but a reviewer may simply ask: “Is there any reason to expect that household-level savings habits correlate with their disclosure engagement? If so, why use random effects?” Have your Hausman test results and a substantive argument for why the assumption is plausible.
Challenge 2 — “What does the random intercept variance tell you?” The ICC — the fraction of total variance attributable to between-household differences — is itself a scientific finding. If \(\hat\sigma_u^2 / (\hat\sigma_u^2 + \hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2) = 0.40\), then 40% of the variance in monthly savings is explained by stable household characteristics, before any predictor enters. Reviewers will ask what this means substantively and whether it is consistent with prior literature. Report and interpret \(\hat\sigma_u\) alongside \(\hat\beta_1\).
Challenge 3 — “Did you check the normality of your random effects?” With 30 households, the Q-Q plot for random intercepts only has 30 points — departures from normality are hard to detect with confidence. A reviewer will note that your inference for \(\hat\sigma_u^2\) depends heavily on the normality assumption, which is untestable with small \(n\). A sensitivity analysis using a non-parametric bootstrap or Bayesian estimation with heavy-tailed priors on random effects can address this concern.

title: Random Slopes
text: Random Slopes

title: Random Slopes
text:
When Effects Vary Across Units
The random-intercept model assumes that the slope — the relationship between a predictor and the outcome — is identical across all units. Only the baseline level differs from unit to unit. This is often an unrealistic assumption.
Consider two research settings:
Longitudinal panel data. A financial coaching program tracks households across monthly waves. The average effect of disclosure engagement on savings may be positive — households that read more of the disclosure tend to save more that month. But some households are highly responsive: reading one extra page pushes them to act on the advice. Others are dismissive: they read the same pages but do not change their behaviour. The slope of disclosure → savings varies across households.
Within-subjects experiments. A price-framing study asks participants to complete WTP tasks under either a “high anchor” or “neutral” framing. On average, the anchor condition increases WTP. But individual responses to the manipulation vary considerably — some participants are strongly anchored, others barely register a difference. The treatment effect itself is heterogeneous across participants.
The random-slope model addresses this directly. Rather than fixing one slope for everyone, we treat each unit’s slope as a draw from a distribution, allowing us to estimate:

The average effect across units (the fixed slope, \(\gamma_{10}\))
The variability of that effect across units (the random slope variance, \(\sigma^2_{u_1}\))
The correlation between where units start and how strongly they respond (\(\rho_{u_0, u_1}\))

title: Random Slopes
text:
The Model
Level 1 (observations within units): \[Y_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j} X_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}\]
Level 2 (units): \[\beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}\] \[\beta_{1j} = \gamma_{10} + u_{1j}\]
Combined form: \[Y_{ij} = \underbrace{\gamma_{00}}_{\text{grand mean}} + \underbrace{\gamma_{10} X_{ij}}_{\text{avg slope}} + \underbrace{u_{0j}}_{\text{unit intercept}} + \underbrace{u_{1j} X_{ij}}_{\text{unit slope deviation}} + \varepsilon_{ij}\]
The random effects are assumed to follow a bivariate normal distribution: \[\begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2_{u_0} & \sigma_{u_0 u_1} \\ \sigma_{u_0 u_1} & \sigma^2_{u_1} \end{pmatrix}\right)\]
What does \(u_{1j}\) mean in each context?

Longitudinal: \(u_{1j}\) is household \(j\)’s deviation from the average disclosure sensitivity. A large positive \(u_{1j}\) means this household responds unusually strongly to disclosure — each page read produces a steep increase in savings. A near-zero \(u_{1j}\) means disclosure has its typical (average) effect on this household.
Experimental: \(u_{1j}\) is participant \(j\)’s deviation from the average anchoring effect. A large \(u_{1j}\) signals that this individual is strongly anchored — the framing shifts their WTP far more than average. A near-zero \(u_{1j}\) means the manipulation barely affected them.

title: Random Slopes
section: Longitudinal Example — Heterogeneous Response to Financial Disclosure
text:
Longitudinal Example — Heterogeneous Response to Financial Disclosure
Design: 50 households measured across 8 monthly waves. The predictor is monthly disclosure engagement (pages read, centered at its grand mean of 6). The outcome is monthly savings rate (%). Each household has their own disclosure sensitivity — modeled as a random slope.
The simulation imposes a correlation of −0.3 between intercepts and slopes: households that start with high baseline savings are somewhat less sensitive to disclosure (perhaps because they are already well-informed and the marginal effect of additional reading is smaller).


Code
n_households <- 50
n_waves      <- 8

# Correlated random intercepts and slopes: SD_int = 8, SD_slope = 0.8, rho = -0.3
Sigma_long <- matrix(c(64, -1.92, -1.92, 0.64), nrow = 2)
re_mat     <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_households, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = Sigma_long)

df_diary <- expand_grid(
  household = 1:n_households,
  wave      = 1:n_waves
) |>
  mutate(
    disclosure   = rnorm(n(), mean = 6, sd = 2),
    disclosure_c = disclosure - 6,
    savings      = (25 + re_mat[household, 1]) +
                   (2 + re_mat[household, 2]) * disclosure_c +
                   rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    household    = factor(household)
  )

# Random intercept only
model_ri_diary <- lmer(savings ~ disclosure_c + (1 | household),
                       data = df_diary, REML = TRUE)

# Random intercept + slope
model_rs_diary <- lmer(savings ~ disclosure_c + (disclosure_c | household),
                       data = df_diary, REML = TRUE)

broom.mixed::tidy(model_rs_diary, effects = "ran_pars") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Variance components: disclosure → savings random slope model")

The variance component for disclosure_c at the household level (\(\hat\sigma^2_{u_1}\)) captures how much individual sensitivity to disclosure varies. The correlation term estimates the intercept-slope association.


Code
# Extract OLS estimates per household for visualization
household_lines <- df_diary |>
  group_by(household) |>
  summarise(
    intercept = coef(lm(savings ~ disclosure_c))[[1]],
    slope     = coef(lm(savings ~ disclosure_c))[[2]],
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

disc_range <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.5)

lines_df_long <- household_lines |>
  mutate(
    x = list(disc_range),
    y = map2(intercept, slope, ~ .x + .y * disc_range)
  ) |>
  unnest(c(x, y)) |>
  rename(disclosure_c = x, savings = y)

p_long_slopes <- ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = lines_df_long,
            aes(x = disclosure_c, y = savings, group = household),
            color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.3, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(
    slope     = fixef(model_rs_diary)["disclosure_c"],
    intercept = fixef(model_rs_diary)["(Intercept)"],
    color     = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Longitudinal: disclosure → savings",
    subtitle = "Each line = one household; red = average fixed slope",
    x        = "Disclosure engagement (centered)",
    y        = "Monthly savings rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_long_slopes









The grey lines reveal substantial variation in disclosure sensitivity. Most households show the expected positive slope, but the steepness varies considerably. A few households show near-flat slopes — for them, disclosure engagement may reflect motivation that exists regardless of the specific advice read.
Intercept-slope correlation: A negative correlation means households with higher baseline savings tend to show a weaker positive disclosure effect. High-saving households may already be well-informed, so additional reading yields diminishing returns. Conversely, low-saving households may have the most to gain from each additional page.

title: Random Slopes
text:
Experimental Example — Anchoring and WTP
Design: 60 participants complete 12 WTP tasks each (6 in the high-anchor condition, 6 in the neutral condition, counterbalanced). The predictor is framing condition (anchor = 1, neutral = 0). The outcome is WTP (0–100 scale). Each participant is allowed their own anchoring sensitivity.
The simulation imposes a positive correlation of 0.2 between intercepts and slopes: participants with higher baseline WTP show a slightly stronger anchoring effect (the anchor has more “room” to pull their estimates upward).


Code
n_participants <- 60
n_trials_each  <- 6   # per condition

# Correlated intercepts and slopes: SD_int = 10, SD_slope = 3, rho = 0.2
Sigma_exp  <- matrix(c(100, 6, 6, 9), nrow = 2)
re_mat_exp <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_participants, mu = c(0, 0), Sigma = Sigma_exp)

df_exp <- expand_grid(
  participant = 1:n_participants,
  condition   = c(0, 1),
  trial       = 1:n_trials_each
) |>
  mutate(
    wtp             = (55 + re_mat_exp[participant, 1]) +
                      (8 + re_mat_exp[participant, 2]) * condition +
                      rnorm(n(), 0, 6),
    participant     = factor(participant),
    condition_label = factor(condition, labels = c("Neutral", "Anchor"))
  )

# Random intercept only
model_ri_exp <- lmer(wtp ~ condition + (1 | participant),
                     data = df_exp, REML = TRUE)

# Random intercept + slope for condition
model_rs_exp <- lmer(wtp ~ condition + (condition | participant),
                     data = df_exp, REML = TRUE)

broom.mixed::tidy(model_rs_exp, effects = "ran_pars") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Variance components: anchor framing condition random slope model")

# Extract per-participant anchoring effects (random slope BLUPs + fixed effect)
re_exp     <- ranef(model_rs_exp)$participant
names(re_exp) <- c("u0", "u1")
avg_effect <- fixef(model_rs_exp)["condition"]

re_exp <- re_exp |>
  mutate(person_anchor_effect = avg_effect + u1)

p_hist <- ggplot(re_exp, aes(x = person_anchor_effect)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#457b9d", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = avg_effect, color = "#e63946",
             linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = avg_effect + 0.4, y = Inf,
           label = "avg effect", color = "#e63946",
           vjust = 2, hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of individual anchoring effects on WTP",
    subtitle = "Each bar = how many participants experienced that effect size",
    x        = "Person-level anchoring effect on WTP",
    y        = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_hist









Some participants show almost no anchoring effect; others show a WTP increase exceeding +20 points. The random slope captures this theoretically important heterogeneity — heterogeneity that is invisible in a model that forces the same effect on everyone.


Code
participant_lines <- df_exp |>
  group_by(participant) |>
  summarise(
    intercept = coef(lm(wtp ~ condition))[[1]],
    slope     = coef(lm(wtp ~ condition))[[2]],
    .groups   = "drop"
  )

p_exp_slopes <- ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = participant_lines,
    aes(x = 0, xend = 1,
        y = intercept,
        yend = intercept + slope,
        group = participant),
    color = "#457b9d", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = 0, xend = 1,
        y = fixef(model_rs_exp)["(Intercept)"],
        yend = fixef(model_rs_exp)["(Intercept)"] + fixef(model_rs_exp)["condition"]),
    color = "#e63946", linewidth = 2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), labels = c("Neutral", "Anchor")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Experimental: anchor framing → WTP",
    subtitle = "Each line = one participant's framing effect; red = average",
    x        = "Condition",
    y        = "WTP (0–100)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_exp_slopes















WarningKey Point: Random Slopes and Type I Error in Experiments



Barr, Levy, Scheepers, & Tily (2013) demonstrated that omitting random slopes for within-subjects conditions inflates Type I error rates substantially. The mechanism: if you do not model variation in the treatment effect across participants, that variation is absorbed into the residual — deflating standard errors and making the average effect appear more precise than it is.
The recommendation: In within-subjects designs, include random slopes for all within-subjects factors by default (the “maximal” random effects structure). The random slope is not merely a nuisance parameter — it is the treatment effect heterogeneity, which is often scientifically interesting in its own right.

title: Random Slopes
text:
The Intercept-Slope Correlation
The random-slope model estimates not just variance in intercepts and variance in slopes, but also their covariance — equivalently, the correlation \(\rho_{u_0, u_1}\).
This correlation is substantively meaningful in both contexts.
Longitudinal interpretation. A negative intercept-slope correlation means: households with higher baseline savings tend to show a weaker positive disclosure effect. High-saving households may already implement advice regardless of how much they read — diminishing returns to disclosure. Conversely, low-saving households may have the most to gain from each additional page.
Experimental interpretation. A positive intercept-slope correlation means: participants with higher baseline WTP show a stronger anchoring effect. One interpretation: the anchor provides a reference that is proportionally more relevant when a participant already has a high willingness to pay — more room to be pulled upward.


Code
p_corr_long <- ggplot(household_lines, aes(x = intercept, y = slope)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e63946", se = TRUE, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Longitudinal",
    subtitle = "Negative: high-baseline households less disclosure-sensitive",
    x        = "Intercept (baseline savings rate)",
    y        = "Slope (disclosure effect)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_corr_exp <- ggplot(participant_lines, aes(x = intercept, y = slope)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#457b9d", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e63946", se = TRUE, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Experimental",
    subtitle = "Positive: high-baseline WTP participants more anchor-sensitive",
    x        = "Intercept (neutral condition WTP)",
    y        = "Slope (anchoring effect)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_corr_long + p_corr_exp +
  plot_annotation(title = "Intercept-slope correlations in each design")

title: Random Slopes
text:
The Zero-Correlation Parameterization
By default, (predictor | group) estimates random slope variance and the intercept-slope correlation. When the correlation is near zero, theoretically uninteresting, or causing convergence problems, the zero-correlation parameterization separates the two:
# Full: estimates intercept variance, slope variance, AND their correlation
lmer(savings ~ disclosure_c + (disclosure_c | household), data = df_diary)

# Zero-correlation: estimates both variances, forces correlation to zero
lmer(savings ~ disclosure_c + (1 | household) + (0 + disclosure_c | household), data = df_diary)
Applied to the experimental data:


Code
model_zcp_exp <- lmer(wtp ~ condition +
                        (1 | participant) + (0 + condition | participant),
                      data = df_exp, REML = FALSE)

# Staged LRT: (1) does the random slope variance matter?
#             (2) does the correlation additionally matter?
model_ri_only_ml <- lmer(wtp ~ condition + (1 | participant),
                         data = df_exp, REML = FALSE)
model_zcp_ml     <- lmer(wtp ~ condition +
                           (1 | participant) + (0 + condition | participant),
                         data = df_exp, REML = FALSE)
model_full_rs_ml <- lmer(wtp ~ condition + (condition | participant),
                         data = df_exp, REML = FALSE)

anova(model_ri_only_ml, model_zcp_ml, model_full_rs_ml)

title: Random Slopes
text:
Assumptions of Random-Slope Models






WarningAssumption 1: Multivariate Normality of Random Effects



What it means: The random intercepts and slopes are jointly drawn from a bivariate normal distribution. Severe departures — banana-shaped clouds, truncation, discrete clusters — suggest the normality assumption is violated, and estimates may be biased.
JDM examples: If households fall into two discrete types (highly financially engaged vs. completely disengaged), the random slopes will form two clusters rather than an elliptical cloud. Similarly, if participants in an anchoring study come from two distinct pools (experienced negotiators vs. novices), the slope distribution may be bimodal.
How to check: Plot the BLUP estimates from ranef() as a scatterplot. A well-specified model produces an elliptical cloud centered at the origin.


Code
re_df_exp <- as.data.frame(ranef(model_rs_exp)$participant)
names(re_df_exp) <- c("u0_intercept", "u1_slope")

ggplot(re_df_exp, aes(x = u0_intercept, y = u1_slope)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#457b9d", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(
    title    = "BLUP random effects: experimental model",
    subtitle = "Elliptical cloud centered at (0,0) supports bivariate normality",
    x        = "Random intercept (u0j)",
    y        = "Random slope for condition (u1j)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

















WarningAssumption 2: Correct Random Effects Structure Is Specified



What it means: The model must include random slopes for every predictor whose effect varies meaningfully across units. Omitting a necessary random slope pushes that variability into the residual, deflating standard errors for the fixed effect and producing anti-conservatively small p-values.
How to check: Use likelihood ratio tests (LRT) comparing models with and without the random slope. Models must be fitted with REML = FALSE for valid LRT comparisons.


Code
model_ri_diary_ml <- lmer(savings ~ disclosure_c + (1 | household),
                          data = df_diary, REML = FALSE)
model_rs_diary_ml <- lmer(savings ~ disclosure_c + (disclosure_c | household),
                          data = df_diary, REML = FALSE)

cat("=== Longitudinal: does disclosure slope vary across households? ===\n")

WarningAssumption 3: Convergence



What it means: Complex random-slope models — especially with multiple predictors or crossed random effects — frequently fail to converge. A convergence warning from lme4 signals the optimization algorithm did not find a stable solution. Estimates from non-converged models should not be trusted or reported.
How to check: Use check_convergence() from the performance package.


Code

What to do if convergence fails:

Center and scale continuous predictors
Remove the intercept-slope correlation (see zero-correlation parameterization above)
Try alternative optimizers: control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
Simplify the random effects structure if the LRT supports it (non-significant random slope variance)
Consider Bayesian estimation via brms, which handles complex random-effects structures more robustly

title: Random Slopes
section: Model Comparison — Do You Need Random Slopes?
text:
Model Comparison — Do You Need Random Slopes?
Add random slopes when:

Theory predicts heterogeneous effects. In financial coaching research, household-level differences in disclosure sensitivity are plausible and theoretically interesting — some households act on advice, others do not. In anchoring studies, individual differences in susceptibility to reference points are well-documented.
The LRT supports them. The model with random slopes fits significantly better than the model without (at REML = FALSE).
The design mandates them. In within-subjects experimental designs, random slopes for within-subjects conditions are structurally required to account for heterogeneous treatment effects. Omitting them is not conservative — it inflates Type I error (Barr et al., 2013).
Sample size is adequate. Estimating a random slope requires sufficient variation in the predictor within each unit. Longitudinally: each household must have multiple waves with varying disclosure engagement. Experimentally: each participant must complete trials in multiple conditions.



Code
bind_rows(
  broom.mixed::glance(model_ri_diary_ml) |> mutate(model = "RI only",    setting = "Longitudinal"),
  broom.mixed::glance(model_rs_diary_ml) |> mutate(model = "RI + Slope", setting = "Longitudinal"),
  broom.mixed::glance(model_ri_exp_ml)   |> mutate(model = "RI only",    setting = "Experimental"),
  broom.mixed::glance(model_rs_exp_ml)   |> mutate(model = "RI + Slope", setting = "Experimental")
) |>
  select(setting, model, AIC, BIC, logLik) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1,

TipReviewer Challenge: Three Questions About Your Random Slopes



Challenge 1 — “Is the slope variance scientifically meaningful or just noise?” A significant LRT for the random slope variance tells you that slopes vary across units more than expected by chance. But variance could reflect true heterogeneity in disclosure sensitivity or measurement noise in within-household disclosure estimates. Reviewers will ask: is the \(\hat\sigma_{u_1}\) estimate large enough to be practically meaningful? If the SD of individual slopes is only 0.1 when the average effect is 2.0, the heterogeneity is probably not theoretically important, even if statistically significant. Report \(\hat\sigma_{u_1}\) alongside the fixed slope.
Challenge 2 — “What does the intercept-slope correlation mean for your theory?” A reviewer will ask whether the negative correlation between household baseline savings and disclosure sensitivity is consistent with a theoretical mechanism (diminishing returns) or whether it is an artefact of regression to the mean. Present the correlation with a scatterplot of BLUPs and a substantive interpretation — do not just report the number from the variance-covariance matrix.
Challenge 3 — “Did you test the maximal structure?” If you included a random slope for disclosure engagement but not for other within-household predictors (e.g., season, promotion activity), a reviewer may ask why. The Barr et al. (2013) recommendation is to include random slopes for all within-unit factors. Be ready to justify each slope inclusion or exclusion with a combination of theoretical reasoning and LRT results.

title: Fixed vs. Random: When to Use Which
text:
The Most Frequently Asked Question
If you have been following along, you have noticed that fixed effects and random effects make different assumptions, answer slightly different questions, and have different costs and benefits. The obvious question is: which one should I use?
The honest answer is: it depends on your data and your scientific question. But it is not arbitrary. There are principled criteria for making this decision.

title: Fixed vs. Random: When to Use Which
text:
The Decisive Criterion
The most important question is whether the random effects (unit-level deviations) are correlated with your predictors.

If yes: Random effects models are biased. Use fixed effects.
If no: Random effects models are more efficient. Use them.

The Hausman test formalizes this check (covered in Part 2). But you should also think about it substantively:
Example 1 — Use FE: You are studying whether a financial disclosure policy raises household savings rates across 30 bank branches observed quarterly. Branches adopt the policy at different times, and branches that adopt earlier may serve wealthier, more financially engaged customers (selection into adoption). The random effects (branch-level deviations in savings) are likely correlated with adoption timing. Use fixed effects — or the cluster-mean centering hybrid that partitions within-branch from between-branch effects.
Example 2 — Use RE: You run a field experiment at 20 bank branches randomly assigned to high-touch vs. standard coaching. The branches were randomly assigned, so the random effects (branch-level deviations in mean savings) are unlikely to correlate with the treatment. Use random effects — randomization breaks the confound that makes RE problematic.
crumbs: 11  Fixed vs. Random: When to Use Which

title: Fixed vs. Random: When to Use Which
section: Worked Example: When RE Is Biased and FE Is Not
text:
Worked Example: When RE Is Biased and FE Is Not

Branch Selection into a Disclosure Policy
The abstract argument is clearer with data. Suppose you have 30 bank branches observed over 8 quarters. A new savings disclosure policy was rolled out staggered across branches — but adoption timing was not random: branches serving wealthier, more financially engaged customers adopted earlier. The confound is unobserved: the dataset contains treated (policy active or not) and savings, but not branch_quality (underlying client wealth).


Code
n_branches <- 30
n_quarters <- 8

# Unobserved: branch quality — wealthier, more savings-oriented clients
branch_quality <- rnorm(n_branches, 0, 15)

# Selection: higher-quality branches adopted the policy earlier (smaller quarter number)
adopt_quarter <- pmax(2, pmin(7,
  round(4.5 - 0.20 * branch_quality + rnorm(n_branches, 0, 1.2))))

df_fe_re <- expand_grid(branch = 1:n_branches, quarter = 1:n_quarters) |>
  mutate(
    branch_q = branch_quality[branch],
    adopt_q  = adopt_quarter[branch],
    treated  = as.integer(quarter >= adopt_q),     # disclosure policy active
    # True causal effect = 5; branch quality is the unobserved confound
    savings  = 500 + branch_q + 5 * treated + rnorm(n(), 0, 10),
    branch_f = factor(branch)
  )




Diagnosing the RE Assumption Failure
Before fitting any model, check whether the random effect is correlated with the treatment variable. Since branch_quality is unobserved in the analysis, the proxy is the proportion of quarters each branch spent under the policy: if wealthier branches adopted earlier, they will have both higher baseline savings and a larger proportion of treated quarters.


Code
df_branch_check <- df_fe_re |>
  group_by(branch_f, branch_q) |>
  summarise(prop_treated = mean(treated), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(df_branch_check, aes(x = prop_treated, y = branch_q)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e63946", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title    = "RE assumption failure: branch quality \u2248 treatment rate",
    subtitle = "Higher-quality (wealthier) branches adopted earlier \u2192 more treated quarters\n\u2192 random effect correlated with predictor \u2192 RE is biased",
    x        = "Proportion of quarters with policy active",
    y        = "Branch quality (unobserved client wealth)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









The upward slope is the visual signature of the RE assumption failure: branches with higher unobserved quality (which drives higher baseline savings) were also treated for a larger fraction of the panel. The random intercept and the treatment indicator are correlated.


Comparing FE, RE, and Hybrid Estimates


Code
# Fixed effects: absorbs all branch-level confounds (including unobserved quality)
m_fe <- plm(savings ~ treated,
            data  = df_fe_re |> mutate(branch = as.integer(branch_f)),
            index = c("branch", "quarter"),
            model = "within")

# Random effects: assumes branch random intercept ⊥ treated (violated here)
m_re <- lmer(savings ~ treated + (1 | branch_f), data = df_fe_re)

# Hybrid (cluster-mean centering): correctly partitions within and between
df_fe_re <- df_fe_re |>
  group_by(branch_f) |>
  mutate(
    treated_mean = mean(treated),           # branch-level treatment rate
    treated_cmc  = treated - treated_mean   # within-branch deviation from mean
  ) |>
  ungroup()

m_hybrid <- lmer(savings ~ treated_cmc + treated_mean + (1 | branch_f),
                 data = df_fe_re)

# Compare all three
tibble(
  Model        = c("Random effects (biased)",
                   "Fixed effects (correct)",
                   "Hybrid CMC — within estimate (correct)"),
  Estimate     = c(fixef(m_re)["treated"],
                   as.numeric(coef(m_fe)["treated"]),
                   fixef(m_hybrid)["treated_cmc"]),
  True_effect  = 5
) |>
  mutate(Bias = round(Estimate - True_effect, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               caption = "Disclosure policy effect on savings: true value = 5.0")



Disclosure policy effect on savings: true value = 5.0

The RE estimate is substantially inflated — it conflates the true within-branch disclosure effect with the between-branch quality confound (wealthier branches both adopted earlier and had higher savings all along). The FE estimate and the hybrid CMC within-estimate recover the true effect of approximately 5. The hybrid model additionally estimates the between-branch association as a separate coefficient (treated_mean), making the confound explicit rather than removing it silently.






ImportantWhat Survives If the RE Assumption Fails?



If the RE assumption is violated (random effects correlated with predictors), the RE estimate of your focal predictor is biased. But several quantities remain interpretable:

The fixed-effects within-unit estimate is still valid — it answers “within the same branch, do the quarters when the policy is active show higher savings than the quarters when it is not?”
The variance components (ICC) remain descriptively useful even under RE misspecification — they still tell you how much variance is between units.
The hybrid CMC model’s within-estimate is consistent and additionally makes the between-unit confound visible as a separate coefficient.

What is not interpretable under RE misspecification: - The RE coefficient on the treatment variable (biased by the unobserved branch-quality confound) - Any between-unit comparison that relies on the exchangeability assumption - Predictions for out-of-sample units from the mixed model (these use biased BLUPs)
The practical rule: if your treatment or exposure varies both between and within units, and there is any reason to believe higher-baseline units also received more treatment, treat RE as your baseline hypothesis and test it with the Hausman test — then report FE or the hybrid if it fails.

title: Fixed vs. Random: When to Use Which
text:
A Third Option: Hybrid Models
In many cases, you actually want both: the within-unit consistency of fixed effects and the ability to model between-unit effects. This is achievable using cluster-mean centering, covered in Module 2.
The hybrid approach: 1. Center the predictor around each unit’s mean (within-unit component) 2. Include the unit mean as a separate predictor (between-unit component) 3. Use a random-intercept model
This separates within and between effects explicitly, avoids the confound problem, and retains the ability to study unit-level variation. It is often the best default for panel and longitudinal data.

Beyond the statistical criteria, your scientific question matters:







Question
Preferred Model

Random effects

Random effects (ICC)

Random slopes

title: Fixed vs. Random: When to Use Which
text:
What About Bayesian Approaches?
Bayesian mixed-effects models (brms package) extend the random-effects framework with explicit priors on variance components. They are particularly useful when:

The model is complex and frequentist estimation has convergence problems
You want proper uncertainty quantification for variance components (frequentist intervals for variances can be poorly behaved near zero)
You want to incorporate prior knowledge about reasonable effect sizes

The conceptual structure is identical to the frequentist random-effects model. The assumptions are the same. The key difference is in how uncertainty is expressed and how parameters are estimated.
crumbs: 11  Fixed vs. Random: When to Use Which

title: Fixed vs. Random: When to Use Which
text:
Summary Decision Tree
Is the random effect correlated with your predictors?
├── Yes → Fixed Effects
└── No or Unknown →
    ├── Do you want to estimate unit-level predictor effects?
    │   ├── Yes → Random Effects
    └── ├── Do you care about between-unit variance (ICC)?
        │   ├── Yes → Random Effects
        └── └── Do you want predictions for new units?
                ├── Yes → Random Effects
                └── No → Either (use Hausman test to choose)






TipReviewer Challenge: Three Questions About Your FE vs. RE Choice



Challenge 1 — “Did you run the Hausman test before committing to random effects?” Random effects are only unbiased if cluster effects are uncorrelated with the predictors. If you defaulted to RE because “the clusters are a random sample,” a reviewer will ask whether cluster-level selection processes could plausibly create this correlation. Show the Hausman test result and explain substantively why RE is defensible — or switch to fixed effects or the hybrid CMC model.
Challenge 2 — “What between-cluster information are you discarding with FE?” Fixed effects remove all between-cluster variance. If you want to know whether urban branches respond differently to a disclosure policy than rural branches, FE cannot answer this — branch characteristics are absorbed by the dummies. Be explicit about what between-cluster questions your design can and cannot answer. If between-cluster comparisons matter, the cluster-mean centering hybrid is the right tool.
Challenge 3 — “Is the hybrid model (cluster-mean centering) a better default?” The CMC model gives you both: within-cluster consistency from FE and the ability to model between-cluster effects explicitly. A reviewer may push back on a pure FE or pure RE choice when a hybrid is available. Explain whether the within and between estimates are substantively different enough to warrant the hybrid, and if not, provide the Wald test confirming convergence.

title: Three-Level Structures
text: Three-Level Structures

title: Three-Level Structures
text:
When Two Levels Aren’t Enough
Real data rarely comes in neat two-level packages. The nesting structures encountered in organizational research and experimental science are often deeper, and collapsing them to two levels misattributes variance in ways that affect both inference and interpretation.
Three-level structures arise in two distinct research contexts:
Consumer panel data nested within service branches. Monthly observations (L1) are nested within customers (L2), who are nested within bank branches (L3). The ICC at L3 tells you how much branches differ in customer financial outcomes — a direct measure of branch-level influence. Local economic conditions, advisor quality, branch program availability, and community effects all contribute to this branch-level variance. Ignoring the branch level means assuming that all customers within the same branch are no more similar to each other than customers at different branches — an implausible assumption when branches shape the advice received, the peers observed, and the local financial environment.
Multi-site experimental research. Trials (L1) are nested within participants (L2), who are nested within labs or research sites (L3). The ICC at L3 tells you how much results vary across labs — a direct measure of the replication generalizability problem. A multi-site replication study — increasingly common in psychological science as a response to the replication crisis — is structurally a three-level model. Ignoring the lab level treats site-to-site variation as random noise attributable to participants or trials, misattributing variance and producing overconfident estimates.

title: Three-Level Structures
text:
The Model
Level 1 (observations within level-2 units): \[Y_{ijk} = \beta_{0jk} + \beta_1 X_{ijk} + e_{ijk}\]
Level 2 (level-2 units within level-3 groups): \[\beta_{0jk} = \gamma_{00k} + u_{0jk}\]
Level 3 (groups): \[\gamma_{00k} = \delta_{000} + v_{0k}\]
Combined form: \[Y_{ijk} = \underbrace{\delta_{000}}_{\text{grand mean}} + \underbrace{\beta_1 X_{ijk}}_{\text{L1 predictor}} + \underbrace{v_{0k}}_{\text{org/lab RE}} + \underbrace{u_{0jk}}_{\text{employee/participant RE}} + \underbrace{e_{ijk}}_{\text{residual}}\]
Three variance components:

\(\sigma^2_v\): variance at level 3 (between organizations or labs)
\(\sigma^2_u\): variance at level 2 (between employees or participants, within groups)
\(\sigma^2_e\): variance at level 1 (within employees or participants, across occasions or trials)

The total variance in \(Y\) is \(\sigma^2_v + \sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_e\), and each component can be expressed as a proportion of this total to obtain the ICCs.

title: Three-Level Structures
section: Longitudinal Example — Consumer Savings Panel in Bank Branches
text:
Longitudinal Example — Consumer Savings Panel in Bank Branches
Design: 8 bank branches × 15 customers × 6 monthly waves = 720 observations. The three levels are:

Level 1: monthly observation (savings rate, disclosure engagement)
Level 2: customer (random intercept per customer, nested within branch)
Level 3: branch (random intercept per branch)

Research question: How much of total savings variance is attributable to branch-level differences vs. stable customer-level differences vs. month-to-month fluctuation within customers? And after partitioning variance, is within-customer disclosure engagement associated with higher savings?


Code
n_branches  <- 8
n_customers <- 15   # customers per branch
n_waves     <- 6    # monthly observations per customer

# Level-3 random effects (branch)
branch_effects <- rnorm(n_branches, 0, 5)          # SD = 5 between branches
                                                    # (local economy, advisor quality)

# Level-2 random effects (customer within branch)
cust_effects <- rnorm(n_branches * n_customers, 0, 4)  # SD = 4 between customers within branch

df_3l <- expand_grid(
  branch   = 1:n_branches,
  customer = 1:n_customers,
  wave     = 1:n_waves
) |>
  mutate(
    cust_id    = (branch - 1) * n_customers + customer,
    disclosure = rnorm(n(), mean = 5, sd = 2),
    disc_c     = disclosure - 5,
    savings    = 25 +
                 branch_effects[branch] +
                 cust_effects[cust_id] +
                 0.8 * disc_c +
                 rnorm(n(), 0, 3),            # SD = 3 within-customer monthly noise
    branch  = factor(branch,  labels = paste0("Branch",  1:n_branches)),
    cust_id = factor(cust_id)
  )

# Three-level model: waves within customers within branches
model_3l <- lmer(savings ~ disc_c + (1 | branch/cust_id),
                 data = df_3l)

summary(model_3l)

Reading the variance components:

branch: How much of total savings variance is explained by which branch a customer belongs to? This is the branch-level ICC (ICC\(_3\)). It captures local economic conditions, advisor quality, branch program availability, and community savings norms.
cust_id:branch: How much is explained by stable differences between customers within the same branch — persistent individual differences in income, financial habits, risk tolerance.
Residual: How much is month-to-month fluctuation within the same customer — the portion that varies over time and could be affected by disclosure engagement.

A large branch-level ICC (ICC\(_3 > 0.10\)) means branches matter substantially for customer savings — suggesting branch-level interventions (coaching quality, program design, community outreach) have real impact beyond individual-level characteristics.

title: Three-Level Structures
text:
Experimental Example — Multi-Lab Replication Study
Design: 5 labs × 20 participants × 8 trials = 800 observations. The three levels are:

Level 1: trial (decision quality score, condition: scarcity vs. control)
Level 2: participant (random intercept per participant, nested within lab)
Level 3: lab (random intercept per lab)

Research question: How much variance in decision quality is attributable to lab differences, participant differences within labs, and trial-to-trial fluctuation? The lab-level ICC quantifies how much the results depend on where the study was run.


Code
n_labs    <- 5
n_par     <- 20   # participants per lab
n_trials  <- 8    # trials per participant

# Level-3 random effects (lab)
lab_effects <- rnorm(n_labs, 0, 3)             # SD = 3 between labs

# Level-2 random effects (participant within lab)
par_effects <- rnorm(n_labs * n_par, 0, 5)    # SD = 5 between participants within lab

df_multilab <- expand_grid(
  lab         = 1:n_labs,
  participant = 1:n_par,
  trial       = 1:n_trials
) |>
  mutate(
    par_id    = (lab - 1) * n_par + participant,
    condition = rep(c(0, 1), times = n_trials / 2)[trial],
    dq        = 65 +
                lab_effects[lab] +
                par_effects[par_id] +
                -4 * condition +
                rnorm(n(), 0, 4),            # SD = 4 within-participant trial noise
    lab        = factor(lab,  labels = paste0("Lab", 1:n_labs)),
    par_id     = factor(par_id),
    condition  = factor(condition, labels = c("control", "scarcity"))
  )

# Three-level model: trials within participants within labs
model_multilab <- lmer(dq ~ condition + (1 | lab/par_id),
                       data = df_multilab)

summary(model_multilab)

Reading the variance components in the experimental case:

lab: Lab-to-lab variability. How much does it matter which lab ran the study? If this is high, the same nominal procedure produces meaningfully different baseline decision quality across sites — suggesting lab culture, participant pools, or local implementation differences are consequential.
par_id:lab: Individual differences between participants within the same lab. In a within-subjects design this is typically the largest component.
Residual: Trial-to-trial noise within a participant — random fluctuation from one decision to the next.

The connection to the replication crisis. If ICC\(_3 = 0.15\), then 15% of variance in decision quality is due to which lab a participant was tested in — independent of the scarcity manipulation. A single-lab study that happens to be run in a high-performing lab will systematically overestimate baseline scores, and if the manipulation interacts with lab characteristics, will also misestimate the effect size. Many replication failures occur because the original study had high lab-level variance: the effect was real in lab A but not lab B. Three-level models quantify this risk directly.

title: Three-Level Structures
text:
ICC Decomposition for Three-Level Models
In a three-level model, there are two ICCs to report and interpret:
Level-3 ICC (variance attributable to the highest-level unit alone): \[\text{ICC}_3 = \frac{\sigma^2_v}{\sigma^2_v + \sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_e}\]
Level-2 ICC (variance attributable to level-2 and above): \[\text{ICC}_2 = \frac{\sigma^2_v + \sigma^2_u}{\sigma^2_v + \sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_e}\]
The difference \(\text{ICC}_2 - \text{ICC}_3\) is the variance uniquely attributable to level-2 units after removing level-3 variance.

icc_exp  <- icc(model_multilab)

title: Three-Level Structures
text:
Cross-Level Interactions
Three-level models allow testing whether higher-level variables moderate lower-level effects — some of the most theoretically interesting questions in multilevel research.

Longitudinal: Does branch coaching intensity moderate disclosure → savings?
Hypothesis: In branches with intensive financial coaching programs (high-touch advisors, regular follow-ups), the positive effect of disclosure engagement on savings may be stronger — because the advice is reinforced by personal contact. In low-touch branches, disclosure alone may not be enough to change behaviour.

Heisig & Schaeffer (2019) showed that when a cross-level interaction involves a level-1 predictor, you must include a random slope for that predictor to obtain unbiased estimates of the interaction. Without the random slope, the cross-level interaction estimate absorbs variance that should be attributed to individual-level heterogeneity.
In practice: if you include disc_c * high_touch, you should also include (disc_c | branch/cust_id) or at minimum allow the disclosure slope to vary across branches. This model requires more data to estimate reliably, but it is the correctly specified model.

title: Three-Level Structures
text:
Assumptions of Three-Level Models
All two-level model assumptions carry over — normality of random effects at each level, correct specification of fixed effects, independence of residuals conditional on random effects. Three additional concerns become prominent with three levels.






WarningAssumption 1: Correct Level Specification



What it means: The model must correctly identify which units belong to which level. If customers are incorrectly assigned to branches (data linkage errors, customers who switch branches mid-study), variance components will be misattributed between levels.
In experimental designs: Participants must be uniquely and correctly assigned to labs. Cross-site contamination — participants completing a study at one lab but attributed to another — corrupts the level-3 variance estimate.
How to check: Cross-tabulate your level-2 and level-3 identifiers. In a pure nested hierarchy, each level-2 unit belongs to exactly one level-3 unit. Any rows returned below signal a cross-classified or misassigned structure.


Code
# Longitudinal: each customer should belong to exactly one branch
df_3l |>
  distinct(cust_id, branch) |>
  group_by(cust_id) |>
  filter(n() > 1)   # should return 0 rows






cust_id
branch








Code
# Experimental: each participant should belong to exactly one lab
df_multilab |>
  distinct(par_id, lab) |>
  group_by(par_id) |>
  filter(n() > 1)   # should return 0 rows






par_id
lab








Zero rows confirms a clean nested hierarchy. If rows appear, you have a cross-classified structure requiring a different model specification (e.g., (1 | branch) + (1 | cust_id) instead of (1 | branch/cust_id)).








WarningAssumption 2: Sufficient Sample Size at Each Level



What it means: Variance components at higher levels require sufficient numbers of higher-level units to be estimated reliably. With only 5 labs or 6 organizations, the level-3 variance estimate is extremely noisy — confidence intervals for \(\sigma^2_v\) will be very wide.
Why it matters: Type I error rates for fixed effects are also affected. With very few level-3 units, the degrees of freedom for branch- or lab-level effects are essentially the number of level-3 units minus the number of predictors at that level.
How to check: Count units at each level explicitly.

WarningAssumption 3: Minimum Clusters at L3



Rule of thumb: ≥ 20 units at L3 for reliable variance estimation at the top level. Below this threshold, the level-3 ICC estimate has very wide confidence intervals, and Wald-type standard errors for level-3 predictors can be severely anti-conservative.

Practical implication for multi-lab research: With only 5 labs (as in our example), the lab-level ICC is estimated with very low precision. This is not a reason to avoid three-level models — a biased two-level model that ignores labs is worse — but it is a reason to:

Report wide confidence intervals for the lab ICC
Avoid strong claims about the magnitude of lab-level effects
Plan future multi-site studies with more labs rather than more participants per lab, if cross-site generalizability is the scientific goal

For Bayesian approaches with informative priors on variance components, smaller level-3 samples can be handled more gracefully. The brms package provides a natural extension.

TipReviewer Challenge: Three Questions About Your Three-Level Model



Challenge 1 — “How precise is your branch-level ICC?” With only 8 branches, the branch-level variance (\(\hat\sigma_v^2\)) is estimated from 8 data points. Confidence intervals for the ICC at level 3 will be very wide. A reviewer will note this and may ask for a sensitivity analysis — reporting how your fixed-effect estimates change if you instead treat branches as fixed effects (branch dummies) rather than a random effect. If the coefficient on your focal predictor (disclosure engagement) shifts substantially, the branch-level random effect is doing a lot of heavy lifting and deserves scrutiny.
Challenge 2 — “Is the cross-level interaction identified?” The interaction between disclosure engagement (L1) and branch coaching intensity (L3) claims that the disclosure slope is moderated by a branch-level characteristic. But there are only 8 branches — 4 high-touch and 4 standard. With 4 data points per group at L3, detecting a genuine interaction requires strong effect sizes. Reviewers will ask whether the interaction is robust to removing any single branch from the analysis (leave-one-branch-out sensitivity), and whether the pattern is consistent with the individual branch means rather than driven by one outlier branch.
Challenge 3 — “Did you include the L2 random slope for the cross-level interaction?” Heisig & Schaeffer (2019) showed that cross-level interactions involving a L1 predictor must include a random slope for that predictor at L2, otherwise the interaction estimate is biased. If you include disc_c * high_touch but not (disc_c | branch/cust_id), you are assuming that every customer’s disclosure sensitivity is identical within branches — which contradicts the premise of the interaction. A reviewer who knows this literature will ask why the full random slope was not included.

title: Crossed Random Effects
text:
Crossed Random Effects
Pure hierarchies assume each lower-level unit belongs to exactly one higher-level unit. But many real data structures — in both experimental consumer research and longitudinal panel research — have units that belong to multiple grouping factors simultaneously. This chapter covers two major instances of crossed random effects:
Both cases share the same formal structure. Both produce badly wrong standard errors when one of the crossed grouping factors is omitted.

title: Crossed Random Effects
section: Part A: Crossed Random Effects in Experimental Designs
text:
Part A: Crossed Random Effects in Experimental Designs

Design Schematic: Crossed vs. Nested
Before fitting a model, it helps to visualise the difference between a nested structure and a crossed structure. The distinction is about whether every participant evaluates every product (crossed) or each participant evaluates a unique subset of products (nested).


Code
# 6 participants × 6 products for illustration
n_p <- 6; n_m <- 6

# Crossed: every participant evaluates every product
df_crossed <- expand_grid(participant = 1:n_p, product = 1:n_m) |>
  mutate(observed = TRUE, design = "Crossed (every P evaluates every product)")

# Nested: each participant evaluates a unique set of 3 products (no overlap)
df_nested <- bind_rows(
  expand_grid(participant = 1:2, product = 1:3),
  expand_grid(participant = 3:4, product = 4:6),
  expand_grid(participant = 5:6, product = c(1, 3, 5))
) |>
  mutate(observed = TRUE, design = "Nested (each P evaluates a unique subset)")

# Add unobserved cells to nested design for visual contrast
df_nested_full <- expand_grid(participant = 1:n_p, product = 1:n_m) |>
  left_join(df_nested |> mutate(observed = TRUE),
            by = c("participant", "product")) |>
  replace_na(list(observed = FALSE)) |>
  mutate(design = "Nested (each P evaluates a unique subset)")

bind_rows(
  df_crossed |> mutate(observed = TRUE),
  df_nested_full
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(product), y = factor(participant),
             fill = observed)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#2166ac", "FALSE" = "#f0f0f0"),
                    labels = c("TRUE" = "Observed", "FALSE" = "Not observed"),
                    name   = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ design, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title    = "Crossed vs. nested: which cells are observed?",
    subtitle = "Crossed designs fill the full participant \u00d7 product grid — every cell is blue.\nNested designs leave gaps — products are not shared across participants.",
    x = "Product", y = "Participant"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid = element_blank())









In a crossed design the grid is fully filled: every participant–product cell is observed. Both grouping factors are fully shared, so variance can be cleanly partitioned into participant differences, product differences, and residual. In a nested design there is no product sharing across participants — you cannot separate “this product is generally liked” from “this participant generally likes things,” because the two effects are aliased.
Why it matters for R syntax: In a crossed design, lme4 formula (1 | participant) + (1 | product) fits two independent random intercepts and partitions variance correctly. In a nested design with partial overlap, the same formula would be misspecified — crossed syntax on a partially nested structure can produce severely wrong standard errors. Always draw (or print) your data grid before choosing a formula.


The Problem with Treating Messages as Fixed
A consumer research experiment: 40 participants each evaluate 80 pricing messages. Each observation belongs to one participant AND one message. Participants are not nested within messages. Messages are not nested within participants. Both grouping factors are fully crossed.
If you only include a random effect for participants, you are assuming that all variance due to messages is captured by the residual. But messages differ systematically — some promotional offers are more compelling due to framing quality, discount depth, or scarcity cues. This message-level variance inflates your residuals and biases your standard errors.
Judd, Westfall, and Kenny (2012, 2017) showed that failing to include random effects for stimuli is one of the most widespread sources of Type I error inflation in social and cognitive psychology. The same logic applies directly to consumer research: when messages (or products, or offers) are the stimuli, they must be treated as a random factor.


The Model
For observation \(y_{ps}\) from participant \(p\) evaluating message \(s\):
\[
Y_{ps} = \underbrace{\gamma_{00}}_{\text{grand mean}} + \underbrace{\beta_1 X_{ps}}_{\text{predictor}} + \underbrace{u_{0p}}_{\text{participant RE}} + \underbrace{w_{0s}}_{\text{message RE}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon_{ps}}_{\text{residual}}
\]
Where:

\(u_{0p} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_u)\): participant random intercepts (some people have higher baseline WTP)
\(w_{0s} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_w)\): message random intercepts (some offers are more compelling overall)
\(\varepsilon_{ps}\): trial-level residual noise



Code
# Simulate a consumer WTP study: participants × product messages
n_participants <- 40
n_messages     <- 80

participant_effects <- rnorm(n_participants, 0, 15)   # people differ in baseline WTP
message_effects     <- rnorm(n_messages, 0, 12)        # messages differ in baseline WTP
discount_depth      <- runif(n_messages, 0, 40)        # discount depth predictor (0-40%)

df_promo <- expand_grid(
  participant = 1:n_participants,
  message     = 1:n_messages
) |>
  mutate(
    participant_eff = participant_effects[participant],
    message_eff     = message_effects[message],
    discount_depth  = discount_depth[message],
    wtp             = 80 + 0.8 * discount_depth +
                      participant_eff + message_eff +
                      rnorm(n(), 0, 15),
    participant     = factor(participant),
    message         = factor(message)
  )




Code
# Without message random effects (wrong)
model_no_msgs <- lmer(wtp ~ discount_depth + (1 | participant),
                      data = df_promo)

# With message random effects (correct: crossed)
model_crossed <- lmer(wtp ~ discount_depth + (1 | participant) + (1 | message),
                      data = df_promo)

summary(model_crossed)

0.109





When message-level variance is ignored, the standard error for the discount depth effect is smaller — the model treats message-level variance as residual noise, artificially deflating uncertainty. This produces anti-conservative inference: p-values are too small.


The Assumptions of Crossed Random-Effects Models






WarningAssumption 1: Independence of Participant and Message Random Effects



What it means: The random effect for participant \(p\) and the random effect for message \(s\) are assumed to be independent. Person 7 having an unusually high WTP is not related to whether message 42 is unusually compelling.
How to check: In a balanced fully-crossed design, this is usually reasonable. In unbalanced designs (not all participants see all messages), check whether missingness is systematic — for example, whether higher-WTP participants were more likely to complete high-discount evaluations.








WarningAssumption 2: Random Effects are Independent of the Predictor



What it means: The random intercepts for participants and messages should be uncorrelated with discount depth. Discount level should not predict which messages were seen by which participants — in a balanced design, it cannot.
Why this is usually satisfied in experiments: In a fully-crossed, counterbalanced design, every participant evaluates every message, so assignment is orthogonal to message characteristics. This is one reason well-designed experiments support random-effects modeling.








WarningAssumption 3: The Same Model Applies to All Participant–Message Pairs



What it means: The discount depth effect is assumed to be the same for all participants unless a random slope for discount depth by participants is included. If some participants are more deal-sensitive than others — for example, high price-consciousness individuals respond more strongly to deeper discounts — a random slope is needed.
How to check: Use likelihood ratio tests and theoretical reasoning.


Code
model_maximal <- lmer(wtp ~ discount_depth + (discount_depth | participant) + (1 | message),
                      data    = df_promo,
                      control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

anova(model_crossed, model_maximal)
