title: Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)
section: The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
text:
The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference
Before introducing regression at all, consider the true object of scientific interest: the causal effect of X on Y for a specific unit \(i\).
Under the potential outcomes framework (Rubin, 1974), every unit has two potential outcomes:
\[
\underbrace{\tau_i}_{\substack{\text{causal effect} \\ \text{for unit } i}} = \underbrace{Y_i(1)}_{\substack{\text{outcome if} \\ \text{treated}}} - \underbrace{Y_i(0)}_{\substack{\text{outcome if} \\ \text{not treated}}}
\]
The fundamental problem: we can never observe both \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\) for the same unit at the same time. A household either received a financial coaching program or it did not. A country either adopted a mandatory disclosure policy or it did not. We observe one potential outcome and must infer the other.
Regression estimates the average treatment effect (ATE):
\[
\text{ATE} = E[\tau_i] = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]
\]
For regression to estimate the ATE correctly, the observed difference in outcomes between treated and untreated units must equal the counterfactual difference between what would have happened to those same units under both conditions. This requires that who gets treated is independent of the potential outcomes.
When this independence fails — when who gets X is related to Y through pathways other than X itself — the regression coefficient is endogenous and does not estimate the causal effect.
crumbs: 19  Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)

title: Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)
text:
What is Endogeneity?
Endogeneity means your predictor X is correlated with the error term \(\varepsilon\) in your regression:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i \quad \text{where } \text{Cov}(X_i, \varepsilon_i) \neq 0
\]
When this happens, \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is biased. It estimates not just the effect of X on Y but a blend of that effect and all the other pathways through which X and Y are connected.
There are four main sources.
crumbs: 19  Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)

title: Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)
text:
Source 1: Omitted Variable Bias (OVB)
A variable Z influences both X and Y, but Z is not in your model. The path Z → Y gets attributed to X because X and Z are correlated.

The Bias Formula
The expected value of the biased coefficient is:
\[
\underbrace{E[\hat{\beta}_1]}_{\substack{\text{what we} \\ \text{estimate}}} = \underbrace{\beta_1}_{\substack{\text{true} \\ \text{effect}}} + \underbrace{\delta_{ZY}}_{\substack{Z \text{'s effect} \\ \text{on } Y}} \cdot \underbrace{\tilde{\rho}_{XZ}}_{\substack{\text{correlation of} \\ X \text{ and } Z}}
\]
where \(\delta_{ZY}\) is the effect of Z on Y (holding X constant) and \(\tilde{\rho}_{XZ}\) is the correlation of Z with X after partialling out other covariates.
The bias formula has a critical practical use: even without data on Z, if you know the sign of both \(\delta_{ZY}\) and \(\tilde\rho_{XZ}\), you can predict the direction of the bias on your estimate.


Code
# Bias direction table
tibble(
  Example         = c("Budget tracker → savings", "Promotion → purchase", "Investment advice → returns"),
  Confounder_Z    = c("Platform quality", "Consumer wealth", "Financial sophistication"),
  `Sign Z→X`      = c("+", "+", "-"),
  `Sign Z→Y`      = c("+", "+", "+"),
  `Bias direction` = c("Positive (↑ est.)", "Positive (↑ est.)", "Negative (↓ est.)")
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "OVB bias direction: multiply signs to get bias direction")

NoteReading the Bias Table



Sign(Z→X) × Sign(Z→Y) = sign of the bias: - Both positive → positive bias (estimate is too large) - Both negative → positive bias (two negatives multiply to positive) - Mixed signs → negative bias (estimate is too small or reversed)
You can use this qualitatively even before collecting data: “If my estimate is already large, and the likely omitted confound would produce positive bias, my true effect is probably smaller than I think.”




Same Observables, Two Stories
The same scatter of data points can support two completely different causal interpretations. The visualization below shows this directly: in panel (A), pooled data suggest that budget-tool use predicts higher savings. In panel (B), the same points are colored by financial literacy tertile — and within each literacy group, the relationship disappears. Financial literacy drives both budget-tool use and savings; the pooled slope is pure confounding.
When you have not measured the confounder — which is the typical case — you see only panel (A) and cannot make the comparison that panel (B) reveals.









This is the OVB core: the observed X–Y correlation in the left panel is entirely explained by Z. When Z is unmeasured, the naive estimate is a biased blend of the (zero) true effect and the Z-driven confounding. The simulations below show this numerically across three financial services examples.


Three Demonstrations


Code
n <- 500

# Example 1: Budget tracker / savings rate / platform quality
# Platform quality attracts more engaged users AND produces better financial outcomes
# True effect of using the tracker = 0; it is the platform quality that matters
Z_quality     <- rnorm(n, 50, 10)
X_tracker     <- 0.3 * Z_quality + rnorm(n, 0, 5)
Y_savings     <- 0.5 * Z_quality + rnorm(n, 0, 8)  # true X effect = 0

m_biased_1  <- lm(Y_savings ~ X_tracker)
m_correct_1 <- lm(Y_savings ~ X_tracker + Z_quality)

# Example 2: Premium promotional message exposure / purchase intention / consumer wealth
# Wealthy consumers are targeted more AND have higher purchase intentions for premium products
# True X effect = 0.15; wealth inflates this upward
Z_wealth      <- rnorm(n, 50, 10)
X_promo       <- 0.4 * Z_wealth + rnorm(n, 0, 8)
Y_intention   <- 0.6 * Z_wealth + 0.15 * X_promo + rnorm(n, 0, 10)

m_biased_2  <- lm(Y_intention ~ X_promo)
m_correct_2 <- lm(Y_intention ~ X_promo + Z_wealth)

# Example 3: Investment advice uptake / portfolio return / financial sophistication
# Sophisticated investors avoid advice (prefer self-directed) AND perform better
# True X effect = +0.5 (advice genuinely helps); sophistication biases estimate downward
Z_sophist     <- rnorm(n, 50, 10)
X_advice      <- -0.5 * Z_sophist + rnorm(n, 0, 2)   # sophisticated investors avoid advice
Y_returns     <- 0.4 * Z_sophist + 0.5 * X_advice + rnorm(n, 0, 8)

m_biased_3  <- lm(Y_returns ~ X_advice)
m_correct_3 <- lm(Y_returns ~ X_advice + Z_sophist)

bind_rows(
  tidy(m_biased_1)  |> filter(term == "X_tracker") |>
    mutate(example = "Budget tracker (true=0)",       model = "Omits Z"),
  tidy(m_correct_1) |> filter(term == "X_tracker") |>
    mutate(example = "Budget tracker (true=0)",       model = "Includes Z"),
  tidy(m_biased_2)  |> filter(term == "X_promo")   |>
    mutate(example = "Promotion (true=0.15)",          model = "Omits Z"),
  tidy(m_correct_2) |> filter(term == "X_promo")   |>
    mutate(example = "Promotion (true=0.15)",          model = "Includes Z"),
  tidy(m_biased_3)  |> filter(term == "X_advice")  |>
    mutate(example = "Investment advice (true=0.5)",   model = "Omits Z"),
  tidy(m_correct_3) |> filter(term == "X_advice")  |>
    mutate(example = "Investment advice (true=0.5)",   model = "Includes Z")
) |>
  select(example, model, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "OVB across three examples: omitting Z biases estimates in predictable directions")

In every case, adding the confounder pulls the estimate toward the true value. The bias direction matches the prediction from the sign table.
The budget-tracking example illustrates a common error in consumer finance research: users of a platform feature (tracker) appear to save more, but the actual driver is platform quality — better platforms attract more financially engaged users who would have saved more regardless. The promotion example shows upward bias: promotions genuinely increase purchase intentions, but the naive estimate is inflated because wealth drives both targeting and intention. The investment advice example shows downward bias: advice genuinely improves portfolio returns, but financially sophisticated investors avoid advice while also outperforming — so the advice-returns correlation in cross-sectional data understates the true benefit.






WarningAssumption: No Omitted Variables Correlated with Both X and Y



How to check: Draw a causal diagram. List every plausible cause of Y. Ask: is any of these also correlated with X? This requires substantive reasoning about the DGP — you cannot test it purely from data.
In nested data: OVB is especially insidious because the omitted variable often varies at a higher level. Studying whether branch-level disclosure intensity predicts household savings while omitting branch-level financial literacy programming biases your estimate; the omitted variable is a branch-level characteristic that clustering creates — households within high-intensity-disclosure branches are also more likely to receive financial coaching.
What to do: Add the variable if measurable. Use fixed effects to absorb all stable unit-level confounders. Use IV, RDD, or DiD if the confound is unmeasurable (covered in Parts 2–6).








NoteReviewer Challenge: Omitted Variable Bias




“Your interpretation assumes you have controlled for all common causes of X and Y. What unmeasured variable could simultaneously predict your predictor and your outcome?”

Pattern that invites the challenge: When X and Y are both desirable outcomes (higher savings AND higher engagement; better decisions AND more information), reviewers will ask what stable individual characteristic could explain both.
What to show: The OVB bias formula tells you the direction of the problem even without the data: Sign(Z→X) × Sign(Z→Y) = sign of your bias. Report this logic explicitly. If you have plausible confounders, bound the bias using coefficient stability (Oster, 2019) or sensitivity analysis (E-values).

title: Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)
text:
Source 2: Simultaneity / Reverse Causality
X causes Y, but Y also causes X. The causal arrow runs in both directions, creating a feedback loop that OLS cannot untangle.


Code
n_sim <- 300
set.seed(42)

# Consumer trust → financial engagement (positive), but engagement → trust (positive)
# Simulate equilibrium: customer who engages more trusts the institution more,
# but the institution also targets more-trusting customers with higher engagement offers
time_pts <- tibble(
  t          = 1:10,
  engagement = c(30, 35, 38, 40, 41, 42, 43, 43, 43, 43) + rnorm(10, 0, 2),
  trust      = c(60, 55, 52, 50, 49, 48, 47, 47, 47, 47) + rnorm(10, 0, 2)
)

p_sim <- time_pts |>
  pivot_longer(-t) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = t, y = value, color = name, group = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#e63946", "#1e3a5f"),
                     labels = c("Platform Engagement", "Consumer Trust")) +
  labs(title = "Simultaneity: trust → engagement AND engagement → trust",
       subtitle = "OLS on cross-sectional data picks up both arrows simultaneously",
       x = "Time", y = "Level", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_sim









JDM example: Consumer trust in a financial institution increases platform engagement — but engagement also builds trust (repeated positive experiences reinforce confidence). A cross-sectional regression of engagement on trust picks up both directions simultaneously and gives a confounded estimate.
The same dynamic appears in advertising: promotional messaging drives purchase intent (awareness → intention), but purchase history drives the volume of targeted promotions a customer receives (purchase history → ad targeting). A cross-sectional regression of purchase intent on messaging frequency cannot identify whether messaging causes intent or prior purchasing causes targeting. Longitudinal designs with lagged predictors are required.






WarningAssumption: No Reverse Causality



How to check: Ask: could Y at time \(t\) plausibly influence X at time \(t\) or \(t+1\)? If yes, simultaneity is a concern.
What to do: - Use lagged predictors (\(X_{t-1}\) predicting \(Y_t\)) in panel data - Use instrumental variables (Part 2) to isolate the causal direction - Use cross-lagged panel models (Module 4, Part 6) which model both causal arrows explicitly








NoteReviewer Challenge: Reverse Causality




“Your model assumes X causes Y, but couldn’t Y cause X? What tells us the arrow runs in the direction you claim?”

Pattern that invites the challenge: Cross-sectional data, outcomes that could plausibly influence the predictor, or settings where timing is ambiguous (e.g., both variables are measured at the same moment).
What to show: Lagged predictors (\(X_{t-1}\) predicting \(Y_t\)) rule out same-period reverse causality. Natural experiments or randomized instruments that shift X but cannot respond to Y rule out the reverse path. The cross-lagged panel model (Module 4, Part 6) makes both causal arrows estimable.
crumbs: 19  Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)

title: Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)
text:
Source 3: Selection Effects
The observations in your dataset are not a random sample of the population. Who ends up in your data — and which treatment they receive — is systematically related to both X and Y.
Self-selection: Customers who choose to open a premium bank account are systematically different from those who don’t — they may be more financially literate, more savings-oriented, or already wealthier. Comparing premium account holders to standard customers conflates the effect of the account type with all these pre-existing differences.
Survivorship bias: You only observe the financial products that survived long enough to be in your dataset. Products that were discontinued due to poor uptake are absent. Conclusions about product design drawn from current survivors are biased because you are conditioning on market survival.
Attrition in longitudinal studies: Participants who drop out of a financial diary study are often systematically different from completers. If the most financially distressed households stop reporting because their situation is worsening, the observed trajectory among completers overstates average financial health improvement.
This source of endogeneity is covered in depth in Part 3.






NoteReviewer Challenge: Selection Effects




“Who is in your sample, and why? Are the people you observed the same as the population your theory is about?”

Pattern that invites the challenge: Studies of platform users, program participants, survey respondents, or experimental volunteers — any setting where participation is voluntary or observable only for a subset.
What to show: Compare baseline characteristics of participants to the eligible population (if known). Report participation rates. In longitudinal designs, compare baseline characteristics of completers to dropouts. If selective participation seems likely, use IPW (Module 3, Part 6) or bound the estimate under selection-on-observables.
crumbs: 19  Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)

title: Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)
text:
Source 4: Collider Bias
This source is frequently overlooked but is just as dangerous as the others. Conditioning on a collider — a variable caused by both X and Y — creates a spurious association between X and Y even when none exists.
A collider is a variable C where two causal arrows “collide”:
\[X \rightarrow C \leftarrow Y\]
When you condition on C (include it as a control, restrict your sample to a subset defined by C, or analyze a non-random sample selected on C), you open a spurious backdoor path between X and Y.


Code
n_col <- 1000

# True DGP: X and Y are uncorrelated
X_col <- rnorm(n_col)
Y_col <- rnorm(n_col)  # truly independent of X

# Collider C is caused by both X and Y
C_col <- X_col + Y_col + rnorm(n_col, 0, 0.5)

# Full sample: no correlation
r_full <- cor(X_col, Y_col)

# Conditioning on C: restrict to top half of C
high_C <- C_col > median(C_col)
r_cond <- cor(X_col[high_C], Y_col[high_C])

tibble(
  Sample           = c("Full sample (no conditioning)", "Restricted to high-C (conditioning)"),
  `Cor(X, Y)`      = c(round(r_full, 3), round(r_cond, 3)),
  Interpretation   = c("True: X and Y are unrelated",
                        "Spurious: conditioning on C creates negative correlation")
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Collider bias: conditioning on C creates a spurious X-Y association")



Collider bias: conditioning on C creates a spurious X-Y association







Sample
Cor(X, Y)
Interpretation




Full sample (no conditioning)
0.005
True: X and Y are unrelated


Restricted to high-C (conditioning)
-0.372
Spurious: conditioning on C creates negative correlation





The publish-or-perish example: Prolificacy (X) and idea quality (Y) may be uncorrelated in the full population of researchers. But publication (C) is caused by both — prolific researchers with good ideas get published. If you study only published papers (conditioning on C), you’ll observe that prolificacy and idea quality are negatively correlated within the published set, even though they’re unrelated in the population.


Code
df_col <- tibble(X = X_col, Y = Y_col, C_high = high_C)

p_full <- ggplot(df_col, aes(x = X, y = Y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Full sample", subtitle = paste0("r = ", round(r_full, 3)),
       x = "X", y = "Y") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_cond <- ggplot(df_col |> filter(C_high), aes(x = X, y = Y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, color = "#2d6a4f") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Conditioned on high C", subtitle = paste0("r = ", round(r_cond, 3)),
       x = "X", y = "Y") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_full + p_cond















TipJDM Collider: Analyzing Only Platform Engagers



In a study of platform users, promotional sensitivity (X) and consumer wealth (Y) may be uncorrelated in the broader population. But both predict active platform engagement (C). If you analyze only high-engagement users — restricting your sample based on C — you introduce a spurious negative correlation between X and Y within your sample. Wealthier users who are also promo-sensitive are over-represented; the model sees this as a negative relationship between wealth and promo-sensitivity within the active user pool. This is collider bias from sample restriction, not from including C as a covariate.
The same logic applies any time you analyze a selected subset: only people who purchased, only participants who completed all waves, only firms that survived.








WarningAssumption: No Conditioning on Colliders



How to check: Draw a DAG. For every variable you are controlling for or selecting on, ask: is this caused by X, by Y, or by both? If caused by both, it is a collider — do not condition on it.
Common mistake: “Kitchen sink” regressions that add every available covariate. If any of those covariates is a collider, adding it creates bias where none existed.








NoteReviewer Challenge: Collider / Bad Control Bias




“The variable you added to your model — are you sure it’s a confounder and not a collider? Could controlling for it have opened a backdoor path rather than closed one?”

Pattern that invites the challenge: “Kitchen sink” regressions; controlling for behavioral outcomes that happen after X; restricting samples based on an outcome-related criterion (only analyzing purchasers, only active users, only completers).
What to show: Draw the causal diagram. For every covariate included, confirm it is caused by neither X nor Y (confounder), not caused by both (collider), and not on the causal path from X to Y (mediator). If uncertain, run the analysis with and without the suspect variable.

title: Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)
section: Pearl’s Causal Framework: Three Types of Paths
text:
Pearl’s Causal Framework: Three Types of Paths
Judea Pearl’s causal graph (DAG) framework provides a systematic way to identify endogeneity. Every causal graph has three fundamental path structures:


Code
make_dag_panel <- function(nodes, edges_df, title, note = NULL) {
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 18,
               shape = 21, fill = "#deebf7", color = "#1e3a5f", stroke = 1.5) +
    geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), size = 3.8,
              fontface = "bold", color = "#1e3a5f")
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(edges_df))) {
    p <- p + annotate("segment",
                      x    = edges_df$x1[i], xend = edges_df$x2[i],
                      y    = edges_df$y1[i], yend = edges_df$y2[i],
                      arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")),
                      color = edges_df$color[i], linewidth = 1.2)
  }
  # Place note text inside the plot area (below nodes) — avoids patchwork overflow
  if (!is.null(note)) {
    p <- p + annotate("text", x = 2, y = 1.1, label = note,
                      size = 2.55, color = "gray30", hjust = 0.5, vjust = 1,
                      lineheight = 1.3)
  }
  p + labs(title = title) +
    xlim(0.3, 3.7) + ylim(0.1, 2.8) + theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, hjust = 0.5,
                                    margin = margin(b = 4)))
}

# Nodes shifted upward so text annotation sits cleanly below them
nodes_fork  <- tibble(label = c("Z", "X", "Y"), x = c(2, 1, 3), y = c(2.3, 1.6, 1.6))
edges_fork  <- tibble(x1 = c(1.85, 2.15), x2 = c(1.2,  2.8),
                      y1 = c(2.20, 2.20), y2 = c(1.70, 1.70),
                      color = c("#e63946", "#e63946"))
p_fork <- make_dag_panel(nodes_fork, edges_fork, "Fork (Confounder)",
  "Z → X  and  Z → Y\nCreates spurious X-Y correlation\nEx: literacy (Z) → disclosure (X)\n   and risky choice (Y)\nFix: control for Z")

nodes_chain <- tibble(label = c("X", "M", "Y"), x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1.7, 1.7, 1.7))
edges_chain <- tibble(x1 = c(1.2, 2.2), x2 = c(1.8, 2.8),
                      y1 = c(1.7, 1.7), y2 = c(1.7, 1.7),
                      color = c("#1e3a5f", "#1e3a5f"))
p_chain <- make_dag_panel(nodes_chain, edges_chain, "Chain (Mediator)",
  "X → M → Y\nM is on the causal path\nEx: auto-enroll (X) → savings habit (M)\n   → long-term savings (Y)\nFix: do NOT control for M")

nodes_coll  <- tibble(label = c("X", "C", "Y"), x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(1.7, 1.7, 1.7))
edges_coll  <- tibble(x1 = c(1.2, 2.8), x2 = c(1.8, 2.2),
                      y1 = c(1.7, 1.7), y2 = c(1.7, 1.7),
                      color = c("#1e3a5f", "#1e3a5f"))
p_coll <- make_dag_panel(nodes_coll, edges_coll, "Collider",
  "X → C ← Y\nConditioning on C opens a backdoor\nEx: promo sensitivity (X) →\nplatform activity (C) ← wealth (Y)\nFix: do NOT control for C")

p_fork + p_chain + p_coll


















Path Type
Structure
What it means
What to do




Fork
Z → X and Z → Y
Z confounds X-Y relationship
Block by controlling for Z


Chain
X → M → Y
M mediates X’s effect on Y
Do NOT block (it carries the effect)


Collider
X → C ← Y
C is caused by both X and Y
Do NOT block (conditioning opens a backdoor)



The goal of every identification strategy in the rest of this module is to block all backdoor paths (forks) without blocking causal paths (chains) and without conditioning on colliders.

title: Endogeneity: Why Regression Lies (and How to Catch It)
text:
The Backdoor Criterion
A set of variables S satisfies Pearl’s backdoor criterion for estimating the effect of X on Y if:

S blocks every path between X and Y that has an arrow into X (i.e., all backdoor paths)
S does not include any descendant of X on a causal path to Y (no colliders, no mediators on the X→Y path)

When you can find such a set S from measured variables, controlling for S gives you the causal effect. When you cannot — because the confounders are unmeasured — you need the identification strategies in Parts 2–6.






ImportantBefore Running Any Regression



Draw a causal diagram. Every arrow is a hypothesis about the DGP. Then ask:

Are there any forks (confounders) not in my model? → OVB
Could the outcome affect the predictor? → Simultaneity
Is my sample selected on something related to both X and Y? → Selection
Am I controlling for anything caused by X or Y? → Collider bias

Answering these four questions before looking at your results will save you from the most common errors in applied regression.








TipObservational → Experimental Translation



In observational nested data: The predictor X is almost never exogenous. Employees who participate in training programs are not randomly selected — they tend to be younger, more motivated, and employed at better-resourced firms. The OVB formula quantifies how much the naive estimate is inflated by this selection.
In randomized experiments: Random assignment solves the endogeneity problem for the assigned condition — but not for everything downstream. Actual treatment receipt (compliance), session attendance, engagement level, and follow-up completion all reintroduce endogeneity after randomization. The residual endogeneity in experiments is the subject of Modules 5 Parts 8 and 9.
Same diagnosis, different source: In both settings, the question is identical: Is there a variable that simultaneously predicts X and Y, that I have not accounted for? In observational data, this is about confounders in the sampling. In experiments, it is about post-randomization processes that reintroduce selection.

title: Instrumental Variables
section: When Endogeneity Cannot Be Removed by Fixed Effects
text:
When Endogeneity Cannot Be Removed by Fixed Effects
Module 1’s fixed effects model removes time-invariant confounders by exploiting within-unit variation over time. But fixed effects are not a universal cure for endogeneity. Two failure modes are especially common.
In longitudinal panel research, the endogeneity can be time-varying: bank branches that are on an upward savings trajectory are exactly the branches most likely to adopt new financial planning tools — they have the motivated staff, engaged customer base, and organizational energy to implement them. Branch fixed effects absorb stable branch quality, but they cannot absorb a time-varying engagement shock that simultaneously drives tool adoption and savings improvement. Even after demeaning, the estimate remains confounded.
In experiments, randomization solves endogeneity for assignment — but not always for treatment receipt. Participants randomly offered access to a financial planning tool may never log in. Customers sent a disclosure summary may never open it. When compliance is imperfect, the simple comparison of assigned groups underestimates the effect of actually using the tool.
In both cases, an instrument is a variable that provides exogenous variation in treatment uptake — variation that is not driven by the confounders affecting outcomes.

Longitudinal context: The scheduled wave in which a branch received an IT infrastructure upgrade provides exogenous variation in financial planning tool adoption. Branches in Wave 1 adopted the tool at higher rates not because of their savings trajectory but because of administrative scheduling order. The rollout wave does not directly affect household savings — only the tool adoption it enables does.
Experimental context: Random assignment to an encouragement condition (a structured outreach protocol with personalized prompts) provides exogenous variation in actual financial tool use. Whether you were randomized to encouragement does not directly improve your savings decisions — logging in and engaging with the tool does.

title: Instrumental Variables
section: The IV Structure: Permitted and Forbidden Pathways
text:
The IV Structure: Permitted and Forbidden Pathways
The instrumental variables strategy works by tracing exactly which paths between Z, X, and Y are permitted and which must be blocked. The diagram below shows this structure for the branch savings example.


Code
library(ggplot2)

# Node positions
nodes <- tibble(
  label = c("Z\n(IT rollout\nwave)", "X\n(Tool\nadoption)", "Y\n(Savings\nrate)", "U\n(Branch\nquality)"),
  x = c(0, 2.5, 5, 2.5),
  y = c(2,   2,  2,   0)
)

arrow_end <- 0.45   # shorten arrow ends to not overlap node circles

ggplot() +
  # --- permitted arrows (blue) ---
  # Z → X  (relevance)
  annotate("segment", x=0.45, xend=2.05, y=2, yend=2,
           arrow=arrow(length=unit(.25,"cm"), type="closed"),
           color="#1e3a5f", linewidth=1.3) +
  # X → Y  (causal effect — what we identify)
  annotate("segment", x=2.95, xend=4.55, y=2, yend=2,
           arrow=arrow(length=unit(.25,"cm"), type="closed"),
           color="#1e3a5f", linewidth=1.3) +
  # U → X  (confound)
  annotate("segment", x=2.5, xend=2.5, y=0.45, yend=1.55,
           arrow=arrow(length=unit(.25,"cm"), type="closed"),
           color="#888888", linewidth=1, linetype="dashed") +
  # U → Y  (confound)
  annotate("segment", x=2.95, xend=4.55, y=0.2, yend=1.65,
           arrow=arrow(length=unit(.25,"cm"), type="closed"),
           color="#888888", linewidth=1, linetype="dashed") +
  # --- FORBIDDEN arrow: Z → Y (dashed red, exclusion violation) ---
  annotate("segment", x=0.45, xend=4.55, y=1.7, yend=1.7,
           arrow=arrow(length=unit(.25,"cm"), type="closed"),
           color="#cc0000", linewidth=1, linetype="dotted") +
  annotate("text", x=2.5, y=1.45, label="FORBIDDEN\n(exclusion restriction)",
           size=3.2, color="#cc0000", fontface="bold") +
  # --- FORBIDDEN link: Z ↔ U (dashed orange, independence violation) ---
  annotate("segment", x=0.45, xend=2.1, y=1.65, yend=0.35,
           arrow=arrow(length=unit(.25,"cm"), type="closed"),
           color="#e67e00", linewidth=1, linetype="dotted") +
  annotate("text", x=0.7, y=0.85, label="FORBIDDEN\n(independence)", hjust=0,
           size=3.2, color="#e67e00", fontface="bold") +
  # --- node circles ---
  geom_point(data=nodes, aes(x=x, y=y), shape=21, size=14,
             fill=c("#d4e6f5","#d4e6f5","#d4e6f5","#fce8cc"),
             color=c("#1e3a5f","#1e3a5f","#1e3a5f","#a05000"),
             stroke=1.5) +
  geom_text(data=nodes, aes(x=x, y=y, label=label), size=3.3, lineheight=0.9) +
  # --- path labels ---
  annotate("text", x=1.25, y=2.18, label="Relevance\n(Z predicts X)",
           size=3.2, color="#1e3a5f") +
  annotate("text", x=3.75, y=2.18, label="Causal path\n(what IV identifies)",
           size=3.2, color="#1e3a5f") +
  annotate("text", x=3.5,  y=0.9,  label="Confounders\n(U affects X and Y)",
           size=3.2, color="#888888") +
  xlim(-0.5, 5.7) + ylim(-0.4, 2.8) +
  labs(
    title    = "IV causal diagram: permitted paths and forbidden pathways",
    subtitle = "Blue = valid paths (Z identifies X→Y effect)    Red/orange = paths that must be blocked for IV to be valid"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title    = element_text(size=13, face="bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size=11, color="#555555"),
        plot.margin   = margin(5, 5, 5, 5))









The blue arrows show the structure IV exploits: Z creates exogenous variation in X (relevance), and X causally affects Y. The grey dashed arrows show the endogeneity problem: U confounds both X and Y, so naive OLS is biased. The red dotted arrow (Z → Y directly) is the exclusion restriction violation — if this path exists, Z affects Y through channels other than X, and the IV estimate is biased. The orange dotted arrow (Z → U) is the independence violation — if Z is correlated with the very confounders it is meant to bypass, it is not truly exogenous.
When all three forbidden pathways are blocked, the IV estimate recovers the causal effect of X on Y.

title: Instrumental Variables
text:
The Three IV Assumptions






WarningAssumption 1: Relevance



What it means: The instrument Z must actually cause the endogenous treatment X to change. An instrument that does not predict treatment is useless — it produces inflated standard errors and, when weak, can bias estimates in unpredictable directions.
How to check: Regress X on Z (the “first stage”). The F-statistic on Z must exceed 10. Below that threshold, the instrument is “weak.”
Longitudinal context: The IT rollout wave must meaningfully predict whether branches adopt the financial planning tool. Wave 1 branches should adopt at substantially higher rates than Wave 2 branches during the observation window.
Experimental context: Being randomized to the encouragement condition must meaningfully predict actual tool use. If the encouragement protocol is so feeble that it does not increase log-ins and engagement, it cannot serve as an instrument.








WarningAssumption 2: Exclusion Restriction



What it means: Z affects Y only through X — not through any other pathway. This is the core untestable assumption. No statistical test can verify it; it requires theoretical argument and domain knowledge.
How to scrutinize: Trace every conceivable path from Z to Y that bypasses X. Each such path is a potential violation.
Longitudinal context: The IT rollout wave must not directly affect household savings rates. It should matter only because it determines which branches have the financial planning tool available. A potential violation: Wave 1 branches may have been selected because they were in larger, more urban markets — advantages that raise savings rates regardless of whether the tool is adopted.
Experimental context: Random assignment to the encouragement condition must not improve savings decisions except through actual tool use. A potential violation: receiving a personalized outreach message might itself prompt reflection on financial goals — a direct effect on savings behavior that bypasses the tool entirely, even if the participant never logs in.








WarningAssumption 3: Independence (Exogeneity of the Instrument)



What it means: Z is as-good-as-randomly assigned — it is not caused by the same confounders that affect X and Y.
How to check: Verify that Z is balanced across observable pre-treatment characteristics. In a natural experiment, check whether the instrument predicts baseline covariates.
Longitudinal context: The IT rollout wave should not be correlated with branch quality or growth trajectory. Branches did not self-select into Wave 1 based on their savings performance potential — the order was determined by infrastructure scheduling. In practice: check whether baseline savings rates and branch size predict wave assignment.
Experimental context: In a proper encouragement design, Z is genuinely randomized — independence holds by construction. The practical threat is post-randomization contamination (e.g., differential attrition by encouragement condition — less financially engaged customers more likely to drop out of the encouraged group) or a failed randomization procedure.

title: Instrumental Variables
section: Section 3: Longitudinal IV — Budgeting Tool Adoption and Household Savings
text:
Section 3: Longitudinal IV — Budgeting Tool Adoption and Household Savings

The Setup
200 bank branches are observed over 6 years. The research question is whether adopting a financial planning tool increases branch-level household savings rates. The identification problem: branches on an upward savings trajectory — engaged staff, motivated customer base — are exactly the ones most likely to implement new tools proactively. A naive OLS regression overestimates the tool’s causal effect.
Even adding branch fixed effects does not fully resolve this: if branches experiencing a positive engagement shock (a new community outreach manager, an unusually successful financial literacy event) respond by deploying the tool, within-branch variation in adoption is still confounded by this time-varying engagement shock.
The instrument is rollout wave — a staggered IT infrastructure upgrade that determined which branches could deploy the tool first. The wave order was set by administrative scheduling (server installation logistics), not by branch savings performance. Branches in Wave 1 adopted the tool at much higher rates than Wave 2 branches during the early years.


Code
n_branches <- 200
n_years    <- 6

branch_quality <- rnorm(n_branches, 0, 5)   # unobserved branch engagement quality
# Wave 1 vs. Wave 2 (1 = early rollout, 0 = later rollout) — as-good-as-random
wave1          <- rbinom(n_branches, 1, 0.5)

df_panel <- expand_grid(branch = 1:n_branches, year = 1:n_years) |>
  mutate(
    bq       = branch_quality[branch],
    wave     = wave1[branch],
    # High-quality branches AND Wave 1 branches adopt the tool more
    p_adopt  = plogis(-0.5 + 0.4 * (bq / sd(branch_quality)) + 0.8 * wave +
                        rnorm(n(), 0, 0.3)),
    adopted  = rbinom(n(), 1, p_adopt),
    # True causal effect of tool adoption = 4 pp savings gain; quality also helps
    savings  = 50 + 4 * adopted + 2.5 * bq + rnorm(n(), 0, 4),
    branch   = factor(branch),
    year     = factor(year)
  )




First Stage: Instrument Relevance


Code
m_first <- lm(adopted ~ wave, data = df_panel)
f_stat  <- summary(m_first)$fstatistic[1]
cat("First-stage F-statistic:", round(f_stat, 1), "\n")


First-stage F-statistic: 43.8 


Code
cat("(Rule of thumb: F > 10 indicates a relevant instrument)\n")


(Rule of thumb: F > 10 indicates a relevant instrument)


Wave 1 is a strong positive predictor of tool adoption (Wave 1 branches adopt at substantially higher rates). F > 10 confirms the instrument is not weak.


OLS vs. IV


Code
# Naive OLS: inflated by branch engagement confound
m_ols <- lm(savings ~ adopted, data = df_panel)

# IV via Two-Stage Least Squares: uses only wave-driven variation in adoption
m_iv  <- ivreg(savings ~ adopted | wave, data = df_panel)

bind_rows(
  tidy(m_ols) |> filter(term == "adopted") |>
    mutate(model = "OLS (confounded — true = 4)"),
  tidy(m_iv)  |> filter(term == "adopted") |>
    mutate(model = "IV / TSLS (consistent under exclusion restriction)")
) |>
  select(model, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "Panel IV: effect of tool adoption on savings rate (true effect = 4). OLS is biased upward by branch quality; IV is consistent but with larger SE.")



Panel IV: effect of tool adoption on savings rate (true effect = 4). OLS is biased upward by branch quality; IV is consistent but with larger SE.








model

p.value

0.000


IV / TSLS (consistent under exclusion restriction)
6.096

OLS overestimates the tool’s effect because branch engagement simultaneously drives adoption and savings improvement. IV isolates only the exogenous, wave-driven variation in adoption. IV is consistent — its bias shrinks to zero as \(N \to \infty\) — but in any single finite sample the estimate can be above or below the truth. The larger standard error reflects this uncertainty honestly.

title: Instrumental Variables
section: Section 4: Two-Stage Least Squares — The Mechanics
text:
Section 4: Two-Stage Least Squares — The Mechanics
TSLS makes the IV logic explicit in two regression steps.
Stage 1: Regress the endogenous treatment X on the instrument Z (and any controls W):
\[\hat{X}_i = \hat{\gamma}_0 + \hat{\gamma}_1 Z_i + \hat{\gamma}_2 W_i\]
This produces fitted values \(\hat{X}\) that contain only the variation in X that is driven by Z — the “clean,” exogenous part of treatment uptake.
Stage 2: Regress Y on \(\hat{X}\) (and controls W):
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \hat{X}_i + \beta_2 W_i + \varepsilon_i\]
Because \(\hat{X}\) contains no endogenous variation, \(\hat{\beta}_1\) is a consistent causal estimate.


Code
# Manual TSLS to show the mechanics
# Stage 1: predict tool adoption from rollout wave
stage1    <- lm(adopted ~ wave, data = df_panel)
df_panel  <- df_panel |> mutate(adopted_hat = fitted(stage1))

# Stage 2: regress savings on predicted adoption
stage2    <- lm(savings ~ adopted_hat, data = df_panel)

cat("Manual TSLS (Stage 2 coefficient on adopted_hat):",
    round(coef(stage2)["adopted_hat"], 3), "\n")


Manual TSLS (Stage 2 coefficient on adopted_hat): 6.096 


Code
cat("ivreg() coefficient (should match):",
    round(coef(m_iv)["adopted"], 3), "\n")


ivreg() coefficient (should match): 6.096 








NoteNote: Standard Errors in Manual TSLS



The coefficients from manual TSLS match ivreg(), but the standard errors do not. The second-stage regression uses \(\hat{X}\) (a generated regressor), so residuals are computed against the wrong quantity. Always use ivreg() or an equivalent dedicated IV function to obtain correct standard errors.



Connection to Module 1 Fixed Effects
Panel fixed effects absorb time-invariant branch-level confounders. But if tool adoption responds to time-varying branch engagement shocks, fixed effects alone are insufficient. Adding IV on top of FE handles both:
\[\underbrace{\text{FE removes}}_{\substack{\text{time-invariant} \\ \text{confounders}}} \quad + \quad \underbrace{\text{IV removes}}_{\substack{\text{time-varying} \\ \text{endogeneity}}}\]


Code
# Panel FE-IV: year fixed effects as controls; rollout wave as instrument
m_fe_iv <- ivreg(savings ~ adopted + year | wave + year, data = df_panel)
cat("FE-IV estimate (adopted):", round(coef(m_fe_iv)["adopted"], 3), "\n")


FE-IV estimate (adopted): 6.096 


By including year fixed effects in both stages, we account for common time trends while using rollout wave to instrument tool adoption within each year.

title: Instrumental Variables
section: Section 5: Experimental IV — Encouragement Designs and LATE
text:
Section 5: Experimental IV — Encouragement Designs and LATE
In experiments, the instrument is the random assignment Z itself. When all participants comply, the simple comparison of assigned groups gives an unbiased causal estimate. But when compliance is imperfect, Z becomes an instrument for actual treatment receipt D.

The Wald Estimator
\[\text{LATE} = \frac{\underbrace{E[Y \mid Z=1] - E[Y \mid Z=0]}_{\text{Intent-to-treat effect (ITT)}}}{\underbrace{E[D \mid Z=1] - E[D \mid Z=0]}_{\text{Compliance rate (first stage)}}}\]
The Intent-to-treat (ITT) effect — the effect of assignment, regardless of compliance — is an unbiased estimate of the causal effect of being assigned to treatment. Dividing by the compliance rate scales the ITT up to recover the LATE: the causal effect of actually using the tool, among those who comply.


Compliance Classes
When Z = random assignment and D = actual tool use, participants fall into four latent types:









Type
D if Z = 0
D if Z = 1
Description




Complier
0
1
Uses tool iff encouraged — IV identifies this group


Always-taker
1
1
Uses tool regardless — uninformative


Never-taker
0
0
Never uses tool even when encouraged — uninformative


Defier
1
0
Does the opposite of assignment — assumed absent (monotonicity)



Only compliers contribute to the IV estimate. LATE is the effect of using the tool, for compliers only.


Simulation: Financial Planning Tool Encouragement Design
160 customers are randomized to encouragement (n = 80, receives personalized outreach and prompts to use the budgeting tool) or control (n = 80, standard materials). Of those encouraged, 70% actually engage with the planning tool; none in the control group have access. The true causal effect of actually using the tool is a 10-percentage-point improvement in savings rate.


Code
n <- 160
Z <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 80)  # random assignment to encouragement

# One-sided noncompliance: encouraged participants use tool at 70%
D <- ifelse(Z == 1, rbinom(80, 1, 0.70), 0)

# True effect of using the tool = +10 pp savings improvement
# Self-selected tool users (always-takers) are more financially motivated — biases as-treated
savings_rate <- 40 + 10 * D + rnorm(n, 0, 8)
df_exp       <- tibble(Z = factor(Z), D = factor(D), savings_rate, id = 1:n)

# Three estimators
m_itt  <- lm(savings_rate ~ Z, data = df_exp)         # ITT: effect of assignment
m_at   <- lm(savings_rate ~ D, data = df_exp)         # As-treated: biased by selection
m_late <- ivreg(savings_rate ~ D | Z, data = df_exp)  # LATE: IV estimate

bind_rows(
  tidy(m_itt)  |> filter(term == "Z1") |>
    mutate(model = "ITT — effect of assignment (diluted, unbiased)"),
  tidy(m_at)   |> filter(term == "D1") |>
    mutate(model = "As-treated — biased by self-selection"),
  tidy(m_late) |> filter(term == "D1") |>
    mutate(model = "IV / LATE — consistent estimate for compliers")
) |>
  select(model, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "Encouragement design: three estimators (true tool effect = +10). ITT is diluted; as-treated overstates due to self-selection; LATE is consistent but individual samples can deviate from truth.")

# Manual Wald estimator: confirms IV equals ITT / compliance rate
itt_effect <- mean(savings_rate[Z == 1]) - mean(savings_rate[Z == 0])
compliance <- mean(D[Z == 1] == 1) - mean(D[Z == 0] == 1)
wald_late  <- itt_effect / compliance

cat("ITT (numerator)         :", round(itt_effect, 3), "\n")


ITT (numerator)         : 5.895 


Code
cat("Compliance (denominator):", round(compliance, 3), "\n")


Compliance (denominator): 0.675 


Code
cat("Wald LATE               :", round(wald_late, 3), "\n")


Wald LATE               : 8.733 


Code
cat("ivreg() LATE            :", round(coef(m_late)["D1"], 3), "\n")


ivreg() LATE            : 8.733 


The ITT is approximately +7: diluted because only 70% of encouraged customers actually used the tool. The as-treated estimate is biased upward — customers who chose to engage with the tool are likely more financially motivated than the average participant, so they would have saved more regardless. The IV/LATE is consistent under the exclusion restriction: on average across many samples it targets +10, though any single sample estimate can deviate from the truth due to sampling variability.

title: Instrumental Variables
text:
Section 6: The LATE Interpretation
The IV estimand is always a LATE — the causal effect for compliers only. This has concrete implications in both research contexts.
What LATE means in the longitudinal case: The estimate applies specifically to branches that adopted the financial planning tool because they happened to be in Wave 1 of the rollout — not to branches that would have adopted regardless (always-takers: highly engaged branches that would find a way to deploy the tool in any scenario) or those that would never have adopted regardless (never-takers: branches with too little infrastructure or staff capacity). If Wave-1-compliant branches are mid-sized, moderately engaged branches, the LATE describes the effect for that marginal segment — it may not generalize to either the most or least engaged branches.
What LATE means in the experimental case: The estimate applies to customers who engaged with the financial planning tool because they were encouraged — not to always-takers who would have logged in and used it on their own initiative, and not to never-takers who would not engage even with personalized outreach. If compliers are ambivalent but malleable (responsive to prompts, but not intrinsically financially motivated), the LATE may understate how much the tool helps self-selected always-takers, while overstating how much it would help confirmed never-takers if somehow compelled to use it.
Generalizability: LATE is a valid causal estimate, but it is local. Policy conclusions drawn from LATE assume that the complier subpopulation is relevant to the policy question. When it is not — when you need to know the ATE for everyone — IV alone is insufficient.

title: Instrumental Variables
text:
Section 7: Finding Good Instruments
The exclusion restriction is the bottleneck. Common instrument classes in social science:









Instrument class
Longitudinal example
Experimental example
Why valid




Administrative assignment
IT rollout wave for budgeting tool
Site randomization in multi-site trials
Order set by logistics, not branch quality


Natural experiment
Weather shock disrupting branch operations
Random lottery for waitlisted customers
Random by nature or design


Regulatory / eligibility threshold
Credit score cutoff for prime-rate access
Financial distress screening cutoff (RDD–IV)
Arbitrary administrative rule


Time-based shock
Policy change or fee structure revision
Seasonal or day-of-week variation in study timing
Exogenous timing


Geographic variation
Distance to nearest financial literacy center
Experimenter assignment in multi-advisor designs
Not chosen by customer or branch



The mathematics of TSLS are straightforward. Finding a credible instrument — one whose exclusion restriction can be defended from theory and whose relevance can be demonstrated empirically — requires deep domain knowledge and careful thinking about the data-generating process. A weak but credible instrument is preferable to a strong instrument with a plausible exclusion-restriction violation. The first produces inflated standard errors; the second produces biased point estimates.

title: Selection Effects & Attrition
text: Selection Effects & Attrition

title: Selection Effects & Attrition
section: When Your Sample is Not Your Population
text:
When Your Sample is Not Your Population
Even with a perfectly specified model, if your observations are not representative of the population you care about, your conclusions may be wrong. Selection effects are the family of processes by which observations non-randomly enter, remain in, or leave your dataset.
Selection is especially dangerous in nested and longitudinal data because the same processes that structure the data — time, group membership, experimental condition — also drive who stays in it. The threats that follow apply across research contexts, but the way they manifest differs.





flowchart TD
    A["Eligible population<br/>All consumers / study-eligible participants"]
    --> B["Sampling frame<br/>Those reachable by recruitment"]
    B --> C["Enrolled / baseline sample<br/>Those who agreed to participate"]
    C --> D["Active participants<br/>Retained through key time points"]
    D --> E["Analyzed sample<br/>Complete-case or available-case dataset"]

    A --> |"Representativeness bias:<br/>systematic gap between eligible and reachable"| B
    B --> |"Self-selection bias:<br/>volunteers differ from decliners"| C
    C --> |"Attrition bias:<br/>high-distress, high-burden participants drop"| D
    D --> |"Exclusion bias:<br/>non-random post-hoc criteria"| E

    style A fill:#deebf7,stroke:#1e3a5f
    style E fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#c0392b






Each narrowing step in the funnel is a potential source of selection bias. The question at each step is: are the people who disappear systematically different from those who remain, in ways that predict the outcome? If yes, the analyzed sample is not representative of the population the researcher wants to generalize to. The types below catalog the main mechanisms.

title: Selection Effects & Attrition
text:
Type 1: Representativeness Bias
Your sampling frame does not cover the full population you want to generalize to.
In longitudinal research: Panel databases draw from specific registers (e.g., publicly traded firms, firms above an employment threshold). Private, small, or young firms are systematically absent. Trends in the observed panel may not generalize to the full firm population.
In experimental research: Convenience samples from university subject pools (WEIRD populations — Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) over-represent young, highly educated, and cognitively flexible participants. Reactions to scarcity, authority, or social norms that are measured in the lab may not generalize to broader populations.






WarningAssumption: Sampling Frame Covers the Population of Interest



How to check: Compare your sample’s distributions on key variables to known population statistics. Are any groups systematically over- or under-represented?
What to do: Acknowledge the limitation explicitly. Use stratified sampling or post-stratification weights if population distributions are known. Consider whether your research question and theoretical claims are appropriately scoped to your sampling frame.

title: Selection Effects & Attrition
text:
Type 2: Self-Selection and Non-Response Bias
Participants choose whether to enter your study based on factors related to your variables of interest.
The landmark example: the 1936 Literary Digest poll predicted Landon would defeat Roosevelt by a landslide, based on 2.4 million responses. Their sampling frame (telephone directories and car registration lists) over-represented wealthy Republicans. Roosevelt won in a historic landslide.
In longitudinal research: Firms that agree to participate in a panel survey are often larger, more stable, and more administratively capable than firms that decline. If firm size and stability predict your outcome, effect estimates from the panel will not generalize to the true firm population.
In experimental research: Participants who volunteer for a study on “decision-making and well-being” may be more introspective, more compliant, and more psychologically attuned to the constructs you measure. They are not a random draw from the population of people to whom your theory applies.
Financial well-being studies are especially vulnerable to self-selection. Financially sophisticated individuals are more likely to enroll — they know what the study is about, find it interesting, and have positive associations with financial topics. Because sophistication also predicts better financial outcomes, the study sample systematically overestimates the population-level financial health.


Code
n_total    <- 1000
fin_sophist <- rnorm(n_total, 50, 10)  # latent financial sophistication (unobserved)

# Financially sophisticated people are more likely to volunteer for a finance study
p_participate <- plogis(-2 + 0.06 * fin_sophist)
participated  <- rbinom(n_total, 1, p_participate)

# Outcome: monthly savings rate, partly caused by financial sophistication
savings_rate <- 10 + 0.5 * fin_sophist + rnorm(n_total, 0, 8)

tibble(
  Group = c("Full population", "Self-selected sample"),
  N     = c(n_total, sum(participated)),
  Mean_savings_rate = c(mean(savings_rate),
                        mean(savings_rate[participated == 1]))
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
    caption = "Self-selection inflates estimated savings rate in the study sample")

Demand Characteristics in Nested Experimental Designs
Self-selection is not only about who enters the study — it also operates within the study as a behavioral process. Demand characteristics are a form of selection into behavior: participants selectively display responses that confirm the hypothesis they have inferred from the study design, the experimenter’s demeanor, or prior experimental experience.
In a standard between-subjects design, demand characteristics inflate both conditions equally and partially cancel out. But in within-subjects (repeated-measures) designs, participants can observe their own behavior across conditions, infer the hypothesis more easily, and respond accordingly. This is especially pernicious because it can masquerade as a real treatment effect.
In JDM research, within-subjects designs are especially common — participants make repeated choices under gain framing, loss framing, scarcity cues, abundance cues, or different disclosure formats. The hypothesis is often obvious to participants (“they want me to choose the safe option” or “this study is about whether scarcity changes my behavior”). Demand-susceptible participants systematically inflate or suppress their responses in the expected direction.
How demand characteristics create bias in within-subjects designs:
Some participants are systematically more susceptible to demand — those higher in agreeableness, more experienced with experiments, or more motivated to please the experimenter. These participants inflate their responses in the treatment condition more than in the control condition. This creates a pattern that looks like a treatment × participant interaction in the data: susceptible participants show larger “effects” not because the treatment worked better for them, but because they responded more to perceived expectations.
This inflated variance is absorbed by the random slope for condition, but it also biases the fixed effect estimate of the treatment itself — pulling the overall effect in the direction of the demand hypothesis.


Code
n_par          <- 80
n_trials_per   <- 6
susceptible    <- c(rep(FALSE, 60), rep(TRUE, 20))  # 25% demand-susceptible

df_demand <- expand_grid(
  participant = 1:n_par,
  condition   = c("control", "scarcity"),
  trial       = 1:n_trials_per
) |>
  mutate(
    demand_sus  = susceptible[participant],
    # True scarcity effect = -3 (scarcity reduces willingness to pay via threat)
    # Demand-susceptible participants inflate scarcity condition WTP by +8
    demand_bias = ifelse(demand_sus & condition == "scarcity", 8, 0),
    wtp         = 70 + (-3) * (condition == "scarcity") + demand_bias +
                    rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    participant = factor(participant),
    condition   = factor(condition, levels = c("control", "scarcity"))
  )

# Pooled model: mixes susceptible and non-susceptible participants
m_pooled <- lmer(wtp ~ condition + (1 | participant), data = df_demand,
                 REML = FALSE)

# Split by susceptibility to reveal the true effect vs. demand inflation
m_non_sus <- lmer(wtp ~ condition + (1 | participant),
                  data = df_demand |> filter(!demand_sus), REML = FALSE)
m_sus     <- lmer(wtp ~ condition + (1 | participant),
                  data = df_demand |> filter(demand_sus),  REML = FALSE)

bind_rows(
  tidy(m_pooled,  effects = "fixed") |> filter(term == "conditionscarcity") |>
    mutate(group = "Pooled (all participants)"),
  tidy(m_non_sus, effects = "fixed") |> filter(term == "conditionscarcity") |>
    mutate(group = "Non-susceptible participants (true effect ≈ −3)"),
  tidy(m_sus,     effects = "fixed") |> filter(term == "conditionscarcity") |>
    mutate(group = "Demand-susceptible participants (inflated)")
) |>
  select(group, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "Demand characteristics attenuate the pooled scarcity effect toward zero")

The pooled estimate is attenuated toward zero: the 25% of participants who inflate their scarcity-condition responses mask the true negative effect among the other 75%. The estimate for non-susceptible participants cleanly recovers the true effect of −3. The susceptible participants show near-zero or positive effects — the demand inflation swamps the true effect for them.
This is especially important in pricing and WTP studies. If participants in the scarcity condition are trying to appear “rational” or “prudent” by moderating their stated WTP, the pooled estimate will understate the true scarcity effect among non-susceptible participants. Suspicion checks and implicit behavioral measures (e.g., actual purchase decisions rather than stated intentions) reduce this threat.
Practical remedies: Within-subjects designs employ deception (concealing the true hypothesis), filler tasks (obscuring the critical conditions), post-hoc suspicion checks (screening out participants who guessed the hypothesis), and implicit measures (which are harder to consciously manipulate). In the mixed model framework, demand characteristics manifest as systematic participant × condition interactions. This is why you should always examine the random slope variance for condition: a large random slope variance in a within-subjects design is a warning sign that participants are responding heterogeneously in ways that may reflect demand rather than true effect heterogeneity.



Hawthorne Effects and Experimenter Effects in Multi-Site Designs
In financial decision research, participants who know they are being monitored may become more price-conscious, more risk-averse, or more “responsible” in their choices. A consumer tracked in a spending diary study may spend differently than they normally would — especially in categories they consider socially undesirable (impulse purchases, luxury goods, vices). This behavioral change due to monitoring inflates the apparent effect of any intervention delivered during the monitoring period.
This Hawthorne effect is a between-experimenter confound in multi-experimenter or multi-site studies: some experimenters elicit stronger Hawthorne effects because of their demeanor, perceived authority, or enthusiasm for the study.
Practical implication for nested experimental data: Experimenter is a level-2 clustering variable. If some experimenters consistently elicit stronger Hawthorne effects, their participants will show elevated treatment effects regardless of the actual manipulation. Adding experimenter random intercepts (covered in Module 5, Part 4) absorbs experimenter-level Hawthorne effects. If experimenter is not modeled, its variance inflates the treatment effect standard error and potentially biases the point estimate.
The same logic applies in multi-site longitudinal studies: the site or observer conducting the repeated assessments is a clustering variable. Observer drift (systematic change in measurement practice over time) and observer effects (participants performing differently for different assessors) are level-2 and cross-level confounds, not nuisance.






WarningAssumption: Observer Effects Are Negligible or Modeled



How to check: Test whether experimenter / site / assessor identity predicts outcomes after controlling for treatment. A significant experimenter effect signals that Hawthorne-type confounds are operating.
What to do: Include experimenter or site as a random effect. Pre-train experimenters to a behavioral protocol to minimize between-experimenter variation. In longitudinal studies, keep the same assessor across waves where possible.

title: Selection Effects & Attrition
text:
Type 3: Survivorship Bias
You only observe units that survived some selection filter correlated with your outcome.
The canonical example: World War II analysts studied bullet-hole patterns on returning planes to determine where to add armor. Abraham Wald pointed out that the relevant evidence came from planes that did not return. The areas with no bullet holes on returning planes were the critical spots — hits there were fatal. The returning planes were a survivor-selected sample.
In longitudinal research: Studying predictors of firm innovation using currently existing firms excludes all firms that failed. If early failure is systematically related to your predictors (e.g., low R&D investment), estimates of those predictors are biased in the surviving sample.
In experimental research: Analyzing only participants who completed all sessions of a multi-session experiment excludes those who dropped out. If dropout is related to the treatment (e.g., participants who find the task aversive are more likely to withdraw), the completed-cases analysis represents a survivorship-selected sample — typically the more motivated, more compliant, or less affected participants.






WarningAssumption: No Survivorship Bias



How to check: Ask whether your outcome is systematically related to the probability of appearing in your dataset. If yes, you likely have survivorship bias.
What to do: Obtain historical data including non-survivors. In longitudinal research, use survival analysis (Module 6, Part 3) to model time-to-exit explicitly. In experiments, report and analyze dropout patterns and compare dropouts to completers on baseline characteristics.

title: Selection Effects & Attrition
section: Type 4: Attrition Bias in Longitudinal Data
text:
Type 4: Attrition Bias in Longitudinal Data
Participants drop out of your study non-randomly over time. This is one of the most serious threats to longitudinal research — and a direct consequence of the nested structure of time.
In longitudinal panel research: Participants in a financial diary study facing higher financial distress may withdraw because tracking spending is burdensome and emotionally aversive when finances are under stress. High-performing firms may exit the panel because they no longer need advisory services. In both cases, later waves of the panel over-represent lower-distress or higher-performing units.
In experimental repeated-measures research: Participants who find the experimental task aversive, boring, or demanding are more likely to withdraw after the first session. If task aversiveness is related to the treatment (e.g., a high-cognitive-load manipulation is more exhausting for lower-capacity participants), dropout is informatively related to both condition and outcome.


Code
n_people <- 200
n_waves  <- 5

fin_distress <- rnorm(n_people, 50, 10)  # higher = more financially stressed
treatment    <- rbinom(n_people, 1, 0.5) # treatment = received budgeting intervention

df_long <- expand_grid(person = 1:n_people, wave = 1:n_waves) |>
  mutate(
    baseline  = fin_distress[person],
    treat     = treatment[person],
    # Higher distress → lower baseline savings; treatment slowly increases savings over time
    # True treatment-wave slope = 3/5 = 0.6 per wave
    savings_pct = 20 - 0.3 * baseline + 3 * treat * (wave / n_waves) + rnorm(n(), 0, 4)
  )

# People with lower savings (more distressed) are more likely to drop out
df_long <- df_long |>
  group_by(person) |>
  mutate(
    drop_risk   = plogis(-3 - 0.04 * mean(savings_pct)),
    dropped_out = cummax(rbinom(n(), 1, drop_risk)),
    observed    = dropped_out == 0 | wave == 1
  ) |>
  ungroup()

complete_cases <- df_long |>
  group_by(person) |> filter(all(observed)) |> ungroup()

tibble(
  Sample   = c("All (Wave 1)", "Completers only"),
  N        = c(n_distinct(df_long$person[df_long$wave == 1]),
               n_distinct(complete_cases$person)),
  Mean_baseline_savings = c(
    mean(20 - 0.3 * fin_distress),
    mean(unique(20 - 0.3 * complete_cases$baseline))
  )
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
    caption = "Attrition: completers have higher baseline savings rate than the full sample")

# The correct estimand is the treat × wave interaction, not a main effect of treat.
m_completers <- lm(savings_pct ~ treat * wave + baseline, data = complete_cases)
m_all        <- lm(savings_pct ~ treat * wave + baseline,
                   data = df_long |> filter(observed))

  tidy(m_completers) |> filter(term == "treat:wave") |>
    mutate(model = "Complete cases only"),
  tidy(m_all) |> filter(term == "treat:wave") |>
    mutate(model = "All observed data (available-case)")
) |>
  select(model, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>

    caption = "Treatment × wave interaction: complete-case vs. available-case. True slope = +0.6 per wave unit (reaches +3 at wave 5). On average across samples, available-case analysis is less biased under MAR — individual draws may vary.")

WarningAssumption: Dropout Mechanism is Ignorable



MCAR (Missing Completely At Random): Dropout is unrelated to any variable — observed or unobserved. Very rare in practice.
MAR (Missing At Random): Dropout depends only on observed variables. If MAR holds, mixed-effects models using all available data (not just completers) give valid estimates. This is a reasonable assumption when you have rich baseline data.
MNAR (Missing Not At Random): Dropout depends on the unobserved outcome itself (e.g., people drop out because their savings situation worsened, not because of any measured variable). Requires sensitivity analysis or selection models (Heckman correction).
How to check: Compare baseline characteristics of completers vs. dropouts. If they differ substantially on predictors of the outcome, the dropout mechanism is non-ignorable and complete-cases analysis is biased.

title: Selection Effects & Attrition
text:
Type 5: Exclusion Bias
The researcher removes observations non-randomly — typically based on criteria correlated with the outcome.
In longitudinal research: Removing firm-year observations where productivity was “unusually low” because the firm was going through a restructuring is a form of exclusion bias if restructuring itself is the phenomenon you are studying. Excluding outlier years based on outcome values selectively removes exactly the high-variance observations that may be most informative.
In experimental research: Removing participants who “clearly did not understand the task” based on their responses — after you have seen the data — is exclusion bias if the misunderstanding or non-compliance rate differs systematically by condition. Post-hoc exclusions that benefit the hypothesis are a particularly consequential form of researcher degrees of freedom.
The key principle: Any data deletion that is non-random introduces selection bias. This includes:

Removing “outliers” based on outcome values
Excluding protocol violators after seeing results
Dropping units that seem “too different” from the main pattern
Selectively trimming conditions that inflate the standard error







TipPre-Registration as a Defense



Pre-registering exclusion criteria before data collection prevents post-hoc rationalization of exclusions that benefit your hypothesis. It does not eliminate the statistical bias if exclusions are necessary, but it prevents the researcher from inadvertently introducing bias by making exclusion decisions under the influence of the results. Pre-registered exclusion criteria are also far more credible to reviewers and readers than post-hoc criteria.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text: Regression Discontinuity Design

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
The Threshold as a Quasi-Experiment
Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) exploits a rule: treatment is assigned when a continuous running variable crosses a known threshold. Observations just below and just above the threshold are nearly identical in every respect except treatment status — because small differences in the running variable near the cutoff are essentially random noise in the data-generating process.
The key insight: Right at the threshold, treatment is as-good-as-randomly assigned. The jump in outcomes at the cutoff is the causal effect of treatment for units near the threshold.
RDD appears in two distinct forms across the research contexts this course covers. In longitudinal research, the running variable is often time itself (Interrupted Time Series) or a cumulative score that triggers a policy intervention. In experimental research, the running variable is often a continuous eligibility screening score, and the cutoff determines who qualifies for a treatment arm.

Why Local Comparison Is Valid: The Bandwidth Argument
The central claim of RDD is that units near the cutoff are comparable in a way that units far from the cutoff are not. A borrower with a credit score of 648 and a borrower with a credit score of 652 are separated by what amounts to random noise in the data-generating process — a single missed payment, a dispute that cleared, a month’s credit utilization that ticked slightly in one direction. Their underlying creditworthiness is essentially identical. But a borrower with a score of 600 and a borrower with a score of 700 differ systematically in creditworthiness, payment history, income stability, and many other factors that independently predict financial outcomes.
This means comparing all borrowers above the cutoff to all borrowers below the cutoff conflates the treatment effect with all the real differences between high- and low-credit-score individuals. The RDD narrows the comparison to a bandwidth around the cutoff where assignment is effectively local and the confounders are approximately balanced.









The bandwidth is not arbitrary — rdrobust selects it optimally to balance the bias-variance trade-off: a wider bandwidth increases sample size (lower variance) but includes more units far from the cutoff where the “approximately random” claim is weaker (higher bias). The density test and falsification tests below check whether the local-randomization assumption holds.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
section: Part A: RDD in Longitudinal Research
text:
Part A: RDD in Longitudinal Research

Sharp RDD: Credit Score Threshold and Prime-Rate Loan Access
A common financial services RDD uses a credit score threshold to assign access to a preferential loan product. Borrowers whose score meets or exceeds the cutoff (e.g., 650) qualify for the prime-rate product with lower interest; those below do not. Borrowers just below and just above an arbitrary administrative cutoff are nearly identical in their actual creditworthiness — the cutoff is a bureaucratic rule, not a true discontinuity in financial behavior.
The outcome of interest: 12-month improvement in financial health (a composite of savings rate and debt reduction). If access to the prime-rate product improves financial health, a jump should appear precisely at the threshold.






WarningAssumption: Continuity of Potential Outcomes at the Threshold



What it means: In the absence of treatment, the expected outcome must be a continuous function of the running variable at the cutoff. The only reason outcomes should jump at the threshold is the treatment itself — prime-rate access.
Why it fails:

Sorting/manipulation: If borrowers can manipulate their credit score to cross the threshold (paying down a specific account, disputing a single error), those just above and just below are no longer comparable. The density test catches this: a spike in the density just above 650 indicates strategic score management.
Other policies at the same cutoff: If a second product (e.g., a fee waiver) also triggers at credit score 650, you cannot separate the effects.
Anticipation effects: If borrowers anticipate the cutoff and change their financial behavior before crossing it (e.g., deferring large purchases until they qualify), the pre-threshold trend is distorted.

What survives if this assumption fails: You can still describe the average difference between borrowers just above and below the threshold — but you cannot interpret it as causal. If sorting is limited to a narrow band, the estimate may still be approximately valid with a tighter bandwidth.
How to check: McCrary density test — a spike in the density just above the cutoff indicates strategic score manipulation.




Code
n <- 1000
# Running variable: credit score, centered at cutoff = 0 (e.g., 650 in real units)
credit_score  <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
prime_access  <- as.integer(credit_score >= 0)
# True causal effect of prime-rate access on 12-month financial health = 8 points
fin_health    <- 50 + 5 * credit_score + 8 * prime_access + rnorm(n, 0, 5)

df_rdd <- tibble(credit_score, prime_access, fin_health)

ggplot(df_rdd, aes(x = credit_score, y = fin_health, color = factor(prime_access))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 2), se = TRUE,
              linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black",
             linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#aec6e8", "#1e3a5f"),
                     labels = c("Standard rate (score < cutoff)",
                                "Prime rate (score ≥ cutoff)")) +
  labs(title = "RDD: financial health vs. credit score",
       subtitle = "Jump at the dashed cutoff = causal effect of prime-rate access",
       x = "Credit Score (centered at cutoff)", y = "12-month financial health score",
       color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)











Code
rdd_result <- rdrobust(y = df_rdd$fin_health, x = df_rdd$credit_score, c = 0)
summary(rdd_result)
