rdrobust uses local polynomial regression with an automatically selected optimal bandwidth. The estimated jump at the cutoff recovers the true causal effect of approximately 8 financial health units.


The Density Test


Code
ggplot(df_rdd, aes(x = credit_score)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#1e3a5f", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.2,
             linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Density test: check for manipulation at the credit score cutoff",
       subtitle = "A spike just right of the dashed line = borrowers gaming their score",
       x = "Credit Score (centered at cutoff)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









The distribution is smooth through the cutoff — no evidence of strategic score manipulation. In real credit data, a spike just above the threshold would indicate that borrowers near the margin are paying down specific accounts, disputing errors, or taking other targeted actions to cross it.


Falsification Tests
Run the RDD on pre-treatment covariates (account tenure, age). These cannot be caused by getting prime-rate access. A jump at the threshold in a covariate means something else is discontinuous there — a serious threat to validity.


Code
df_rdd <- df_rdd |> mutate(acct_tenure = 5 + rnorm(n, 0, 2))
fake   <- rdrobust(y = df_rdd$acct_tenure, x = df_rdd$credit_score, c = 0)
cat("Jump in account tenure at cutoff (should be ~0):", round(fake$coef[1], 3),
    "| p =", round(fake$pv[1], 3), "\n")


Jump in account tenure at cutoff (should be ~0): -0.164 | p = 0.656 




Bandwidth Sensitivity
The estimate should be stable as you vary the bandwidth around the default. Dramatic changes signal dependence on functional form assumptions near the threshold.


Code
bws  <- seq(0.3, 1.5, by = 0.2)
ests <- sapply(bws, \(bw)
  rdrobust(y = df_rdd$fin_health, x = df_rdd$credit_score, c = 0, h = bw)$coef[1])

tibble(Bandwidth = bws, Estimate = ests) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Bandwidth, y = Estimate)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 8, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e63946") +
  labs(title = "Bandwidth sensitivity (red dashed = true effect = 8)",
       x = "Bandwidth", y = "Estimated Discontinuity") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)












Interrupted Time Series as Temporal RDD
A special form of RDD uses time as the running variable. When a policy takes effect at a known date, observations before that date serve as “control” and observations after as “treated.” The continuity assumption becomes: absent the policy, the pre-existing time trend would have continued smoothly through the policy date.
This design is called an Interrupted Time Series (ITS) and is especially valuable in longitudinal panel data where a policy is applied to all units simultaneously.
The ITS model separates three distinct quantities:
\[Y_t = \underbrace{\beta_0 + \beta_1 t}_{\text{pre-policy trend}} + \underbrace{\beta_2 D_t}_{\text{level jump at policy date}} + \underbrace{\beta_3 (t - c) D_t}_{\text{post-policy slope change}} + \varepsilon_t\]

\(\beta_1\): the pre-policy trend (the counterfactual slope — what would have continued)
\(\beta_2\): the immediate level jump at the policy date (the “intercept shift”)
\(\beta_3\): the change in slope after the policy (whether the policy altered the trajectory)



Code
n_stores <- 30
n_months <- 30
store_eff <- rnorm(n_stores, 0, 6)  # store-level random intercepts

df_its <- expand_grid(store = 1:n_stores, month = 1:n_months) |>
  mutate(
    post    = as.integer(month >= 16),          # policy starts at month 16
    t_post  = pmax(month - 15, 0),              # time since policy, 0 pre-policy
    store_u = store_eff[store],
    # True: level jump = +5, slope change = +0.3/month
    sales   = 60 + 0.8 * month + 5 * post + 0.3 * t_post + store_u +
                rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    store   = factor(store)
  )

m_its <- lmer(sales ~ month + post + t_post + (1 | store), data = df_its,
              REML = FALSE)
summary(m_its)$coefficients |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("term") |>
  filter(term %in% c("month", "post", "t_post")) |>
  rename(estimate = Estimate, std.error = `Std. Error`, t = `t value`) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "ITS model: pre-trend, level jump (post), and slope change (t_post)")

  annotate("text", x = 22, y = 84, label = expression(beta[3] ~ "(slope change)"),

  scale_color_manual(values = c("#aec6e8", "#1e3a5f"),
                     labels = c("Pre-policy", "Post-policy")) +

       x = "Month", y = "Mean Sales", color = NULL) +

\(\hat{\beta}_2 \approx 5\): The policy caused an immediate, step-change increase in sales at implementation.
\(\hat{\beta}_3 \approx 0.3\): The policy also increased the monthly sales growth rate by 0.3 units per month compared to the pre-policy trend.
\(\hat{\beta}_1 \approx 0.8\): The counterfactual — in the absence of the policy, sales would have continued rising by 0.8 units per month.

The ITS design cannot rule out other events that happened exactly at month 16. The strongest threats are contemporaneous shocks (another policy, a market event) that coincide precisely with the policy date.
The density-test equivalent for ITS: Check for unusual clustering of observations just before the policy implementation date. Firms that anticipate a pricing policy may accelerate purchases or delay inventory, creating a temporary spike in the outcome in periods 14–15. Plot the distribution of the outcome in the 3–4 periods immediately before implementation and compare to the pre-trend expectation.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
section: Part B: RDD in Experimental Research
text:
Part B: RDD in Experimental Research
RDD logic appears in applied studies when eligibility for an intervention is determined by crossing a continuous screening threshold. Unlike the observational RDD — where the cutoff is an exogenous administrative rule — this version uses the cutoff to create a natural comparison group within a structured study.

Eligibility Threshold: Financial Distress Screening and Coaching Access
A financial services organization screens applicants for an intensive debt-counseling program using a Financial Vulnerability Index (FVI) — a composite of debt-to-income ratio, payment history, and account balances scored 0–30 (higher = more financially distressed). Applicants scoring ≥ 15 are offered access to the intensive coaching program; those scoring below 15 receive standard informational materials.
This creates an RDD: applicants just above and just below FVI = 15 are nearly identical in their actual financial situation — the cutoff is an administrative rule, not a true behavioral discontinuity. The outcome is savings rate improvement over six months.
The FVI RDD is sharp if the cutoff is strictly enforced. It becomes fuzzy if advisors exercise discretion — some below-threshold clients are enrolled based on advisor judgment, some above-threshold clients decline. In the fuzzy case, the cutoff becomes an instrument for actual program participation, and the estimand is a LATE.






WarningAssumption: Sharp vs. Fuzzy Cutoff



Sharp RDD: Crossing the threshold deterministically assigns treatment. The discontinuity directly identifies the causal effect for units near the cutoff.
Fuzzy RDD: The cutoff changes the probability of treatment receipt — some above-threshold clients decline, some below-threshold clients are enrolled by advisor discretion. Fuzzy RDD gives a LATE via IV: the cutoff is an instrument for actual program participation. Use rdrobust(..., fuzzy = enrolled) for fuzzy designs.
What survives if neither version holds cleanly: If enforcement is very fuzzy (the threshold is essentially ignored), the first stage is weak and the RDD estimate is unreliable. Report the first-stage jump in participation probability alongside the outcome estimate. A first-stage F below 10 is a red flag.
The key diagnostic: does crossing the threshold produce a large, discontinuous jump in the probability of participation?




Code
n   <- 600
fvi <- round(runif(n, 0, 30))        # FVI scores from 0 to 30
enrolled <- as.integer(fvi >= 15)    # sharp: ≥15 enrolled in intensive coaching

# True causal effect for applicants near the threshold = 6 pp savings improvement
# Underlying trend: more distressed applicants have lower baseline savings gains
savings_gain <- 8 - 0.2 * fvi + 6 * enrolled + rnorm(n, 0, 4)

df_coaching <- tibble(fvi, enrolled, savings_gain)

rdd_coaching <- rdrobust(y = df_coaching$savings_gain, x = df_coaching$fvi, c = 15)
summary(rdd_coaching)


Call: rdrobust

Sharp RD estimates using local polynomial regression.

Code
ggplot(df_coaching, aes(x = fvi, y = savings_gain, color = factor(enrolled))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 15, linetype = "dashed", color = "black",
             linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#aec6e8", "#1e3a5f"),
                     labels = c("Standard materials (FVI < 15)",
                                "Intensive coaching (FVI ≥ 15)")) +
  labs(title = "RDD: savings gain at Financial Vulnerability Index cutoff = 15",
       subtitle = "Jump at the cutoff = causal effect of coaching for applicants near FVI = 15",
       x = "Financial Vulnerability Index (FVI)", y = "6-month savings rate improvement (%)",
       color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)











Density Test: Did Applicants Game Their FVI Score?
If applicants believe that scoring ≥ 15 gives them access to a desirable coaching program, they might strategically misreport their financial situation (understating income, overstating debts) to cross the threshold. A spike in the density just above 15 indicates this gaming behavior.


Code
ggplot(df_coaching, aes(x = fvi)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 31, fill = "#1e3a5f", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 15, color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.2,
             linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Density test: Financial Vulnerability Index distribution",
       subtitle = "A spike just above 15 (red dashed) = applicants gaming their score to qualify",
       x = "Financial Vulnerability Index (FVI)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









In this simulation there is no spike — the distribution is smooth through the cutoff, consistent with the continuity assumption.


Falsification Test: No Jump in Pre-Screening Covariates
Run the RDD on account tenure — a pre-screening covariate that cannot be caused by coaching enrollment. A discontinuity at FVI = 15 in account tenure would indicate that something other than financial distress drives the threshold assignment.


Code
df_coaching <- df_coaching |>
  mutate(acct_tenure = 5 + rnorm(n, 0, 3))

fake_coaching <- rdrobust(y = df_coaching$acct_tenure, x = df_coaching$fvi, c = 15)
cat("Jump in account tenure at FVI = 15 (should be ~0):",
    round(fake_coaching$coef[1], 3),
    "| p =", round(fake_coaching$pv[1], 3), "\n")


Jump in account tenure at FVI = 15 (should be ~0): -0.869 | p = 0.505 




The LATE Interpretation for the Coaching RDD
Like all RDD estimates, this is a Local Average Treatment Effect for applicants near FVI = 15 — those at the margin of financial distress. The treatment effect for severely distressed applicants (FVI = 25+) may be very different: they face structural financial constraints that intensive coaching may not overcome, or alternatively, they may benefit most. But RDD cannot speak to them — they are far from the threshold.
The practical implication: The RDD estimate tells you whether coaching helps marginally distressed applicants — exactly the population where the program’s benefit is most uncertain and contested. It cannot tell you whether to expand the program to the most severely distressed, who would need a different identification strategy (e.g., randomized waitlist).

RDD is most credible when the threshold is truly arbitrary from the unit’s perspective, when the running variable cannot be precisely manipulated, and when the bandwidth is narrow enough that treated and control units are genuinely comparable. The narrower the bandwidth, the more credible the local randomization — but also the smaller the sample and the larger the standard errors.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text: Difference-in-Differences

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
The Core Idea
A savings nudge rolls out at some bank branches; others serve as controls. You have monthly transaction data from before and after. Can you estimate the nudge’s effect on savings behavior?
The naive approach — compare treated and control branches after the rollout — is biased if they were already different. Difference-in-Differences (DiD) subtracts the control group’s change from the treated group’s change:
\[\hat{\tau}_{DiD} = \underbrace{(\bar{Y}_{T,\text{post}} - \bar{Y}_{T,\text{pre}})}_{\text{treated group change}} - \underbrace{(\bar{Y}_{C,\text{post}} - \bar{Y}_{C,\text{pre}})}_{\text{control group change}}\]
The control group’s change serves as the counterfactual: what would have happened to treated units in the absence of the nudge?

The counterfactual timeline





flowchart LR
    A["Pre-period\n(baseline)"] --> B["Treatment onset\n(policy rollout)"]
    B --> C["Post-period\n(observed)"]
    B --> D["Counterfactual\n(unobserved)"]
    style D fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#f39c12,stroke-dasharray:5 5
    style B fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2d6a4f






The dashed box is the missing data problem. The treated group’s counterfactual post-period outcome — what they would have done without the nudge — is never observed. DiD fills that gap by assuming the control group’s trajectory is a valid proxy.
DiD appears in two distinct research contexts that share this same logic:

Longitudinal panel data: households, consumers, or bank branches tracked across calendar time, with a policy affecting some units.
Repeated-measures experimental data: participants randomized to treatment vs. control and measured both before and after.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Part A: Panel DiD

Setup and Simulation
We simulate a savings nudge rolled out at 40 of 80 bank branches over 6 waves (waves 1–3: pre; 4–6: post). The true nudge effect is a +10 unit increase in average monthly savings. Branches differ in their baseline savings rates and all follow a common upward time trend.


Code
n_branches <- 80
n_waves    <- 6  # waves 1–3 pre; 4–6 post

branch_treat <- c(rep(1, 40), rep(0, 40))
branch_base  <- rnorm(n_branches, 50, 8)

df_did <- expand_grid(branch = 1:n_branches, wave = 1:n_waves) |>
  mutate(
    treat          = branch_treat[branch],
    post           = as.integer(wave > 3),
    baseline       = branch_base[branch],
    trend          = (wave - 3.5) * 1.5,
    te             = treat * post * 10,
    avg_savings    = baseline + trend + te + rnorm(n(), 0, 4)
  )




The Core Assumption: Parallel Trends






WarningAssumption: Parallel Trends



Plain-language meaning: In the absence of the nudge, treated branches would have followed the same savings trajectory as control branches. They can start at different levels — DiD accounts for that with fixed effects. But their rate of change over time must be the same.
What the model is assuming away: Any pre-existing divergence in trends — treated branches might have been on a steeper growth trajectory already, making the post-treatment gap look like a nudge effect when it would have appeared anyway.
JDM example: If a bank selectively rolled out the savings nudge at high-momentum branches (those already gaining customers and growing savings), treated branches were on a faster pre-trend. The post-period gap partly reflects that pre-existing momentum, not just the nudge.
Experimental analog: In a randomized pre-post experiment, parallel trends is guaranteed in expectation by random assignment. In panel observational data, it is an assumption you must argue and test.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Why should the treatment and control branches have had the same underlying savings growth trajectory if the rollout was not random? Were higher-growth branches systematically chosen for the nudge?”
Observable warning sign: Treated and control group trends visibly diverging before the treatment onset in a raw data plot; significant treatment-period interactions in pre-treatment-only regressions.
What to check: 1. Plot pre-treatment trends for both groups — they should look parallel. 2. Regress outcome on treat × wave using only pre-treatment observations — significant interactions indicate pre-trend differences. 3. Estimate an event study (period-specific treatment effects) — pre-period coefficients should be statistically indistinguishable from zero.
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The sign of the effect may still be correct if the pre-trend divergence is modest. But the magnitude is unreliable, and the direction can reverse if treated units were on a faster upward trend that would have created a post-period gap regardless.











In the left panel, both groups rise at the same rate before treatment — the DiD estimate cleanly captures only the jump caused by the policy. In the right panel, treated units were already on a steeper trajectory. The DiD estimate would be inflated because part of the post-period gap would have materialised even without the nudge. The pre-trend test and event study distinguish these two situations.


Code
group_means <- df_did |>
  group_by(wave, treat) |>
  summarise(mean_sav = mean(avg_savings), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(group = ifelse(treat == 1, "Nudge branches", "Control branches"))

ggplot(group_means, aes(x = wave, y = mean_sav, color = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.6, y = max(group_means$mean_sav) - 1,
           label = "Nudge rollout", hjust = 0, color = "gray40", size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#aec6e8", "#1e3a5f")) +
  labs(
    title    = "DiD: parallel pre-trends, divergence post-rollout",
    subtitle = "Parallel pre-period trends support the counterfactual substitution; post-period gap = DiD estimate",
    x        = "Wave",
    y        = "Mean monthly savings (branch average)",
    color    = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)











Regression Implementation: Two-Way Fixed Effects
The regression implementation of DiD is the Two-Way Fixed Effects (TWFE) model:
\[Y_{it} = \underbrace{\alpha_i}_{\text{branch FE}} + \underbrace{\lambda_t}_{\text{time FE}} + \underbrace{\delta \cdot D_{it}}_{\text{nudge effect}} + \varepsilon_{it}\]
Branch fixed effects \(\alpha_i\) absorb all time-invariant differences across branches (e.g., branch size, local income demographics). Time fixed effects \(\lambda_t\) absorb all common temporal trends (e.g., macroeconomic changes affecting all branches). The treatment indicator \(D_{it}\) captures the DiD estimate net of both.
In the 2×2 case (one treated group, one pre and one post period), treat:post in an OLS interaction model is algebraically identical to the DiD estimator. With multiple periods and multiple units, the TWFE formulation generalises naturally.


Code
m_did_fe <- lm(avg_savings ~ treat * post + factor(branch) + factor(wave),
               data = df_did)

tidy(m_did_fe) |>
  filter(term == "treat:post") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "`treat:post` = DiD estimate via TWFE (true effect = 10)")

In DiD with panel data, residuals within the same branch are correlated across waves — the same branch’s errors co-vary over time. Ignoring this inflates precision. Cluster at the branch level:

m_did_basic <- lm(avg_savings ~ treat * post + baseline, data = df_did)

coeftest(m_did_basic, vcov = vcovCL(m_did_basic, cluster = ~branch)) |>

  filter(term == "treat:post") |>

Event Study Plot
An event study estimates a separate treatment effect for each period, omitting one reference pre-period. Pre-period coefficients near zero confirm parallel trends; post-period coefficients trace the dynamic effect of the nudge.


Code
m_ev  <- lm(avg_savings ~ treat * factor(wave) + baseline, data = df_did)
ev_df <- tidy(m_ev, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "treat:factor")) |>
  mutate(
    wave = as.integer(str_extract(term, "[0-9]+")),
    pre  = wave <= 3
  )

ggplot(ev_df, aes(x = wave, y = estimate, color = pre)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "#aec6e8", "FALSE" = "#1e3a5f"),
    labels = c("TRUE"  = "Pre-treatment (should ≈ 0)",
               "FALSE" = "Post-treatment (nudge effect)")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Event study: pre-period near zero, post-period shows nudge effect",
    subtitle = "Pre-period balance confirms parallel trends; post-period estimates trace effect trajectory",
    x        = "Wave",
    y        = "Estimated treatment effect (vs. wave 1 reference)",
    color    = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)











A Note on Staggered Adoption
When different branches (or households) adopt treatment at different calendar times, the standard TWFE estimator produces a weighted average of all pairwise DiD comparisons — including “forbidden comparisons” where already-treated units serve as controls for later-treated units. If nudge effects are heterogeneous across cohorts or build up over time, this weighting can produce a biased and even sign-reversed estimate.






WarningStaggered DiD: A Critical Limitation of Plain TWFE



Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) and related estimators address this by computing group-time average treatment effects \(ATT(g, t)\) for each cohort \(g\) (defined by adoption timing) at each post-treatment period \(t\), then aggregating appropriately. If you have staggered adoption, check whether the did or staggered packages are appropriate before relying on plain TWFE. See Roth et al. (2023) for a comprehensive review.
JDM context: If a financial education program rolls out to different consumer cohorts at different times (e.g., some households enrolled in January, others in April), and the program’s effect builds over time, plain TWFE will produce a distorted average. The Callaway–Sant’Anna approach estimates the cohort-specific effect at each relative time period, then aggregates.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Part B: Experimental DiD

DiD Logic in Pre-Post Controlled Experiments
DiD logic appears directly in experimental designs when you have both a between-subjects factor (treatment vs. control) and a within-subjects time factor (baseline vs. follow-up). This is the standard pre-post controlled experiment — and it is structurally a DiD.
\[\hat{\tau}_{DiD} = \underbrace{(\bar{Y}_{T,\text{post}} - \bar{Y}_{T,\text{pre}})}_{\text{treatment group change}} - \underbrace{(\bar{Y}_{C,\text{post}} - \bar{Y}_{C,\text{pre}})}_{\text{control group change}}\]
In a randomized experiment, pre-test differences are zero in expectation. Random assignment supports parallel trends. Under random assignment, no differential attrition, stable measurement, and no spillovers, the treatment-by-time interaction consistently estimates the average causal contrast for this pre-post design — often interpreted as the average treatment effect on change.
Adding the pre-test makes the estimate more efficient than a post-only comparison: the participant random intercept absorbs baseline heterogeneity, reducing residual variance. This matters most in smaller samples where chance baseline imbalance is nontrivial.


The Experimental DiD as a Mixed Model
Pre-post data are nested: measurements within participants within conditions. The correct model includes a random intercept for participant:
\[Y_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{10} \cdot \text{time}_{ij} + \gamma_{01} \cdot \text{cond}_j + \underbrace{\gamma_{11} \cdot \text{time}_{ij} \times \text{cond}_j}_{\text{DiD estimate}} + u_{0j} + \varepsilon_{ij}\]
The random effect \(u_{0j}\) absorbs between-person variance in the outcome level, just as unit fixed effects do in the panel TWFE model. Both absorb stable individual heterogeneity; the DiD interaction identifies the treatment effect net of that heterogeneity.


Worked Example: Savings Disclosure Intervention
120 participants (60 disclosure, 60 standard) are measured at baseline and at an 8-week follow-up. The outcome is wtp (willingness to invest in a recommended product, 0–100 scale). The disclosure condition receives an expected-value breakdown of investment options; the standard condition receives the usual product description. The true DiD effect is +8: disclosure increases WTP 8 points more than the standard condition.


Code
n_per <- 60

df_disc <- tibble(
  participant = rep(1:(n_per * 2), each = 2),
  condition   = rep(c("standard", "disclosure"), each = n_per * 2),
  wave        = rep(c("pre", "post"), times = n_per * 2),
  u0          = rep(rnorm(n_per * 2, 0, 8), each = 2)
) |>
  mutate(
    time_num  = as.integer(wave == "post"),
    treat_num = as.integer(condition == "disclosure"),
    wtp       = 50 + u0 + 1 * time_num + 8 * time_num * treat_num + rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    participant = factor(participant),
    wave        = factor(wave, levels = c("pre", "post")),
    condition   = factor(condition, levels = c("standard", "disclosure"))
  )

Comparing Estimation Strategies

                  data = df_disc |> filter(wave == "post"))

df_wide <- df_disc |>
  select(participant, condition, wave, wtp) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = wave, values_from = wtp) |>
  rename(wtp_pre = pre, wtp_post = post)

m_ancova <- lm(wtp_post ~ condition + wtp_pre, data = df_wide)

bind_rows(
  tidy(m_post_only)       |> filter(term == "conditiondisclosure") |>
    mutate(model = "Post-only"),
  tidy(m_ancova)          |> filter(term == "conditiondisclosure") |>
    mutate(model = "ANCOVA"),
  tidy(m_exp_did, effects = "fixed") |>
    filter(str_detect(term, "wave.*condition|condition.*wave")) |>
    mutate(model = "Mixed DiD")
) |>

Experimental Event Study: Multiple Waves
With three or more measurement waves, you can estimate separate wave-specific effects — the experimental analog of the panel event study. Pre-intervention coefficients should be near zero (confirming randomization succeeded); post-intervention estimates trace the trajectory of the effect and whether it persists or fades.


Code
df_long <- tibble(
  participant = rep(1:(n_per * 2), each = 4),
  condition   = rep(c("standard", "disclosure"), each = n_per * 2 * 2),
  wave        = rep(c("pre", "mid", "post", "followup"), times = n_per * 2),
  u0          = rep(rnorm(n_per * 2, 0, 8), each = 4)
) |>
  mutate(
    wave_num  = case_when(wave == "pre" ~ 0, wave == "mid" ~ 1,
                          wave == "post" ~ 2, wave == "followup" ~ 3),
    treat_num = as.integer(condition == "disclosure"),
    true_did  = case_when(wave == "pre" ~ 0, wave == "mid" ~ 4,
                          wave == "post" ~ 8, wave == "followup" ~ 5),
    wtp         = 50 + u0 + 1 * wave_num + true_did * treat_num + rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    wave        = factor(wave, levels = c("pre", "mid", "post", "followup")),
    participant = factor(participant),
    condition   = factor(condition, levels = c("standard", "disclosure"))
  )

m_ev_exp <- lmer(wtp ~ wave * condition + (1 | participant), data = df_long)

ev_exp <- tidy(m_ev_exp, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "wave.*condition")) |>
  mutate(
    wave = str_extract(term, "mid|post|followup"),
    wave = factor(wave, levels = c("mid", "post", "followup"))
  )

ggplot(ev_exp, aes(x = wave, y = estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  labs(
    title    = "Experimental event study: disclosure effect at each post-wave",
    subtitle = "Pre-period reference = 0 by construction; wave 'pre' is the omitted category",
    x        = "Wave (relative to pre-period)",
    y        = "DiD estimate (differential change vs. pre)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









The effect builds from mid-intervention, peaks at post, and partially fades at follow-up — consistent with an information effect that decays without reinforcement. This trajectory cannot be detected with a simple two-wave pre-post design.

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Shared Assumptions






WarningAssumption: SUTVA — No Spillovers



Plain-language meaning: Treatment of unit A should not affect the outcomes of unit B. If nudged branches compete with control branches for the same customer base, improvements at nudged branches may come partly at control branches’ expense — contaminating the control trend.
JDM example: A financial education program at some bank branches may cause customers to switch from non-program branches, raising the program-branch savings rate partly through selection rather than education.
Experimental analog: In within-subjects experiments, SUTVA violation is called carryover effects: completing the disclosure condition may make participants more financially attentive in later trials, including control trials. This creates an asymmetry that the DiD estimate cannot separate from the disclosure effect.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Is there any reason to believe that treated branches and control branches are drawing from the same local customer pool? If so, the control group trend is contaminated.”
How to manage (experimental): Randomize condition order; include filler tasks between conditions; use between-subjects designs when carryover is likely.
How to check (panel): Test whether control units near treated units trend differently from geographically distant controls.








WarningAssumption: Stable Group Composition



Plain-language meaning: The composition of treated and control groups should not change differentially after treatment. If the savings nudge causes higher-balance customers to switch into nudged branches (because they value the service), the post-period treated group is a different population.
JDM example: After a fee waiver rolls out to some branches, financially sophisticated customers may actively seek out those branches. Post-period comparisons then partly capture customer self-selection, not just the fee waiver effect.
Experimental analog: Differential attrition at follow-up — if financially distressed participants in the disclosure condition drop out before the post-test, the remaining disclosure group is a non-representative survivor sample.
What to check: Test whether observable baseline characteristics predict differential attrition or switching behavior. If they do, consider IPW to correct for non-random compositional change (see Part 6).

title: Difference-in-Differences
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “How do you know the branches would have followed parallel trends without the nudge?” The parallel trends assumption is untestable for the post-period — you never observe the treated group’s counterfactual. The pre-period test (event study coefficients near zero before treatment) provides necessary but not sufficient evidence. A reviewer will want to know whether the rollout was random or selective, and whether treated and control branches look systematically different in observable characteristics.
Challenge 2: “Aren’t you using already-treated branches as controls for later-treated branches in your staggered TWFE?” Yes, in a staggered adoption setting. This is the Callaway–Sant’Anna critique: with staggered timing and heterogeneous effects, the TWFE weights can be negative for some (g,t) cells, potentially sign-reversing the estimate. If your rollout was staggered, use cohort-time estimators and present the event study disaggregated by cohort.
Challenge 3: “Your experimental DiD treats missing-at-random dropout as acceptable — but what if high-WTP participants in the standard condition dropped out because they found the baseline session discouraging?” Differential dropout by the outcome of interest is MNAR, not MAR. The DiD estimate from completers would be biased. Sensitivity analysis comparing the completer estimate to an IPW-weighted estimate (and reporting the two together) is the appropriate response.

title: Propensity Scores & Matching
text: Propensity Scores & Matching

title: Propensity Scores & Matching
text:
The Problem PSM Solves
You want to estimate whether enrolling in a digital budgeting program increases household savings, using observational data from a financial services platform. Households self-selected into the program — financially motivated, more tech-comfortable, higher-income households are more likely to enroll. A naive comparison of enrollees vs. non-enrollees will overestimate the program’s benefit.
Propensity score methods reduce this bias by constructing a comparison group similar to the treated group on all observed confounders. They work by estimating the probability that each household enrolled — the propensity score — then matching or weighting on that score.
\[e(X) = P(\text{Enrolled} = 1 \mid X)\]
Key result (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983): conditioning on \(e(X)\) is equivalent to conditioning on all elements of \(X\) — you do not need to match on every covariate separately.

The selection funnel





flowchart TD
    A["All platform households\nN = 2,000"] --> B["Eligible for program\n(active accounts)\nN = 1,400"]
    B --> C["Aware of program\n(received notification)\nN = 900"]
    C --> D["Enrolled\n(treated)\nN = 180"]
    C --> E["Did not enroll\n(control pool)\nN = 720"]
    style D fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2d6a4f
    style E fill:#f0f0f0,stroke:#888888






At each stage, who disappears is not random. Financially savvy households stay eligible; engaged households see the notification; motivated households enroll. The enrolled group is the product of multiple successive selection filters — and the naive comparison confounds all of those filters with the program effect itself.

Part A: Propensity Scores in Observational Data

Simulation: Digital Budgeting Program

n <- 600

financial_literacy <- rnorm(n, 50, 12)
income_percentile  <- rnorm(n, 50, 15)
baseline_savings   <- rnorm(n, 40, 10)

# Enrollment probability driven by observed confounders
p_enroll  <- plogis(-4 + 0.06 * financial_literacy + 0.04 * income_percentile
                       + 0.03 * baseline_savings)
enrolled  <- rbinom(n, 1, p_enroll)

# True ATE = 8 (program increases monthly savings by 8 units)
savings_change <- 0.2 * financial_literacy + 0.15 * income_percentile
               + 8 * enrolled + rnorm(n, 0, 7)

                enrolled, savings_change)

m_naive <- lm(savings_change ~ enrolled, data = df_ps)
cat("Naive estimate:", round(coef(m_naive)["enrolled"], 2),
    "  |  True effect = 8\n")


Naive estimate: 2.81   |  True effect = 8


The naive estimate is substantially inflated because it conflates financial literacy and income with the program effect — financially literate, higher-income households save more regardless of the program.



Step 1: Estimate Propensity Scores and Check Overlap


Code
ps_model <- glm(enrolled ~ financial_literacy + income_percentile + baseline_savings,
                family = binomial, data = df_ps)
df_ps <- df_ps |> mutate(ps = fitted(ps_model))


The overlap plot is the most important diagnostic before any matching or weighting. If the two distributions do not overlap, there are no valid comparison units for some treated households — causal inference is impossible for them.


Code
p_hist <- ggplot(df_ps, aes(x = ps, fill = factor(enrolled))) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.65, bins = 35, position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#aec6e8", "#1e3a5f"),
                    labels = c("Did not enroll", "Enrolled"),
                    name   = NULL) +
  labs(
    title    = "Overlap: propensity score distributions",
    subtitle = "Both groups must cover the same PS range. Non-overlapping tails = no valid comparison.",
    x        = "Propensity score (P(enrolled))",
    y        = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

# Mirrored version for cleaner comparison
p_mirror <- df_ps |>
  mutate(group   = ifelse(enrolled == 1, "Enrolled", "Not enrolled"),
         ps_plot = ifelse(enrolled == 0, -ps, ps)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ps_plot, fill = group)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Enrolled" = "#1e3a5f", "Not enrolled" = "#aec6e8"),
                    name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(-0.6, 0.6, 0.2),
    labels = abs(seq(-0.6, 0.6, 0.2))
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title    = "Mirrored propensity score distribution",
    subtitle = "Non-enrolled below center line; enrolled above. Overlap = similar PS ranges on both sides.",
    x        = "Propensity score (mirrored for not-enrolled)",
    y        = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_hist / p_mirror















WarningAssumption: Overlap (Common Support)



Plain-language meaning: Every enrolled household must have a non-trivial probability of not enrolling, and every non-enrolled household must have a non-trivial probability of enrolling. Without overlap, there are no valid comparison units for the extreme treated households — you are extrapolating, not comparing.
What the model is assuming away: That the enrolled and non-enrolled groups are ever comparable on the propensity score scale. If all households with high financial literacy enrolled, there are no high-literacy non-enrollees to serve as controls.
JDM example: If only households with incomes above $100k ever enrolled in the budgeting program, there is no valid comparison group for those households. Any estimated “effect” for them is pure extrapolation from lower-income non-enrollees who differ in many ways that matter.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Where is the common support? Show the propensity score distributions for treated and control groups — if they barely overlap, the comparison is not credible.”
Observable warning sign: Propensity score histograms with little overlap; many enrolled households with PS > 0.8 while the control group’s PS peaks below 0.3.
What to check: Plot mirrored PS histograms. Trim households outside the common support region (PS < min treated PS, or PS > max control PS). Report how many observations are excluded by trimming and whether results change.




Step 2: Matching and Balance Check


Code
m_out <- matchit(enrolled ~ financial_literacy + income_percentile + baseline_savings,
                 data   = df_ps,
                 method = "nearest",
                 ratio  = 1)

summary(m_out)$sum.matched |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "Balance after nearest-neighbor matching. Standardized mean differences should be < 0.10 after matching.")

Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW)
PSM discards unmatched households, losing information. IPW retains all observations by reweighting so the weighted sample resembles a random draw from the full population:
\[w_i = \frac{D_i}{\hat{e}(X_i)} + \frac{1-D_i}{1-\hat{e}(X_i)}\]
Enrolled households with a low enrollment probability are upweighted (they are surprising enrollees — useful controls for the counterfactual). Non-enrolled households with a high enrollment probability are upweighted (they are surprising non-enrollees — useful controls for what would happen without the program).

  mutate(
    ipw = ifelse(enrolled == 1,
                 1 / fitted(ps_model),
                 1 / (1 - fitted(ps_model)))
  )

            data    = df_ps,

Rosenbaum Sensitivity Analysis
After matching, the critical question is: how large would an unmeasured confounder need to be to overturn the conclusion? The sensitivity parameter \(\Gamma\) quantifies this:

\(\Gamma = 1\): no hidden bias assumed.
\(\Gamma = 2\): an unmeasured confounder could double the odds of enrollment for otherwise-identical households.

A small \(\Gamma\) threshold at significance (say, \(\Gamma = 1.2\)) means the conclusion is fragile — even a modest omitted confounder overturns it. A large threshold (say, \(\Gamma = 3\)) means the conclusion survives substantial unmeasured confounding. The rbounds package implements Rosenbaum bounds for continuous and binary outcomes. Always report the \(\Gamma\) at which your p-value crosses 0.05.

title: Propensity Scores & Matching
section: Part B: Propensity Scores in Experimental Research
text:
Part B: Propensity Scores in Experimental Research
Random assignment guarantees unbiased intent-to-treat estimates at the point of randomization. But three situations arise in practice where PS methods are needed even within an experiment.

Context A: IPW for Non-Random Attrition
This is the most important experimental application. When participants drop out at follow-up and dropout is related to the outcome, the remaining sample is no longer a random subsample. High-debt households may disengage from a financial diary study precisely because their financial situation is worsening — excluding them from the analysis biases the control group’s follow-up average upward.


Code
n_att <- 200
treatment_att    <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 100)
baseline_debt    <- rnorm(n_att, 50, 10)

# High debt + control group → higher dropout
# (distressed households avoid follow-up measurement)
p_remain  <- plogis(2.5 - 0.07 * baseline_debt + 0.8 * treatment_att)
remained  <- rbinom(n_att, 1, p_remain)

# True treatment effect = +6 (financial coaching increases savings)
outcome_att <- 45 + 6 * treatment_att - 0.3 * baseline_debt + rnorm(n_att, 0, 6)

df_att <- tibble(treatment = treatment_att, baseline_debt, remained, outcome_att)

cat("Control retention:  ", round(mean(remained[treatment_att == 0]) * 100, 1), "%\n")


Control retention:   21 %


Code
cat("Treatment retention:", round(mean(remained[treatment_att == 1]) * 100, 1), "%\n")


Treatment retention: 50 %




Code
ps_att     <- glm(remained ~ baseline_debt + treatment, family = binomial, data = df_att)
df_att$ipw_att <- 1 / fitted(ps_att)

df_complete     <- df_att |> filter(remained == 1)
m_naive_att     <- lm(outcome_att ~ treatment, data = df_complete)
m_ipw_att       <- lm(outcome_att ~ treatment, data = df_complete,
                       weights = df_att$ipw_att[df_att$remained == 1])

bind_rows(
  tidy(m_naive_att) |> filter(term == "treatment") |> mutate(method = "Naive complete-case analysis"),
  tidy(m_ipw_att)   |> filter(term == "treatment") |> mutate(method = "IPW-corrected analysis")
) |>
  select(method, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "Attrition bias: naive vs. IPW-weighted (true effect = +6). High-debt control households drop out more, biasing the naive estimate downward. IPW is consistent under MAR.")

TipReporting Attrition IPW



Report both estimates side by side. The naive estimate describes the effect among completers — a potentially biased, surviving subsample. The IPW estimate approximates the intent-to-treat effect for the full randomized sample. A large discrepancy signals material attrition bias.




Context B: PSM for Self-Selected Sub-Treatment Engagement
Random assignment gives households access to the coaching program, but actual engagement is voluntary. Comparing high-engagement to low-engagement households within the treatment arm is an observational comparison — highly engaged participants likely differ systematically in motivation, baseline financial literacy, and financial goals. PSM on pre-randomization covariates makes this comparison more credible.


Context C: Pre-Test Matching for Nonlinear Covariate Relationships
ANCOVA assumes a linear, homogeneous relationship between the pre-test and post-test. When this relationship is nonlinear — for instance, when very high or very low baseline savers change at a different rate — matching on the pre-test creates a comparison group that is directly comparable at baseline, allowing nonparametric change estimation without linear extrapolation.

title: Propensity Scores & Matching
text:
Assumptions






WarningAssumption: No Unmeasured Confounders (Ignorability)



Plain-language meaning: Given the observed covariates in the PS model, enrollment is effectively independent of the potential outcomes. There are no unmeasured variables that both predict enrollment and directly affect savings outcomes.
What the model is assuming away: Any confounding that operates through variables not in your data. Financial self-efficacy, financial anxiety, life-stage savings goals, and partner financial behavior could all simultaneously predict enrollment and savings outcomes — but if they are unmeasured, the PS model cannot account for them.
JDM example: If financially anxious households are both less likely to enroll and have worse savings outcomes for anxiety-related reasons (not program reasons), the PS model is missing the mechanism. Anxiety looks like a confounder but is not measured.
Experimental analog: In a perfectly randomized experiment, this assumption is satisfied by design. In an observational study, it is always an untestable assertion about your data-generating process.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “You controlled for literacy and income — but what about financial self-efficacy? Confidence in managing money predicts both enrollment and savings outcomes independently, and you don’t measure it.”
Observable warning sign: Sensitivity analysis (\(\Gamma\)) showing fragility at values close to 1 — meaning even small amounts of unmeasured confounding overturn the conclusion.
What to check: Report the Rosenbaum \(\Gamma\) or E-value. Discuss which unmeasured confounders are most plausible given domain knowledge. Consider whether any proxy measure can be added to the PS model to reduce confounding exposure.
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The estimate is a lower bound on confounding bias — it shows what you would find if all observed confounders are balanced. The causal interpretation depends on how credible ignorability is given the specific context.








WarningAssumption: Correctly Specified Propensity Score Model



Plain-language meaning: The logistic regression used to estimate PS must include all relevant confounders and model their effects correctly (linear effects, or appropriate transformations and interactions if effects are nonlinear).
What the model is assuming away: Nonlinear confounder effects, important interaction terms, and confounders not in the model.
JDM example: If financial literacy’s effect on enrollment probability has a threshold (below a certain level, almost no one enrolls; above it, nearly everyone does), the logistic model with a linear literacy term will misestimate the PS near the threshold.
What to check: Check balance after matching — if the PS model is correct and the matching is effective, observed confounders should be balanced between matched groups (SMD < 0.10). Poor balance despite matching signals PS model misspecification. Consider non-parametric PS estimation (CBPS or generalized boosted models) as a robustness check.

title: Propensity Scores & Matching
section: What Propensity Score Methods Can and Cannot Do
text:
What Propensity Score Methods Can and Cannot Do






NoteThe Limits of Matching



What you can say after PSM/IPW:

Among households with similar observed characteristics, the enrollment contrast is less confounded by those characteristics.
The estimate approximates what you would find in a randomized study if all confounders were measured and correctly modeled.
For ATT: the effect among enrolled households, relative to a comparison group matched to look like the enrolled group on observables.

What you cannot say:

That enrollment is as good as random — unobserved confounders remain and can dominate the result.
That a large \(\Gamma\) proves confounding is absent — it means you have quantified the threshold for overturning, not ruled out confounding.
That balance on observed covariates implies balance on unobserved ones.

Propensity score methods shift the burden from “I controlled for X” to “I controlled for all confounders” — which is a judgment about the DGP, not a statistical guarantee. Every PS analysis should be accompanied by an explicit argument for why the observed confounders are sufficient given the institutional context.

title: Propensity Scores & Matching
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “You matched on financial literacy and income — but motivation to save is the most obvious confounder and you have no measure of it.” This is the ignorability challenge. The appropriate response is: (1) acknowledge the limitation explicitly, (2) argue why the measured proxies (literacy, baseline savings) partially capture motivation, (3) conduct a sensitivity analysis showing how large an unmeasured confounder would need to be (\(\Gamma\) or E-value), and (4) discuss whether the residual confounding, if present, is likely to be large enough to materially change the conclusion.
Challenge 2: “Your pre-matching balance table shows a large SMD for baseline savings. Why is your matching not working?” Poor post-matching balance indicates either that the PS model is misspecified (wrong functional form, missing interactions) or that the matching ratio is too restrictive. Investigate the caliper setting, consider exact matching on the most influential covariate, or use entropy balancing which targets direct covariate balance rather than going through the PS.
Challenge 3: “Your overlap plot shows that enrolled households have PS mostly above 0.5, while non-enrolled are mostly below 0.2. Is the comparison credible?” This is a common support failure. Matches in the tails are between very different households — the comparisons are not credible there. The honest response is to trim to the common support region, show results on that restricted sample, and acknowledge that the ATT estimate applies only to enrolled households with close matches, not all enrolled households.

title: Propensity Scores & Matching
text:
Reporting Checklist for PS Analyses






TipPS Reporting Checklist




Specify all covariates in the PS model — pre-treatment only; no mediators or post-treatment variables
Report overlap check: mirrored PS histogram or plot by treatment group; note common support violations
Report balance statistics before AND after matching/weighting (standardized mean difference table; target SMD < 0.10)
Specify estimand: ATE (all households), ATT (enrolled only), or ATC (non-enrolled only)? Justify the choice
Report sensitivity analysis (\(\Gamma\) or E-value) to quantify vulnerability to unmeasured confounding
For attrition IPW: report both naive (completer-only) and IPW-corrected estimates side by side
For doubly robust: note which model (PS or outcome) is the primary specification and which provides the robustness guarantee
Discuss the most plausible unmeasured confounders by name and explain why the design reduces their influence

title: Module 4: Longitudinal Data & Change
text: Module 4: Longitudinal Data & Change

title: Module 4: Longitudinal Data & Change
section: Time is the Ultimate Nesting Variable
text:
Time is the Ultimate Nesting Variable
Every person, household, or firm exists within a stream of time. When you measure them repeatedly, your observations are nested within that stream. Each measurement is a snapshot of an ongoing trajectory — the DGP is a time-varying process, and your data is a discrete sample from it.
This is especially clear in JDM research. A household’s spending trajectory reflects stable financial habits, accumulated experience with budgeting tools, and responses to income shocks and policy changes. A consumer’s credit repayment pattern encodes risk preferences, liquidity constraints, and the behavioral effects of disclosure interventions. A product adoption curve traces how decision-makers update their willingness to engage as their information accumulates. A household’s response to a default change — opting out of automatic enrollment in a savings plan, or failing to — unfolds over months, not a single moment.
In each case, the temporal structure is not a nuisance to be controlled. It is the phenomenon.
This creates two profound challenges for analysis:

Observations within a unit are correlated. A household’s spending decision this month is correlated with its spending last month. A consumer’s risk preference today predicts their choice tomorrow. Treating these as independent observations — as standard regression does — violates independence and inflates Type I error.
Change itself is the phenomenon. In many JDM studies, the question is not just “what is the average level?” but “does a disclosure intervention shift risk-taking over time? Do saving trajectories diverge after a policy nudge? Does price sensitivity evolve as consumers gain experience?” A model that treats all observations as exchangeable — ignoring that some come first and some come later — cannot answer these questions.

Module 4 builds the toolkit for modeling change over time correctly.

title: Module 4: Longitudinal Data & Change
text:
What This Module Covers
The module is organized into five clusters. Each cluster addresses a distinct challenge in longitudinal data analysis, building from low-level specification decisions to causal identification.


Cluster 1 — Dependence and Covariance Structure
Part 1: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models — The repeated measures ANOVA that most researchers learned makes a specific assumption about the covariance structure of repeated observations (compound symmetry/sphericity). We show concretely what this assumption means, why it almost always fails, and how mixed-effects models relax it. JDM example: why measuring WTP at three time points — before an information intervention, immediately after, and at a one-month follow-up — cannot be analyzed with standard RM-ANOVA when variance structures differ across measurement occasions.
Part 2: Covariance Structures — The covariance matrix of your repeated observations is not just a nuisance to be controlled — it is a window into the DGP. We catalog the main structures (compound symmetry, AR(1), unstructured, Toeplitz), show what each implies about how measurements relate over time, and explain how to choose among them.


Cluster 2 — Modeling Trajectories and Change
Part 2b: Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles — Before modeling individual trajectories, we need to handle time itself as a potential confounder. This section introduces a single simulated longitudinal dataset — 120 app users tracked for 24 months — and builds a fully disclosed data-generating process with a secular trend, a 12-month seasonal cycle, and staggered non-random treatment enrollment. Five progressively better models are compared against the true DGP. Diagnostic plots (residuals vs. calendar time, residuals vs. month-of-year, ACF of panel-mean residuals) drive each specification improvement, and a final benchmark table shows exactly how much each additional control reduces bias.
Part 3: Growth Curve Models — When the question is how outcomes change over time and whether trajectories differ across people, growth curve models are the right tool. We build from simple linear growth to random slopes, nonlinear trajectories, and predictors of growth. JDM example: modeling individual savings trajectories or credit repayment curves after a financial coaching intervention — does the average trajectory improve, and does the effect differ across households?
Part 4: Latent Growth Curve Models in SEM — The same growth curve model can be estimated in a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework. We show the connection, explain when the SEM approach adds value (modeling measurement error, multiple growth processes), and demonstrate the equivalence using lavaan.
Part 5: Autoregressive Structures — When today’s outcome predicts tomorrow’s, the covariance structure is autoregressive. We explain AR(1) models, how to specify them in nlme, and the assumptions of stationarity. JDM example: today’s risk perception predicts tomorrow’s — AR structures in repeated financial decision tasks and daily diary studies of spending behavior.
Part 6: Cross-Lagged Panel Models — When you want to understand the dynamic relationship between two variables over time — does A cause B, does B cause A, or do they mutually reinforce each other — cross-lagged panel models (and their improved version, the RI-CLPM) provide the framework. JDM example: does financial stress cause reduced discretionary spending, or does reduced spending relieve financial stress? Cross-lagged models for separating the causal order in JDM panel data.


Cluster 3 — Non-Gaussian and Event Outcomes
Part 7: Binary and Count Outcomes Over Time — Many longitudinal outcomes are binary (opted out of the default / did not) or counts (number of late payments in a quarter, number of impulsive purchases per month). GLMMs extend the mixed model framework to handle these correctly using logistic and Poisson/negative-binomial families, with random effects preserving the within-person dependence structure. JDM example: binary choice outcomes — did the consumer opt out of the default enrollment? How many late payments did the household make in a given quarter?
Part 8: Survival Analysis — When the outcome is time until an event, standard regression ignores censoring and misrepresents the DGP. Kaplan-Meier curves, Cox proportional hazards models, and frailty models handle event-time outcomes in nested data. JDM example: time to first default on a credit product, time to churn from a savings app, time to opt out of an automatic fee renewal program — all require survival methods because many households will not experience the event during the observation window.


Cluster 4 — Missingness and Attrition
Part 9: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies — Attrition and intermittent missingness are nearly universal in panel data. We classify mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), show how lmer handles MAR data via full-information maximum likelihood, introduce multiple imputation as a principled alternative, and cover sensitivity analysis for MNAR. JDM example: participants dropping out of financial diary studies because they experience financial distress — precisely the population whose trajectories matter most. App users going inactive after negative financial events. These are MNAR patterns that require explicit sensitivity analysis.


Cluster 5 — Causal Identification in Panel Settings
Part 10: Applied Identification Strategies — The capstone. When the research question is causal — not just descriptive — panel data offer a powerful toolkit: difference-in-differences (TWFE), interrupted time series, panel instrumental variables, and time-varying propensity score matching. Each strategy maps to a specific threat from Module 3 and provides a concrete remedy in the longitudinal context. JDM examples: DiD for evaluating an overdraft fee policy change across banks that adopted the policy at different times; ITS for a sudden regulatory requirement to disclose total annual costs on credit statements; panel IV using randomized encouragement to adopt a budgeting tool as an instrument for actual tool use; time-varying propensity scores for observational financial diary data where engagement with financial advice changes over time.

The module closes with Part 10 as a deliberate capstone: after understanding how longitudinal data are structured, how trajectories are modeled, and how non-standard outcomes and missing data are handled, Part 10 asks the hardest question — can we identify a causal effect? — and provides the tools to answer it.

title: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models
text: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models
crumbs: 26  From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models

title: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models
section: The Standard Approach and Its Hidden Assumption
text:
The Standard Approach and Its Hidden Assumption
Repeated measures ANOVA (RM-ANOVA) has been the default tool for within-subjects designs for decades. It is built into every statistics textbook and available in SPSS, JASP, and R. And it makes an assumption about your data that is almost always wrong.
That assumption is sphericity.
crumbs: 26  From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models

title: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models
text:
What Is Sphericity?
Sphericity constrains the variance-covariance matrix of your repeated measurements. Specifically, it requires that the variances of all pairwise differences between time points are equal.
Consider measuring willingness to pay (WTP) at three time points: before a financial disclosure intervention, immediately after, and at a one-week follow-up. Sphericity requires that:
\[\text{Var}(\text{WTP}_{\text{pre}} - \text{WTP}_{\text{post}}) = \text{Var}(\text{WTP}_{\text{pre}} - \text{WTP}_{\text{follow-up}}) = \text{Var}(\text{WTP}_{\text{post}} - \text{WTP}_{\text{follow-up}})\]
In plain language: the variability in how much people change must be the same regardless of which two time points you compare. This is equivalent to assuming compound symmetry — that all time points correlate equally with each other.
But this is implausible. The pre-to-post change (a few days) captures the immediate disclosure reaction. The pre-to-follow-up change (a week) is noisier because some people’s attention has faded. The post-to-follow-up change (a few days) reflects short-term decay. These three differences have different variances — sphericity is already violated in principle before you collect any data.


Code
library(Matrix)

# Three covariance structures for 4 repeated WTP measurements
CS <- matrix(c(1.0, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5,
               0.5, 1.0, 0.5, 0.5,
               0.5, 0.5, 1.0, 0.5,
               0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0), 4, 4)

rho <- 0.7
AR1 <- outer(1:4, 1:4, FUN = function(i, j) rho^abs(i - j))

US <- matrix(c(1.0, 0.8, 0.6, 0.3,
               0.8, 1.0, 0.7, 0.5,
               0.6, 0.7, 1.0, 0.8,
               0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0), 4, 4)

plot_cov <- function(M, title, subtitle = NULL) {
  lbl <- c("Pre", "Post", "1wk", "1mo")
  as.data.frame(M) |>
    setNames(lbl) |>
    mutate(row = lbl) |>
    pivot_longer(-row, names_to = "col", values_to = "corr") |>
    mutate(row = factor(row, levels = rev(lbl)),
           col = factor(col, levels = lbl)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = col, y = row, fill = corr)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(corr, 1)), size = 4) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#f7fbff", mid = "#6baed6", high = "#08306b",
                         midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle,
         x = "WTP wave", y = "WTP wave", fill = "Corr") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

plot_cov(CS,  "Compound Symmetry",    "All pairs equally correlated.\nSphericity holds. Implausible.") +
plot_cov(AR1, "AR(1)",                "Adjacent waves more similar.\nDecaying with time lag. Common.") +
plot_cov(US,  "Unstructured",         "No constraints. Each pair\nestimated from data.") +
plot_layout(ncol = 3)









The compound symmetry structure (left) forces all off-diagonal entries to be equal — WTP pre-post relates to WTP post-follow-up the same as WTP pre-follow-up. This is the sphericity assumption. AR(1) (middle) lets correlations decay with the time gap. Unstructured (right) imposes no constraints.
Real longitudinal data almost always looks more like AR(1) or unstructured than compound symmetry.
crumbs: 26  From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models

title: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models
section: What Happens When Sphericity Is Violated?
text:
What Happens When Sphericity Is Violated?
When sphericity fails, RM-ANOVA F-tests are anti-conservative — Type I error rates inflate above your stated alpha level.


Code
# Severe violation: AR(1) ρ = 0.85 over 5 measurement occasions.
# With ρ = 0.7 and 4 occasions (as in the diagram above), the violation is
# mild because the average AR(1) correlation (≈ 0.54) is close to the
# CS assumption (0.50). Using ρ = 0.85 and 5 occasions makes the
# heterogeneity in pairwise correlations (0.85 at lag 1 vs. 0.52 at lag 4)
# large enough to produce substantial Type I error inflation.
rho_viol  <- 0.85
n_occ     <- 5
AR1_viol  <- outer(1:n_occ, 1:n_occ, FUN = function(i, j) rho_viol^abs(i-j))

# CS benchmark: all off-diagonal equal to the average AR(1) off-diagonal
cs_avg   <- mean(AR1_viol[lower.tri(AR1_viol)])
CS_viol  <- matrix(cs_avg, n_occ, n_occ); diag(CS_viol) <- 1

extract_pval <- function(y_mat) {
  n_p <- nrow(y_mat); n_t <- ncol(y_mat)
  df_aov <- data.frame(
    Y      = c(y_mat),
    time   = factor(rep(seq_len(n_t), each = n_p)),
    person = factor(rep(seq_len(n_p), n_t))
  )
  s <- tryCatch(
    summary(aov(Y ~ time + Error(person / time), data = df_aov)),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(s)) return(NA_real_)
  tryCatch(s[["Error: person:time"]][[1]][["Pr(>F)"]][1],
           error = function(e) NA_real_)
}

set.seed(99)
n_sims <- 3000
type1_spherical <- logical(n_sims)
type1_violated  <- logical(n_sims)

for (i in seq_len(n_sims)) {
  y_sph <- MASS::mvrnorm(50, mu = rep(0, n_occ), Sigma = CS_viol  * 4)
  y_vio <- MASS::mvrnorm(50, mu = rep(0, n_occ), Sigma = AR1_viol * 4)
  p_sph <- extract_pval(y_sph);  p_vio <- extract_pval(y_vio)
  type1_spherical[i] <- isTRUE(p_sph < 0.05)
  type1_violated[i]  <- isTRUE(p_vio < 0.05)
}

t1_cs  <- mean(type1_spherical, na.rm = TRUE)
t1_ar1 <- mean(type1_violated,  na.rm = TRUE)

tibble(
  Condition = c("Sphericity holds (CS)",
                "Sphericity violated (AR1, ρ = 0.85, 5 occasions)"),
  `Type I Error Rate` = c(t1_cs, t1_ar1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "Type I error at nominal α = 0.05. Strong AR(1) data inflates the rejection rate more than three-fold.")



Type I error at nominal α = 0.05. Strong AR(1) data inflates the rejection rate more than three-fold.


Condition
Type I Error Rate




Sphericity holds (CS)
0.047


Sphericity violated (AR1, ρ = 0.85, 5 occasions)
0.080





Code
tibble(
  Condition = factor(c("Compound\nSymmetry\n(sphericity holds)",
                        "AR(1), ρ = 0.85\n(5 occasions,\nsphericity violated)"),
                     levels = c("Compound\nSymmetry\n(sphericity holds)",
                                "AR(1), ρ = 0.85\n(5 occasions,\nsphericity violated)")),
  rate = c(t1_cs, t1_ar1)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Condition, y = rate, fill = Condition)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.45) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1, color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.0f%%", rate * 100)),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.35),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(round(x * 100), "%")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2d6a4f", "#cb181d")) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.053, hjust = 0, size = 3.5,
           label = "Nominal 5% threshold") +
  labs(title = "RM-ANOVA Type I error rate\nunder sphericity vs. violation",
       subtitle = "n = 50, 3 000 simulations — null is true in both conditions",
       x = NULL, y = "Observed Type I error rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 11, lineheight = 1.2))









With strong AR(1) data (ρ = 0.85, five occasions), RM-ANOVA produces Type I error rates more than three times the nominal 5%. The violation is severe because the pairwise correlation at lag 1 (0.85) and at lag 4 (0.85^4 ≈ 0.52) differ greatly, yet RM-ANOVA assumes they are equal. The Greenhouse–Geisser correction adjusts the degrees of freedom to compensate — but the better remedy is to switch to a mixed model, which does not require sphericity at all.

title: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models
text:
Assumption: Sphericity






WarningAssumption: Sphericity (RM-ANOVA Only)



Plain-language meaning: All pairwise differences between time points have the same variance. Equivalent to compound symmetry: every pair of WTP waves correlates equally, regardless of the time gap separating them.
What the model is assuming away: The natural structure of most longitudinal data, where adjacent observations are more similar than distant ones. A WTP measurement taken immediately after a disclosure should correlate more strongly with a 1-week follow-up than with a 6-month follow-up.
JDM example: In a disclosure experiment with pre, immediate post, 1-week, and 1-month follow-ups, sphericity requires that the correlation structure is flat across all time gaps. But 1-week WTP should resemble immediate-post WTP more than it resembles baseline WTP.
Experimental analog: In an observational panel study of weekly savings behavior, sphericity would require that week 1 and week 4 savings correlate as strongly as week 1 and week 2 savings. This is never realistic.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “You used RM-ANOVA with four waves and report a significant time × condition interaction — did you test sphericity? With decaying correlations across waves, RM-ANOVA F-tests will be anti-conservative.”
Observable warning sign: Mauchly’s W is significant (p < .05). Or simply: you have more than 2 repeated measurements and time points are separated by unequal gaps.
What to check: Run Mauchly’s test as a preliminary check. But note: it is underpowered in small samples and overpowered in large ones. The better move is to switch to a mixed model — then the sphericity assumption is not required at all.
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The direction of effects is usually robust. The p-value is too small under violation, so a conclusion that “just barely” passes a threshold is suspect.
crumbs: 26  From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models

title: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models
text:
Mixed-Effects Models: No Sphericity Required
A mixed-effects model makes no sphericity assumption. The random effects structure and residual covariance together determine what the model implies about how measurements co-vary — and you can specify the structure that fits the data rather than forcing compound symmetry.


Code
# Simulate a WTP study: 3 waves, AR(1) correlation (sphericity violated)
n_people <- 60
n_times  <- 3
Sigma_ar <- AR1[1:3, 1:3] * 4  # true structure is AR(1), not CS

# Null data: no true time effect
wtp_data <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_people, mu = c(50, 50, 50), Sigma = Sigma_ar) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  setNames(c("pre", "post", "follow_up")) |>
  mutate(person = 1:n_people) |>
  pivot_longer(-person, names_to = "time", values_to = "WTP") |>
  mutate(
    time_num = case_when(time == "pre" ~ 1, time == "post" ~ 2, TRUE ~ 3),
    person   = factor(person)
  )

# RM-ANOVA
m_anova <- aov(WTP ~ factor(time_num) + Error(person / factor(time_num)),
               data = wtp_data)

# Mixed-effects model with AR(1) covariance
m_mlm <- lme(WTP ~ factor(time_num),
             random      = ~1 | person,
             correlation = corAR1(),
             data        = wtp_data)

cat("RM-ANOVA p (time):", round(
  summary(m_anova)$`Error: person:factor(time_num)`[[1]]["factor(time_num)", "Pr(>F)"], 4), "\n")


RM-ANOVA p (time): 0.0169 


Code
cat("MLM p (time):     ", round(anova(m_mlm)["factor(time_num)", "p-value"], 4), "\n")


MLM p (time):      0.0226 


When the true covariance structure is AR(1), the mixed-effects model gives more accurate p-values — because it uses the correct covariance structure rather than assuming an implausible flat one.

title: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models
section: The Key Advantages of Mixed Models Over RM-ANOVA
text:
The Key Advantages of Mixed Models Over RM-ANOVA








Feature
RM-ANOVA
Mixed-Effects Model




Assumes sphericity?
Yes — almost always violated
No — covariance is modeled


Handles missing data?
No — requires complete cases at every wave
Yes — uses all available observations


Allows continuous time?
No — time must be discrete categories
Yes


Models individual trajectories?
No
Yes (random slopes)


Handles unbalanced designs?
Poorly
Gracefully


Can include level-2 predictors?
No
Yes


Generalizes to non-normal outcomes?
No
Yes (GLMM)



The only reason to prefer RM-ANOVA is familiarity. For most real longitudinal designs, mixed-effects models are more flexible, more transparent about assumptions, and better able to handle unequal spacing and missing data.

title: From RM-ANOVA to Mixed Models
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “You measured WTP at 4 waves and analyzed with RM-ANOVA — did you test for sphericity? If it’s violated, your interaction p-value is too small.” The correct response: switch to a mixed model (or at minimum apply Greenhouse-Geisser correction). A mixed model with AR(1) residuals is both more flexible and more honest about the covariance structure than corrected RM-ANOVA.
Challenge 2: “You have 12% missing data at wave 3 and excluded those cases. How does that affect the RM-ANOVA result?” RM-ANOVA requires complete cases — excluding wave-3 dropouts creates a biased subsample. The mixed model with available-case estimation (all participants at their observed waves) is unbiased under MAR and should be the primary analysis.
Challenge 3: “Why do you need random effects for person in a within-subjects design where each person appears multiple times?” The random intercept for person absorbs between-person variance in baseline WTP, reducing residual noise and improving power. Without it, that between-person variance inflates the residual, making the condition effect look less precise. The random intercept is not optional in a within-subjects mixed model — it is the direct translation of the design into the model.
