title: Covariance Structures
section: The Covariance Matrix Is a Scientific Statement
text:
The Covariance Matrix Is a Scientific Statement
When you measure the same person at multiple time points, those measurements co-vary. How they co-vary is not a nuisance parameter — it is a substantive statement about the DGP. The choice of covariance structure encodes an assumption about how the process unfolds over time.
A useful starting question: “If I knew Person A’s WTP in week 1, how much does that tell me about their WTP in week 2 versus week 8?” The answer depends on the persistence of the underlying state being measured:

Short-lived state (e.g., momentary risk perception after seeing a shocking news headline): week 1 barely predicts week 4. Adjacent observations are only a bit more similar than distant ones.
Persistent individual tendency (e.g., stable financial risk tolerance): week 1 predicts week 8 almost as well as week 2. Observations are broadly similar regardless of lag.
Gradually decaying memory or habit (e.g., recall of a disclosure or momentum of a savings habit): week 2 is more similar to week 1 than week 8 is, and the similarity decays smoothly with lag.

Each of these stories implies a different covariance structure.

title: Covariance Structures
text:
The Main Structures

1. Compound Symmetry (CS)
All variances equal. All covariances equal regardless of lag.
\[\Sigma_{CS} = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma^2 & \sigma^2\rho & \sigma^2\rho \\ \sigma^2\rho & \sigma^2 & \sigma^2\rho \\ \sigma^2\rho & \sigma^2\rho & \sigma^2 \end{pmatrix}\]
The DGP story: Each person has a stable individual level, and every observation is equally predictable from every other. The WTP at month 1 tells you as much about month 6 as it tells you about month 2.
JDM setting: Most appropriate when what you are measuring is a fixed individual trait that shows no dynamic persistence or decay — for example, a stable risk-preference score that does not drift meaningfully across sessions. In practice this is rare; most repeated JDM measurements show some decay structure.
When it fails: Whenever observations are more similar to adjacent ones than to distant ones — which is almost always true in longitudinal JDM studies.



2. Autoregressive Order 1 — AR(1)
Correlations decay exponentially with time lag. Observations one step apart correlate \(\rho\); two steps apart, \(\rho^2\); \(k\) steps apart, \(\rho^k\).
\[\Sigma_{AR1} = \sigma^2\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho & \rho^2 \\ \rho & 1 & \rho \\ \rho^2 & \rho & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]
The DGP story: Each observation partially inherits from the previous one. Yesterday’s state predicts today’s, but the influence decays at a constant rate. A financial decision made under a disclosure effect carries partial memory into the next measurement, but fades over longer gaps.
JDM settings: - Daily spending diary: today’s spending predicts tomorrow’s more than next week’s - Weekly savings rate: this week’s savings are correlated with last week’s, but the correlation decays with the lag - Risk perception during a market fluctuation: day-to-day persistence that gradually loses predictive power
When it fits: When your measurement intervals are equal and the process has smooth geometric decay in correlations.



3. Unstructured (UN)
No constraints. Every variance and covariance is estimated freely from the data.
The DGP story: The data speak for themselves. There is no assumed decay pattern or symmetry.
JDM settings: Reasonable when you have a small number of waves (3–4) and a large sample — the model has enough data to estimate every pairwise correlation without exploding the parameter count.
When it fails: With many waves or small samples, the unstructured model is severely overparameterized. With 5 waves and 50 people, you are estimating 15 covariance parameters from data where each person contributes only 5 observations. The estimates are unstable and the model often fails to converge.



4. Toeplitz
Like AR(1) but without the geometric constraint: each lag has its own correlation, but the correlation depends only on the lag size, not the absolute time point.
The DGP story: Lag-1 observations are more similar than lag-2, which are more similar than lag-3 — but the rate of decay does not have to be exponential. A financial decision’s influence might fade quickly at first (week 1 to week 2) and then more slowly (week 3 to week 6), which AR(1) cannot capture but Toeplitz can.

title: Covariance Structures
text:
Visualizing the Structures


Code
make_cov_plot <- function(Sigma, title, subtitle = NULL) {
  n <- nrow(Sigma)
  D <- diag(1 / sqrt(diag(Sigma)))
  Corr <- D %*% Sigma %*% D
  wlabs <- paste0("W", 1:n)

  data.frame(Corr) |>
    setNames(wlabs) |>
    mutate(row = wlabs) |>
    pivot_longer(-row, names_to = "col", values_to = "r") |>
    mutate(row = factor(row, levels = rev(wlabs)),
           col = factor(col, levels = wlabs)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = col, y = row, fill = r)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 3.5) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#f7fbff", mid = "#4292c6", high = "#08306b",
                         midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(-0.1, 1)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

n <- 5
rho <- 0.6

CS   <- matrix(rho, n, n); diag(CS) <- 1; CS <- CS * 4
AR1  <- outer(0:(n-1), 0:(n-1), function(i, j) rho^abs(i-j)) * 4
Toep <- outer(0:(n-1), 0:(n-1), function(i, j) {
  c(1, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2)[abs(i-j)+1]
}) * 4
UN <- matrix(c(4.0, 2.4, 1.8, 1.4, 1.0,
               2.4, 4.2, 2.2, 1.6, 1.1,
               1.8, 2.2, 4.5, 2.4, 1.5,
               1.4, 1.6, 2.4, 4.8, 2.2,
               1.0, 1.1, 1.5, 2.2, 5.0), n, n)

(make_cov_plot(CS,   "Compound Symmetry",
               "Flat correlations — any wave\npredicts any other equally") +
 make_cov_plot(AR1,  "AR(1)",
               "Geometric decay — adjacent\nwaves most similar")) /
(make_cov_plot(Toep, "Toeplitz",
               "Free decay by lag — flexible\nbut still lag-dependent") +
 make_cov_plot(UN,   "Unstructured",
               "No constraints — data-driven\nbut needs large N"))









The heatmaps show how correlation between waves (W1–W5) changes under each structure. AR(1) and Toeplitz capture the realistic pattern where similarity decreases as the time gap grows.

title: Covariance Structures
text:
Specifying Covariance Structures in R
lme4 does not support custom covariance structures beyond the random effects structure. For explicit covariance modeling, use nlme:


Code
# Simulate WTP data from a savings study: 5 waves with AR(1) correlation
n_people <- 50
n_times  <- 5
rho_true <- 0.7

Y_ar1 <- MASS::mvrnorm(n_people, rep(50, n_times),
                        outer(0:(n_times-1), 0:(n_times-1),
                              function(i, j) rho_true^abs(i-j)) * 9)

df_long <- as.data.frame(Y_ar1) |>
  setNames(paste0("wave", 1:n_times)) |>
  mutate(person = 1:n_people) |>
  pivot_longer(-person, names_to = "wave", values_to = "WTP") |>
  mutate(wave_num = as.integer(str_extract(wave, "[0-9]")),
         person   = factor(person))

# Fit four competing models
m_cs  <- gls(WTP ~ factor(wave_num),
             correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~1 | person),
             data = df_long)
m_ar1 <- gls(WTP ~ factor(wave_num),
             correlation = corAR1(form = ~wave_num | person),
             data = df_long)
m_un  <- gls(WTP ~ factor(wave_num),
             correlation = corSymm(form = ~wave_num | person),
             weights = varIdent(form = ~1 | factor(wave_num)),
             data = df_long)

tibble(
  Model = c("Compound Symmetry", "AR(1)", "Unstructured"),
  AIC   = c(AIC(m_cs), AIC(m_ar1), AIC(m_un)),
  BIC   = c(BIC(m_cs), BIC(m_ar1), BIC(m_un))
) |>
  arrange(AIC) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1,
    caption = "Model comparison: AR(1) fits best when data has geometric decay in correlations (lower AIC/BIC = better)")

title: Covariance Structures
text:
Assumptions






WarningAR(1) Assumption: Stationarity



Plain-language meaning: The mean and variance of the outcome are constant across time, and the correlation between any two observations depends only on how far apart they are — not on when in the study they fall. An AR(1) with \(|\phi| < 1\) is stationary by construction.
What the model is assuming away: Trending means (e.g., WTP systematically rising over time due to growing familiarity with the product) or trending variance (e.g., participants becoming more variable later in a long task when fatigue sets in).
JDM example: If participants in a repeated savings task become more financially confident across waves — so WTP increases for all participants regardless of condition — the mean is trending. The AR(1) model will confound this trend with the outcome trajectory unless time is included as a fixed effect.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “You modeled repeated savings willingness with AR(1) — but if participants are becoming more engaged with the study instrument over time, the mean is trending and stationarity fails.”
Observable warning sign: Plot wave-by-wave means. If the mean increases or decreases systematically across waves, stationarity is violated for the raw outcome. Including wave as a fixed effect typically restores stationarity for the residuals.
What to check: Plot means and variances by wave. Fit a model with time as a fixed effect and check whether residuals are stationary. Use the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test for stationarity on per-person residual series.
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The direction of the condition effect is usually robust. The autoregressive coefficient estimate and its confidence interval may be biased if stationarity is violated.








WarningUnstructured Assumption: Sufficient Sample Size



Plain-language meaning: The unstructured model estimates \(T(T+1)/2\) covariance parameters for \(T\) waves. With 5 waves, that is 15 parameters — just for the covariance structure. These must be estimated from the data.
What the model is assuming away: Any parsimony. The unstructured model places no restrictions on how measurements co-vary.
JDM example: A 6-wave savings diary study with 60 participants requires estimating 21 covariance parameters from a sample that has only 360 observations. That is fewer than 17 observations per covariance parameter — estimates will be noisy and models may fail to converge.
What to check: Compare the number of observations to the number of covariance parameters (aim for at least 10:1). If the unstructured model fails to converge, start with AR(1) and use AIC to evaluate whether the more constrained model fits acceptably.

text:
Model Selection Strategy

  `Params (T=5)`    = c("2", "2", "5", "15"),
  `Best for`         = c(
    "Stable trait; no decay; rarely appropriate",
    "Regular intervals; geometric decay; default starting point",
    "Irregular decay; flexible but tractable; good middle ground",

Recommended workflow:

title: Covariance Structures
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “You fitted a random intercept model with lme4. What covariance structure does that imply for your repeated WTP measurements?” A random intercept model in lme4 implies compound symmetry — all waves correlate equally at \(\rho = \sigma^2_u / (\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_\varepsilon)\). If adjacent waves should correlate more than distant ones (almost always true), this model misspecifies the covariance structure. Switch to nlme with corAR1() for longitudinal data with meaningful time ordering.
Challenge 2: “Why did you choose AR(1) over unstructured?” The data-driven answer: AIC/BIC favored AR(1) and the unstructured model showed convergence issues (too many parameters for the sample). The conceptual answer: WTP decay after a disclosure intervention is well described by geometric fading — the psychological mechanism supports AR(1) structure.
Challenge 3: “Your AR(1) estimate is \(\hat{\rho} = 0.72\) — doesn’t that suggest the waves are measuring a stable trait rather than a dynamic process?” High AR(1) correlation does not necessarily mean it is a fixed trait. It means the process has strong short-term persistence. A Bayesian risk-tolerance parameter might show \(\rho = 0.72\) across weeks while still responding to information interventions — the AR structure describes the baseline persistence, not the treatment effect.

title: Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles
text:
One Dataset, Many Models
This section works differently from most of the module. We build one realistic longitudinal dataset, disclose the true data-generating process completely, then run it through five progressively better specifications. Each model section follows the same five-step inferential workflow:

Assumptions — what does this model assume about the data?
Pre-fit checks — what can we verify before fitting?
Fitting the model — code and key output
Against the DGP — how well does this model recover the truth?
Interpreting the results — what do the coefficients mean, and what errors would we make stopping here?

All residual diagnostic plots use the same y-axis scale, so the shrinking of residuals across models is directly visible.
crumbs: 28  Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles

title: Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles
text:
The True Data-Generating Process
A fintech app tracks monthly spending ($) for 120 US users over 24 months (January 2023 through December 2024). The platform introduced a voluntary Loyalty Program partway through, and the research question is: does program membership cause higher spending?






TipTrue DGP Parameters






Parameter
Symbol
True value




Loyalty program effect
\(\beta_{\text{loyalty}}\)
$35


Background drift (per month)
\(\beta_{\text{drift}}\)
$3


Seasonal amplitude
\(A\)
$60


Between-person SD
\(\sigma_u\)
$80


Within-person residual SD
\(\sigma_e\)
$40


Person baseline mean
\(\mu\)
$500



\[
Y_{it} = \underbrace{\alpha_i}_{\text{person baseline}}
       + \underbrace{35 \cdot D_{it}}_{\text{loyalty effect}}
       + \underbrace{3 \cdot t}_{\text{background drift}}
       + \underbrace{60 \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi\, m_t}{12}\right)}_{\text{seasonal cycle}}
       + \underbrace{\varepsilon_{it}}_{\text{noise}}
\]
where \(t\) is the calendar month (1–24), \(m_t\) is the month of year (1–12), and \(\varepsilon_{it} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 40^2)\).



Each row is one user–month. There are \(120 \times 24 = 2{,}880\) rows.
\(\alpha_i \sim \mathcal{N}(500, 80^2)\): the person’s stable monthly baseline spending.
Background drift (\(+\$3\)/month): platform growth and inflation lift everyone’s spending over the 24 months, totalling +$72 by the end regardless of program status.
Seasonal cycle: December spending is $60 above the monthly average; June is $60 below — a $120 annual swing.
Enrollment is staggered and non-random: higher-spending users are more likely to join; a November–December marketing push concentrates enrollment in the highest-spending months. Both create confounding.



Code
set.seed(2025)

n_hh     <- 120
n_months <- 24

# True DGP parameters
true_loyalty   <- 35   # causal program effect ($/month)
true_trend     <- 3    # background drift ($/month)
true_amplitude <- 60   # seasonal amplitude ($)
true_person_sd <- 80   # between-person SD ($)
true_resid_sd  <- 40   # within-person residual SD ($)

# Person baselines
person_baselines <- rnorm(n_hh, 500, true_person_sd)

# Staggered enrollment:
#   (a) higher-spending users enroll earlier
#   (b) Nov/Dec marketing campaign doubles enrollment probability
enroll_month <- rep(NA_integer_, n_hh)
for (hh in seq_len(n_hh)) {
  for (m in 4:22) {
    moy       <- ((m - 1L) %% 12L) + 1L
    p_base    <- 0.025
    p_person  <- max(0, (person_baselines[hh] - 500) / 80) * 0.025
    p_holiday <- if (moy %in% c(11L, 12L)) 0.05 else 0
    p         <- min(p_base + p_person + p_holiday, 0.15)
    if (runif(1) < p) { enroll_month[hh] <- m; break }
  }
}

df <- expand_grid(person = seq_len(n_hh), month = seq_len(n_months)) |>
  mutate(
    month_of_year      = ((month - 1L) %% 12L) + 1L,
    cos_12             = cos(2 * pi * month_of_year / 12),
    sin_12             = sin(2 * pi * month_of_year / 12),
    enroll_m           = enroll_month[person],
    loyalty            = as.integer(!is.na(enroll_m) & month >= enroll_m),
    person_component   = person_baselines[person],
    drift_component    = true_trend * month,
    seasonal_component = true_amplitude * cos_12,
    true_y             = person_component + drift_component +
                         seasonal_component + true_loyalty * loyalty,
    noise              = rnorm(n(), 0, true_resid_sd),
    spending           = true_y + noise,
    person_f           = factor(person)
  )

cat(sum(!is.na(enroll_month)), "of", n_hh,
    sprintf("users enrolled (%.0f%%)\n", 100 * mean(!is.na(enroll_month))))

section: Fitting All Models and Setting a Common Y-Axis
text:
Fitting All Models and Setting a Common Y-Axis


Code
# 3-panel residual dashboard used after every model.
# trend_ok / seasonal_ok drive the green/red colour coding.
# y_lim is shared across all calls so residual shrinkage is visible.

show_diag <- function(model_obj,
                      trend_ok    = FALSE,
                      seasonal_ok = FALSE,
                      y_lim       = global_y) {

  resids  <- residuals(model_obj)
  ok_col  <- "#2d6a4f"
  bad_col <- "#cb181d"
  ci_b    <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n_months)

  make_sub <- function(ok, label_yes, label_no)
    if (ok) paste0("✓ ", label_yes) else paste0("✗ ", label_no)

  # Panel 1 — mean residuals by calendar month
  p1 <- df |> mutate(r = resids) |>
    group_by(month) |> summarise(mr = mean(r), .groups = "drop") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = month, y = mr)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.1,
              color = if (trend_ok) ok_col else bad_col) +
    { if (!trend_ok) list(
        geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linetype = "dotted",
                    color = bad_col, linewidth = 0.8))
      else list() } +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = y_lim) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1,6,12,18,24),
      labels = c("J'23","Jn'23","J'24","Jn'24","D'24")) +
    labs(title = "Residuals by calendar month",
         subtitle = make_sub(trend_ok,
           "Background drift absorbed",
           "Background drift not captured"),
         x = NULL, y = "Mean residual ($)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(
      color = if (trend_ok) ok_col else bad_col, size = 9.5))

  # Panel 2 — mean residuals by month-of-year
  p2 <- df |> mutate(r = resids) |>
    group_by(month_of_year) |> summarise(mr = mean(r), .groups = "drop") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = month_of_year, y = mr)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.1,
              color = if (seasonal_ok) ok_col else bad_col) +
    geom_point(size = 2.2,
               color = if (seasonal_ok) ok_col else bad_col) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = y_lim) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12,
      labels = c("J","F","M","A","M","J","J","A","S","O","N","D")) +
    labs(title = "Residuals by month of year",
         subtitle = make_sub(seasonal_ok,
           "Seasonal cycle absorbed",
           "Seasonal cycle not captured"),
         x = NULL, y = "Mean residual ($)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(
      color = if (seasonal_ok) ok_col else bad_col, size = 9.5))

  # Panel 3 — ACF of panel-mean residuals
  panel_mr <- df |> mutate(r = resids) |>
    group_by(month) |> summarise(mr = mean(r), .groups = "drop") |>
    pull(mr)
  acf_r  <- acf(panel_mr, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 13)
  acf_df <- tibble(lag = as.integer(acf_r$lag[-1]),
                   a   = as.numeric(acf_r$acf[-1]))
  lag12_ok  <- abs(acf_df$a[acf_df$lag == 12]) <= ci_b
  acf_col   <- if (lag12_ok) ok_col else bad_col
  acf_sub   <- if (lag12_ok) "✓ No lag-12 spike"
               else           "✗ Lag-12 spike (annual cycle)"

  p3 <- acf_df |>
    ggplot(aes(x = lag, y = a)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1,1)*ci_b, linetype="dashed", color="#2171b5") +
    geom_segment(aes(xend=lag, yend=0), color="grey60", linewidth=0.7) +
    geom_point(color="grey50", size=1.8) +
    geom_segment(data=filter(acf_df, lag==12),
                 aes(xend=lag, yend=0), color=acf_col, linewidth=1.5) +
    geom_point(data=filter(acf_df, lag==12), color=acf_col, size=3.5) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(2,4,6,8,10,12)) +
    labs(title = "ACF of panel-mean residuals",
         subtitle = acf_sub,
         x = "Lag (months)", y = "Autocorr.") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(color = acf_col, size = 9.5))

  p1 | p2 | p3
}

text:
Pre-Modeling: Understanding the Data
Before fitting anything, explore the raw data. The goal is to see the three confounding structures directly.


Code
set.seed(1)
sample_ids <- sample(seq_len(n_hh), 20)

p_spaghetti <- df |>
  filter(person %in% sample_ids) |>
  mutate(grp = factor(if_else(!is.na(enroll_m),
                               "Enrolls at some point", "Never enrolls"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = spending, group = person, color = grp)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Enrolls at some point" = "#2171b5",
                                "Never enrolls"         = "#cb181d")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1,6,12,18,24),
    labels = c("Jan\n2023","Jun\n2023","Jan\n2024","Jun\n2024","Dec\n2024")) +
  labs(title = "Individual spending trajectories\n(20 sampled users)",
       x = NULL, y = "Monthly spending ($)", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_mean <- df |>
  group_by(month) |> summarise(ms = mean(spending), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = ms)) +
  geom_line(color = "#555", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE, color="#e6550d", linetype="dashed") +
  annotate("text", x=19, y=565,
           label="Background drift\n(+$3/month)", color="#e6550d", size=3.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1,6,12,18,24),
    labels = c("Jan\n2023","Jun\n2023","Jan\n2024","Jun\n2024","Dec\n2024")) +
  labs(title = "Cohort-average spending\nover time",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean spending ($)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

seas_avg <- df |> group_by(month_of_year) |>
  summarise(ms = mean(spending), .groups = "drop")
p_seasonal <- seas_avg |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month_of_year, y = ms)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, color = "#6a51a3") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#6a51a3") +
  annotate("segment", x=12, xend=12,
           y=min(seas_avg$ms), yend=max(seas_avg$ms),
           color="#6a51a3", linetype="dotted") +
  annotate("text", x=11.4, y=max(seas_avg$ms)-4,
           label="Dec\npeak", size=3, color="#6a51a3", hjust=1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=1:12,
    labels=c("J","F","M","A","M","J","J","A","S","O","N","D")) +
  labs(title = "Spending by month of year\n(seasonal pattern)",
       x = "Month of year", y = "Mean spending ($)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_spaghetti | p_mean | p_seasonal









Visible patterns: the average spending line slopes upward (background drift), the month-of-year plot shows a clear $120 annual swing, and blue users (future enrollees) tend to start higher than red users (never-enrollees) — signalling the person-level confound.
The table below makes the person-level confound concrete. Even before enrollment, future loyalty members spend more than those who never join.

title: Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles
text:
Model 1: Naïve Pooled Regression

Step 1 — What this model assumes






WarningModel 1 Assumptions




Independence: Each of the 2,880 user-month rows is an independent draw. Spending by user 47 in March is unrelated to their spending in April.
No omitted variables: Nothing predicts both program enrollment and spending except what is already in the model.
No time trend: Expected spending is constant across all 24 months — no background drift, no seasonal pattern.
No person-level heterogeneity: All users have the same baseline spending; the only thing that differs is loyalty status.

All four are violated here. This model is a deliberate starting point — not a defensible analysis.




Step 2 — Pre-fit checks
The three diagnostic plots above already show the violations: - Average spending slopes upward → background drift exists (assumption 3 fails) - Spending cycles with a ±$60 annual amplitude → seasonal pattern exists (assumption 3 fails) - Future enrollees spend more before enrollment → person-level heterogeneity correlated with enrollment (assumption 4 and 2 fail)


Step 3 — Fitting the model


Code
m1 <- lm(spending ~ loyalty, data = df)

bind_rows(
  tidy(m1) |> filter(term == "loyalty") |>
    mutate(parameter = "Loyalty effect ($)", true_value = true_loyalty),
  tibble(term = "sigma", estimate = sigma(m1), std.error = NA_real_,
         statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_,
         parameter = "Residual SD ($)", true_value = true_resid_sd)
) |>
  mutate(bias = round(estimate - true_value, 2)) |>
  select(parameter, estimate, std.error, true_value, bias) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
    caption = "Model 1 — naïve OLS. True loyalty effect = $35.")



Model 1 — naïve OLS. True loyalty effect = $35.

Step 4 — Against the true DGP


Code
show_diag(m1, trend_ok = FALSE, seasonal_ok = FALSE)









The residual SD (\(\approx\) 102) is roughly 2.5× the true within-person noise of $40 — the model is attributing background drift, seasonal swings, and between-person differences to the residual.


Step 5 — Interpreting the results
The loyalty estimate is roughly $50–60 — far above the true $35. Three biases are compounding:

Person selection: higher-spending users enrolled, so loyal users look wealthier than they are relative to the program.
Drift absorption: enrolled users accumulate more post-enrollment months in the later, higher-drift portion of the window. The model reads the rising tide as a loyalty benefit.
Seasonal absorption: enrollment peaks in November–December, the highest-spending months. The model reads holiday spending as a loyalty benefit.

What you would wrongly conclude: “Loyalty program membership increases monthly spending by $50+.” What is actually true: the causal effect is $35.

title: Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles
text:
Model 2: Controlling for Background Drift

Step 1 — What this model assumes






WarningModel 2 Assumptions (new, on top of Model 1)




(Inherits all Model 1 assumptions except the “no time trend” one)
Linear drift: The background increase in spending is constant at exactly $k/month — it does not accelerate, decelerate, or experience any structural breaks across the 24-month window.

The seasonal cycle assumption is still violated. This model removes one confound but not both time-based confounds.




Step 2 — Pre-fit checks
The left panel from Model 1’s diagnostic above shows a clear upward slope in calendar-month residuals — a textbook symptom of unmodeled linear drift. Adding month as a predictor addresses this directly.


Step 3 — Fitting the model


Code
m2 <- lm(spending ~ loyalty + month, data = df)

bind_rows(
  tidy(m2) |> filter(term %in% c("loyalty", "month")) |>
    mutate(parameter = c("Loyalty effect ($)", "Background drift ($/month)"),
           true_value = c(true_loyalty, true_trend)),
  tibble(term = "sigma", estimate = sigma(m2), std.error = NA_real_,
         statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_,
         parameter = "Residual SD ($)", true_value = true_resid_sd)
) |>
  mutate(bias = round(estimate - true_value, 2)) |>
  select(parameter, estimate, std.error, true_value, bias) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
    caption = "Model 2 — loyalty + linear drift.")

Step 4 — Against the true DGP


Code
show_diag(m2, trend_ok = TRUE, seasonal_ok = FALSE)









The calendar-month panel is now flat — the background drift is absorbed ✓. The seasonal wave in the month-of-year panel is unchanged, and the lag-12 ACF spike remains ✗. The residual SD has shrunk from Model 1 but is still well above $40 because seasonal variance is still in the error.


Step 5 — Interpreting the results
The drift coefficient is close to the true $3/month — the model has correctly recovered that parameter. The loyalty estimate has improved but is still inflated: the seasonal confound is entirely intact. November–December enrollment still creates an artificial positive correlation between loyalty status and spending, because spending is naturally high in those months regardless of the program.
What you would wrongly conclude: “Loyalty program membership increases spending by ~$40–45 after accounting for overall platform growth.” What is actually true: the causal effect is still $35.

title: Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles
text:
Model 3: Capturing the Seasonal Cycle

Step 1 — What this model assumes






WarningModel 3 Assumptions (new, on top of Model 2)




(Inherits drift and independence assumptions from Model 2)
Annual periodicity: The seasonal cycle repeats exactly every 12 months and can be represented by a single Fourier pair.
Single harmonic: One cosine + one sine term at frequency 1/12 per month captures all meaningful periodic variation — there are no quarterly or weekly sub-cycles.

The person-level confound assumption is still violated. Higher-spending users are still more likely to enroll, but this model cannot remove that between-person bias.




Step 2 — Pre-fit checks
The middle and right panels from Model 2 are diagnostic: the seasonal wave (\(\approx \pm\$60\)) and the lag-12 ACF spike both persist after controlling for drift. This motivates the Fourier terms.






NoteWhy Two Terms (Cosine + Sine)?



Any single-frequency cycle can be written as: \[f(t) = A\cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi m_t}{12}\right) + B\sin\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi m_t}{12}\right) = R\cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi m_t}{12} - \phi\right)\] where \(R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2}\) is the amplitude and \(\phi = \arctan(B/A)\) is the phase (peak month). Including both terms lets OLS determine amplitude and peak month from the data without you specifying either. In our DGP the true cycle is pure cosine (\(B = 0\), December peak), so the sine coefficient should estimate near zero.




Step 3 — Fitting the model


Code
m3 <- lm(spending ~ loyalty + month + cos_12 + sin_12, data = df)

bind_rows(
  tidy(m3) |> filter(term %in% c("loyalty","month","cos_12","sin_12")) |>
    mutate(parameter  = c("Loyalty effect ($)", "Background drift ($/month)",
                          "Seasonal cosine ($)", "Seasonal sine ($)"),
           true_value = c(true_loyalty, true_trend, true_amplitude, 0)),
  tibble(term = "sigma", estimate = sigma(m3), std.error = NA_real_,
         statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_,
         parameter = "Residual SD ($)", true_value = true_resid_sd)
) |>
  mutate(bias = round(estimate - true_value, 2)) |>
  select(parameter, estimate, std.error, true_value, bias) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
    caption = "Model 3 — loyalty + drift + Fourier seasonal.")

Both time panels are flat and the lag-12 ACF spike is gone ✓. The residual SD has dropped to near the true $40 — most of the explainable variance is now captured. The loyalty estimate is much closer to $35, but still slightly high.


Step 5 — Interpreting the results
The seasonal cosine coefficient is near the true $60, and the sine is near zero — exactly as the DGP specifies. Both time-based confounds are now resolved.
The remaining upward bias in the loyalty estimate reflects the person-level confound: Model 3 is still comparing higher-spending enrollees to lower-spending non-enrollees. OLS uses the between-person contrast because it has no person controls. The residual SD being close to $40 confirms the time structure is well-captured; the remaining issue is cross-sectional, not temporal.
What you would wrongly conclude: “Loyalty program membership increases spending by ~$38–42 after accounting for platform growth and seasonality.” Closer to the truth, but still inflated by ~$5 from person selection.

title: Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles
section: Model 4: The Full Specification — Person Random Effects
text:
Model 4: The Full Specification — Person Random Effects

Step 1 — What this model assumes






WarningModel 4 Assumptions (new, on top of Model 3)




(Inherits drift, Fourier, and independence assumptions from Model 3)
Normal person random effects: Each user’s stable baseline spending \(\alpha_i\) is drawn from \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_u^2)\).
Independence of person effects and predictors: After conditioning on the drift, seasonal terms, and loyalty status, a user’s random intercept is uncorrelated with the loyalty predictor. This is the exchangeability assumption — the program was not assigned based on unmeasured time-varying characteristics.
Within-person residual independence: After removing person effects, the month-to-month residuals within a person are exchangeable — no remaining autocorrelation.

This is the first model that is correctly specified for our DGP. All four assumptions hold by construction because we simulated the data.




Step 2 — Pre-fit checks
The person-level selection check shown in the pre-modeling section confirmed: future enrollees spent more before enrolling. Model 3’s loyalty estimate is still inflated (see above), even though time is correctly specified. The culprit is between-person confounding — exactly what person random effects address.
The test: does the loyalty coefficient change when person random effects are added? If yes, the between-person contrast was driving part of the Model 3 estimate.


Step 3 — Fitting the model


Code
m4 <- lmer(spending ~ loyalty + month + cos_12 + sin_12 + (1 | person_f),
           data = df)

person_sd_est <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m4)) |>
  filter(grp == "person_f") |> pull(sdcor)

bind_rows(
  tidy(m4, effects = "fixed") |>
    filter(term %in% c("loyalty","month","cos_12","sin_12")) |>
    mutate(parameter  = c("Loyalty effect ($)", "Background drift ($/month)",
                          "Seasonal cosine ($)", "Seasonal sine ($)"),
           true_value = c(true_loyalty, true_trend, true_amplitude, 0)),
  tibble(term = "sigma_person", estimate = person_sd_est,
         std.error = NA_real_, statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_,
         parameter = "Person SD ($)", true_value = true_person_sd),
  tibble(term = "sigma_resid", estimate = sigma(m4),
         std.error = NA_real_, statistic = NA_real_, p.value = NA_real_,
         parameter = "Residual SD ($)", true_value = true_resid_sd)
) |>
  mutate(bias = round(estimate - true_value, 2)) |>
  select(parameter, estimate, std.error, true_value, bias) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
    caption = "Model 4 — full specification: loyalty + drift + Fourier + person RE.")

All three time-based panels pass ✓. The loyalty estimate, all time-structure parameters, person SD, and residual SD are all near their true values. As a final check, plot person-mean residuals against person mean spending — the random intercept should have absorbed all baseline differences.


Code
df |>
  mutate(resid = residuals(m4)) |>
  group_by(person) |>
  summarise(mr = mean(resid), ms = mean(spending), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ms, y = mr)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#2171b5", size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#2171b5", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Person-mean residuals\nvs. person mean spending",
       subtitle = "✓ No pattern — person RE absorbed all baseline differences",
       x = "Person mean spending ($)", y = "Mean residual ($)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#2d6a4f"))











Step 5 — Interpreting the results
Every DGP parameter is now accurately recovered. The key shift from Model 3 to Model 4:

Loyalty estimate: drops from ~$38–42 to ~$35, removing the person-selection upward bias
Person SD: correctly estimates ~$80 — confirming that the model partitioned between-person variance appropriately
Residual SD: near $40 — only genuine within-person noise remains unexplained

The loyalty coefficient now answers: among the same user, does spending rise in months when they are enrolled compared to months when they are not, after accounting for background drift and seasonality? This is a within-person causal comparison, not a cross-sectional average.
Correct conclusion: “Controlling for user-level spending habits, background platform drift, and seasonal cycles, loyalty program membership is associated with ~$35 higher monthly spending.”

title: Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles
text:
Model 5: Period Fixed Effects (Month Dummies)

Step 1 — What this model assumes






WarningModel 5 Assumptions




Each calendar month has its own intercept, absorbing all calendar-period effects — no parametric shape assumed for the time function.
Each person has their own intercept (person dummies), absorbing all stable between-person differences.
Loyalty effect is homogeneous: The program effect is the same for all users in all months. No user-specific or time-varying treatment effect.
Strict exogeneity: After removing person and month fixed effects, loyalty status is uncorrelated with the residual.

Model 5 is more robust to misspecification of the time structure than Model 4 (no assumption of linearity or periodicity), but less efficient (23 extra parameters for month dummies vs. 3).




Step 2 — Pre-fit checks
Model 4 already passes all residual diagnostics — this model serves as a robustness check, not a correction. The question is whether relaxing the parametric time assumption changes the loyalty estimate materially.


Step 3 — Fitting the model


Code
m5 <- lm(spending ~ loyalty + factor(month) + factor(person_f), data = df)

tidy(m5) |>
  filter(term == "loyalty") |>
  mutate(parameter  = "Loyalty effect ($)",
         true_value = true_loyalty,
         bias       = round(estimate - true_loyalty, 2),
         sigma      = round(sigma(m5), 2)) |>
  select(parameter, estimate, std.error, true_value, bias, sigma) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
    caption = "Model 5 — two-way FE: loyalty + month dummies + person dummies.")

Step 4 — Against the true DGP
The loyalty estimate is close to $35, matching Model 4. The residual SD is similar. No residual diagnostic is plotted because the month-dummy FE makes the diagnostic structure trivial — the calendar-month residuals are exactly zero by construction.


Step 5 — Interpreting the results
Model 5 confirms Model 4 non-parametrically. The loyalty effect is ~$35 regardless of whether we model the time function as “linear drift + one Fourier pair” or as “unrestricted month intercepts.” This robustness is reassuring: the parametric time assumption in Model 4 is not driving the result.
When to prefer Model 5 over Model 4:







Situation
Prefer

title: Time Structure, Fixed Effects, and Seasonal Cycles
text:
Practical Guide: Diagnostic Sequence
When you encounter a new longitudinal dataset, run these five checks in order:



Five-step diagnostic sequence for longitudinal time structure.








Step
Plot or check
What you are looking for
Remedy




1
Mean outcome by calendar month
Upward or downward slope → background drift present
Add calendar month as a linear predictor


2
Mean outcome by month-of-year
Repeated wave → seasonal cycle present
Add Fourier sin/cos or season-of-year dummies


3
Mean residuals by calendar month
Still drifts after controls → drift not fully captured
Add polynomial trend or period dummies


4
Mean residuals by month-of-year
Still waves after controls → seasonality not captured
Add Fourier terms or seasonal dummies


5
ACF of panel-mean residuals
Spike at lag k → k-period autocorrelation remaining
Model residual autocorrelation (Part 5: AR structures)











WarningReviewer Challenge



What a skeptical reviewer would say: “You control for a linear background drift, but what if the drift is nonlinear — accelerating in the second year or interrupted by a market shock in month 14? Your loyalty estimate could absorb a nonlinear surge that happened to coincide with program rollout.”
Observable warning sign: After adding a linear drift term, residuals vs. calendar month show a curve rather than a flat line.
What claim survives: Direction is likely correct. Magnitude depends on how closely the parametric time model matches the true DGP. Model 5 (period FE) is the robustness check — if it agrees with Model 4, the parametric assumption is not driving the finding.

section: Setting the Stage for Growth Curve Models
text:
Setting the Stage for Growth Curve Models
This section treated time as a confounder to be controlled. The next section, Growth Curve Models, treats time as the phenomenon: how does each person’s trajectory unfold, and why do trajectories differ across people?
The same five-step inferential workflow — assumptions, pre-fit checks, fitting, DGP comparison, interpretation — applies to every model in the rest of the module. The diagnostic toolkit (residual-by-time, seasonal check, ACF) remains the standard first pass before interpreting any parameter estimate.

title: Growth Curve Models
text: Growth Curve Models

title: Growth Curve Models
text:
Trajectories as the Target
Standard repeated measures models ask: “Is the mean outcome different across time points?” Growth curve models ask something richer: “How does each unit’s trajectory unfold over time, and what explains variation in those trajectories?”
The shift in framing is fundamental. We are not trying to estimate one average change — we are trying to recover the distribution of individual change processes that generated the data. Each person has their own DGP; growth curve models estimate the parameters of that distribution.

title: Growth Curve Models
text:
The Unconditional Growth Model
Start with no predictors. Just time and people.


Code
n_people <- 60
n_times  <- 6  # weeks

# Each person has a random baseline (intercept) and random rate of change (slope)
person_intercepts <- rnorm(n_people, 50, 8)
person_slopes     <- rnorm(n_people, -2, 1.5)  # average decline of 2/week

df_growth <- expand_grid(person = 1:n_people, week = 0:(n_times-1)) |>
  mutate(
    stress = person_intercepts[person] +
             person_slopes[person] * week +
             rnorm(n(), 0, 4),
    person = factor(person)
  )

# Plot individual trajectories
sample_people <- sample(levels(df_growth$person), 12)

ggplot(df_growth |> filter(person %in% sample_people),
       aes(x = week, y = stress, group = person, color = person)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) + geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(data = df_growth, aes(group = NULL, color = NULL),
              method = "lm", color = "black", linewidth = 1.5, se = TRUE) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Growth curve: individual stress trajectories over 6 weeks",
       subtitle = "Colored lines = 12 individuals; black line = average trajectory",
       x = "Week", y = "Stress (0-100)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

m_growth <- lmer(stress ~ week + (week | person), data = df_growth)
summary(m_growth)

title: Growth Curve Models
text:
Nonlinear Growth
Some processes do not change linearly. Symptoms might improve rapidly at first, then plateau. Performance curves often show diminishing returns. The growth curve framework accommodates nonlinearity.


Code
# Quadratic growth
df_growth_q <- expand_grid(person = 1:n_people, week = 0:8) |>
  mutate(
    person_int    = rep(rnorm(n_people, 50, 8), each = 9),
    person_lin    = rep(rnorm(n_people, -5, 2), each = 9),
    person_quad   = rep(rnorm(n_people, 0.5, 0.3), each = 9),
    stress        = person_int + person_lin * week + person_quad * week^2 + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),
    person        = factor(person)
  )

# Fit with quadratic time
m_quad <- lmer(stress ~ week + I(week^2) + (week | person), data = df_growth_q)

# Plot average predicted trajectory
df_growth_q <- df_growth_q |>
  mutate(fitted_stress = fitted(m_quad))

df_growth_q |>
  group_by(week) |>
  summarise(mean_obs = mean(stress), mean_fit = mean(fitted_stress)) |>
  pivot_longer(-week) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = value, color = name, linetype = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#aec6e8", "#1e3a5f"),
                     labels = c("Fitted (quadratic)", "Observed")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed"),
                        labels = c("Fitted (quadratic)", "Observed")) +
  labs(title = "Quadratic growth: curve captures the deceleration",
       x = "Week", y = "Mean Stress", color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)















WarningAssumption: The Growth Function is Correctly Specified



What it means: Linear growth assumes constant rate of change. Quadratic growth assumes a parabolic trajectory. If the true trajectory is neither — e.g., a logarithmic curve or piecewise linear — your model will be misspecified.
How to check: Plot the observed means by time point. Does the pattern look linear? Is there a clear deceleration or acceleration that requires a curve? Use AIC to compare linear vs. quadratic models.








WarningAssumption: Random Slope for Time is Correctly Specified



What it means: Allowing only a random intercept (but not slope) for time assumes everyone changes at exactly the same rate. This is almost always wrong for developmental or therapeutic outcomes.
How to check: Compare the random-intercept-only model to the random-slope model using a likelihood ratio test. Plot individual trajectories — if they clearly fan out or diverge, a random slope is needed.

title: Latent Growth Curve Models (SEM)
text: Latent Growth Curve Models

title: Latent Growth Curve Models (SEM)
section: Two Languages for the Same Model
text:
Two Languages for the Same Model
The growth curve model from Part 3 and the Latent Growth Curve Model (LGC) from structural equation modeling are mathematically equivalent. They answer the same questions using different parameterizations and different software.
Understanding both languages is valuable because: 1. Many psychology researchers encounter LGC models in SEM training (Mplus, lavaan) before they encounter MLM-based growth models 2. The SEM framing makes certain things explicit that are implicit in MLM — particularly the role of measurement error and the ability to model multiple growth processes simultaneously 3. Reviewing both frames deepens understanding of what the model is actually doing

title: Latent Growth Curve Models (SEM)
text:
The SEM Framing
In the latent growth curve model, the trajectory is represented by two latent variables: - Intercept factor (η_i): The latent initial level for each person - Slope factor (η_s): The latent rate of change for each person
Observed scores at each time point are modeled as: \[Y_{ti} = 1 \cdot \eta_i + \lambda_t \cdot \eta_s + \varepsilon_{ti}\]
where \(\lambda_t\) are factor loadings that encode the time metric (e.g., \(\lambda_1 = 0, \lambda_2 = 1, \lambda_3 = 2\) for linear growth), and \(\varepsilon_{ti}\) are measurement residuals.
The intercept factor has loadings of 1.0 at all time points. The slope factor has loadings equal to the time coding.

title: Latent Growth Curve Models (SEM)
section: Fitting an LGC Model in lavaan
text:
Fitting an LGC Model in lavaan

JDM Context: Savings Growth After Loyalty Program Enrollment
A financial services firm tracks 150 customers’ monthly net savings for 5 months after they enroll in a loyalty-and-coaching program. The key substantive questions:

On average, how much do customers save at enrollment, and how fast does savings grow?
How much do they vary? Do some customers start high and stay high? Do some start low but grow quickly?
Do initial level and growth rate covary? Customers who start with high savings might grow more slowly (ceiling effects) or more quickly (financially engaged customers who compound good habits).

These are precisely the questions the latent growth curve model answers. The intercept factor captures each customer’s baseline savings level; the slope factor captures their personal savings growth trajectory.


Code
# 150 loyalty program customers tracked for 5 months
# Outcome: monthly net savings (€)
n <- 150
intercepts <- rnorm(n, 500, 80)   # wide between-customer variation in baseline savings
slopes     <- rnorm(n,  15, 12)   # some customers grow savings fast; others plateau

Y <- sapply(0:4, function(t) intercepts + slopes * t + rnorm(n, 0, 35))
colnames(Y) <- paste0("savings_m", 1:5)   # monthly savings at months 1–5
df_lgc <- as.data.frame(Y)




Visualizing What the Latent Factors Mean
Before fitting the model, it helps to see what the intercept and slope factors represent in individual trajectories.


Code
# Draw 12 representative individual trajectories
df_vis <- tibble(
  id        = 1:12,
  intercept = c(intercepts[1:12]),
  slope     = c(slopes[1:12])
) |>
  expand_grid(time = 0:4) |>
  mutate(savings = intercept + slope * time + rnorm(n(), 0, 25),
         id = factor(id))

grand_intercept <- mean(intercepts)
grand_slope     <- mean(slopes)

ggplot(df_vis, aes(x = time, y = savings)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = id), alpha = 0.35, color = "#4393c3") +
  geom_point(aes(group = id), alpha = 0.35, color = "#4393c3", size = 1.5) +
  # Mean growth line
  geom_abline(intercept = grand_intercept, slope = grand_slope,
              color = "#d73027", linewidth = 1.5) +
  # Label: intercept at time = 0
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = grand_intercept, color = "#d73027", size = 4) +
  annotate("text",  x = 0.15, y = grand_intercept - 30,
           label = paste0("Mean intercept: \u20ac", round(grand_intercept), "/month at enrollment"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3.5, color = "#d73027") +
  # Label: slope (one-month increment on mean line)
  annotate("segment", x = 3, xend = 4,
           y = grand_intercept + 3 * grand_slope,
           yend = grand_intercept + 4 * grand_slope,
           color = "#d73027", linewidth = 1.2,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), ends = "last")) +
  annotate("text",  x = 4.05, y = grand_intercept + 3.5 * grand_slope,
           label = paste0("Mean slope:\n+\u20ac", round(grand_slope), "/month"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3.5, color = "#d73027") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:4,
                     labels = paste0("Month ", 1:5)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Latent growth curve model: loyalty program savings trajectories",
    subtitle = "Blue = individual customer trajectories; Red = average growth line\nIntercept = baseline savings; Slope = monthly growth rate",
    x = NULL, y = "Monthly net savings (\u20ac)"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 4.8)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









Each blue line is one customer. The intercept (red dot at month 1) is their individual starting level; the slope is how steeply their line rises. The model estimates both factors’ means, variances, and covariance.


Code
# Latent growth curve model in lavaan
lgc_model <- '
  # Intercept factor (loadings all fixed to 1)
  intercept =~ 1*savings_m1 + 1*savings_m2 + 1*savings_m3 + 1*savings_m4 + 1*savings_m5

  # Slope factor (loadings = time coding: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4)
  slope     =~ 0*savings_m1 + 1*savings_m2 + 2*savings_m3 + 3*savings_m4 + 4*savings_m5

  # Means of latent factors (the fixed effects)
  intercept ~ 1
  slope     ~ 1

  # Variances of latent factors (random effects variance)
  intercept ~~ intercept
  slope     ~~ slope

  # Covariance between intercept and slope
  intercept ~~ slope

  # Residual variances (constrained equal across time for simplicity)
  savings_m1 ~~ a*savings_m1
  savings_m2 ~~ a*savings_m2
  savings_m3 ~~ a*savings_m3
  savings_m4 ~~ a*savings_m4
  savings_m5 ~~ a*savings_m5
'

m_lgc <- growth(lgc_model, data = df_lgc)
summary(m_lgc, fit.measures = TRUE)

text:
The Equivalence with MLM


Code
# Fit equivalent MLM
df_long_lgc <- df_lgc |>
  mutate(id = 1:n) |>
  pivot_longer(-id, names_to = "wave", values_to = "savings") |>
  mutate(time = as.integer(str_extract(wave, "[0-9]")) - 1,
         id   = factor(id))

m_mlm <- lmer(savings ~ time + (time | id), data = df_long_lgc)

# Compare estimates
tibble(
  Parameter        = c("Mean intercept (baseline savings)", "Mean slope (monthly growth)",
                       "Var(intercept)", "Var(slope)"),
  `MLM estimate`   = c(fixef(m_mlm),
                        as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_mlm))$vcov[1:2]),
  `LGC estimate`   = c(
    lavInspect(m_lgc, "mean.lv")[c("intercept", "slope")],
    diag(lavInspect(m_lgc, "cov.lv"))[c("intercept", "slope")]
  )

title: Latent Growth Curve Models (SEM)
section: When the SEM Framing Adds Value
text:
When the SEM Framing Adds Value






NoteAdvantage 1: Modeling Measurement Error



In the SEM framework, each observed score \(Y_{ti}\) has a residual \(\varepsilon_{ti}\) that can be interpreted as measurement error — the gap between the true latent trajectory and the imperfect observed score. This is explicit in the LGC model.
In standard MLM, the residual is treated as a mix of measurement error and genuine within-person fluctuation. If your outcome is a measured construct (scale scores, ratings, test scores), the SEM framing forces you to be explicit about measurement.








NoteAdvantage 2: Multiple Growth Processes



With SEM, you can model two interrelated growth curves simultaneously. A natural JDM application: how app engagement and monthly savings co-evolve over the first 5 months of a loyalty program. The covariance between the two intercept factors tells you whether customers who were already engaging heavily at enrollment also started with higher savings. The covariance between the two slope factors tells you whether customers whose engagement grew faster also showed steeper savings growth — that is, whether engagement and savings amplify each other over time.
This is difficult to do cleanly in standard MLM, which would require a multivariate response formulation or a separate bivariate outcome model.

title: Latent Growth Curve Models (SEM)
text:
Assumptions of LGC Models






WarningAssumption: Correctly Specified Factor Loadings



What it means: The factor loadings for the slope factor encode the time metric. Linear loadings (0, 1, 2, 3…) assume linear growth. If growth is nonlinear, you can free some loadings to be estimated from the data — but the intercept must still be defined by fixing at least two loadings.
How to check: Test alternative loading patterns (free vs. fixed) and compare model fit using CFI, RMSEA, and SRMR.








WarningAssumption: Multivariate Normality



What it means: SEM estimation (default ML) assumes the observed variables are multivariate normal. Severely skewed outcomes or floor/ceiling effects can bias estimates.
How to check: Check univariate skewness and kurtosis. Use robust ML estimators (MLR in lavaan) if normality is questionable.

title: Autoregressive Structures
text: Autoregressive Structures

title: Autoregressive Structures
text:
The Memory of Time
Some outcomes carry their history. Today’s daily spending predicts tomorrow’s. This week’s savings rate predicts next week’s. A consumer’s current risk perception reflects last week’s perception, adjusted for new information. This temporal dependence — the “memory” of the process — is not just a nuisance. It is a feature of the DGP that your model must account for.
When you ignore serial dependence and treat residuals as independent:

Your standard errors are biased — usually too small if residuals are positively correlated
You are misrepresenting the process — claiming the outcome at each time point arises fresh, unconnected from what came before
You cannot distinguish persistence (genuine temporal carry-over) from trend (a steady directional shift)

title: Autoregressive Structures
text:
What AR(1) Means
In an autoregressive order-1 (AR(1)) process, each observation is a linear function of the immediately preceding observation plus random noise:
\[Y_t = \phi \cdot Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon)\]
The parameter \(\phi\) is the autoregressive coefficient — how strongly the past predicts the present. When \(\phi = 0\), observations are independent. When \(\phi = 0.8\), yesterday’s financial state strongly predicts today’s.
JDM examples where AR(1) is plausible:

Daily risk perception: a spike in risk perception triggered by a market event slowly decays back toward a person’s baseline over subsequent days
Weekly savings rate: savings behavior in one week partially inertially carries forward to the next
Daily spending: expenditure patterns show week-to-week habit inertia
Price sensitivity across promotional cycles: a consumer’s sensitivity in one promotional period partially predicts their sensitivity in the next



Code
# Simulate AR(1) process for one person: 30 days of daily risk perception
phi   <- 0.75
sigma <- 3
n_t   <- 30

Y <- numeric(n_t)
Y[1] <- rnorm(1, 50, 5)
for (t in 2:n_t) Y[t] <- phi * Y[t-1] + rnorm(1, 0, sigma)

p1 <- tibble(day = 1:n_t, risk_perception = Y) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = day, y = risk_perception)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title    = paste0("Daily risk perception: AR(1) with φ = ", phi),
    subtitle = "Each day's value depends on the previous — shows smooth persistence",
    x = "Day", y = "Risk perception"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

acf_vals <- acf(Y, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 10)
p2 <- tibble(lag = 0:10, acf = acf_vals$acf[,1,1]) |>
  filter(lag > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(n_t),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#e63946") +
  labs(
    title    = "Autocorrelation function (ACF)",
    subtitle = "Geometric decay is the signature of AR(1)",
    x = "Lag (days)", y = "ACF"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p1 + p2









The geometric decay in the ACF — strong at lag 1, weaker at lag 2, gradually dying out — is the signature pattern of an AR(1) process.

title: Autoregressive Structures
section: Trend Versus Persistence: A Critical Distinction
text:
Trend Versus Persistence: A Critical Distinction
AR(1) is about persistence — today’s deviation from the trend carries into tomorrow. This is fundamentally different from a trend — a systematic directional movement over time. Confusing the two leads to a common misspecification:


Code
t_vals <- 1:30
# Trend: mean drifts upward, residuals are independent
y_trend <- 40 + 0.8 * t_vals + rnorm(30, 0, 3)

# Persistence: stationary mean, AR(1) residuals
phi_p <- 0.8
y_pers <- numeric(30)
y_pers[1] <- 50
for (t in 2:30) y_pers[t] <- 50 * (1 - phi_p) + phi_p * y_pers[t-1] + rnorm(1, 0, 3)

p_trend <- tibble(day = t_vals, y = y_trend) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = day, y = y)) +
  geom_line(color = "#e67e22", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#c0392b", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title    = "Trend (not AR)",
    subtitle = "Mean drifts. Residuals are independent.",
    x = "Day", y = "Outcome"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_pers <- tibble(day = t_vals, y = y_pers) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = day, y = y)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed", color = "#888") +
  labs(
    title    = "Persistence (AR(1))",
    subtitle = "Stationary mean. Residuals carry memory.",
    x = "Day", y = "Outcome"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

p_trend + p_pers









A trend series looks like it has AR(1) structure — it autocorrelates — but the correct model includes time as a fixed effect, after which the residuals may be independent. AR(1) applies to the residuals around the trend, not to the raw series.
JDM diagnostic question: Is the serial correlation in your outcome driven by a steady directional shift (trend), or by short-term inertia around a stable mean (persistence)? The answer determines whether you need a trend term in your fixed effects, an AR(1) residual structure, or both.

title: Autoregressive Structures
text:
Assumptions






WarningAssumption: Stationarity



Plain-language meaning: The mean and variance of the process are constant over time, and the autocorrelation depends only on the lag size — not on where you are in the study timeline. An AR(1) with \(|\phi| < 1\) is stationary by construction.
What the model is assuming away: Any systematic drift in the mean (trend) or variance (heteroskedasticity over time). If consumers’ risk perception is trending upward across a study because financial anxiety is increasing nationwide, the process is non-stationary.
JDM example: If daily risk perception increases during a financial crisis period within the study window, the mean is trending. AR(1) applied naively will have non-stationary residuals.
Experimental analog: In a daily diary experiment running across 8 weeks, if the pre-post intervention change creates a structural break in the mean, the AR(1) process applies separately within the pre- and post-intervention periods.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “You applied AR(1) to a 12-week panel of financial diary data — but the data spans both the pre-policy and post-policy period. Did you account for the structural break in the mean at the policy change date?”
Observable warning sign: Wave-by-wave mean plots that show a systematic trend; ACF of raw residuals that does not decay to zero (persistent autocorrelation at long lags).
What to check: Include time as a fixed effect first. Examine whether residual ACF shows geometric decay (AR(1)) or long-run persistence (non-stationary). Use unit root tests if trend is suspected.
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The sign and rough magnitude of the treatment effect are usually robust. The AR coefficient estimate and its confidence interval may be biased.








WarningAssumption: Lag-1 Dependence Only



Plain-language meaning: AR(1) assumes that \(Y_{t-2}\) predicts \(Y_t\) only through \(Y_{t-1}\) — once you know yesterday’s value, knowing the day before yesterday adds nothing.
What the model is assuming away: Longer-range memory. A consumer’s spending behavior this week may depend on both last week and two weeks ago — a second-order AR process.
JDM example: Promotional spending behavior may have a two-week purchase cycle: today’s spending is influenced by purchases from both last week (direct) and two weeks ago (restock timing), requiring AR(2).
What to check: Examine the partial autocorrelation function (PACF). If significant spikes appear at lag 2 or beyond after fitting AR(1), the model needs a higher order.


Code
pacf_vals <- pacf(Y, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 10)
tibble(lag = 1:10, pacf = pacf_vals$acf[,1,1]) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lag, y = pacf)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1e3a5f", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(n_t),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#e63946") +
  labs(
    title    = "Partial ACF: only lag-1 significant = AR(1) is sufficient",
    subtitle = "Spikes at lag 2+ would indicate AR(2) or higher order",
    x = "Lag", y = "Partial ACF"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

title: Autoregressive Structures
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “Your AR(1) coefficient is \(\hat{\phi} = 0.72\). Does that mean consumers’ financial decisions are mostly determined by their previous decision rather than your manipulation?” A high AR(1) coefficient means the baseline level of the process is persistent — which is expected for daily financial behavior. The treatment effect is estimated on top of this persistence, as a departure from the AR trajectory. The AR coefficient describes the DGP’s background noise structure, not the causal mechanism.
Challenge 2: “How do you distinguish AR(1) persistence from an unmodeled time trend that creates the appearance of autocorrelation?” By including time as a fixed effect first. AR(1) persistence appears in residuals after removing trends. If the apparent AR disappears once time is included as a covariate, the “persistence” was actually a trend. Inspect the partial ACF after including time in the model — if lag-1 PACF is no longer significant, the trend was the source of apparent autocorrelation.
Challenge 3: “You estimated AR(1) for a daily 20-day series per person. With only 20 observations per person, how stable is the per-person autocorrelation estimate?” Individual-level AR estimates are indeed noisy with short series. The nlme approach pools information across persons (assuming common AR structure), which is more stable than person-specific estimates. This is an advantage of the multilevel AR approach over fitting AR models separately per person.

title: Cross-Lagged Panel Models
text: Cross-Lagged Panel Models

title: Cross-Lagged Panel Models
text:
Two Variables, Evolving Together
Suppose you want to understand the relationship between financial stress and risky borrowing behavior over time. Does financial stress push people toward riskier borrowing? Or does risky borrowing create financial strain? Or do they mutually reinforce each other?
To answer this, you need data on both variables at multiple time points, and you need a model that can disentangle the temporal ordering of their relationship. The cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) is the standard tool for this question.

title: Cross-Lagged Panel Models
text:
The Classic CLPM
In a two-wave, two-variable CLPM with variables S (financial stress) and B (risky borrowing):
\[S_{t+1} = a_{SS} \cdot S_t + a_{SB} \cdot B_t + \varepsilon_{S,t+1}\] \[B_{t+1} = a_{BB} \cdot B_t + a_{BS} \cdot S_t + \varepsilon_{B,t+1}\]
Four parameters: - \(a_{SS}\), \(a_{BB}\): autoregressive effects — stability of each variable over time - \(a_{SB}\): cross-lagged effect of B at time \(t\) on S at time \(t+1\) - \(a_{BS}\): cross-lagged effect of S at time \(t\) on B at time \(t+1\)


Code
# Simulate 3-wave panel data
n <- 200
n_waves <- 3

# True DGP: financial stress -> risky borrowing (not the reverse)
S <- matrix(NA, n, n_waves)
B <- matrix(NA, n, n_waves)

S[, 1] <- rnorm(n, 50, 8)   # baseline financial stress
B[, 1] <- rnorm(n, 45, 7)   # baseline borrowing propensity

for (t in 2:n_waves) {
  S[, t] <- 0.6 * S[, t-1] + 0.1 * B[, t-1] + rnorm(n, 0, 5)  # small B->S effect
  B[, t] <- 0.6 * B[, t-1] + 0.3 * S[, t-1] + rnorm(n, 0, 5)  # strong S->B effect
}

df_clpm <- as.data.frame(cbind(S, B)) |>
  setNames(c(paste0("S", 1:3), paste0("B", 1:3)))




Code
# Classic CLPM in lavaan
clpm_model <- '
  # Autoregressive effects
  S2 ~ a_SS * S1
  S3 ~ a_SS * S2
  B2 ~ a_BB * B1
  B3 ~ a_BB * B2

  # Cross-lagged effects
  S2 ~ a_SB * B1
  S3 ~ a_SB * B2
  B2 ~ a_BS * S1
  B3 ~ a_BS * S2

  # Residual covariances (within same wave)
  S2 ~~ B2
  S3 ~~ B3

  # Variance of wave 1
  S1 ~~ S1
  B1 ~~ B1
  S1 ~~ B1
'

m_clpm <- sem(clpm_model, data = df_clpm)
parameterEstimates(m_clpm) |>
  filter(op == "~") |>
  select(lhs, rhs, label, est, se, pvalue) |>

    caption = "CLPM: cross-lagged path from S→B is strong; B→S is weak")

title: Cross-Lagged Panel Models
text:
The Problem with Classic CLPM
The classic CLPM conflates within-person dynamics with between-person differences. Consider: people who are chronically financially stressed tend to also engage in chronically riskier borrowing (stable between-person correlation). The cross-lagged paths in the classic CLPM pick up both this stable between-person covariation and the genuine within-person dynamic — they cannot be separated.
This means even if there is no within-person causal relationship between financial stress and risky borrowing (i.e., changes in financial stress within a person do not cause changes in borrowing behavior), the classic CLPM can show significant “cross-lagged” effects simply because chronically stressed people also tend to borrow more riskily.

The Same Observed Pattern, Three Different Stories
The same observed correlations between financial stress and risky borrowing across waves are consistent with three completely different causal stories. The classic CLPM cannot distinguish them without extending the model.









All three stories produce the same bivariate correlation pattern between \(S_t\) and \(B_{t+1}\), and between \(B_t\) and \(S_{t+1}\). The classic CLPM cannot distinguish them because it does not separate stable between-person covariation (Story C) from genuine within-person dynamics (Stories A and B). The RI-CLPM separates these sources explicitly, making it the correct model for the within-person question.

title: Cross-Lagged Panel Models
text:
The Random Intercept CLPM (RI-CLPM)
Hamaker, Kuiper, & Grasman (2015) proposed the Random Intercept CLPM, which solves this by separating two sources of variation:

Between-person: Stable trait levels (random intercepts) that explain why some people are chronically higher on S or B
Within-person: Fluctuations around each person’s stable level, and the cross-lagged dynamics among those fluctuations



Code
ri_clpm_model <- '
  # Random intercepts (stable between-person levels)
  RI_S =~ 1*S1 + 1*S2 + 1*S3
  RI_B =~ 1*B1 + 1*B2 + 1*B3

  # Within-person components (deviations from stable level)
  wS1 =~ 1*S1; wS2 =~ 1*S2; wS3 =~ 1*S3
  wB1 =~ 1*B1; wB2 =~ 1*B2; wB3 =~ 1*B3

  # Constrain observed variances to 0 (all captured by RI + within)
  S1 ~~ 0*S1; S2 ~~ 0*S2; S3 ~~ 0*S3
  B1 ~~ 0*B1; B2 ~~ 0*B2; B3 ~~ 0*B3

  # Within-person cross-lagged dynamics
  wS2 ~ a_SS*wS1 + a_SB*wB1
  wS3 ~ a_SS*wS2 + a_SB*wB2
  wB2 ~ a_BB*wB1 + a_BS*wS1
  wB3 ~ a_BB*wB2 + a_BS*wS2

  # Random intercept variances and covariance
  RI_S ~~ RI_S; RI_B ~~ RI_B; RI_S ~~ RI_B

  # Within-person residual variances
  wS1 ~~ wS1; wB1 ~~ wB1
  wS2 ~~ wS2; wB2 ~~ wB2
  wS3 ~~ wS3; wB3 ~~ wB3
  wS2 ~~ wB2; wS3 ~~ wB3

  # Mean structure
  RI_S ~ 1; RI_B ~ 1
  wS1 ~ 0; wB1 ~ 0
'

m_ri_clpm <- sem(ri_clpm_model, data = df_clpm, estimator = "ML")

parameterEstimates(m_ri_clpm) |>
  filter(op == "~", lhs %in% c("wS2","wS3","wB2","wB3")) |>
  select(lhs, rhs, label, est, se, pvalue) |>

What it means: The CLPM (and RI-CLPM) typically constrains cross-lagged effects to be equal across waves. This assumes the dynamics do not change over the study period.
How to check: Fit an unconstrained model (different path coefficients at each wave) and compare fit to the constrained model.








WarningAssumption: No Omitted Dynamics



What it means: Both models assume all relevant variables are included. An omitted third variable that drives both S and B could produce spurious cross-lagged effects.
How to check: Think carefully about what else changes over time that could explain both variables. Include plausible third variables as additional nodes.

title: Binary and Count Outcomes Over Time
text: Binary and Count Outcomes Over Time
crumbs: 33  Binary and Count Outcomes Over Time

title: Binary and Count Outcomes Over Time
section: When the DGP Does Not Generate Continuous Data
text:
When the DGP Does Not Generate Continuous Data
Every model we have used in this module so far assumes something about your outcome: that the true data-generating process (DGP) produces values that, after accounting for predictors and random effects, are normally distributed. That assumption is perfectly reasonable for outcomes like stress scores, reaction times, or cognitive performance — values that can in principle be any real number.
But many longitudinal outcomes in consumer behavior and financial research are not continuous. They are binary — did the customer make a purchase this week? Did they make a late payment this month? Did they adopt the recommended savings allocation? Or they are counts — how many times did a customer open the app this week? How many transactions did they make? How many overdraft events occurred this month?
When the DGP generates binary or count data, a linear mixed model imposes a structure that does not match the outcome’s constraints. Predicted probabilities can fall outside [0, 1]. Residuals cannot be normally distributed. The Gaussian linear model is misspecified for binary and count outcomes — it does not respect the bounded, discrete DGP. Predicted probabilities can fall outside [0, 1], the mean-variance relationship is wrong, and standard errors and effect interpretations can be misleading. A GLMM is the appropriate primary model.
Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) extend the mixed model framework to non-normal outcomes. They combine:

A random effects structure (exactly as in lmer) to handle nesting and repeated measures
A link function that transforms the linear predictor to the appropriate scale
A distributional family that matches the DGP

The longitudinal setting makes GLMMs especially important, because tracking people over time almost guarantees you will encounter binary events and count outcomes alongside the usual continuous measures.

Why Not Just Use a Linear Mixed Model?
The chart below shows what happens when you fit a linear mixed model to a binary outcome versus a logistic mixed model. Both models are fit to the same data: 60 customers, binary purchase outcome, one predictor (loyalty program × baseline purchase tendency). The problem is immediate: the linear model produces predicted probabilities below 0 for customers with low baseline purchase tendency, and potentially above 1 for customers with high tendency and program membership. These are impossible predicted probabilities — and they make confidence intervals and counterfactual predictions unreliable.









The linear model is sometimes used as a “linear probability model” in economics — it gives approximately correct marginal effects near the center of the distribution. But in longitudinal research with repeated measures, the out-of-bounds predictions propagate through the random effects structure, distorting the variance partitioning and making ICC and \(\tau^2\) estimates meaningless. The logistic GLMM is the correct choice whenever the outcome is binary.
crumbs: 33  Binary and Count Outcomes Over Time

title: Binary and Count Outcomes Over Time
section: Part 1: Binary Longitudinal Outcomes — The Logistic Mixed Model
text:
Part 1: Binary Longitudinal Outcomes — The Logistic Mixed Model

The Model
For a binary outcome \(Y_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\) measured at occasion \(i\) for person \(j\), the logistic mixed model is:
\[\text{logit}\bigl(P(Y_{ij} = 1)\bigr) = \underbrace{\beta_0}_{\substack{\text{average log-odds} \\ \text{at baseline}}} + \underbrace{u_{0j}}_{\substack{\text{person's deviation} \\ \text{from average}}} + \underbrace{\beta_1 \cdot \text{week}_{ij}}_{\substack{\text{change in log-odds} \\ \text{per week}}} + \underbrace{\beta_2 \cdot \text{treatment}_j}_{\substack{\text{treatment effect} \\ \text{on log-odds scale}}}\]
where:

\(\text{logit}(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p}\) is the log-odds of the event
\(u_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)\) is a person-level random intercept — capturing the fact that some people are generally more likely to have an episode, regardless of treatment or time
The fixed effects \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) operate on the log-odds scale, so we exponentiate them to get odds ratios

This is exactly the linear mixed model, but with a logit link function wrapping the left-hand side.


Simulating a Longitudinal Loyalty Experiment
We simulate 60 customers tracked over 6 weeks. Half are randomly enrolled in a loyalty reward program. The outcome is binary: whether the customer made at least one purchase that week. The loyalty program is expected to roughly double the weekly purchase odds.


Code
n_people  <- 60
n_weeks   <- 6
treatment <- rep(c(0, 1), each = n_people / 2)

# Person-level random intercepts (on log-odds scale) — some customers are
# habitual shoppers, others rarely purchase regardless of program
u0 <- rnorm(n_people, 0, 0.8)

df_binary <- expand_grid(
  person = 1:n_people,
  week   = 0:(n_weeks - 1)
) |>
  mutate(
    treatment = treatment[person],
    u0        = u0[person],
    # True log-odds: intercept + loyalty program effect + habituation over time + RE
    log_odds  = -0.5 + u0 + 0.7 * treatment - 0.05 * week,
    prob      = plogis(log_odds),
    purchased = rbinom(n(), 1, prob),
    person    = factor(person),

Marginal Predicted Probabilities
Odds ratios describe the model’s internal logic, but audiences (and your future self) think in probabilities, not log-odds. ggeffects::ggpredict() computes marginal predicted probabilities — averaging over the random effects distribution rather than conditioning on a specific individual.


Code
preds_binary <- ggpredict(m_binary, terms = c("week", "treatment"), type = "fixed")

    x = "Week", y = "Predicted purchase probability", color = "Group", fill = "Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)











Marginal vs. Conditional Effects
This distinction matters more in GLMMs than in linear models, because the logit link is nonlinear.

A conditional effect asks: “For a specific person (with a specific \(u_{0j}\)), what is the predicted probability?” It conditions on knowing that person’s random intercept.
A marginal effect asks: “For an average person drawn from this population, what is the predicted probability?” It averages over the distribution of random effects.

The conditional effect is the right answer for individual-level prediction — predicting whether this patient will have an episode. The marginal effect is the right answer for policy-level inference — estimating the population-average impact of a treatment.
ggpredict(..., type = "fixed") gives marginal effects. ggpredict(..., type = "random") gives predictions for an average individual (random effects set to zero). Neither is wrong — they answer different questions.






Warning



Assumption: Correct link function
Logistic regression assumes the log-odds of the outcome are a linear function of the predictors. For bounded probabilities near 0 or 1, this is usually reasonable. The probit link is an alternative if you have theoretical reasons to prefer it (probit assumes a latent Gaussian threshold; logistic assumes a logistic latent distribution). In practice, they rarely differ much.








Warning



Assumption: No overdispersion in binomial outcomes
Binomial outcomes (0/1 per trial) cannot be overdispersed in the strict statistical sense — by definition, a Bernoulli draw has variance \(p(1-p)\). However, if your outcome is a proportion based on multiple trials (e.g., 3 out of 5 tasks completed), overdispersion can occur. Check it with Pearson \(\chi^2\) / df. For strict 0/1 data, this is not a concern.








Warning



Assumption: Normality of random effects on the log-odds scale
The random intercepts \(u_{0j}\) are assumed to follow a normal distribution on the log-odds scale — not on the probability scale. This means a person with \(u_{0j} = 2\) is simply a person with systematically higher log-odds. The distribution of random effects is not directly observable, but you can inspect BLUPs (Best Linear Unbiased Predictors) for gross departures from normality.
