title: Binary and Count Outcomes Over Time
section: Part 2: Count Longitudinal Outcomes — Poisson and Negative Binomial
text:
Part 2: Count Longitudinal Outcomes — Poisson and Negative Binomial

Why Counts Need Different Models
Count outcomes (0, 1, 2, 3, …) have two properties that break standard regression assumptions:

Non-negativity. Counts cannot be negative. A linear model can happily predict −2 hospitalizations.
Mean-variance relationship. For a Poisson process, the variance equals the mean. Higher-count people are intrinsically more variable. A linear model assumes constant variance.

The Poisson mixed model handles both:
\[\log\bigl(\mu_{ij}\bigr) = \underbrace{\beta_0}_{\substack{\text{log expected count} \\ \text{at baseline}}} + \underbrace{u_{0j}}_{\substack{\text{person's log-rate} \\ \text{deviation}}} + \underbrace{\beta_1 \cdot \text{visit}_{ij}}_{\substack{\text{change in log-count} \\ \text{per visit}}} + \underbrace{\beta_2 \cdot \text{treatment}_j}_{\substack{\text{treatment effect} \\ \text{on log-count scale}}}\]
The log link ensures predicted counts are always positive. Exponentiating fixed effects gives rate ratios (also called incidence rate ratios).


Simulating Longitudinal Count Data
We simulate 80 customers tracked over 8 weeks. The count outcome is the number of times they open a budgeting app each week. Half are randomly assigned to a push-notification feature that encourages regular check-ins. The treatment is expected to approximately double weekly app opens — the true log rate ratio is \(\exp(0.5) \approx 1.65\).


Code
n_customers <- 80
n_weeks_c   <- 8
treatment_c <- rep(c(0, 1), each = n_customers / 2)

# Customer-level random intercepts on log-count scale
# Some customers are habitual checkers; others rarely open the app
u0_count <- rnorm(n_customers, 0, 0.5)

df_count <- expand_grid(
  customer = 1:n_customers,
  week     = 1:n_weeks_c
) |>
  mutate(
    treatment  = treatment_c[customer],
    u0         = u0_count[customer],
    log_mu     = 0.8 + u0 + 0.5 * treatment - 0.04 * week,
    mu         = exp(log_mu),
    app_opens  = rpois(n(), mu),
    customer   = factor(customer),
    treatment  = factor(treatment, labels = c("Control", "Push notifications"))
  )

# Observed mean app opens by week and treatment
df_count |>
  group_by(week, treatment) |>
  summarise(mean_opens = mean(app_opens), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = mean_opens, color = treatment, group = treatment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#1e3a5f", "#e63946")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Mean weekly app opens by push-notification enrollment",
    subtitle = "Observed means by treatment group",
    x = "Week", y = "Mean weekly app opens", color = "Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)











Fitting the Poisson Mixed Model

m_poisson <- glmmTMB(
  app_opens ~ week + treatment + (1 | customer),
  data   = df_count,
  family = poisson
)

Checking for Overdispersion
The Poisson model assumes variance = mean. If your data are more variable than this (which is common in practice — people differ in unmeasured ways), the model will underestimate standard errors and produce overconfident p-values. This is called overdispersion.
A simple check: compute the Pearson statistic divided by the residual degrees of freedom. If this ratio is substantially greater than 1 (a common rule of thumb is > 1.5), overdispersion is present.


Code
# Pearson statistic / residual df
pearson_resid <- residuals(m_poisson, type = "pearson")
dispersion_ratio <- sum(pearson_resid^2) / df.residual(m_poisson)

cat("Dispersion ratio (Pearson χ² / df):", round(dispersion_ratio, 3), "\n")

Interpretation: values near 1.0 indicate no overdispersion;

cat("values > 1.5 suggest the negative binomial model is preferred.\n")


values > 1.5 suggest the negative binomial model is preferred.




Negative Binomial Model
The negative binomial adds a dispersion parameter (\(\theta\)) that allows variance to exceed the mean:
\[\text{Var}(Y) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\theta}\]
When \(\theta \to \infty\), the negative binomial reduces to Poisson. Smaller \(\theta\) means more overdispersion (more between-person variance in counts beyond what the Poisson allows).

  app_opens ~ week + treatment + (1 | customer),
  data   = df_count,

What About Zero-Inflation?
In many longitudinal count outcomes, there are far more zeros than a Poisson or negative binomial distribution would predict. For example, in an app engagement study, a meaningful share of enrolled users never open the app at all — they are structural zeros. A standard count model will underfit these zeros and overfit the counts from active users.
glmmTMB handles this cleanly with a zero-inflation component:
# Zero-inflated negative binomial (not run — for illustration)
m_zinb <- glmmTMB(
  app_opens ~ week + treatment + (1 | customer),
  ziformula = ~1,        # intercept-only zero-inflation model
  family    = nbinom2,
  data      = df_count
)
The zero-inflation formula ziformula models the probability that an observation comes from the “always zero” process (e.g., a customer who enrolled but never opened the app at all) rather than the count-generating process. You can make this a function of predictors — for instance, the zero-inflation probability might itself depend on whether the customer was in the push-notification group.






Warning



Assumption: Correct distributional family
Start with Poisson. Check the dispersion ratio. If > 1.5, switch to negative binomial (nbinom2). If you have many more zeros than either model predicts (compare prop_zero in your data to mean(predict(..., type="response") == 0)), add zero-inflation. The model should match the DGP that generated your outcome.








Warning



Assumption: Log link is appropriate
The log link assumes that predictor effects are multiplicative on the count scale (each unit increase in X multiplies the expected count by \(e^\beta\)). This is usually sensible for rate outcomes. If you have strong theoretical reasons to expect additive effects on the count scale, the identity link is possible but numerically unstable with count data.

text:
Putting It Together: GLMMs and the DGP
The key insight is that GLMMs are not a special case of mixed models — they are a more faithful representation of the DGP when your outcome is binary or a count. Forcing binary or count data into a linear mixed model is equivalent to saying “I know the DGP generates counts, but I will pretend it generates continuous normal data.” The parameter estimates you get from that misspecified model are biased and not meaningful.
GLMMs respect the DGP:

In every case, the random effects structure stays exactly as it would be in a linear mixed model: participants are nested within themselves across time, and the random intercept (or random slope, if you have one) captures stable individual differences in the outcome on the transformed scale.

title: Survival Analysis for Longitudinal Events
text:
When the Outcome Is Time-to-Event
Many JDM outcomes of interest are not continuous scores but events with timing:

A customer churns from a financial app — leaves the platform
A borrower defaults on their first late payment
A household opts out of a default enrollment they were automatically placed in
A consumer makes their first purchase after receiving a marketing offer
A subscriber cancels automatic fee renewal

For each of these, the scientific question concerns when the event happens and what speeds or slows the rate. Standard regression applied to the event indicator (event = 1/0) ignores timing entirely. Standard regression applied to the elapsed time until the event ignores censoring — participants who have not yet experienced the event by the end of the study. Discarding them as “incomplete data” would introduce systematic bias (the longer-surviving, more loyal customers would vanish from the analysis).
Survival analysis handles both: it models the hazard function over time while correctly incorporating information from participants who have not yet churned, defaulted, or opted out.

What Survival Data Look Like: Censoring in Practice
The diagram below shows why standard regression fails for time-to-event outcomes. Each row is a customer. Some churn at a known time (red ✕). Others are still active when the study ends, or leave for reasons unrelated to churn — these are censored (grey dot). Dropping censored customers would systematically remove the most loyal users and overstate churn rates. Survival analysis retains them, using their partial observation: the fact that they survived at least as long as they were observed.









Customers B and G survive the full 180 days — they contribute positive information about surviving through day 180 without implying they never churn. Customers D and I withdrew early for unrelated reasons — they contribute positive information through their last observed day. Excluding either group would remove the most persistent users and produce a biased estimate of the survival function.
crumbs: 34  Survival Analysis for Longitudinal Events

title: Survival Analysis for Longitudinal Events
text:
The Hazard and Survival Functions
The survival function \(S(t)\) gives the probability of surviving (not experiencing the event) past time \(t\): \[S(t) = P(T > t)\]
The hazard function \(h(t)\) gives the instantaneous rate of the event at time \(t\), given survival to that point: \[h(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{P(t \leq T < t + \Delta t \mid T \geq t)}{\Delta t}\]
They are linked by: \[S(t) = \exp\left(-\int_0^t h(u)\, du\right)\]
JDM intuitions:

Churn hazard: typically highest in the first weeks after account opening (buyer’s remorse / friction with the app), then declining as engaged users settle in — a decreasing hazard.
Default hazard: may increase over time as debt accumulates and financial stress compounds — an increasing hazard.
First purchase hazard: may peak a few days after an offer arrives (immediate response window), then decay as the offer recedes from attention — a non-monotone hazard.
crumbs: 34  Survival Analysis for Longitudinal Events

title: Survival Analysis for Longitudinal Events
text:
Step 1: The Kaplan-Meier Estimator
The Kaplan-Meier (KM) estimator is the nonparametric estimate of the survival function. It makes no assumptions about the shape of the hazard and handles censoring correctly.

Simulating Time-to-Churn Data
We simulate 120 customers: 60 assigned to a standard onboarding flow, 60 to an enhanced onboarding with a personalized savings goal feature. We track days until app churn over a 180-day observation window. Customers who have not churned by day 180 are censored.


Code
n_customers <- 120
condition   <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 60)   # 0 = standard, 1 = enhanced onboarding

# True churn times: exponential with condition-dependent rate
rate_standard <- 0.012  # average churn ~83 days
rate_enhanced <- 0.006  # enhanced roughly halves churn rate

churn_time <- ifelse(
  condition == 0,
  rexp(n_customers, rate = rate_standard),
  rexp(n_customers, rate = rate_enhanced)
)

# Censoring at day 180
follow_up  <- 180
event_time <- pmin(churn_time, follow_up)
event      <- as.integer(churn_time <= follow_up)   # 1 = churned, 0 = censored

df_surv <- tibble(
  customer  = 1:n_customers,
  days      = event_time,
  churned   = event,
  condition = factor(condition, labels = c("Standard onboarding", "Enhanced onboarding"))
)

df_surv |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(
    n_churned    = sum(churned),
    n_retained   = sum(1 - churned),
    median_days  = median(days[churned == 1]),
    .groups      = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Churn summary by onboarding condition")

plot_data <- broom::tidy(km_fit)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = time, y = estimate, color = strata, fill = strata)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("#1e3a5f", "#2d6a4f"),
    labels = c("Standard onboarding", "Enhanced onboarding"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("#1e3a5f", "#2d6a4f"),
    labels = c("Standard onboarding", "Enhanced onboarding"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title    = "Kaplan-Meier survival curves: time to app churn",
    subtitle = "Shaded = 95% CI. Steps at each churn event. Customers not yet churned are censored at day 180.",
    x        = "Days since account opening",
    y        = "P(still active on platform)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









The KM curve starts at \(S(0) = 1\) (everyone active) and steps down at each churn event. The median survival time is the day at which the curve crosses 0.50 — half the customers in that condition have churned by that point. Censored customers (still active at day 180) contribute their partial information: they reduce the “at risk” count at later times without contributing a step down.

title: Survival Analysis for Longitudinal Events
section: Step 3: The Cox Proportional Hazards Model
text:
Step 3: The Cox Proportional Hazards Model
The Cox model is the standard regression tool for survival outcomes:
\[h(t \mid X_j) = \underbrace{h_0(t)}_{\substack{\text{baseline hazard} \\ \text{(unspecified)}}} \cdot \exp(\beta_1 X_{1j} + \beta_2 X_{2j} + \cdots)\]
Each \(\exp(\beta_k)\) is a hazard ratio: the multiplicative factor by which the instantaneous churn rate changes for a one-unit increase in \(X_k\).

HR = 0.5: the treatment halves the churn rate at every time point
HR = 1.0: no effect on the churn rate
HR = 2.0: the predictor doubles the churn rate



Code
cox_model <- coxph(Surv(days, churned) ~ condition, data = df_surv)

broom::tidy(cox_model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Cox model: hazard ratio for enhanced vs. standard onboarding. HR < 1 means lower churn rate."
  )



Cox model: hazard ratio for enhanced vs. standard onboarding. HR < 1 means lower churn rate.

The Proportional Hazards Assumption
The Cox model assumes the hazard ratio between conditions is constant over time. If the enhanced onboarding’s protective effect fades after month 3 (customers disengage with their savings goal), the curves would converge in later periods — violating proportional hazards.


Code
cox_test <- cox.zph(cox_model)

title: Survival Analysis for Longitudinal Events
section: Step 4: Frailty Models — Handling Clustered Churn Data
text:
Step 4: Frailty Models — Handling Clustered Churn Data
When customers are nested in contexts — bank branches, geographic regions, or platform versions — standard Cox models assume independence that is violated. Customers from the same branch may churn for similar branch-level reasons (local economic shock, branch closure, manager change). The survival analogue of a random intercept is a frailty — a latent multiplicative factor that shifts the churn hazard up or down for everyone in a cluster.
\[h_{ij}(t) = h_0(t) \cdot \exp(\beta X_{ij}) \cdot Z_j, \quad Z_j \sim \text{Gamma}(1, \theta)\]
\(Z_j\) is the frailty for branch \(j\). If \(Z_j > 1\), all customers in that branch have higher churn risk — perhaps because local economic conditions make financial management more stressful for everyone there.


Code
n_branches   <- 15
n_per_branch <- 8
n_total      <- n_branches * n_per_branch

branch       <- rep(1:n_branches, each = n_per_branch)
condition_b  <- rep(rep(c(0, 1), each = n_per_branch / 2), n_branches)

# Branch-level frailty (some branches have structurally higher churn)
branch_frailty <- rgamma(n_branches, shape = 2, rate = 2)  # variance = 0.5

base_rate   <- 0.010
churn_time_b <- rexp(
  n_total,
  rate = base_rate * branch_frailty[branch] * exp(0.5 * (1 - condition_b))
)

df_frailty <- tibble(
  customer  = 1:n_total,
  branch    = factor(branch),
  days      = pmin(churn_time_b, follow_up),
  churned   = as.integer(churn_time_b <= follow_up),
  condition = factor(condition_b, labels = c("Standard", "Enhanced"))
)

cox_frailty <- coxph(
  Surv(days, churned) ~ condition + frailty(branch, distribution = "gamma"),
  data = df_frailty
)

title: Survival Analysis for Longitudinal Events
text:
Assumptions






WarningAssumption: Non-Informative Censoring



Plain-language meaning: Censoring must be independent of the event process. Customers who are censored (still active at the end of the observation window) must not systematically differ in their imminent churn risk from those who have not yet been censored.
What the model is assuming away: Any relationship between the reason for censoring and the rate of the event. If customers who are about to churn disengage from the app before formally churning — becoming inactive but not yet counted as churned — they are effectively informatively censored.
JDM example: If financially distressed customers frequently delete the app before their account officially lapses (a soft churn that precedes the hard churn event), the observed churn times underrepresent the actual churning rate. Customers with high churn risk are leaving the observation window early for risk-related reasons.
Experimental analog: In a lab study of time-to-abandonment of a financial task, participants who give up before completing it but whose abandonment does not trigger the “event” (task abandonment) are informatively censored.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Why would customers who are about to churn be equally likely to remain in your observation window as customers who are loyal? If pre-churn disengagement precedes formal churn, your censoring is informative.”
Observable warning sign: Censored customers show systematically lower engagement metrics or different baseline characteristics than event-experiencing customers — suggesting informative censoring.
What to check: Compare baseline characteristics (account age, engagement score, demographics) between censored and churned customers. If they differ substantially, consider sensitivity analyses or inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting (IPCW).
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The KM estimates and Cox HRs are biased (usually toward underestimating the true event rate). If censoring depends on latent event risk, both effect magnitude and direction can be distorted.








WarningAssumption: Proportional Hazards (Cox Model Only)



Plain-language meaning: The hazard ratio between conditions is constant over time. The enhanced onboarding’s protective effect at day 30 is the same multiplier as at day 120.
What the model is assuming away: Time-varying treatment effects — for example, an onboarding boost that fades after initial engagement, or a default enrollment whose effect builds as habits solidify.
JDM example: A personalized savings goal feature may prevent early churn (when customers are still learning the app) but have weaker effects later once the novelty fades. The hazard ratio would drift toward 1 over time, violating PH.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Why should the effect of enhanced onboarding on churn be a fixed multiplier at all time points? Surely the benefit is concentrated in the first weeks when onboarding is salient.”
What to check: cox.zph() test and Schoenfeld residual plot. If violated, add a time-by-treatment interaction (tt() in survival) or stratify the baseline hazard by condition.








WarningAssumption: Correct Frailty Distribution



Plain-language meaning: The frailty model assumes branch-level random effects follow a Gamma distribution (the standard choice). If the actual distribution of branch-level churn propensity is very different — heavily skewed or multimodal — the Gamma frailty may not fit well.
What to check: Examine residuals from the frailty model. Compare fitted and observed survival curves within branches. For robustness, consider log-normal frailty as an alternative (available in coxme or frailtyEM).

title: Survival Analysis for Longitudinal Events
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “You defined churn as account closure — but isn’t disengagement (stopping app use) the more behaviorally relevant event, and it would be much harder to define?” This is a latent event timing problem. Formally measured churn is a discrete, observable event; meaningful disengagement happens earlier and more continuously. Sensitivity analyses using alternative event definitions (e.g., 30-day inactivity vs. formal account closure) help assess whether conclusions depend on the event definition.
Challenge 2: “Your observation window is 180 days, but many customers are still active at the end. Doesn’t that mean you can’t actually estimate median survival for the enhanced condition?” Correct — if the KM curve does not cross 0.50 within the observation window, the median is undefined from the data. Report the 25th percentile survival time (the day by which 25% of customers have churned) instead, or report survival probabilities at specific time points (e.g., “60% of enhanced customers were still active at day 120”).
Challenge 3: “The frailty variance estimate is large — does that mean your treatment effect is confounded with branch-level variation?” Not confounded, but attenuated. The frailty absorbs between-branch variance that would otherwise inflate residual variance. The treatment effect (HR) is estimated conditional on branch frailty — it represents the within-branch contrast, which is the more precise and causally interpretable estimate. A large frailty variance is an argument for the frailty model, not against it.

title: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies
section: Why Longitudinal Data Are Especially Prone to Missingness
text:
Why Longitudinal Data Are Especially Prone to Missingness
Cross-sectional studies have one chance to collect data. Longitudinal studies have multiple waves — and at each wave, participants can fail to provide data. Even modest per-wave dropout compounds dramatically:

90% retention per wave × 4 waves = 66% completing all waves
80% retention per wave × 4 waves = 41% completing all waves

The complete-case sample — participants with data at every wave — can be a small, highly selected subset of the original enrollment.
The central problem: Why people drop out is rarely random. Financially stressed households are more likely to disengage from financial diary studies precisely because their situation is worsening and they are avoiding measurement. App users with the worst savings outcomes are often the least engaged users — and the first to stop logging. These are mechanisms that create systematic relationships between missingness and the outcome trajectory.
crumbs: 35  Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies

title: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies
section: The Three Mechanisms of Missing Data
text:
The Three Mechanisms of Missing Data

Missing Completely At Random (MCAR)
Whether an observation is missing is independent of everything — both observed and unobserved variables. Complete-case analysis is unbiased under MCAR, but still inefficient.
JDM example: Data are missing because a server outage prevented 15% of responses from being saved at wave 2. The outage has nothing to do with who the participants are or how they were responding.


Missing At Random (MAR)
Whether an observation is missing depends on observed variables in the dataset, but not on the missing value itself after conditioning on those variables. Modern methods (available-case maximum likelihood via lmer, multiple imputation) can be valid under MAR when the model is correctly specified and predictors of missingness are included. Note: lmer uses all observed outcomes under the model’s likelihood — this is not identical to SEM-style FIML but shares the core MAR property.
JDM example: Households with higher baseline debt are more likely to drop out of a financial diary study. Higher debt is observed. Once you condition on observed baseline debt, dropout is independent of the unobserved future financial behavior. The dropout is predictable from what you have — but it is not driven by the unseen future outcome.


Missing Not At Random (MNAR)
Whether an observation is missing depends on the missing value itself, even after conditioning on all observed variables. This is the dangerous case.
JDM example: App users stop logging their transactions because their spending worsened — and the worsened spending that caused them to disengage is the exact outcome you would have measured. The missingness is caused by the unobserved outcome. No standard method corrects for this.


The MAR/MNAR Distinction Visualized





flowchart TD
    A["Enrolled participants\nN = 200"] --> B["Wave 2 complete\nN = 160"]
    A --> C["Dropped out at wave 2\nN = 40"]
    B --> D["Wave 3 complete\nN = 128"]
    B --> E["Dropped out at wave 3\nN = 32"]
    C --> F_mar["MAR: dropout predicted by\nobserved baseline debt"]
    C --> F_mnar["MNAR: dropout caused by\nunobserved spending shock"]
    style F_mar fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2d6a4f
    style F_mnar fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#c0392b






Under MAR, the cause of dropout sits in your observed data — you can model it. Under MNAR, the cause is invisible — it is the thing you failed to measure.






WarningAssumption: MAR or Better



Plain-language meaning: Multiple imputation and available-case ML via lmer are only valid if the data are MAR — missing for reasons explainable by observed variables — or MCAR. If dropout is driven by the unobserved outcome trajectory, these methods reduce but cannot eliminate bias.
What the model is assuming away: The possibility that the financially distressed households who disappeared from wave 3 had worse outcomes than predicted from their observed characteristics — and dropped out specifically because of that unobserved worsening.
JDM example: If app users disengage specifically after large overdraft events (which are unobserved in your data), their missing wave 3 savings behavior is not explained by their observed baseline debt level. The dropout is MNAR.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Your imputation is valid under MAR — but why would a financial diary dropout be MAR? The people who stop logging finances are arguably the ones whose finances are getting worse in ways your baseline measures don’t fully capture.”
Observable warning sign: Significant differences in observed baseline variables between completers and dropouts (consistent with MAR, but also consistent with MNAR); dropout rates that increase across waves; dropout concentrated in the control arm.
What to check: Compare observed baseline characteristics between completers and dropouts. If they differ, MAR is possible but MNAR cannot be ruled out. Run sensitivity analysis to bound the MNAR bias.
crumbs: 35  Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies

title: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies
text:
Step 1: Diagnosing Missingness


Code
n_people <- 150
n_waves  <- 4

person_baseline <- rnorm(n_people, 50, 10)
person_trt      <- rep(c(0, 1), each = n_people / 2)

df_full <- expand_grid(person = 1:n_people, wave = 1:n_waves) |>
  mutate(
    baseline  = person_baseline[person],
    treatment = person_trt[person],
    Y_true    = baseline - 3 * (wave - 1) + 5 * treatment * (wave - 1) + rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    person    = factor(person)
  )

# MAR mechanism: households with lower baseline savings drop out more over time
dropout_prob <- plogis(-2 + 0.03 * (50 - person_baseline[as.integer(df_full$person)])
                          + 0.4 * (df_full$wave - 1))
missing_flag <- rbinom(nrow(df_full), 1, dropout_prob)

df_obs <- df_full |>
  mutate(Y_obs = ifelse(missing_flag == 1, NA, Y_true))

df_obs |>
  group_by(wave) |>
  summarise(
    n_total   = n(),
    n_missing = sum(is.na(Y_obs)),
    pct_miss  = round(mean(is.na(Y_obs)) * 100, 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Missingness rates per wave — attrition compounds across waves")

title: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies
text:
Step 2: Complete-Case vs. Available-Case Analysis
Complete-case analysis: use only participants with data at every wave. Simple, but biased when dropouts differ from completers — and they almost always do in financial panel studies.
Available-case analysis: use all available data at each wave. lmer uses this by default (FIML-like estimation), and it is unbiased under MAR when the model correctly includes the observed predictors of dropout.


Code
# Complete cases only
df_cc <- df_obs |>
  group_by(person) |>
  filter(sum(!is.na(Y_obs)) == n_waves) |>
  ungroup()

m_cc <- lmer(Y_obs ~ wave * treatment + (1 | person), data = df_cc)
m_ac <- lmer(Y_obs ~ wave * treatment + (1 | person), data = df_obs)

bind_rows(
  broom.mixed::tidy(m_cc, effects = "fixed") |>
    filter(str_detect(term, "wave.*treatment")) |>
    mutate(approach = "Complete-case"),
  broom.mixed::tidy(m_ac, effects = "fixed") |>
    filter(str_detect(term, "wave.*treatment")) |>
    mutate(approach = "Available-case (lmer)")
) |>
  select(approach, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Treatment × wave interaction: complete-case vs. available-case. True effect ≈ 5. Available-case is closer under MAR."
  )

title: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies
text:
Step 3: Multiple Imputation
Multiple Imputation (MI) is a principled approach for MAR data with three steps:

Impute: Create \(m\) plausible complete datasets, with missing values filled by draws from the posterior predictive distribution given observed data
Analyze: Run your analysis model on each of the \(m\) complete datasets
Pool: Combine estimates using Rubin’s rules, propagating imputation uncertainty into the final standard errors







NoteMI for Longitudinal Outcomes



For repeated-measures longitudinal outcomes where the missing data are the outcome at specific waves, FIML via lmer() using all available observations is usually the preferred approach under MAR — it directly maximizes the likelihood over observed data without requiring a separate imputation model.
Full multilevel MI that respects the time-series structure (e.g., mice with 2l.pan or Bayesian multilevel imputation) is technically superior when auxiliary variables not in the analysis model predict missingness. But it is considerably more complex to implement correctly.
The illustration below uses a simplified person-level imputation to demonstrate Rubin’s rules pooling mechanics. It is a didactic toy example, not a recommended workflow for longitudinal outcomes.




Code
df_person <- df_obs |>
  group_by(person, treatment, baseline) |>
  summarise(mean_Y = mean(Y_obs, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

imp <- mice(
  df_person |> select(treatment, baseline, mean_Y),
  method = "pmm",
  m      = 20,
  maxit  = 10,
  print  = FALSE
)

results_list <- lapply(1:20, function(k) {
  df_imp_person <- complete(imp, k) |>
    mutate(person = df_person$person)

  df_long_imp <- df_obs |>
    left_join(df_imp_person |> select(person, mean_Y_imp = mean_Y), by = "person") |>
    mutate(Y_mi = ifelse(is.na(Y_obs), mean_Y_imp + rnorm(n(), 0, 3), Y_obs))

  lmer(Y_mi ~ wave * treatment + (1 | person), data = df_long_imp, REML = FALSE)
})

pooled <- pool(results_list)

summary(pooled) |>
  filter(term == "wave:treatment") |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "MI pooled estimate: treatment × wave interaction. True effect ≈ 5."
  )



MI pooled estimate: treatment × wave interaction. True effect ≈ 5.

Rubin’s Rules
The pooled estimate from \(m\) imputations is the average: \[\hat{\beta}_{pool} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{k=1}^m \hat{\beta}_k\]
The pooled variance combines within-imputation variance and between-imputation variance: \[V_{pool} = \bar{W} + \left(1 + \frac{1}{m}\right) B\]
The between-imputation variance \(B\) captures uncertainty from the imputed values themselves. Unlike complete-case analysis, MI correctly accounts for the fact that imputed values are estimated, not observed — standard errors are appropriately wider.
crumbs: 35  Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies

title: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies
text:
Step 4: Sensitivity Analysis for MNAR
When you suspect MNAR, the honest response is not to claim the problem is solved — it is to characterize how much the MNAR mechanism would need to deviate before your conclusions change.
Tipping point analysis: Shift the imputed missing values by a parameter \(\delta\) (representing how much worse the dropouts’ outcomes were relative to MAR predictions) and observe when the key estimate loses significance.


Code
delta_values <- seq(-10, 0, by = 2)

sensitivity_results <- purrr::map_dfr(delta_values, function(delta) {
  results_delta <- lapply(1:10, function(k) {
    df_imp_person <- complete(imp, k) |>
      mutate(person = df_person$person)

    df_long_imp <- df_obs |>
      left_join(df_imp_person |> select(person, mean_Y_imp = mean_Y), by = "person") |>
      mutate(
        Y_mi = ifelse(
          is.na(Y_obs),
          mean_Y_imp + delta + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),   # delta = MNAR shift
          Y_obs
        )
      )

    lmer(Y_mi ~ wave * treatment + (1 | person), data = df_long_imp, REML = FALSE)
  })

  pooled_d <- pool(results_delta)
  est <- summary(pooled_d) |> filter(term == "wave:treatment")
  tibble(delta = delta, estimate = est$estimate, p_value = est$p.value)
})

ggplot(sensitivity_results, aes(x = delta, y = estimate)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = estimate - 1, ymax = estimate + 1), alpha = 0.1, fill = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e63946") +
  labs(
    title    = "MNAR sensitivity analysis: tipping point for treatment × time effect",
    subtitle = "Delta = assumed additional penalty for dropouts (0 = MAR; negative = dropouts fared worse)",
    x        = "MNAR shift parameter δ (units worse than MAR prediction)",
    y        = "Estimated treatment × time interaction"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









The tipping point is the \(\delta\) at which the estimate drops to zero (or the p-value crosses 0.05). If that requires implausibly large deviations from MAR — for example, assuming dropouts averaged 8 units worse than their observed predictors suggest — the conclusion is relatively robust to MNAR. If the tipping point is \(\delta = -2\), the finding is fragile.
crumbs: 35  Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies

title: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies
text:
Step 5: Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML)
An alternative to MI is Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML). Instead of imputing missing values, FIML uses the likelihood of the observed data — but the likelihood is computed across all available time points for each person.
In practice, lmer on all available observations already implements FIML-like estimation. For structural equation models with missing data, lavaan’s missing = "fiml" argument provides explicit FIML.
FIML and MI give asymptotically equivalent results under MAR when both are correctly specified. For standard mixed models with MAR data, available-case lmer is the simpler and preferred approach.
crumbs: 35  Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies

title: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies
text:
Decision Framework






TipMissing Data Analysis Workflow




Diagnose: What is the missingness rate by wave? Do dropouts differ from completers on observed baseline characteristics?
Classify mechanism: MCAR (server outage, lost data), MAR (dropout predicted by observed variables), or MNAR (dropout driven by the very outcome being studied)?
Choose primary analysis:

Under MCAR or MAR: available-case lmer is unbiased (as long as the model includes observed predictors of dropout as covariates)
Add MI when auxiliary variables predict missingness beyond the main model

Run sensitivity analysis: Tipping-point analysis shows how much MNAR bias would reverse your conclusions. Report the tipping point explicitly.
Report: State the missingness rate, the mechanism assumption, the analytic approach, and the sensitivity analysis. Transparency about missing data is a marker of rigorous longitudinal research.

title: Missing Data in Longitudinal Studies
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “You assumed MAR and used available-case estimation. But the most financially stressed households — the ones who dropped out — are exactly the ones whose trajectories matter most. If they dropped out because they’re worse off, that’s MNAR.” This is the hardest challenge in financial panel research. The appropriate response: (1) show that dropouts and completers differ on observed baseline characteristics (consistent with but not proving MAR), (2) include those observed characteristics in the model to control for predictable dropout, and (3) conduct a tipping point sensitivity analysis showing how much the MNAR effect would need to be to change conclusions.
Challenge 2: “Your multiple imputation imputed the wave 3 outcome — but what was the imputation model? Did it include baseline debt, income, and treatment status?” Correct specification of the imputation model is critical. The imputation model should include all variables in the analysis model plus any auxiliary variables that predict missingness. If baseline debt predicts dropout and is in the imputation model, the resulting imputations will correctly reflect the mechanism. If it is omitted, the imputations are misspecified.
Challenge 3: “With 35% missing at wave 4, can you trust any estimates from that wave?” High missingness does not automatically invalidate inference — what matters is the mechanism. Under well-supported MAR with a rich set of observed predictors, 35% missingness with lmer or MI can still produce unbiased estimates. But the uncertainty is larger (fewer observed data points), and MNAR sensitivity analysis is more important. Report the mechanism argument, not just the imputation procedure.

text:
Section 1: Introduction — Module 3 Meets Panel Data
Module 3 covered six sources of endogeneity and six identification strategies. The discussion there was largely cross-sectional: a researcher observes units at one point in time and tries to isolate causal effects despite confounding. This chapter applies each of those strategies to longitudinal panel data from a JDM perspective: consumer finance panels, policy rollout datasets, and platform-level behavioral data. The time dimension allows us to difference out stable individual differences (fixed effects) and exploit policy announcement dates (DiD, ITS) or randomized encouragement (IV) to recover causal estimates in settings where simple regression fails.
The table below maps Module 3 threats to their panel-data solutions.

title: Applied Identification Strategies for Panel Data
section: Section 2: Panel DiD with Two-Way Fixed Effects
text:
Section 2: Panel DiD with Two-Way Fixed Effects

Setup and simulation
The two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimator is the workhorse of panel difference-in-differences. It absorbs unit fixed effects (removing stable confounders) and time fixed effects (removing common shocks), then estimates the treatment effect from within-unit, within-period variation.


Code
did_viz <- tibble(
  month = rep(1:8, 3),
  group = rep(c("Treated (observed)", "Control (observed)", "Treated (counterfactual)"), each = 8),
  savings = c(
    # Treated: parallel before month 5, then jumps up
    c(11.8, 12.1, 11.9, 12.2, 20.4, 20.8, 21.1, 21.4),
    # Control: gradual drift
    c(11.9, 12.0, 12.1, 12.0, 12.3, 12.4, 12.6, 12.7),
    # Counterfactual: treated would have followed control's path
    c(11.8, 12.1, 11.9, 12.2, 12.5, 12.6, 12.8, 12.9)
  ),
  linetype_val = rep(c("solid", "solid", "dashed"), each = 8)
)

ggplot(did_viz, aes(x = month, y = savings,
                    color = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, data = did_viz |> filter(group != "Treated (counterfactual)")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray40") +
  annotate("segment",
           x = 7, xend = 7,
           y = 12.8, yend = 21.1,
           arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.15, "cm")),
           color = "#c0392b", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 7.15, y = 17,
           label = "ATT estimate\n(DiD)", color = "#c0392b",
           hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.65, y = 22,
           label = "Policy rollout\n(month 5)", color = "gray40",
           hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Treated (observed)"        = "#1e3a5f",
               "Control (observed)"        = "#aec6e8",
               "Treated (counterfactual)"  = "#e67e22")
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Treated (observed)"        = "solid",
               "Control (observed)"        = "solid",
               "Treated (counterfactual)"  = "dashed")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Difference-in-Differences: counterfactual logic",
    subtitle = "Parallel trends assumption: absent the policy, treated households would have followed the orange dashed path",
    x        = "Month",
    y        = "Monthly savings rate (%)",
    color    = NULL, linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")





DiD logic: the control group’s path estimates what treated households would have done absent the savings policy. The treatment effect (ATT) is the gap between the observed treated path and the dashed counterfactual.




The dashed orange line is the counterfactual — the path treated households would have taken if the policy had never been introduced. It is not observed. The DiD estimator borrows the control group’s post-period trend as a proxy for this counterfactual path (the parallel trends assumption). The ATT is the gap between where treated households actually ended up and where the counterfactual says they would have been.


Setup and simulation
We simulate 60 households observed over 8 months. Thirty households are enrolled in a default savings program at month 5 by their employer. The true average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) is 8 percentage points of additional monthly savings.


Code
n_hh       <- 60
n_months   <- 8

hh_eff      <- rnorm(n_hh, 0, 4)         # stable household saving habits
month_eff   <- rnorm(n_months, 0, 2)     # macroeconomic month shocks

df_twfe <- expand_grid(household = 1:n_hh, month = 1:n_months) |>
  mutate(
    treated     = as.integer(household <= 30),
    post        = as.integer(month >= 5),
    D           = treated * post,
    h_eff       = hh_eff[household],
    m_eff       = month_eff[month],
    savings_pct = 12 + 8 * D + h_eff + m_eff + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),
    household   = factor(household),
    month       = factor(month)
  )




Three equivalent estimators


Code
# 1. Manual 2x2 DiD
did_manual <- with(
  df_twfe |>
    group_by(treated, post) |>
    summarise(y = mean(savings_pct), .groups = "drop"),
  (y[treated == 1 & post == 1] - y[treated == 1 & post == 0]) -
    (y[treated == 0 & post == 1] - y[treated == 0 & post == 0])
)
cat("Manual DiD estimate:", round(did_manual, 2), "\n")


Manual DiD estimate: 8.03 


Code
# 2. Regression DiD with household-clustered SEs
m_reg_did  <- lm(savings_pct ~ treated * post, data = df_twfe)
se_cluster <- coeftest(m_reg_did, vcov = vcovCL(m_reg_did, cluster = ~household))

# 3. TWFE via plm (two-way within)
pdata_twfe <- pdata.frame(
  df_twfe |> mutate(hh_id = as.integer(household), mo = as.integer(month)),
  index = c("hh_id", "mo")
)
m_twfe <- plm(savings_pct ~ D, data = pdata_twfe,
              model = "within", effect = "twoways")





All three approaches target the true ATT ≈ 8. Clustered SEs account for within-household correlation of savings shocks over time; they may be larger or smaller than naive SEs depending on the dependence structure.


Method
Estimate
Std. Error




Manual DiD

Regression DiD (naive SE)

Regression DiD (clustered SE)

WarningWhy Cluster Standard Errors in Panel DiD?



Observations within the same household are not independent — savings behavior shocks persist over time. Treating them as independent (naive OLS SEs) understates uncertainty and inflates Type I error rates. The rule of thumb: cluster at the level of treatment assignment. Here, treatment varies at the household level, so we cluster on household. With fewer than ~30 clusters, consider wild cluster bootstrap (fwildclusterboot package).




Event study: testing parallel trends
The parallel trends assumption — that treated and control households would have followed the same savings trajectory absent the enrollment policy — is not directly testable, but we can look for violations by checking whether pre-treatment differences in trends are already present.


Code
m_event <- lm(savings_pct ~ treated * factor(month), data = df_twfe)

event_df <- broom::tidy(m_event, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "treated:")) |>
  mutate(
    month = as.integer(str_extract(term, "[0-9]+")),
    pre   = month < 5
  )

ggplot(event_df, aes(x = month, y = estimate, color = pre)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray30") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#1e3a5f", "TRUE" = "#aec6e8"),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "Post-enrollment", "TRUE" = "Pre-enrollment (should \u2248 0)")
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.7, y = max(event_df$conf.high) * 0.9,
           label = "Default\nenrollment", hjust = 0, size = 3.5, color = "gray30") +
  labs(
    title   = "Event study: pre-period near zero supports parallel trends in savings behavior",
    subtitle = "Post-period coefficients trace the materializing treatment effect",
    x       = "Month",
    y       = "Estimated treatment effect vs. Month 1",
    color   = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









Pre-period interaction coefficients (light blue) are scattered around zero — consistent with parallel pre-trends. Post-period coefficients (dark blue) step up after month 5 and hover near the true effect of 8. If the pre-period coefficients showed a systematic upward or downward slope, that would be evidence of pre-existing differential trends and would undermine the DiD identification assumption.






TipReading an Event Study Plot




Pre-period coefficients near zero: parallel trends plausible. Fail this check and DiD is suspect.
Sharp jump at treatment date: consistent with an immediate treatment effect.
Gradual post-period increase: treatment effect builds over time (dynamic effects).
Anticipation effects (pre-period coefficients trending upward before treatment): households may be responding in advance; adjust the “post” indicator.

title: Applied Identification Strategies for Panel Data
text:
Section 3: Interrupted Time Series (Temporal RDD)

Concept
Interrupted Time Series (ITS) applies the RDD logic to time rather than a continuous running variable. When a policy takes effect at a known calendar date \(c\), we look for a discontinuity in the time series at that date — a sudden level jump and/or a change in slope. The key identification assumption mirrors RDD’s continuity assumption: absent the policy, the time trend would have continued smoothly through \(c\).
The ITS model decomposes the response into:
\[Y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \underbrace{\beta_2 D_t}_{\text{level jump}} + \underbrace{\beta_3 (t - c)\, D_t}_{\text{slope change}} + u_{0i} + \varepsilon_{it}\]
where \(D_t = \mathbf{1}[t \geq c]\), \(t - c\) is time elapsed since the intervention (zero before), \(u_{0i}\) is a unit random intercept (absorbing stable unit differences), and \(\varepsilon_{it}\) is idiosyncratic error.

\(\beta_1\): pre-regulation monthly trend in customer retention
\(\beta_2\): immediate level change at month \(c\) (jump in retention when regulation takes effect)
\(\beta_3\): additional slope change after regulation (change in rate of improvement)



Simulation
We simulate 40 financial service branches observed for 30 months. A fee-transparency disclosure regulation takes effect at month 16. The true DGP has a \(+4\) percentage point level jump in customer retention rate and a \(+0.2\)/month additional improvement in retention rate slope.


Code
n_branches <- 40
n_months   <- 30
branch_eff <- rnorm(n_branches, 0, 4)

df_its <- expand_grid(branch = 1:n_branches, month = 1:n_months) |>
  mutate(
    post      = as.integer(month >= 16),
    t_post    = pmax(month - 15, 0),       # months elapsed since regulation; 0 before
    b_eff     = branch_eff[branch],
    retention = 72 + 0.3 * month + 4 * post + 0.2 * t_post + b_eff + rnorm(n(), 0, 4),
    branch    = factor(branch)
  )




Code
m_its <- lmer(retention ~ month + post + t_post + (1 | branch), data = df_its)

broom.mixed::tidy(m_its, effects = "fixed") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "ITS model: pre-trend (month), level jump (post), slope change (t_post). True values: 0.3, 4, 0.2.")

Pre-trend test
The ITS equivalent of the RDD density (McCrary) test is to check whether the pre-intervention trend is genuinely linear, or whether a non-linear pre-trend exists that could masquerade as a level jump. If the pre-trend in retention was already curving before month 16, the jump at the cutoff could reflect a pre-existing trend rather than the regulation.


Code
df_pre <- df_its |> filter(month < 16)
m_pretrend <- lmer(retention ~ month + I(month^2) + (1 | branch), data = df_pre)
broom.mixed::tidy(m_pretrend, effects = "fixed") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4,
               caption = "Pre-period model with quadratic term. If I(month^2) is far from zero, the pre-trend is curved and the level-jump interpretation is suspect.")

title: Applied Identification Strategies for Panel Data
text:
Section 4: Panel IV

When fixed effects are not enough
Unit fixed effects remove time-invariant confounders. But if a confounder varies both across units and across time — and is correlated with the predictor — FE alone is insufficient. Panel IV combines the within-unit differencing of FE with an instrument that shifts the endogenous predictor but has no direct path to the outcome.


Simulation: budgeting tool use and savings
We simulate 200 platform customers over 6 months. Customers voluntarily use a budgeting tool (endogenous — customers with higher saving disposition use it more). Platform encouragement push (amount the platform pushes tool reminders) serves as the instrument: it is relevant (push increases tool use), excludes directly (platform push affects savings only through tool use), and is as-good-as-randomly assigned at the feature level.


Code
n_c  <- 200
n_m  <- 6                               # months
base_saving    <- rnorm(n_c, 0, 5)     # unobserved saving disposition (quality analog)
platform_push  <- rnorm(10, 0, 2)[rep(1:10, each = n_c/10)]  # feature-level push intensity

df_piv <- expand_grid(customer = 1:n_c, month = 1:n_m) |>
  mutate(
    bs      = base_saving[customer],
    # Time-varying disposition shock (FE removes base_saving mean, not this shock)
    bs_tv   = bs + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),
    push    = platform_push[customer] + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5),  # customer-month realization
    # Budgeting tool usage: endogenous — higher disposition + higher push -> more usage
    tool_use = 20 + 2 * bs_tv + 3 * push + rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    # Savings rate: causal effect of tool_use = 0.4; also depends on disposition
    savings_rate = 5 + 0.4 * tool_use + 1.5 * bs_tv + rnorm(n(), 0, 3),
    customer = factor(customer),
    month    = factor(month)
  )


OLS + FE removes stable customer effects, but if saving disposition varies over time (a good-month disposition leads to more tool use AND more saving), fixed effects alone cannot isolate the causal effect of the tool.


Code
# OLS + FE: still biased by time-varying disposition-tool correlation
m_ols_fe <- lm(savings_rate ~ tool_use + customer + month, data = df_piv)

# Panel IV: instrument = platform push
m_iv <- ivreg(savings_rate ~ tool_use + customer + month | push + customer + month,
              data = df_piv)

# First-stage F-statistic
fs <- lm(tool_use ~ push + customer + month, data = df_piv)
fs_F <- summary(fs)$fstatistic[1]
cat("First-stage F on instrument:", round(fs_F, 1), "\n")


First-stage F on instrument: 14.4 





Panel IV: platform push as instrument for budgeting tool usage. True causal effect = 0.4 per unit of tool use. OLS + FE is biased by time-varying saving disposition (bs_tv), which customer fixed effects cannot remove. First-stage: platform push strongly predicts tool usage (F > 10). Exclusion: push affects savings only through the tool (by design of the instrument).

Std. Error

WarningWeak Instruments in Panel Data



Panel fixed effects remove between-unit variation and retain only within-unit variation. This can substantially weaken an instrument that looked strong in cross-sectional data: the platform push intensity varies mostly across feature groups, and much of that cross-group variation is soaked up by the customer fixed effects. Always check the first-stage \(F\)-statistic using the demeaned (within-transformed) data, not the raw data. The conventional threshold is \(F > 10\); for inference-robust methods (Anderson-Rubin test), the threshold matters less.
# Safe check: first stage on demeaned data via plm
pdata_piv   <- pdata.frame(df_piv |> mutate(cust_id=as.integer(customer), mo=as.integer(month)),
                             index=c("cust_id","mo"))
fs_within   <- plm(tool_use ~ push, data=pdata_piv, model="within", effect="twoways")
summary(fs_within)

title: Applied Identification Strategies for Panel Data
text:
Section 5: Time-Varying Propensity Score Matching
When units adopt a treatment at different waves — a staggered rollout rather than a single cutoff — the two-by-two DiD logic breaks down because the “post” period differs across treated units. Two-way FE with staggered adoption can produce negatively-weighted treatment effect estimates when treatment effects are heterogeneous across cohorts (the “negative weighting” problem documented by Callaway & Sant’Anna, 2021).
One practical alternative is time-varying propensity score matching, which handles staggered adoption explicitly:
Step 1: For each adoption wave \(w\), identify: - Households (or customers) that just enrolled in wave \(w\) (the “treated” at wave \(w\)). - Households that have not yet enrolled by wave \(w\) (the “not-yet-treated” controls).
Step 2: Compute the propensity score at wave \(w\) among eligible units:
glm(enrolled_now ~ lag_outcome + income + age + region,
    family = binomial,
    data   = eligible_at_wave_w)
Step 3: Match treated households to the most similar not-yet-treated households at that wave using nearest-neighbor matching within the wave-specific pool.
Step 4: Estimate the ATT on the matched sample, using the matched controls’ post-enrollment outcomes as the counterfactual.
This approach produces a cohort-specific ATT for each adoption wave, which can be aggregated into an overall ATT. It is conceptually equivalent to the Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) estimator (available in the did package) and is doubly robust when combined with outcome regression.






TipPS-Weighted DiD: Doubly Robust Panel Estimation



Combining time-varying PS weighting with DiD regression produces an estimator that is doubly robust: consistent if either (a) the propensity score model is correctly specified, or (b) parallel trends holds conditional on covariates. Neither assumption alone is sufficient for ordinary DiD; neither alone is sufficient for ordinary PSM. The combination of both provides extra insurance. See drdid package for implementation.

title: Module 5: Experimental Designs with Nesting
text:
Experiments Are Not Flat
A well-designed randomized experiment is often treated as the gold standard for causal inference. And it is — when properly analyzed. The problem is that most experiments are analyzed as if every observation is an independent draw from a single population. They are not.
Even the simplest between-subjects experiment has nesting baked in:

Participants are a sample from a population of possible participants, each carrying stable preferences, risk attitudes, and prior experience that shape their responses
Stimuli — product descriptions, price disclosures, policy messages, risk displays, or lottery gambles — are a sample from a population of possible stimuli, each with its own expected value, framing properties, and saliency
Conditions may be nested within advisors, coaching groups, platforms, or lab sites, introducing clustering at a level above the individual participant

When stimuli are treated as fixed — as if your 20 gamble descriptions are the only 20 that exist — the generalization to other stimuli is silent. Your p-values are too small because stimulus-level variance is being absorbed into the residual, artificially tightening standard errors.
A concrete JDM example: In a study of gain vs. loss framing, each participant sees multiple product offers (stimuli), some framed as gains and others as losses. The offers are sampled from a larger set of possible framings that vary in magnitude, probability, and domain. Ignoring stimulus-level clustering — treating each offer response as an independent observation rather than as one draw from a participant-by-stimulus interaction — inflates Type I error for the framing effect. The apparent precision of the estimate is false.
Judd, Westfall, & Kenny (2012, 2017) documented that this mistake is pervasive in social psychology and leads to systematic Type I error inflation. The same critique applies directly to JDM research using repeated-stimulus designs.
crumbs: 37  Module 5: Experimental Designs with Nesting

title: Module 5: Experimental Designs with Nesting
text:
What This Module Covers
The module is organized into three clusters, moving from design-structure modeling through inferential planning to handling real-world experimental imperfections.


Cluster 1 — Design Structure and Model Specification
Part 1: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments — Why stimuli are random, what happens when you treat them as fixed, and how to fix it with crossed random effects models in lme4. Every JDM experiment that presents multiple gambles, product messages, or policy stimuli to each participant requires this approach.
Part 2: Partially Nested Designs — When one condition has nesting and the other does not, standard MLM misspecifies the design. The Bauer et al. partially nested model handles this correctly. JDM example: when one condition receives advisor-led financial coaching sessions and the other receives a self-serve information module, the treatment arm has within-group clustering by advisor that the control arm entirely lacks. Standard MLM, which assumes symmetric nesting, will misattribute advisor-level variance and produce incorrect standard errors for the treatment effect.
Part 3: Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects — The Barr et al. (2013) vs. Matuschek et al. (2017) debate: how complex should your random effects structure be? When does complexity help and when does it hurt?
Part 4: Multi-Site Experiments — When the same experiment runs at multiple sites (labs, countries, platforms), sites introduce clustering. The many-labs design and how to model treatment effect heterogeneity across sites. JDM example: a multi-site framing study run across five university labs and two online platforms — site-level variance in base rates of risk-taking must be modeled, and the treatment effect estimate should reflect average heterogeneity across sites rather than a single-site result.


Cluster 2 — Planning and Inference
Part 5: Power Analysis for Nested Designs — Why standard power formulas are wrong for nested data, the role of ICC, simulation-based power analysis, and practical sample size guidance for JDM experiments with repeated stimuli or multi-site designs.
Part 6: Binary and Count Outcomes in Experiments — When experimental outcomes are binary (chose the risky option / chose the safe option; opted out of the default / remained enrolled) or counts (number of risky choices out of a block of ten), GLMMs with the correct link function are required. Logistic and Poisson mixed models with crossed random effects for participants and stimuli.
Part 7: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility — Standardized effect sizes for mixed models, \(R^2\) decomposition by level, translating log-odds to probability for binary JDM outcomes, and pre-registration practices that make nested-data analyses credible.


Cluster 3 — Imperfect Randomization and Quasi-Experimental Fixes
The final two parts form a self-contained mini-unit on what to do when randomization does not work exactly as planned.
Part 8: Non-Compliance — ITT and LATE — When participants are randomized but not all comply with their assigned condition, the naive treatment-vs-control comparison is diluted or biased. This part covers the intent-to-treat estimand (ITT), the complier average causal effect (LATE) via instrumental variables, the Wald estimator, and the compliance typology (compliers, always-takers, never-takers). JDM example: randomized assignment to a budgeting tool — some participants never activate the tool despite being assigned to the treatment condition (non-compliance). ITT = the effect of being offered the tool, averaged over compliers and non-compliers; LATE = the effect for those whose activation status changed because of the offer. The two estimands answer different questions and require different assumptions.
Part 9: Quasi-Experimental Methods for Applied Researchers — The broader toolkit for experiments with observational features. JDM examples: DiD logic applied to a WTP pre-post design where a subset of participants received an unexpected information shock between measurement occasions; IPW to correct for non-random dropout from a repeated risky-choice study where higher-risk participants dropped out at greater rates; PSM within the treatment arm to estimate dose-response effects of financial tool engagement (comparing heavy users to light users while controlling for pre-treatment risk profiles); RDD using a credit score threshold or account balance cutoff that determines eligibility for a financial product, enabling causal inference at the margin. Each method maps to a specific randomization failure and provides a principled remedy.

Parts 8 and 9 together cover the full arc from “randomization was imperfect” to “here is the estimand you can credibly claim and the method to estimate it.” Readers who have worked through Modules 1–5 will recognize how each quasi-experimental tool inherits from the broader mixed-model and identification framework built earlier in the workshop.

title: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments
text: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments
crumbs: 38  Crossed Random Effects in Experiments

title: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments
text:
The Stimuli-Are-Random Problem
Every JDM experiment that presents multiple stimuli — gain- and loss-framed messages, product descriptions, gamble pairs, disclosure formats, price offers, policy options — has the same structural feature: the stimuli you used are a sample from a larger population of possible stimuli.
A gain-frame study uses, say, 12 gain-framed messages. Those 12 were chosen (or written) by the researcher. Some turned out to be unusually compelling. Others fell flat. If you happened to write gain-framed messages that were particularly vivid and loss-framed messages that were blandly written, your “framing effect” captures both the actual psychological effect of framing and the luck of your specific stimulus draw.
The problem: If you treat your stimuli as fixed — as if these 12 messages were the only 12 that could ever represent gain framing — then stimulus-level variability is absorbed into the residual error term. The residual looks small and the treatment effect looks precise. But that precision is false.
The fix: Treat stimuli as a random factor, just like participants. Model both sources of random variability explicitly: participants vary in their baseline tendencies; stimuli vary in their baseline effectiveness. The treatment effect is estimated net of both.
crumbs: 38  Crossed Random Effects in Experiments

title: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments
text:
Crossed, Not Nested
In most within-subjects experiments, participants and stimuli are crossed: every participant sees multiple stimuli, and every stimulus is seen by multiple participants. Neither factor is nested within the other.
This is different from the nested structures in Modules 1–2. In a nested design, each participant belongs to one group and each observation belongs to one participant. In a crossed design, participants and stimuli form a matrix — each cell is a (participant × stimulus) observation:

Stimulus random effects capture stable differences in how stimuli perform (e.g., a particularly vivid message consistently gets higher responses). The treatment effect — gain vs. loss framing — is what remains after removing both sources of variance.
When participants only see a subset of stimuli, the design is partially crossed. The analysis is the same; lme4 handles incomplete designs automatically.

title: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments
section: Simulation: Gain vs. Loss Framing and WTP
text:
Simulation: Gain vs. Loss Framing and WTP
We simulate a framing experiment: 60 participants each see 12 of 24 gain/loss-framed messages describing financial product benefits. They rate their willingness to adopt the product. The true framing effect is +3 points (loss framing increases adoption intent). Both participants and messages have their own stable variance.


Code
n_participants <- 60
n_messages     <- 24  # 12 gain-framed, 12 loss-framed

participant_effects <- rnorm(n_participants, 0, 8)   # SD = 8 (large between-person spread)
message_effects     <- rnorm(n_messages, 0, 6)        # SD = 6 (meaningful between-message spread)
message_condition   <- rep(c("gain", "loss"), each = 12)

# Partial crossing: each participant sees approximately half the messages
set.seed(2025)
df_exp <- expand_grid(
  participant = 1:n_participants,
  message     = 1:n_messages
) |>
  slice_sample(prop = 0.5) |>   # each participant sees ~12 messages
  mutate(
    condition   = message_condition[message],
    p_eff       = participant_effects[participant],
    m_eff       = message_effects[message],
    WTP         = 50 + 3 * (condition == "loss") + p_eff + m_eff + rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    participant = factor(participant),
    message     = factor(message)
  )



Two models, two answers


Code
# Incorrect: ignores stimulus variance
m_wrong <- lmer(WTP ~ condition + (1 | participant), data = df_exp)

# Correct: both participant and message as crossed random effects
m_correct <- lmer(WTP ~ condition + (1 | participant) + (1 | message), data = df_exp)

bind_rows(
  broom.mixed::tidy(m_wrong,   effects = "fixed") |>
    filter(term == "conditionloss") |>
    mutate(model = "Incorrect: participant RE only\n(ignores message variance)"),
  broom.mixed::tidy(m_correct, effects = "fixed") |>
    filter(term == "conditionloss") |>
    mutate(model = "Correct: participant + message RE\n(crossed random effects)")
) |>
  select(model, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
    caption = "Ignoring message variance produces an overconfident SE. The correct crossed model reveals the true uncertainty about the framing effect across all possible messages of this type.")



Ignoring message variance produces an overconfident SE. The correct crossed model reveals the true uncertainty about the framing effect across all possible messages of this type.

The incorrect model looks more precise — but its SE is too small because it attributes stimulus-level variance to residual noise instead of a proper separate component. This is a false precision that will not replicate when a different message set is used.


Visualizing the two variance components


Code
# Extract variance components from the correct model
vc_df <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_correct)) |>
  filter(grp != "Residual") |>
  mutate(
    component = case_when(
      grp == "participant" ~ "Between-participant variance\n(stable individual tendencies)",
      grp == "message"     ~ "Between-message variance\n(stimulus quality differences)",
      TRUE                 ~ grp
    ),
    sd = sdcor
  )

vc_res <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_correct)) |>
  filter(grp == "Residual") |>
  mutate(component = "Within-cell residual\n(unexplained individual × message variation)", sd = sdcor)

vc_all <- bind_rows(vc_df, vc_res) |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, levels = c(
    "Between-participant variance\n(stable individual tendencies)",
    "Between-message variance\n(stimulus quality differences)",
    "Within-cell residual\n(unexplained individual × message variation)"
  )))

ggplot(vc_all, aes(x = component, y = sd, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1e3a5f", "#2d6a4f", "#cccccc")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Variance components: participant, message, and residual",
    subtitle = "The incorrect model collapses the message component into residual — shrinking the SE artificially",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "SD (variance component)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments
text:
The Judd–Westfall–Kenny (2012) Argument
Judd, Westfall & Kenny (2012) documented a systematic error in social psychology experiments: researchers treat stimuli (words, faces, messages, images) as fixed rather than random. They labeled this the “stimuli-as-fixed-effects fallacy.” The same problem applies directly to JDM research:

A study of risk communication using 8 gamble descriptions treats those 8 as the only possible gambles — when they are clearly a sample
A study of disclosure effects on WTP using 6 product descriptions generalizes implicitly to all product descriptions — but the model does not account for stimulus-level variance
A study of default effects using 4 enrollment forms treats those 4 forms as exhaustive — underestimating between-form variance

The consequence is systematic Type I error inflation that is not corrected by increasing sample size alone. Adding more participants does not help if the binding constraint is stimulus-level variance.
crumbs: 38  Crossed Random Effects in Experiments

title: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments
section: Power Depends on Both N and Number of Stimuli
text:
Power Depends on Both N and Number of Stimuli
Westfall, Kenny & Judd (2014) showed that in crossed designs, statistical power is jointly determined by the number of participants and the number of stimuli. With only a few stimuli, adding more participants eventually yields diminishing returns because stimulus-level variance remains the binding constraint.


Code
# Schematic: how SE changes with N_stimuli vs. N_participants
# (simplified illustration, not simulation-calibrated)
se_grid <- expand_grid(
  n_stim = c(4, 8, 16, 32),
  n_part = seq(20, 200, by = 20)
) |>
  mutate(
    # Approximate SE ∝ 1/sqrt(n_part) + 1/sqrt(n_stim), simplified
    approx_se = sqrt(64 / n_part + 36 / n_stim),
    n_stim    = factor(paste(n_stim, "stimuli"), levels = paste(c(4, 8, 16, 32), "stimuli"))
  )

ggplot(se_grid, aes(x = n_part, y = approx_se, color = n_stim, group = n_stim)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("#c0392b", "#e67e22", "#2d6a4f", "#1e3a5f"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "SE of treatment effect as function of N participants and N stimuli",
    subtitle = "With few stimuli, adding participants has limited impact. Expand the stimulus set.",
    x        = "Number of participants",
    y        = "Approximate SE of treatment effect"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)









Practical implication: If you are planning a framing experiment and you have only 6 message pairs, consider doubling the message set before doubling the participant count. The precision of your framing-effect estimate depends heavily on how many distinct stimuli you have sampled.

title: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments
text:
Assumptions






WarningAssumption: Stimuli Are a Representative Sample From the Population of Interest



Plain-language meaning: The crossed model generalizes the treatment effect to new participants and to new stimuli drawn from the same population. This is only valid if your stimuli were sampled in a way that represents the full range of relevant stimuli — not cherry-picked to maximize or demonstrate an effect.
What the model is assuming away: The possibility that you selected stimuli precisely because they produced the pattern you expected — in which case the stimulus “sample” is not a random draw from the population of all possible stimuli.
JDM example: A framing researcher writes 12 gain messages and 12 loss messages. If the loss messages were unconsciously written to be more concrete and vivid (because the researcher was more practiced at loss language), the between-condition difference reflects both framing and writing quality.
Experimental analog in observational work: In observational stimulus-response data (e.g., consumer responses to real advertisements), stimuli are not randomly sampled — they are produced by advertisers with incentives to optimize. The crossed model would still be appropriate for inference about the sample, but generalization to “all possible ads” requires caution.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “How were your stimuli selected? Were they piloted and retained based on effect-size criteria? If so, the crossed-effects estimate may overstate how well the manipulation generalizes.”
Observable warning sign: Between-stimulus variance that is unusually low (suggesting pre-selection of comparable stimuli) or unusually high (suggesting highly heterogeneous stimuli from different populations).
What to check: Report stimulus-level ICC: \(\sigma^2_{\text{message}} / (\sigma^2_{\text{message}} + \sigma^2_{\text{residual}})\). If it is effectively zero, message variance is negligible and the concern is less pressing. If it is large, the stimulus sample matters a lot and should be defended.
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The treatment effect estimate for these specific stimuli is still valid. Generalization to the population of stimuli depends on representativeness.








WarningAssumption: Random Effects for Participants and Stimuli Are Independent of the Manipulation



Plain-language meaning: The model assumes that which stimuli end up in the gain condition versus the loss condition is unrelated to their “natural strength” as stimuli. In other words, the assignment of stimuli to conditions was not influenced by stimulus quality.
What the model is assuming away: Any correlation between stimulus random intercepts and condition assignment — which would exist if, for example, researchers assigned their best-quality messages to the manipulation they expected to produce the larger effect.
JDM example: If a researcher piloted messages and assigned the most persuasive ones to the loss-frame condition (expecting loss aversion to need less help), the loss condition starts with a built-in quality advantage.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Were stimuli randomly assigned to conditions, or were they constructed for their assigned condition from the start? If constructed, the random-effects independence assumption requires that condition-specific writing quality is negligible.”
What to check: In a fully counterbalanced design (where each message can appear in either condition across participants), this assumption is guaranteed by design. In a design where stimuli were created for a specific condition, the assumption must be argued conceptually.

title: Crossed Random Effects in Experiments
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “You have only 8 messages per condition. Isn’t that too few to treat messages as random?” The answer is: too few for high power, yes — but that is an argument for adding more stimuli, not for treating the existing stimuli as fixed. Treating 8 messages as fixed asserts that those exact messages are the population of interest, which makes the result entirely non-generalizable. A small number of stimuli produces low power with correct random effects; it produces false precision with fixed effects.
Challenge 2: “Your message random effect variance is larger than your participant variance. Does that mean messages matter more than participants?” Not necessarily — it means there is more heterogeneity across your message set than across your participant sample. This could reflect genuine message quality differences, or it could reflect that your message set was less homogeneous than your participant pool. Either way, the correct model accounts for both.
Challenge 3: “Why not just average across messages and analyze at the participant level?” Averaging loses information and implicitly weights all messages equally, which is rarely justified. More importantly, it only corrects participant-level inference — it does not account for the possibility that the results are specific to this particular message set rather than generalizing to the population of possible messages. Averaging kills the second random effect.
