title: Partially Nested Designs
text: Partially Nested Designs

title: Partially Nested Designs
section: When Only One Condition Has Clustering
text:
When Only One Condition Has Clustering
Consider a financial coaching field experiment. The treatment group receives group financial coaching: 8 participants share a coach, 15 coaches total. The control group receives a self-serve information module — there is no coach and no shared group structure. Control participants are fully independent of each other.
This design is partially nested: only the treatment condition has a natural cluster structure.

Why this creates a modeling problem
If you fit a standard two-level model treating all participants the same way, you are forced into one of two bad choices:

Ignore clustering in the treatment group — deflating standard errors and inflating Type I error for the treatment effect
Apply random effects to all participants — misspecifying the control group, which has no actual clustering

Neither is honest about what the design actually looks like. The correct description of the design is asymmetric: one arm has coach-induced dependence; the other does not.


The design structure





flowchart TD
    A["Participants — N = 240"] --> B["Coaching condition\nN = 120"]
    A --> C["Self-serve condition\nN = 120"]
    B --> D["Coach 1\n8 participants"]
    B --> E["Coach 2\n8 participants"]
    B --> F["...Coach 15\n8 participants"]
    C --> G["Participant A\n(independent)"]
    C --> H["Participant B\n(independent)"]
    C --> I["...Participant N\n(independent)"]
    style D fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2d6a4f
    style E fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2d6a4f
    style F fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2d6a4f
    style G fill:#f0f0f0,stroke:#888888
    style H fill:#f0f0f0,stroke:#888888
    style I fill:#f0f0f0,stroke:#888888






Green boxes share a coach — their outcomes are correlated. Grey boxes are fully independent. A model that treats green and grey identically is wrong about both.


The key intuition
Each coach is a shared environment. A particularly effective coach lifts all eight of their clients’ outcomes together. A disengaged or poorly trained coach drags them all down. This coach-induced similarity is variance at the cluster level, not at the individual level. It inflates observed similarity within coaching groups beyond what you would expect from individual-level randomness alone.
The control group has no equivalent of this shared-environment effect. Each self-serve participant experiences the same information materials independently. There is no coach, no shared context, and no reason for outcomes to be correlated across control participants.

title: Partially Nested Designs
text:
Simulating a Partially Nested Design


Code
n_coaches    <- 15
n_per_group  <- 8
n_control    <- n_coaches * n_per_group  # same total N = 120

# Treatment group: participants nested in coaching groups
# Coach effects introduce within-group similarity
coach_effects <- rnorm(n_coaches, 0, 3)  # SD = 3 → ICC ≈ 0.20

df_treatment <- tibble(
  condition        = "coaching",
  coach            = rep(1:n_coaches, each = n_per_group),
  participant      = 1:(n_coaches * n_per_group),
  coach_eff        = rep(coach_effects, each = n_per_group),
  savings_increase = 5 + 5 + coach_eff + rnorm(n_coaches * n_per_group, 0, 6)
  # true mean = 10 (baseline 5 + treatment effect 5); coach effect varies around that
)

# Control group: independent participants — no coach, no shared structure
df_control <- tibble(
  condition        = "self_serve",
  coach            = NA_integer_,
  participant      = 1:n_control + max(df_treatment$participant),
  coach_eff        = 0,
  savings_increase = 5 + rnorm(n_control, 0, 6)
)

df_pn <- bind_rows(df_treatment, df_control)

title: Partially Nested Designs
section: Fitting the Partially Nested Model in lme4
text:
Fitting the Partially Nested Model in lme4
The trick is to create cluster IDs that correctly represent the design’s actual structure:

Coaching participants: share the coach ID
Control participants: each gets a unique “cluster” ID of their own — indicating no shared context

A random effect estimated on this ID variable will pick up coach-level variance in the coaching condition, but will estimate near-zero variance for control participants (because each has their own “cluster” and there is nothing to share).


Code
df_pn <- df_pn |>
  mutate(
    cluster_id = ifelse(condition == "coaching",
                        paste0("Coach", coach),
                        paste0("Ctrl", participant))
  )

# Partially nested: the cluster_id random effect operates only meaningfully
# in the coaching condition; control participants each have a singleton cluster
m_pn    <- lmer(savings_increase ~ condition + (1 | cluster_id), data = df_pn)

# Compare to naive model — ignores all clustering
m_naive <- lm(savings_increase ~ condition, data = df_pn)





Partially nested model: the SE for the coaching effect is larger than the naive model because coaching-group dependence is correctly accounted for. The naive model treats coaching groups as if participants were independent — producing an overconfident SE and inflated Type I error.


model
estimate
std.error
p.value








Visualizing coach-level variance
The coach random effects plot shows the between-coach spread. This is exactly the shared-environment variance that the naive model erroneously absorbed into the residual:


Code
# Extract BLUP estimates for coaching groups
re_df <- ranef(m_pn)$cluster_id |>
  rownames_to_column("cluster") |>
  rename(blup = `(Intercept)`) |>
  filter(str_starts(cluster, "Coach")) |>
  mutate(coach_id = as.integer(str_remove(cluster, "Coach"))) |>
  arrange(blup)

ggplot(re_df, aes(x = reorder(cluster, blup), y = blup)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#888888") +
  geom_point(color = "#2d6a4f", size = 3) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = cluster, y = 0, yend = blup),
               color = "#2d6a4f", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title    = "Estimated coach effects (random intercepts)",
    subtitle = "Coach-level deviations from the coaching-condition mean. Spread = ICC-generating variance.",
    x        = "Coach",
    y        = "Estimated coach effect (BLUP)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))









The spread in these estimates is what the naive model ignores. It treats participants from an effective coach and participants from an ineffective coach as if they were drawn from the same independent distribution — understating uncertainty about the coaching condition’s overall effect.

title: Partially Nested Designs
text:
The Observational–Experimental Bridge
The partial-nesting problem is not unique to experiments. It appears in observational studies whenever one subgroup has clustering and another does not. Common examples:

Branch-level program availability: households near a branch offering a financial planning service are clustered within that branch environment; households without branch access are independent
Advisor assignment in financial services: clients assigned to human advisors share an advisor context; clients in a self-service portal do not
Message delivery via teams: consumers receiving a financial message through a group workshop share a facilitator; those receiving it individually do not

In each case, the same diagnostic question applies: does one group have shared context that induces outcome correlation, while the other group does not? If yes, the partially nested model is the right choice, whether the clustering arose from experimental design or from a naturally occurring asymmetry in the observational data.

title: Partially Nested Designs
text:
Assumptions






WarningAssumption: Correct Identification of Which Condition is Clustered



Plain-language meaning: You must correctly specify which condition has clustering and which does not. The model is asymmetric by design — you are asserting that one arm has group-level variance and the other does not. Getting this backwards or applying symmetric random effects is a misspecification.
What the model is assuming away: The possibility that control participants also share latent clustering — common recruiters, common geographic contexts, or common information environments that induce correlation even without an explicit group structure.
JDM example: In this coaching experiment, control participants all receive the same self-serve module via an online platform. If the platform itself introduces shared behavior (e.g., participants recruited through the same community forum tend to be more financially engaged), control outcomes may also be correlated despite the absence of an explicit coach.
Experimental analog in observational work: In an observational study comparing advisor-served versus self-directed investors, the self-directed group may still share regional or platform-level environments that induce dependence.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “How do you know the control group is truly unstructured? Could shared recruitment channels, neighborhoods, or platform environments create clustering in the ‘independent’ arm?”
Observable warning sign: If the ICC for control-arm residuals is nontrivially positive after fitting the partially nested model — or if control participants from identifiable subgroups look more similar than chance — the flat-variance assumption for the control arm may be incorrect.
What to check: Fit a version with cluster random effects in both arms and compare the estimated control-arm ICC to zero. If it is detectably nonzero, consider modeling residual clustering there too.
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The direction and rough magnitude of the treatment effect remain interpretable. The standard error may be underestimated if the control arm also has unmodeled clustering.








WarningAssumption: Homogeneity of Within-Cluster Variance



Plain-language meaning: The standard partially nested model assumes the residual variance (after removing coach effects) is the same in the coaching and self-serve groups. Only the random-effect variance differs across conditions; the individual-level noise is treated as equivalent.
What the model is assuming away: The possibility that the coaching experience fundamentally changes how much outcome variance exists within each coaching group — for example, that effective coaches reduce individual variation (by standardizing their approach) or that the coaching process introduces new individual-level idiosyncrasies.
JDM example: If coaching sessions involve highly interactive financial goal-setting, some participants may be very responsive while others remain unmoved — creating greater within-group residual variance in the coaching arm than in the self-serve arm, where everyone receives the same neutral module.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Why should individual-level noise be the same in a group coaching experience as in a passive self-serve module? Coach interactions could easily change within-person variability.”
Observable warning sign: Standard deviations of residuals that differ noticeably across conditions in a simple linear model, or a Levene test for residual variance equality.
What to check: Compare within-group residual standard deviations across conditions. If they differ substantially, fit a heteroskedastic residual model (e.g., using nlme::lme() with weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | condition)) to allow different residual variances.
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The treatment effect estimate is still interpretable. The standard errors for the treatment effect may be slightly off; the heteroskedastic version is preferred if residual variances clearly differ.








WarningAssumption: Coach Effects Are Exchangeable (Random, Not Systematic)



Plain-language meaning: The model treats coach effects as draws from a common distribution rather than as fixed, systematic differences. This is appropriate when coaches are a sample from a broader population of potential coaches and you want to generalize the treatment effect beyond this specific set of 15 coaches.
What the model is assuming away: The possibility that coaches were deliberately selected to differ in ways that matter (e.g., some coaches were selected because they were known to be ineffective, as a robustness test), or that coach assignment was not independent of participant characteristics.
JDM example: If higher-baseline-savings participants were assigned to better-trained coaches (perhaps as a program-efficiency decision), the coach random effects are confounded with participant pre-treatment characteristics.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Were coaches randomly assigned to groups, or were they matched to participant characteristics? If matched, the coach random effect is conflated with participant-level selection.”
What to check: Verify that coach assignment was independent of participant characteristics. If there is coach–participant matching in the design, include matched participant characteristics as covariates, or reframe the coach effect as fixed.

title: Partially Nested Designs
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “Why not just include coach fixed effects?” Fixed effects for coaches would absorb all between-coach variance and correctly account for clustering — but they consume 14 degrees of freedom, cannot generalize to new coaches, and cannot estimate the between-coach variance component that characterizes the program’s implementation fidelity. Random effects are preferred when coaches are a sample from a population and the goal is generalizable inference about the coaching condition overall.
Challenge 2: “Your SE is bigger with the partially nested model — how do I know you are not just being conservative arbitrarily?” The partially nested SE is not arbitrary conservatism — it is a consequence of the design. Participants within a coaching group are not independent sources of evidence about the coaching condition; they are partially redundant because they share a coach. The effective sample size for the coaching condition is n coaching groups, not n × 8 individual participants. The inflated SE correctly reflects that the design has less statistical power than naive sample sizes suggest.
Challenge 3: “What if between-coach differences just reflect participant sorting into coaching groups?” If participants self-selected coaches rather than being randomly assigned, the coach random effect conflates coach quality with the characteristics of coach-seekers. In the experimental context here, participants are randomly assigned to coaches — so the coach effects are not confounded with pre-existing participant differences. In an observational study with self-selected coaches, this concern would require explicit investigation.

title: Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects
text: Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects
crumbs: 40  Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects

title: Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects
text:
The Debate
In 2013, Barr, Levy, Scheepers, & Tily published an influential paper titled “Random Effects Structure for Confirmatory Hypothesis Testing: Keep It Maximal.” Their argument:

To control Type I error at the nominal level, researchers should include the maximal random effects structure — every random slope that is justified by the experimental design.

In a within-subjects design where every participant sees every condition, you must include a random slope for condition by participants. Omitting this random slope will produce anti-conservative p-values.
Two years later, Matuschek, Kliegl, Vasishth, Baayen, & Bates (2017) pushed back in a paper titled “Balancing Type I Error and Power in Linear Mixed Models.” Their argument:

Maximal models frequently fail to converge or produce degenerate variance components. Over-parameterized models can actually have worse power than well-specified parsimonious models. Use likelihood ratio tests to decide what to include.

Both papers are correct. The question is when each applies.
crumbs: 40  Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects

title: Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects
text:
Why Maximal Models Can Fail


Code
# Simulate a within-subjects design
# Each participant sees each condition 4 times (trials)
# 40 participants × 3 conditions × 4 trials = 480 observations
# Random effects needed: 40 × 3 = 120 — well below 480
n_participants <- 40
n_conditions   <- 3
n_trials       <- 4

participant_intercepts <- rnorm(n_participants, 50, 8)
# Small (but nonzero) random slopes
participant_slopes     <- rnorm(n_participants, 0, 0.5)

df_within <- expand_grid(
  participant = 1:n_participants,
  condition   = 1:n_conditions,
  trial       = 1:n_trials
) |>
  mutate(
    condition_eff = c(-2, 0, 2)[condition],  # condition effect
    p_slope       = participant_slopes[participant],
    Y = participant_intercepts[participant] + condition_eff +
        p_slope * condition_eff + rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    participant = factor(participant),
    condition   = factor(condition)
  )

# Maximal model
m_max <- lmer(Y ~ condition + (condition | participant),
              data    = df_within,
              control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

# Does it converge?
library(performance)
check_convergence(m_max)

title: Maximal vs. Parsimonious Random Effects
text:
The Decision Framework
The current consensus among methodologists:






NoteWhen to Use Maximal Random Effects




Within-subjects experimental manipulations: Always include random slopes for within-subjects factors. This is the critical case. Barr et al. (2013) are correct: omitting random slopes for within-subject conditions inflates Type I error.
When theory or pilot data suggests heterogeneous effects: If you have prior reason to believe the treatment effect varies substantially across participants, include the random slope.
Large samples: With enough data, complex models converge and the efficiency loss from over-parameterization is small.









NoteWhen to Simplify (Parsimonious)




Convergence failures: If the maximal model does not converge, you must simplify. Start by removing the correlation between random intercept and slope ((1 | participant) + (0 + condition | participant)). Then consider removing the random slope itself.
Degenerate variance components: If the random slope variance is estimated at exactly zero (or very near), it is contributing nothing and can be dropped.
Very small variance components: Use an LRT to test whether the random slope significantly improves fit. If not, the parsimonious model is appropriate.

WarningAssumption: The Random Effects Structure Matches the Design



What it means: The random effects you include should reflect the actual nesting structure of your design. A random slope for a between-subjects factor makes no statistical sense (between-subjects factors cannot vary within a subject).
Common mistake: Including a random slope for a between-subjects condition. This will either produce a degenerate model or absorb all variance in a nonsensical way.
How to check: For each predictor, ask: does this variable vary within the grouping unit (participant, stimulus)? If yes, it can have a random slope for that unit. If no (between-subjects), it cannot.

title: Multi-Site Experiments
text: Multi-Site Experiments

title: Multi-Site Experiments
text:
Generalizability is a Nesting Problem
The replication crisis in psychology revealed that many findings were fragile — they held at one university, with one sample, run by one experimenter, but failed to replicate elsewhere. The problem is that site is a nesting variable that standard analysis ignores.
A multi-site experiment (also called a many-labs design) runs the same study across multiple locations: different universities, countries, online platforms, or time periods. Each site contributes data. Sites are treated as a random sample from a larger population of sites.
This design answers a richer question: not “does this effect occur at location X?” but “does this effect occur, on average, across the population of contexts?” And it allows you to ask: how much does the effect size vary across sites?

title: Multi-Site Experiments
text:
The Model
Sites are random. The treatment effect may vary across sites (cross-level interaction between treatment and site).
\[Y_{ijk} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{10} \text{Treat}_{ij} + u_{0k} + u_{1k} \text{Treat}_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}\]
Where: - \(k\) = site; \(j\) = participant; \(i\) = observation - \(u_{0k}\): site-level random intercept (baseline differences across sites) - \(u_{1k}\): site-level random slope for treatment (heterogeneity in treatment effect) - \(\gamma_{10}\): average treatment effect across sites


Code
n_sites       <- 20
n_per_site    <- 40  # 20 treatment, 20 control

site_intercepts <- rnorm(n_sites, 50, 5)   # sites differ in baseline
site_effects    <- rnorm(n_sites, 5, 3)    # treatment effect varies across sites
# Average effect = 5; some sites show 8, some show 2

df_ml <- expand_grid(
  site = 1:n_sites,
  participant = 1:n_per_site
) |>
  mutate(
    treatment   = rep(c(rep(0, 20), rep(1, 20)), n_sites),
    site_base   = site_intercepts[site],
    site_effect = site_effects[site],
    outcome     = site_base + site_effect * treatment + rnorm(n(), 0, 6),
    site        = factor(site)
  )




Code
# Random intercepts and slopes for sites
m_ml <- lmer(outcome ~ treatment + (treatment | site), data = df_ml)

broom.mixed::tidy(m_ml, effects = "fixed") |>

title: Multi-Site Experiments
text:
The ICC for Treatment Effects
The random slope for treatment tells you how much the effect varies across sites. The I² statistic (from meta-analysis) provides a related measure: what proportion of the total variation in effect size estimates is due to genuine heterogeneity vs. sampling error?


Code
# Variance of the treatment effect across sites

cat("Standard deviation of treatment effect across sites:",
    round(sqrt(var_treatment_effect), 2), "\n")

    round(fixef(m_ml)["treatment"] - 2*sqrt(var_treatment_effect), 1),
    "to",
    round(fixef(m_ml)["treatment"] + 2*sqrt(var_treatment_effect), 1),
    "across sites\n")


Effect ranges approximately from -0.4 to 10.4 across sites








WarningAssumption: Sites are a Representative Sample



What it means: The multi-site model generalizes to the population of sites from which your sites were drawn. If your 20 labs are all top-10 research universities, the results generalize to that population — not to community colleges, online platforms, or international contexts.
How to check: Describe your site-selection process. Were sites systematically sampled? Opportunistically recruited? The inference should match the selection.








WarningAssumption: Treatment Procedure is Comparable Across Sites



What it means: The “treatment” must be operationally equivalent across sites. If different labs implemented the procedure differently — different materials, different timing, different experimenter instructions — site-to-site variability reflects procedure differences, not true effect heterogeneity.
How to check: Pre-specify and enforce standardized protocols. Measure implementation fidelity. Include implementation fidelity as a moderator.

title: Power Analysis for Nested Designs
text: Power Analysis for Nested Designs
crumbs: 42  Power Analysis for Nested Designs

title: Power Analysis for Nested Designs
section: Why Standard Power Formulas Are Wrong
text:
Why Standard Power Formulas Are Wrong
Standard power formulas (Cohen’s power tables, G*Power) assume independent observations. They compute: given my expected effect size and desired power, how many participants do I need?
In nested data, this question is incomplete. You also need to know: - How many clusters? (classrooms, firms, sites, therapists) - How many observations per cluster? - What is the ICC? (how similar are observations within clusters)
The ICC and cluster size together determine the design effect (DEFF), which shrinks your effective sample size:
\[N_{effective} = \frac{N}{1 + (n_{cluster} - 1) \times \text{ICC}}\]
Ignoring this leads to severely underpowered studies.
crumbs: 42  Power Analysis for Nested Designs

title: Power Analysis for Nested Designs
text:
The ICC-Power Relationship


Code
# Power as a function of ICC, for a fixed N = 300 in clusters of 15
compute_power <- function(icc, n_total = 300, cluster_size = 15, effect = 0.3, alpha = 0.05) {
  deff    <- 1 + (cluster_size - 1) * icc
  n_eff   <- n_total / deff
  # Two-sample t-test power with effective N
  power.t.test(n = n_eff / 2, delta = effect, sd = 1, sig.level = alpha)$power
}

icc_vals <- seq(0, 0.5, by = 0.01)
power_vals <- sapply(icc_vals, compute_power)

tibble(ICC = icc_vals, Power = power_vals) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ICC, y = Power)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1e3a5f", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e63946") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.35, y = 0.82, label = "80% power threshold",
           color = "#e63946", size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "Power declines as ICC increases (N = 300, cluster size = 15)",
    subtitle = "Even modest ICC substantially reduces effective power",
    x        = "ICC",
    y        = "Statistical Power"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)









At ICC = 0, you have the expected power for 300 independent observations. At ICC = 0.2, power drops below 80% — you would need more observations to compensate.






WarningDesign-Effect Conversion Is an Approximation



The design-effect formula DEFF = 1 + (m − 1) × ICC assumes equal cluster sizes and that assignment is at the cluster level. It is a useful heuristic for back-of-envelope planning, but it can mislead in several common situations:

Unequal cluster sizes: Power is lower than the equal-size formula predicts when cluster sizes vary substantially.
Assignment below the cluster level: In within-subjects designs (participants × stimuli), DEFF does not straightforwardly apply — you need to account for the stimulus-level random effect separately.
Multiple random effects: Three-level designs have two ICCs; collapsing to a single design effect loses information.

For decision-quality power planning — grant applications, pre-registrations, trial designs — use simulation under your exact assignment unit, cluster structure, and analysis model (see the simulation section below). The design-effect shortcut is a starting point, not a final answer.
crumbs: 42  Power Analysis for Nested Designs

title: Power Analysis for Nested Designs
text:
Simulation-Based Power Analysis
For complex nested designs, analytic formulas do not always exist. The gold standard is simulation-based power analysis: generate data from the assumed DGP, fit the model, check whether the effect is significant, repeat 1000 times.


Code
simulate_power <- function(n_clusters, n_per_cluster, icc,
                            true_effect = 0.3, n_sims = 500) {
  sigma_between <- sqrt(icc)
  sigma_within  <- sqrt(1 - icc)

  p_values <- replicate(n_sims, {
    # Simulate two groups of clusters
    n_c <- ceiling(n_clusters / 2)
    cluster_effects <- rnorm(n_clusters, 0, sigma_between)

    df <- tibble(
      cluster = rep(1:n_clusters, each = n_per_cluster),
      group   = ifelse(cluster <= n_c, 0, 1)
    ) |>
      mutate(
        Y = true_effect * group + cluster_effects[cluster] +
            rnorm(n(), 0, sigma_within)
      )

    tryCatch({
      m <- lmer(Y ~ group + (1 | cluster), data = df, REML = FALSE)
      coef(summary(m))["group", "Pr(>|t|)"]
    }, error = function(e) NA_real_,
       warning = function(w) {
         m <- lmer(Y ~ group + (1 | cluster), data = df, REML = FALSE)
         tryCatch(coef(summary(m))["group", "Pr(>|t|)"],
                  error = function(e) NA_real_)
       })
  })
  p_values <- p_values[!is.na(p_values)]

  mean(p_values < 0.05)
}

# Power across different designs
designs <- expand_grid(
  n_clusters      = c(10, 20, 30, 40),
  n_per_cluster   = c(10, 20),
  icc             = c(0.05, 0.15)
) |>
  mutate(
    power = pmap_dbl(
      list(n_clusters, n_per_cluster, icc),
      ~simulate_power(..1, ..2, ..3, n_sims = 200)  # reduce for speed
    ),
    total_N = n_clusters * n_per_cluster,
    design  = paste0("ICC=", icc, ", n/cluster=", n_per_cluster)
  )

ggplot(designs, aes(x = n_clusters, y = power, color = design, linetype = design)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dotted", color = "gray50") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title    = "Power by number of clusters (simulated)",
    subtitle = "Effect size d = 0.3; n_sims = 200 per design",
    x        = "Number of Clusters",
    y        = "Power",
    color    = "Design", linetype = "Design"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

title: Power Analysis for Nested Designs
section: The simr Package for Complex Designs
text:
The simr Package for Complex Designs
For multilevel models with random slopes, crossed random effects, or other complex structures, the simr package provides a convenient simulation-based power analysis directly from a fitted model:


Code
library(simr)

# Fit a model with your expected parameters
m_pilot <- lmer(Y ~ group + (1 | cluster),
                data = your_pilot_data)

# Change the effect size to your expected value
fixef(m_pilot)["group"] <- 0.3

# Simulate power for different sample sizes
power_curve <- powerCurve(m_pilot,
                           along = "cluster",   # vary number of clusters
                           nsim  = 200)
plot(power_curve)
crumbs: 42  Power Analysis for Nested Designs

title: Power Analysis for Nested Designs
text:
Key Takeaways for Power Planning






NoteRules of Thumb




More clusters > more per cluster when ICC is high. If ICC = 0.20, doubling the number of clusters gains much more power than doubling the size of each cluster.
The ICC threshold: If ICC > 0.10 and cluster size > 10, standard power formulas underestimate required N by 50–100%.
For crossed designs (participants × stimuli): Power depends on both the number of participants and the number of stimuli. Westfall, Kenny & Judd (2014) showed that many published studies are severely underpowered on the stimulus side.
Collect pilot ICC estimates: Run a small pilot study and compute the ICC before committing to a full design.

title: Binary and Count Outcomes in Experiments
section: When Experimental Outcomes Are Not Continuous
text:
When Experimental Outcomes Are Not Continuous
JDM experiments frequently produce non-continuous outcomes:

Binary choices: Did the participant opt into the default? Choose the risky gamble? Adopt the recommended product?
Counts within a block: How many of 10 gambles did the participant accept? How many disclosure warnings did the consumer respond to?
Binary flags: Did the household enroll in automatic savings? Did the participant choose the gain-framed option?

Fitting a standard linear mixed model to these outcomes is not just statistically suboptimal — it misspecifies the data-generating process. The probability of opting in cannot genuinely be negative, but a linear model will predict it below zero for low-baseline participants. The count of risky choices in a 10-gamble block is bounded above at 10, but a linear model will sometimes predict above that bound.
Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) handle this correctly. The nesting structure — observations within participants, participants possibly nested in groups or crossed with stimuli — is modeled with the same random effects as before. The difference is the link function (which maps the linear predictor to the outcome scale) and the distributional family (which describes how the outcomes are distributed given the mean).
crumbs: 43  Binary and Count Outcomes in Experiments

title: Binary and Count Outcomes in Experiments
section: What Is a Link Function? A Plain-Language Visual
text:
What Is a Link Function? A Plain-Language Visual
Before diving into models, it helps to see what a link function actually does. The link function is what converts the linear predictor (a number that can take any value, positive or negative) into the scale of the outcome (which has a restricted range — a probability must be between 0 and 1; a count must be non-negative).


Code
x_seq <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 200)

df_links <- bind_rows(
  # Identity link (linear model): predicted value = linear predictor (no constraint)
  tibble(
    linear_predictor = x_seq,
    predicted        = x_seq,
    link  = "Identity link\n(Linear model — continuous outcome)",
    note  = "No constraint: predicted value\ncan be negative or > 1"
  ),
  # Logit link (logistic model): maps log-odds to probability ∈ (0, 1)
  tibble(
    linear_predictor = x_seq,
    predicted        = plogis(x_seq),
    link  = "Logit link\n(Logistic model — binary 0/1 outcome)",
    note  = "S-curve: predicted stays in (0, 1)\nSlope flattest at extremes"
  ),
  # Log link (Poisson model): maps log-rate to non-negative count
  tibble(
    linear_predictor = x_seq,
    predicted        = exp(x_seq),
    link  = "Log link\n(Poisson model — count outcome \u2265 0)",
    note  = "Exponential: predicted always positive\nVariance scales with mean"
  )
) |>
  mutate(link = factor(link, levels = unique(link)))

ggplot(df_links, aes(x = linear_predictor, y = predicted)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.4, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_hline(data = tibble(link = factor("Logit link\n(Logistic model — binary 0/1 outcome)",
                                          levels = levels(df_links$link)),
                            y = c(0, 1)),
             aes(yintercept = y), color = "#e63946", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(data = tibble(link = factor("Log link\n(Poisson model — count outcome \u2265 0)",
                                          levels = levels(df_links$link)),
                            y = 0),
             aes(yintercept = y), color = "#e63946", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", color = "#aaa", linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ link, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title    = "Three link functions: how the linear predictor maps to the outcome scale",
    subtitle = "Red dashed lines = constraints on the outcome (0/1 for binary; \u22650 for counts)\nThe curve between the linear predictor (x-axis) and predicted value (y-axis) IS the link function",
    x = "Linear predictor (\u03b2\u2080 + \u03b2\u2081X + random effects)",
    y = "Predicted outcome value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10.5),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))









Why this matters for interpretation:

The identity link (linear model) produces a straight line: a one-unit increase in X always shifts the predicted outcome by the same amount (\(\beta_1\)), regardless of where you are on the scale.
The logit link produces an S-curve: the same log-odds change (\(\beta_1\)) produces a smaller probability change when the baseline probability is near 0 or 1, and a larger change when it is near 0.5. This is why odds ratios do not translate directly to probability differences without knowing the baseline.
The log link produces an exponential curve: the same log-rate change (\(\beta_1\)) produces a larger count change when the baseline count is high. This is why Poisson models produce rate ratios, not count differences.

The experimental implication: in a GLMM, the fixed effect \(\beta_1\) lives on the link scale (log-odds or log-rate), not the outcome scale. Always report both the link-scale estimate (for comparability and meta-analysis) and the back-transformed predicted outcome (for interpretability).
crumbs: 43  Binary and Count Outcomes in Experiments

title: Binary and Count Outcomes in Experiments
section: Part 1: Binary Outcomes — Logistic Mixed Model
text:
Part 1: Binary Outcomes — Logistic Mixed Model

The model
For a binary outcome \(Y_{ij} \in \{0,1\}\) at trial \(i\) for participant \(j\) in a within-subjects design:
\[\text{logit}\bigl(P(Y_{ij} = 1)\bigr) = \beta_0 + u_{0j} + \beta_1 \cdot \text{condition}_{ij}\]
The random intercept \(u_{0j}\) captures stable individual differences in baseline response tendency — some participants are generally more risk-accepting or more opt-in-prone than others. Omitting this term ignores the within-person dependence from repeated measurements, deflating standard errors and inflating Type I error.


Example: Loss framing and risky financial choices
We simulate a within-subjects framing experiment. 80 participants each evaluate 16 gambles — half framed as potential gains (“Win $200 with probability 0.5; win nothing otherwise”), half framed as potential losses (“Lose nothing with probability 0.5; lose $200 otherwise”). The outcome is binary: did the participant accept the gamble (1) or decline (0)?
The true framing effect is an odds ratio of 1.8: loss-framed gambles have 80% higher odds of acceptance (consistent with loss aversion driving risk-seeking under losses). Participants differ substantially in their baseline risk tolerance.


Code
n_participants <- 80
n_trials_each  <- 8   # 8 gain-framed + 8 loss-framed trials per person

u0_person <- rnorm(n_participants, 0, 1.2)   # individual risk tolerance differences

df_gamble <- expand_grid(
  participant = 1:n_participants,
  framing     = c("gain", "loss"),
  trial       = 1:n_trials_each
) |>
  mutate(
    u0            = u0_person[participant],
    framing_dummy = as.integer(framing == "loss"),
    log_odds      = -0.5 + u0 + 0.59 * framing_dummy,   # log(1.8) ≈ 0.59
    prob          = plogis(log_odds),
    accepted      = rbinom(n(), 1, prob),
    participant   = factor(participant),
    framing       = factor(framing, levels = c("gain", "loss"))
  )

df_gamble |>
  group_by(framing) |>
  summarise(
    n_trials       = n(),
    acceptance_rate = mean(accepted),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Observed gamble acceptance rates by framing condition")

Fitting the logistic mixed model

m_gamble <- glmer(
  accepted ~ framing + (1 | participant),
  data   = df_gamble,
  family = binomial
)

broom.mixed::tidy(m_gamble, effects = "fixed", exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Framing effect as odds ratio. True OR = 1.8; loss framing increases gamble acceptance odds."
  )

Translating to the probability scale
Odds ratios are the correct internal currency of the logistic model — but they are unintuitive. Report predicted probabilities for audiences not comfortable with odds:


Code
preds_gamble <- ggpredict(m_gamble, terms = "framing", type = "fixed")

plot(preds_gamble) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#1e3a5f", "#e63946")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Predicted gamble acceptance by framing condition",
    subtitle = "Marginal predictions (averaging over individual risk tolerance)",
    x        = "Framing condition",
    y        = "Predicted probability of accepting gamble"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)











The nonlinearity of marginal effects
A constant odds ratio translates to different probability differences depending on the baseline probability. The same OR of 1.8 produces a larger absolute increase in acceptance when the baseline probability is 0.5 than when it is near 0 or 1. This means:

Sub-populations with different baseline risk tolerance will show different absolute probability effects of framing — even if the log-odds effect is homogeneous.
A single marginal probability difference from a regression table is only a population-average summary, not a universal statement about all participants.



Code
tibble(
  baseline_logodds = seq(-3, 3, by = 0.25),
  baseline_prob    = plogis(baseline_logodds),
  treatment_prob   = plogis(baseline_logodds + log(1.8)),
  prob_difference  = plogis(baseline_logodds + log(1.8)) - plogis(baseline_logodds)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = baseline_prob, y = prob_difference)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3, color = "#1e3a5f") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#888") +
  labs(
    title    = "Same log-odds effect → different probability differences by baseline",
    subtitle = "OR = 1.8 (log-odds effect = 0.59). Probability difference peaks near p = 0.5.",
    x        = "Baseline probability of accepting gamble",
    y        = "Probability increase due to loss framing"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

title: Binary and Count Outcomes in Experiments
section: Part 2: Count Outcomes — Poisson and Negative Binomial Mixed Models
text:
Part 2: Count Outcomes — Poisson and Negative Binomial Mixed Models

The model
For a count outcome \(Y_{ij} \geq 0\) (e.g., number of risky choices out of a block of 10 gambles):
\[\log\bigl(E[Y_{ij}]\bigr) = \beta_0 + u_{0j} + \beta_1 \cdot \text{condition}_{ij}\]
Exponentiating \(\beta_1\) gives the rate ratio — the multiplicative factor by which the expected count changes in the treatment condition relative to control.


Example: Information disclosure and count of risky choices
We simulate a between-subjects experiment: 100 participants (50 per arm) complete a block of 10 gambles. The control arm receives standard framing; the treatment arm receives an information disclosure showing the expected value of each gamble. Disclosures are expected to reduce risky choice frequency: true rate ratio = 0.65 (35% reduction in accepted gambles).


Code
n_per_cond <- 50

df_risky <- tibble(
  participant = 1:(n_per_cond * 2),
  condition   = rep(c("control", "disclosure"), each = n_per_cond)
) |>
  mutate(
    u0          = rnorm(n(), 0, 0.4),

When Poisson is not enough: overdispersion
In within-subjects designs, the same participant makes repeated choices across multiple blocks. Individual heterogeneity generates more variance than a Poisson model allows — variance exceeds the mean. This overdispersion requires a negative binomial family:

n_par_within  <- 60
n_blocks      <- 6   # 6 blocks of 10 gambles per condition

  condition   = c("control", "disclosure"),

  mutate(

    risky_count = rpois(n(), mu * phi),
    participant = factor(participant),
    condition  = factor(condition, levels = c("control", "disclosure"))
  )

m_nb_within <- glmmTMB(
  risky_count ~ condition + (1 | participant),
  data   = df_risky_within,
  family = nbinom2
)

section: Part 3: Mixed Factorial Designs with Non-Normal Outcomes
text:
Part 3: Mixed Factorial Designs with Non-Normal Outcomes
Many JDM experiments combine a between-subjects factor (e.g., standard vs. gain-frame disclosure) with a within-subjects factor (e.g., high-stakes vs. low-stakes gamble blocks). When outcomes are binary or counts, GLMMs handle this naturally.


Code
n_par_mf <- 100   # 50 per between-subjects condition
n_items   <- 4    # items per within-subjects condition

df_mf <- expand_grid(
  participant  = 1:n_par_mf,
  stakes       = c("low", "high"),
  item         = 1:n_items
) |>
  mutate(
    disclosure = ifelse(participant <= 50, "standard", "gain_frame"),
    u0         = rnorm(n_par_mf, 0, 0.9)[participant],
    log_odds   = -0.3
      + u0
      + 0.5 * (stakes == "high")                              # high stakes increases risk-seeking
      + 0.4 * (disclosure == "gain_frame")                    # gain frame shifts toward acceptance
      + 0.3 * (stakes == "high") * (disclosure == "gain_frame"), # interaction
    prob          = plogis(log_odds),
    chose_risky   = rbinom(n(), 1, prob),
    participant   = factor(participant),
    stakes        = factor(stakes, levels = c("low", "high")),
    disclosure    = factor(disclosure, levels = c("standard", "gain_frame"))
  )

m_mf <- glmer(
  chose_risky ~ stakes * disclosure + (1 | participant),
  data   = df_mf,
  family = binomial
)

broom.mixed::tidy(m_mf, effects = "fixed", exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Mixed factorial GLMM: stakes × disclosure framing on risky choice (odds ratios). Interaction OR > 1 means the disclosure effect is larger under high stakes."
  )

title: Binary and Count Outcomes in Experiments
text:
Assumptions






WarningAssumption: Correct Link Function and Distributional Family



Plain-language meaning: The model assumes that log-odds (logistic) or log-count (Poisson/NB) are linearly related to predictors. This is a reasonable default for most JDM outcomes, but the choice of family should match how you believe the outcomes were generated.
What the model is assuming away: The possibility that outcomes cluster near boundaries (very high or very low acceptance rates) in ways the standard logit link fits poorly, or that counts have structural excess zeros (many participants who never accept any gamble).
JDM example: If the gamble task is very easy and all participants accept most gambles (base rate near 0.95), the logit model is working in the nonlinear tails where slight misspecification matters more. A complementary log-log link might fit better.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “You used a logistic model — but with acceptance rates consistently above 90%, all your odds ratios are in the highly compressed region of the probability scale. Can you verify the link function is appropriate?”
Observable warning sign: Predicted probabilities consistently near 0 or 1; the model struggling to converge; or large odds ratios that translate to tiny probability differences.
What to check: Plot observed proportions against predicted probabilities. For count outcomes, compare the observed distribution of counts to the predicted distribution from the fitted model. Check the dispersion ratio (should be near 1.0 for Poisson; switch to negative binomial if > 1.5).
What claim survives if the assumption is doubtful: The direction of the effect is usually robust. The exact magnitude on the probability scale may be sensitive to the link function when outcomes are near boundaries.








WarningAssumption: No Complete Separation



Plain-language meaning: For logistic models, maximum likelihood estimation requires that both outcome values (0 and 1) occur across the range of predictors. Complete separation — where one condition perfectly predicts the outcome — causes the estimated log-odds to diverge to infinity and standard errors to blow up.
What the model is assuming away: The practical possibility that an experimental manipulation is so strong, or a sample is so small, that one cell has all 0s or all 1s.
JDM example: If all participants in the loss-frame condition declined every gamble (all 0s) and all participants in the gain-frame condition accepted every gamble (all 1s), the logistic model has no finite solution.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “Your condition-level acceptance rates are 0% and 98% — are your results artifacts of near-complete separation?”
Observable warning sign: Extremely large estimated coefficients (in the hundreds) with enormous standard errors; a warning from glmer() about convergence or Hauck-Donner effects.
What to check: Inspect condition-level contingency tables before fitting. If any cell is empty or near-empty, use Firth’s penalized likelihood (brglm2 package) or Bayesian estimation.








WarningAssumption: Correct Distributional Family for Count Outcomes



Plain-language meaning: Poisson assumes mean = variance. Negative binomial relaxes this, allowing variance > mean (overdispersion). Zero-inflated models further allow excess structural zeros.
What the model is assuming away with Poisson: That individual-level heterogeneity in choice propensity does not create extra variance in counts beyond what a simple rate model predicts.
JDM example: In a repeated gamble task, participants with generally low risk tolerance will contribute many near-zero blocks while participants with high risk tolerance contribute many near-10 blocks. This cross-person heterogeneity creates overdispersion relative to Poisson.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “The Poisson model assumes variance equals mean for your choice counts, but in a within-subjects design with individual differences, this seems implausible. Did you check for overdispersion?”
Observable warning sign: Dispersion ratio > 1.5; residual variance plots showing systematic patterns.
What to check: Report the dispersion ratio explicitly. If > 1.5, switch to nbinom2 in glmmTMB(). If the count distribution has excess zeros beyond the model prediction, add a zero-inflation component.








WarningAssumption: Sufficient Within-Person Observations for Stable Random Effects



Plain-language meaning: The logistic random intercept is estimated from each participant’s repeated choices. With very few observations per participant (e.g., 2 binary trials), the individual-level log-odds are estimated very imprecisely and the random-effects variance is unstable.
JDM example: In a 2-trial binary choice experiment, each participant contributes only two observations — one per condition. The random intercept for that participant is essentially identified by a single data point. The random-effect variance estimate will be very noisy.
What a skeptical reviewer might say: “With only 4 trials per participant per condition, how reliable are your random-effects estimates?”
What to check: Aim for at least 5–10 binary trials per participant per condition for stable random-effects estimation. With fewer, consider Bayesian estimation (brms) which regularizes the random effects via priors and handles small-cluster GLMMs more stably.

title: Binary and Count Outcomes in Experiments
text:
Reviewer Challenge






TipWhat a Reviewer Would Ask



Challenge 1: “Why not just analyze the proportion correct / proportion accepted as a continuous outcome?” Converting binary outcomes to proportions and using a linear model is a common shortcut. It produces approximately correct inference when proportions are in the 0.2–0.8 range, but fails near the boundaries where the probability scale becomes nonlinear. More importantly, the logistic random intercept correctly models the individual differences on the log-odds scale — which is where the DGP actually operates — rather than forcing normal residuals onto a bounded proportion.
Challenge 2: “Your odds ratios are hard to interpret. Can you just report probability differences?” Both should be reported. Odds ratios are the natural effect size from the model (they are constant across baseline probability levels). Marginal probability differences from ggpredict() are easier to communicate but depend on the reference population. Report odds ratios in the model table and predicted probabilities in the figure. State both.
Challenge 3: “Your random intercept variance is large — could the treatment effect be moderated by individual differences?” Yes, and this is worth examining. A large random intercept variance means participants vary a lot in their baseline tendencies. A random slope model — (1 + framing | participant) — tests whether the framing effect itself varies across participants. If it does, reporting a single average effect misses important heterogeneity. The random slope test is the right diagnostic.

title: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility
text:
Why This Chapter Exists
Nested data creates reporting problems that do not exist in simple ANOVA or OLS regression. When effects are estimated at multiple levels, when random effects have their own variance components, and when outcomes live on transformed scales, the standard playbook for effect sizes (Cohen’s \(d\), \(\eta^2\), \(R^2\)) breaks down or becomes ambiguous.
This chapter covers:

Effect size measures for mixed models — what they mean and how to compute them
Translating fixed effect estimates to interpretable metrics
Conditional vs. marginal \(R^2\)
Reporting standards for nested experimental data
Reproducibility practices: seeds, version pinning, and transparent reporting
crumbs: 44  Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility

title: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility
section: Part 1: Effect Size in Mixed Models
text:
Part 1: Effect Size in Mixed Models

The Problem with Standard Effect Sizes
Cohen’s \(d\) is defined as the standardized mean difference:
\[d = \frac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\sigma}\]
But what is \(\sigma\) in a mixed model? There are multiple variance components: the residual variance \(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\), the random intercept variance \(\tau^2_{00}\), and possibly additional random slope variances. Each gives a different denominator — and therefore a different \(d\).
The answer depends on the question you are asking:

Conditional \(d\): standardizes by the within-cluster (residual) variance. Answers: “How large is the effect within a person/cluster, relative to how much observations vary within that cluster?”
Marginal \(d\): standardizes by the total variance (random effects + residual). Answers: “How large is the effect relative to all variability in the outcome?”

Neither is wrong. They answer different questions.


Cohen’s \(d\) for Experimental Effects in Nested Data
In a typical within-subjects experiment, the effect of interest is the difference between conditions, and the relevant variability is the within-person trial-level variance. The residual SD from the mixed model (not including the random effect variance) is the appropriate standardizer for a within-person \(d\).


Code
# Simulate a within-subjects experiment: 80 participants × 10 trials per condition
n_par  <- 80
n_trial <- 10

df_d <- expand_grid(
  participant = 1:n_par,
  condition   = c("control", "treatment"),
  trial       = 1:n_trial
) |>
  mutate(
    u0          = rnorm(n_par, 0, 8)[participant],  # between-person SD = 8
    residual_sd = 5,
    effect      = 3,  # true within-person effect
    response    = 50 + u0 + effect * (condition == "treatment") + rnorm(n(), 0, residual_sd),
    participant = factor(participant),
    condition   = factor(condition, levels = c("control", "treatment"))
  )

m_d <- lmer(response ~ condition + (1 | participant), data = df_d)

# Extract variance components
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_d))
sigma_residual <- vc$sdcor[vc$grp == "Residual"]     # within-person SD
sigma_person   <- vc$sdcor[vc$grp == "participant"]   # between-person SD
sigma_total    <- sqrt(sigma_person^2 + sigma_residual^2)

# Fixed effect estimate
beta_treatment <- fixef(m_d)["conditiontreatment"]

# Two versions of d
d_conditional <- beta_treatment / sigma_residual
d_marginal    <- beta_treatment / sigma_total

tibble(
  metric         = c("Fixed effect (unstandardized)", "Conditional d (÷ residual SD)", "Marginal d (÷ total SD)"),
  value          = c(beta_treatment, d_conditional, d_marginal),
  denominator    = c("—", round(sigma_residual, 2), round(sigma_total, 2))
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Three ways to express the same treatment effect")



Three ways to express the same treatment effect


metric
value
denominator




Fixed effect (unstandardized)
3.010
—


Conditional d (÷ residual SD)
0.615
4.9


Marginal d (÷ total SD)
0.316
9.53





Interpreting the two \(d\) values: - Conditional \(d\): standardizes within the trial-level noise. A \(d\) of 0.6 here means the treatment shifts the mean by 0.6 trial-level SDs — controlling for stable person differences. - Marginal \(d\): standardizes relative to all variability including between-person differences. This will always be smaller than conditional \(d\) when there is substantial between-person variance, because the denominator is larger. It represents the treatment’s effect size in the full distribution of responses.
The conditional \(d\) is usually more appropriate for experimental reporting, because the design specifically removes between-person variance through random assignment and repeated measurement. Marginal \(d\) deflates the effect by variance that the design was explicitly not trying to explain.

title: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility
section: Part 2: Conditional and Marginal \(R^2\) for Mixed Models
text:
Part 2: Conditional and Marginal \(R^2\) for Mixed Models

The Nakagawa-Schielzeth \(R^2\)
For linear mixed models, Nakagawa & Schielzeth (2013) define two \(R^2\) values:

Marginal \(R^2_m\): Variance explained by fixed effects only — how much the predictors in the model account for, ignoring individual differences.
Conditional \(R^2_c\): Variance explained by fixed effects plus random effects — how much the whole model (predictors + clustering) accounts for.

The difference \(R^2_c - R^2_m\) is the variance uniquely attributable to the random effects (the clustering).


Code
# Compute R² using the performance package
r2_results <- performance::r2(m_d)
print(r2_results)


# R2 for Mixed Models

  Conditional R2: 0.742
     Marginal R2: 0.024




Interpreting \(R^2\) in Nested Designs
Consider what these values tell you:

A large marginal \(R^2\) means your experimental manipulations account for substantial variance in the outcome.
A large gap between conditional and marginal \(R^2\) means individual differences (the random effects) account for substantial variance — much of the outcome is determined by who the person is, not what condition they were in.

In a typical within-subjects experiment, conditional \(R^2\) can be quite high (0.5–0.8) while marginal \(R^2\) is low (0.03–0.15). This is not a sign that the experiment failed — it is a sign that the random effects structure is doing its job, absorbing the stable between-person variance and leaving the experimental effect clearly visible in the residuals.


Code
# Show R² decomposition visually
r2_vals <- performance::r2(m_d)

r2_df <- tibble(
  component = c("Fixed effects (marginal R²)", "Random effects (conditional − marginal)", "Unexplained"),
  proportion = c(
    r2_vals$R2_marginal,
    r2_vals$R2_conditional - r2_vals$R2_marginal,
    1 - r2_vals$R2_conditional
  )
)

ggplot(r2_df, aes(x = "", y = proportion, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1e3a5f", "#4a90d9", "#d0d0d0")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Variance decomposition in the mixed model",
    subtitle = "Fixed effects (marginal R²) + Random effects contribution + Residual unexplained",
    x = NULL, y = "Proportion of total variance", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility
section: Part 3: ICC as an Effect Size
text:
Part 3: ICC as an Effect Size
The Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) — covered in Module 1 — is itself an effect size: it quantifies how much of the outcome’s variance is attributable to the clustering structure.
\[\text{ICC} = \frac{\tau^2_{00}}{\tau^2_{00} + \sigma^2_\varepsilon}\]
In experimental reporting, the ICC tells readers how much stable between-person differences matter:

High ICC (> 0.5): Most variance is between people. Within-subjects designs are very efficient here (they remove the large between-person noise). Between-subjects designs require large samples to detect effects against this noise.
Low ICC (< 0.1): Little between-person clustering. Within- and between-subjects designs are roughly equivalent in power.

Reporting the ICC in an experimental methods section tells readers how much person-to-person variability was present and why a particular design choice (within vs. between subjects) was efficient.

section: Part 4: Translating Model Output to Interpretable Metrics
text:
Part 4: Translating Model Output to Interpretable Metrics

From Log-Odds to Probabilities
For logistic mixed models, the fixed effect is in log-odds units. Always translate to probabilities for reporting:


Code
# Example: framing experiment on donation probability
# Log-odds effect = 0.59 (OR = 1.8)

log_odds_effect    <- 0.59
baseline_log_odds  <- -0.5  # average person's log-odds in control

control_prob   <- plogis(baseline_log_odds)
treatment_prob <- plogis(baseline_log_odds + log_odds_effect)

tibble(
  metric = c("Log-odds effect", "Odds ratio", "Control probability", "Treatment probability", "Probability difference"),
  value  = c(log_odds_effect, exp(log_odds_effect), control_prob, treatment_prob, treatment_prob - control_prob)
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Translating from log-odds to probabilities for reporting")

At the average baseline donation probability of 38%, loss framing increased donation probability by approximately 12 percentage points (to 50%).”


From Log-Counts to Rate Ratios
For Poisson/negative binomial models, exponentiate to get rate ratios:

# Example: scarcity on helping count
# Log effect = -0.43 (rate ratio = 0.65)

log_rate_effect    <- -0.43
baseline_log_count <- 1.8  # average log(expected count) in control

control_count   <- exp(baseline_log_count)
treatment_count <- exp(baseline_log_count + log_rate_effect)

tibble(
  metric = c("Log-count effect", "Rate ratio", "Control mean count", "Treatment mean count", "Count reduction"),
  value  = c(log_rate_effect, exp(log_rate_effect), control_count, treatment_count, control_count - treatment_count)
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Translating from log-counts to counts for reporting")

title: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility
section: Part 5: Reporting Standards for Nested Experimental Data
text:
Part 5: Reporting Standards for Nested Experimental Data

What to Report
A complete report for a mixed model analysis includes:






TipReporting Checklist for Mixed Models



Design description: - [ ] Whether the design is within-subjects, between-subjects, or mixed factorial - [ ] Number of participants, clusters, and observations per cell - [ ] ICC of the outcome (how much between-person variance was present)
Model specification: - [ ] Fixed effects included (and their coding: treatment, contrast, etc.) - [ ] Random effects structure (intercept only? slopes? which predictors vary by person?) - [ ] Software and package versions used
Results for each effect: - [ ] Unstandardized estimate with units - [ ] Standard error and 95% confidence interval - [ ] Test statistic and degrees of freedom (\(t\), \(z\), or \(F\) with Satterthwaite/Kenward-Roger df) - [ ] \(p\)-value - [ ] Effect size (\(d\), \(\eta^2\), OR, RR as appropriate)
Model-level fit: - [ ] Marginal and conditional \(R^2\) - [ ] Variance components (\(\tau^2_{00}\), \(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\), and any random slopes)
For non-normal outcomes: - [ ] Overdispersion check (for count models) - [ ] Predicted probabilities or counts at substantively meaningful covariate values




Example APA-Style Results Paragraph

“We analyzed donation decisions using a logistic mixed model with participant random intercepts, framing condition (gain vs. loss) as a fixed effect, and trial nested within participant. Loss-framing significantly increased donation probability (b = 0.59, OR = 1.81, 95% CI [1.42, 2.31], \(z\) = 4.7, \(p\) < .001). At the sample’s average baseline donation rate (38%), loss framing increased donation probability by approximately 12 percentage points. The ICC was .48, indicating substantial stable individual differences in donation tendency; the random intercept accounted for 31% of total variance (conditional \(R^2_c\) = .35; marginal \(R^2_m\) = .04).”
crumbs: 44  Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility

title: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility
text:
Part 6: Reproducibility Practices

Setting Seeds
Simulations, multiple imputation, bootstrapped CIs, and permutation tests all depend on random number generation. A fixed seed ensures the analysis is reproducible:


Code
# Set seed at the top of every analysis script
set.seed(42)

# For parallel computing, set seeds for each worker explicitly
library(parallel)
RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")  # safe for parallel streams
set.seed(42)


A single set.seed() call at the top of the script is sufficient for non-parallel analyses. Document the seed in the manuscript methods section.


Package Version Pinning
Results can change between package versions (model fitting algorithms improve, bugs are fixed, defaults change). Record the environment at the time of analysis:


Code
# At the end of every analysis script:
sessionInfo()

# Or more concisely:
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), "session_info.txt")


For fully reproducible environments, use renv:
# Initialize renv in the project root
renv::init()

# After installing/updating packages:
renv::snapshot()  # saves renv.lock with exact package versions

# To restore the environment on a new machine:
renv::restore()


Preregistration for Experimental Analyses
Preregistration specifies your analysis plan before data collection, separating confirmatory from exploratory findings. For mixed model experiments, the preregistration should specify:

The exact model formula (including random effects structure)
The primary outcome variable
The family and link function (for GLMMs)
How multiple comparisons will be handled
Any planned sensitivity analyses (e.g., random slopes model as robustness check)

Deviations from the preregistered plan should be disclosed and labeled as exploratory.
crumbs: 44  Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility

title: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility
section: Part 7: Common Reporting Mistakes in Nested Data
text:
Part 7: Common Reporting Mistakes in Nested Data






WarningMistake 1: Reporting Only the Pooled Estimate



If you ran a random-intercepts model but forgot to decompose within- and between-person effects (Module 2), the fixed effect coefficient is a blend of two mechanisms. Report both if they differ.








WarningMistake 2: Using Total SD for Within-Subjects d



Reporting Cohen’s \(d\) using the total SD (including between-person variance) dramatically understates the within-person effect. Use the residual SD from the mixed model for within-subjects standardization.








WarningMistake 3: Interpreting ICC-Corrected SEs Incorrectly



Standard errors from lmer already account for the nested structure. Do not additionally “correct” them for clustering (e.g., by applying cluster-robust SEs on top of a random intercept model). That would double-count the clustering adjustment.








WarningMistake 4: Reporting Conditional R² as the “Effect Size” of a Fixed Effect



Conditional \(R^2\) includes variance explained by the random effects. It is not an effect size for your experimental manipulation. Use marginal \(R^2\) for the fixed-effects explanation, or report individual \(\eta^2\) or \(d\) for specific contrasts.








WarningMistake 5: Omitting the Random Effects Structure from the Methods



Reporting “we used a mixed model” without specifying the random effects structure (intercept only? random slopes for condition?) makes the analysis non-reproducible. Another researcher cannot verify or extend your work without knowing the exact model formula.

title: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility
section: Part 8: What Goes in the Paper vs. the Appendix
text:
Part 8: What Goes in the Paper vs. the Appendix
One of the most practical reporting questions: which parts of the multilevel analysis belong in the main text, and which belong in a supplementary appendix?






TipPaper vs. Appendix Decision Guide



Main text (always include): - The model formula (written out, not just stated as “mixed model”) - Fixed effect estimates with standard errors and p-values for all tested hypotheses - ICC of the primary outcome - Whether random slopes were tested for the focal predictor - Effect size (conditional d, OR, RR) with confidence interval - Software and key package versions
Main text (include when substantively important): - Variance components (\(\tau^2_{00}\), \(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\)) when the research question concerns between-unit variability - Marginal and conditional R² - Hausman test result (when FE vs. RE choice was non-obvious) - Predicted probabilities or counts at theoretically meaningful covariate values (for GLMM)
Appendix (include as standard robustness evidence): - Full model comparison table (null model, main model, saturated model) - Alternative random effects specifications (e.g., random slopes added or removed) - Sensitivity analysis results (e.g., influential cluster removal, model with and without outlier branches) - Multiple imputation details and pooled results when missing data is non-trivial - CMC decomposition results when pooled and within estimates differ
Appendix (include when facing potential reviewer objections): - Fixed effects equivalent model output alongside the random effects model (when exchangeability may be questioned) - Model diagnostics: residual QQ plots, random effects normality plots, variance homogeneity checks - Alternative distributional families (Poisson vs. negative binomial for count outcomes) - Falsification tests (for IV, RDD, DiD contexts)

title: Effect Sizes, Reporting, and Reproducibility
text:
Part 9: Preempting Common Reviewer Misunderstandings
Reviewers who are not mixed-model specialists raise predictable objections. Here is a field guide for the most common ones.






NoteReviewer: “Why not just use repeated-measures ANOVA?”



What they mean: RM-ANOVA is the familiar tool for within-subjects designs.
Why MLM is better: RM-ANOVA requires complete cases (it drops participants with any missing observations). It cannot include continuous time-varying covariates. It assumes compound symmetry or sphericity (homogeneous variance across all time-lag pairs) — an assumption that rarely holds in practice. Mixed models handle all of these naturally.
How to respond: “We used a mixed model rather than RM-ANOVA because (a) 18% of participants had incomplete data at one or more waves, (b) we included continuous within-person time-varying covariates, and (c) preliminary Mauchly tests indicated sphericity was violated.”








NoteReviewer: “Your ICC is small — why does clustering matter?”



What they mean: An ICC of 0.05 looks negligible.
Why it still matters: The relevant quantity is the design effect: DEFF = 1 + (cluster size − 1) × ICC. With 20 observations per cluster and ICC = 0.05, DEFF = 1.95 — your effective N is roughly half your nominal N, and standard errors are inflated by √1.95 ≈ 40%. A “small” ICC with large clusters is a large problem.
How to respond: “Although the ICC was modest (0.05), clusters contained an average of n = 22 observations each, producing a design effect of 2.05. Ignoring clustering would have underestimated standard errors by approximately 43% and inflated Type I error for the focal comparison.”








NoteReviewer: “Why random effects rather than fixed effects? Did you test for this?”



What they mean: They are invoking the RE vs. FE concern from the Hausman tradition.
Why the question matters: If cluster-level random effects are correlated with predictors, RE estimates are biased. FE removes this problem at the cost of between-cluster comparisons.
How to respond: “We assessed the random effects assumption with the Hausman test [χ²(df) = X.XX, p = .XX], which did not support systematic differences between FE and RE estimates. Additionally, our primary predictor was experimentally assigned within clusters, ensuring orthogonality between treatment and cluster random effects by design.”








NoteReviewer: “Why don’t you include random slopes? Barr et al. (2013) say you should.”



What they mean: They have read the “keep it maximal” literature.
When they are right: For a within-subjects predictor (every participant experiences every condition), a random slope for that predictor is theoretically warranted. Omitting it increases Type I error.
When to push back: Maximal models frequently fail to converge with real data. If the random slope variance was estimated near zero and the LRT comparing models was non-significant (p > .10), the simpler model is defensible.
How to respond: “We tested a model with a by-participant random slope for condition; the slope variance was estimated near zero (σ² = 0.003) and the likelihood ratio test did not support the more complex structure (χ²(2) = 0.84, p = .66). We retained the simpler random-intercept model following Matuschek et al. (2017).”








NoteReviewer: “Your random effects are not normally distributed — doesn’t that invalidate the model?”



What they mean: They checked a caterpillar plot and saw non-normality in the BLUP residuals.
Why this is usually not fatal: The normality assumption in mixed models is on the population distribution of random effects, not on the finite-sample BLUPs. Small-to-moderate deviations from normality have limited impact on fixed-effect estimates and standard errors, especially with moderate to large numbers of clusters.
How to respond: “The random effects normality assumption was examined via QQ plots of the conditional modes (BLUPs). We observed [mild left skew / a few outlier clusters], but simulation studies (e.g., Maas & Hox, 2004) show that fixed-effect estimates in MLM are robust to moderate violations of the random-effects normality assumption. Results were substantively unchanged when [the three outlier clusters were excluded / a robust estimation method was used].”
