title: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE
text: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE

title: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE
text:
Section 1: The Compliance Problem
Random assignment supports intent-to-treat (ITT) estimates that are unbiased under standard conditions (no differential attrition, exclusion restriction, no interference) — the effect of being offered or assigned to treatment. But ITT is not always the quantity of interest.
Consider a randomized budgeting tool experiment: half the participants are given access to a digital budgeting tool, the other half to a standard information email. At 3 months, the ITT estimate is the effect of being offered the tool — but if only 65% of offered participants actually activated it, the ITT averages together the tool’s effect with a zero effect for the 35% who never engaged. The ITT underestimates the effect of the budgeting tool itself for people who would comply.
This is the compliance problem: the treatment assigned (\(Z\)) diverges from the treatment received (\(D\)).
Four estimands address this situation, each answering a different question:








Estimand
Definition
Bias?




Intent-to-treat (ITT)
Effect of assignment (\(Z \rightarrow Y\))
Unbiased but attenuated


As-treated (AT)
Compare \(D=1\) to \(D=0\) regardless of \(Z\)
Biased (self-selection into compliance)


Per-protocol
Analyze only observed compliers
Biased (excludes non-compliers non-randomly)


LATE via IV
Effect for compliers, using \(Z\) as instrument for \(D\)
Unbiased for compliers



The as-treated and per-protocol estimators are both biased for the same reason: compliers are not a random subset of assigned participants. People who activate a budgeting tool likely differ from non-activators on financial motivation, savings goals, and prior financial literacy — all of which also predict savings outcomes. Comparing them to non-activators is an observational comparison, not a causal one.

title: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE
text:
Section 2: The Four Compliance Types
To understand what IV recovers, we need to categorize participants by their potential compliance behavior. Imagine each person has a latent compliance type that determines how they respond to each value of the instrument:









Z = 0 (Control assigned)
Z = 1 (Treatment assigned)




D = 0 (no treatment received)
Never-takers & Compliers
Never-takers & Defiers


D = 1 (treatment received)
Always-takers & Defiers
Always-takers & Compliers



The four types:

Compliers: Take treatment when assigned (\(Z=1\)), do not take it when not assigned (\(Z=0\)). Treatment status follows assignment.
Never-takers: Never take treatment regardless of assignment. Their \(D\) is unaffected by \(Z\).
Always-takers: Always take treatment regardless of assignment. Their \(D\) is also unaffected by \(Z\).
Defiers: Do the opposite of their assignment. Assumed away by the monotonicity assumption.

The key insight: only compliers are affected by the instrument. Never-takers and always-takers have the same \(D\) regardless of \(Z\), so the instrument creates no variation in \(D\) for them. Comparing outcomes by \(Z\) among never-takers and always-takers is just noise. The ITT effect is therefore a diluted average: it reflects the treatment effect for compliers but zero for never- and always-takers.
Instrumental variables “zooms in” on compliers by scaling the ITT by the compliance rate.

Visual: What Happens to Each Type When Assignment Changes?


Code
# Visual illustration of the four compliance types
compliance_grid <- tibble(
  type      = rep(c("Compliers", "Never-takers", "Always-takers", "Defiers (assumed absent)"), each = 2),
  condition = rep(c("Z = 0 (Control)", "Z = 1 (Treatment)"), times = 4),
  D         = c(0, 1,   # Compliers: 0 when control, 1 when treatment
                0, 0,   # Never-takers: always 0
                1, 1,   # Always-takers: always 1
                1, 0),  # Defiers: opposite of assignment
  affected  = c(TRUE, TRUE,   # Compliers are affected
                FALSE, FALSE, # Never-takers not affected
                FALSE, FALSE, # Always-takers not affected
                TRUE, TRUE)   # Defiers are affected (but assumed away)
) |>
  mutate(
    D_label    = ifelse(D == 1, "Uses tool (D=1)", "Does not use (D=0)"),
    type       = factor(type, levels = c("Compliers", "Never-takers",
                                         "Always-takers", "Defiers (assumed absent)")),
    condition  = factor(condition, levels = c("Z = 0 (Control)", "Z = 1 (Treatment)"))
  )

fill_colors <- c("Uses tool (D=1)"    = "#1e3a5f",
                 "Does not use (D=0)" = "#d9e8f5")
text_colors <- c("Uses tool (D=1)"    = "white",
                 "Does not use (D=0)" = "#1e3a5f")

ggplot(compliance_grid,
       aes(x = condition, y = type, fill = D_label)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.2, aes(alpha = ifelse(type == "Defiers (assumed absent)", 0.35, 1))) +
  geom_text(aes(label = D_label, color = D_label), size = 3.4, fontface = "bold") +
  # Highlight complier column change
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1.45, xmax = 2.55, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 1.5,
           fill = NA, color = "#e63946", linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("text",  x = 2.62, y = 1, label = "\u2190 LATE\nidentified\nhere",
           hjust = 0, size = 3.2, color = "#e63946", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = fill_colors) +
  scale_color_manual(values = text_colors) +
  scale_alpha_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.4, 2.9)) +
  labs(
    title    = "The four compliance types: what each group does when assignment changes",
    subtitle = "IV identifies the effect for Compliers (red box) — the only group whose D changes with Z.\nNever- and Always-takers contribute noise; Defiers are assumed absent (monotonicity).",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid     = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12))

title: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE
text:
Section 3: The LATE Formula
The Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) — the average causal effect for compliers — is recovered via the Wald estimator:
\[\text{LATE} = \frac{\overbrace{E[Y \mid Z=1] - E[Y \mid Z=0]}^{\text{ITT (reduced form)}}}{\underbrace{E[D \mid Z=1] - E[D \mid Z=0]}_{\text{Compliance rate (first stage)}}}\]
The numerator is the ITT: the effect of assignment on the outcome. The denominator is the first stage: the effect of assignment on treatment receipt, i.e., the share of the sample whose treatment status is changed by the instrument. Dividing by the compliance rate “scales up” the diluted ITT to recover the effect for the sub-population whose treatment changed.
One-sided noncompliance is the special case where the control group has zero take-up (\(E[D \mid Z=0] = 0\) — no always-takers, no crossover). Then:
\[\text{LATE} = \frac{\text{ITT}}{\text{Compliance rate in treatment group}}\]
This simplification applies whenever the control condition makes treatment practically impossible (e.g., access to the tool is gated behind a unique code given only to treatment participants).






TipFour Assumptions for LATE to Be Valid




Relevance: The instrument \(Z\) must affect take-up \(D\) (testable — check first-stage \(F > 10\)).
Exclusion restriction: \(Z\) affects \(Y\) only through \(D\), not directly. This is an untestable assumption that must be justified by design.
Monotonicity: No defiers. Assignment can only push people toward treatment, never away from it.
Independence: \(Z\) is as good as randomly assigned (satisfied by design in an RCT).









WarningWhat LATE Does Not Identify



LATE is precise but narrow. A few things it does not tell you:

The effect for never-takers. People who would not activate the tool regardless of the offer are excluded from the LATE estimate. If uptake is lowest among the most financially distressed users — perhaps those who need it most — LATE reflects the effect for those already inclined to engage.
The average treatment effect (ATE). LATE = ATE only if compliance is universal (everyone assigned to treatment uses it). With partial compliance, LATE estimates the effect for compliers only.
Transportability. Compliers in this experiment may be a self-selected group (motivated, tech-comfortable, low inertia). The LATE from one context may not predict uptake effects in a population with different compliance rates.

The question LATE answers well: “If we offer this tool and some people adopt it because of the offer, how much does adoption help those people?” That is often the right question for evaluating a real-world rollout.

title: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE
section: Section 4: Worked Example — Digital Budgeting Tool Experiment
text:
Section 4: Worked Example — Digital Budgeting Tool Experiment

Simulation
We simulate a budgeting tool experiment: 200 participants randomized 1:1. In the treatment arm, 65% activate and use the tool (one-sided noncompliance — no control participants access the tool). The true causal effect of activating and using the tool is +8 percentage points of monthly savings rate.


Code
n <- 200
Z <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 100)
D <- ifelse(Z == 1, rbinom(100, 1, 0.65), 0)   # one-sided: 65% activate tool
savings_rate <- 10 + 8 * D + rnorm(n, 0, 6)    # true effect for compliers = 8

df_nc <- tibble(id = 1:n, Z = factor(Z), D = factor(D), savings_rate)







flowchart TD
    A["Randomized — N = 200"] --> B["Offered tool<br/>N = 100"]
    A --> C["Control — no offer<br/>N = 100"]
    B --> D["Activated tool<br/>Compliers ≈ 65"]
    B --> E["Did not activate<br/>Never-takers ≈ 35"]
    D --> F["Outcome measured<br/>D = 1: tool users"]
    E --> G["Outcome measured<br/>D = 0: assigned but unused"]
    C --> H["Outcome measured<br/>D = 0: no access"]
    style D fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2d6a4f
    style E fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e67e22
    style H fill:#f0f0f0,stroke:#888888






The ITT estimate contrasts everyone in the offered group (N=100) with everyone in the control group (N=100) — regardless of activation. The LATE estimate uses the offer as an instrument for actual activation, recovering the causal effect for the sub-population whose tool use changed because of the offer (the compliers — roughly 65 of the 100 offered participants). Never-takers and the control group both have D = 0, but for different reasons.


Estimating all three quantities


Code
m_itt  <- lm(savings_rate ~ Z,   data = df_nc)
m_at   <- lm(savings_rate ~ D,   data = df_nc)
m_late <- ivreg(savings_rate ~ D | Z, data = df_nc)





True effect for compliers = 8. ITT is diluted by the 35% non-activators. As-treated is biased upward (activators are more motivated to save). LATE recovers the true complier effect.


method
estimate
std.error
p.value




ITT (assignment)
4.904
0.866
0


As-treated (biased — self-selection)
7.627
0.862
0


LATE via IV (Wald estimator)
8.174
1.319
0







Manual Wald check
The IV estimate should equal ITT divided by the compliance rate:


Code
itt_est   <- coef(m_itt)["Z1"]
comp_rate <- mean(as.integer(as.character(df_nc$D))[Z == 1]) -
             mean(as.integer(as.character(df_nc$D))[Z == 0])

cat("ITT estimate:      ", round(itt_est, 3), "\n")


ITT estimate:       4.904 


Code
cat("Compliance rate:   ", round(comp_rate, 3), "\n")


Compliance rate:    0.6 


Code
cat("Wald LATE:         ", round(itt_est / comp_rate, 3), "\n")


Wald LATE:          8.174 


Code
cat("ivreg LATE:        ", round(coef(m_late)["D1"], 3), "\n")


ivreg LATE:         8.174 


The manual Wald calculation and ivreg() agree (up to rounding). This confirms the mechanics: ivreg() is just solving the Wald formula via two-stage least squares.


Visualization


Code
est_df <- bind_rows(
  broom::tidy(m_itt)  |> filter(term == "Z1") |>
    mutate(method = "ITT"),
  broom::tidy(m_at)   |> filter(term == "D1") |>
    mutate(method = "As-treated"),
  broom::tidy(m_late) |> filter(term == "D1") |>
    mutate(method = "LATE (IV)")
) |>
  mutate(
    method   = factor(method, levels = c("ITT", "As-treated", "LATE (IV)")),
    biased   = method == "As-treated"
  )

ggplot(est_df, aes(x = method, y = estimate, fill = biased)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.55, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - 1.96 * std.error,
                    ymax = estimate + 1.96 * std.error),
                width = 0.18) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 8, linetype = "dashed", color = "#c0392b", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.45, y = 8.5, label = "True effect = 8",
           color = "#c0392b", hjust = 1, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#1e3a5f", "TRUE" = "#e67e22"),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title    = "ITT, as-treated, and LATE estimates — budgeting tool experiment",
    subtitle = "ITT diluted by non-activators; as-treated biased by self-selection; LATE recovers true effect",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Estimated effect on savings rate (pp)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

title: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE
section: Section 5: When Is ITT vs. LATE the Right Estimand?
text:
Section 5: When Is ITT vs. LATE the Right Estimand?
Both ITT and LATE are valid causal estimands — they answer different questions. The choice depends on what the researcher or policymaker actually wants to know.








Estimand
Right for
Policy analog




ITT
“What happens if we offer this program?”
Opt-in program evaluation — you offer it, some take it


LATE
“What is the effect of actually receiving treatment?”
Compliance-based evaluation — effect among those who engage



Policy example 1 — Budgeting tool rollout: A financial platform evaluates whether to offer a budgeting tool to customers. Some will activate it, others will not. The policy assigns the offer, not the tool engagement itself. The ITT (effect of receiving access, even if unused) is the directly relevant estimand for evaluating whether to expand the offer — it captures the real-world effect of deploying the tool at scale.
Policy example 2 — Behavioral effect of tool engagement: A researcher wants to know whether the budgeting tool itself changes savings behavior for users who engage with it. The instrument is random assignment to access; LATE — the effect for those who activated because they were offered access — is the behaviorally relevant quantity. The ITT (effect of the offer) captures the effect of the deployment, which is less informative about whether the tool mechanism itself works.






TipPractical Guidance



When writing up results, report both ITT and LATE. The ITT is interpretable as an “offer effect” that any policymaker can use directly. The LATE is interpretable as the treatment effect for those who would engage, given the design. Report the first-stage compliance rate and the \(F\)-statistic so readers can evaluate the strength of the instrument.

title: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE
text:
Section 6: Two-Sided Noncompliance
Two-sided noncompliance occurs when some control-group participants find the treatment on their own (always-takers, crossover). This is common in studies of freely available digital tools — an app that is publicly downloadable cannot be restricted to the treatment arm. The control group no longer has zero take-up.


Code
n   <- 200
Z   <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 100)
D   <- ifelse(Z == 1,
              rbinom(100, 1, 0.75),   # 75% compliance in treatment
              rbinom(100, 1, 0.10))   # 10% crossover in control
Y   <- 50 - 8 * D + rnorm(n, 0, 7)

df_2s      <- tibble(Z = factor(Z), D = factor(D), Y)
m_late_2s  <- ivreg(Y ~ D | Z, data = df_2s)

broom::tidy(m_late_2s) |>
  filter(term == "D1") |>
  select(estimate, std.error, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Two-sided noncompliance: ivreg() generalizes automatically. True effect = -8.")



Two-sided noncompliance: ivreg() generalizes automatically. True effect = -8.


estimate
std.error
p.value




-7.889
1.526
0





The Wald formula generalizes: the denominator is now \(E[D \mid Z=1] - E[D \mid Z=0] = 0.75 - 0.10 = 0.65\), reflecting that 65% of the sample has their treatment status determined by the instrument (the compliers). ivreg() handles this automatically.






WarningTwo-Sided Non-Compliance Shrinks the Complier Pool



With 10% crossover in the control group, the effective “complier” share drops. The first-stage \(F\)-statistic will be lower than in the one-sided case with the same treatment-group compliance rate, because there is less net variation in \(D\) driven by \(Z\). Monitor the first-stage \(F\)-statistic carefully when crossover is suspected.

title: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE
section: Section 7: Noncompliance in Nested Experimental Designs
text:
Section 7: Noncompliance in Nested Experimental Designs
In multi-site experiments (employees nested in firms, customers nested in bank branches), noncompliance can cluster at the site level: in a multi-employer experiment on financial wellness tools, an entire employer site may implement the tool poorly (IT barriers, low managerial support). Treating compliance as independent across participants in the same site understates uncertainty.
The remedy is cluster-robust standard errors at the site level:


Code
library(sandwich)

# Assume df_nc has a 'site' variable
coeftest(m_late, vcov = vcovCL(m_late, cluster = ~site))


When site-level compliance rates vary substantially, it can also be informative to model compliance as a site-level random effect — sites with low compliance contribute attenuated ITT estimates, and the LATE for each site reflects that site’s compliance rate.






TipSite-Level Compliance in Multi-Site Studies



If site-level compliance is itself of interest (e.g., “does full implementation matter?”), you can model it explicitly:
# Site-level compliance rate as a predictor
site_compliance <- df_nested |>
  filter(Z == 1) |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarise(compliance_rate = mean(as.integer(as.character(D))))

df_nested <- left_join(df_nested, site_compliance, by = "site")
lmer(savings_rate ~ compliance_rate + (1 | site), data = df_nested |> filter(Z == 1))
This is a “dose-response” analysis at the site level and requires its own identification argument (why does compliance vary across sites independent of site characteristics?).

title: Non-Compliance: ITT and LATE
text:
Section 8: Reporting Template
Use the following template for APA-style reporting of ITT and LATE results:

Participants were randomly assigned to receive access to a [digital budgeting tool] (n = 100) or standard information email (n = 100). Compliance was 65% in the treatment group (one-sided noncompliance; no control participants accessed the tool). Intent-to-treat analysis — using treatment assignment as the predictor regardless of compliance — showed a statistically significant but attenuated effect (b = [ITT estimate], SE = [ITT SE], p = [p]). To estimate the effect for participants who complied with treatment, we used instrumental variables regression (two-stage least squares) with treatment assignment as the instrument for treatment receipt. The complier average causal effect (LATE) was b = [LATE estimate], SE = [LATE SE], p = [p], consistent with a [direction and magnitude] effect on savings rate for participants who activated the tool. The first-stage F-statistic (F = [F]) exceeded the conventional weak-instruments threshold of 10, supporting the instrument’s relevance.

section: How Experiments Degrade: A Flow Map
text:
How Experiments Degrade: A Flow Map
A perfectly randomized experiment with full compliance and no attrition requires only the tools from Modules 1–2. But most field experiments accumulate one or more complications. The flowchart below maps how each complication arises and which tool this chapter uses to recover a valid estimate.





flowchart TD
    A["Ideal randomized experiment\nFull compliance · No attrition · Random assignment"]

    A -->|"Experiment runs perfectly"| B["Standard mixed model\nModules 1–2"]

    A -.->|"Differential dropout\nat follow-up"| C["Non-random survivor sample\nControl group deflated or inflated"]
    C --> D["IPW for attrition\nSection 3\nRequires: MAR assumption"]

    A -.->|"Noncompliance:\nassigned ≠ received"| E["ITT diluted;\ntreatment take-up endogenous"]
    E --> F["ITT + LATE via IV\nModule 5 Part 8"]

    A -.->|"Voluntary sub-treatment\nengagement within arm"| G["Within-arm observational\ncomparison (endogenous usage)"]
    G --> H["PSM within treatment arm\nSection 4\nRequires: ignorability on observables"]

    A -.->|"Threshold rule\ndetermines eligibility"| I["Assignment discontinuous\nat running-variable cutoff"]
    I --> J["Regression discontinuity\nSection 5 · Module 3 Part 4\nRequires: continuity assumption"]

    A -.->|"Baseline + follow-up\nwith control group"| K["Pre-post design:\nparallel trends question"]
    K --> L["DiD mixed model\nSection 2\nRequires: parallel trends"]

    style A fill:#deebf7,stroke:#1e3a5f
    style B fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2d6a4f
    style D fill:#fff9c4,stroke:#e67e00
    style F fill:#fff9c4,stroke:#e67e00
    style H fill:#fff9c4,stroke:#e67e00
    style J fill:#fff9c4,stroke:#e67e00
    style L fill:#fff9c4,stroke:#e67e00






Each dashed arrow represents a complication that breaks the ideal randomization; the yellow boxes show the methodological remedy and the key assumption that must hold for the remedy to work.

title: Quasi-Experimental Methods for Applied Researchers
section: Section 1: When Experiments Have Observational Features
text:
Section 1: When Experiments Have Observational Features
A fully randomized experiment with perfect compliance and no attrition is the gold standard for causal inference — but it rarely survives contact with the field intact. In practice, experiments accumulate observational features: participants drop out for reasons related to the treatment, some assigned to treatment never engage, ethical or logistical constraints limit who can be randomized, and field implementations vary substantially across sites.
These complications do not invalidate the experiment. They do require the researcher to reach into the quasi-experimental toolkit that Module 3 introduced for observational studies. The good news: the same tools that handle observational confounding also handle experimental imperfections — often in a cleaner setting, because the original randomization still provides some traction.
The table below maps common experimental complications to their methodological remedies and their Module 3 antecedents:

section: Section 2: DiD as the Logic of Pre-Post Designs
text:
Section 2: DiD as the Logic of Pre-Post Designs

The structural equivalence
The standard randomized pre-post design is a difference-in-differences design. It has:

Two groups: intervention and control (the “treated vs. untreated” dimension of DiD)
Two time points: baseline and follow-up (the “pre vs. post” dimension of DiD)
The DiD estimand: \((\bar{Y}^{\text{post}}_{\text{int}} - \bar{Y}^{\text{pre}}_{\text{int}}) - (\bar{Y}^{\text{post}}_{\text{ctrl}} - \bar{Y}^{\text{pre}}_{\text{ctrl}})\)

Recognizing this equivalence is valuable for two reasons. First, it makes explicit what the pre-post mixed model assumes (parallel trends in the absence of treatment — which randomization supports in expectation across repeated samples, though any realized sample can show chance pre-trend imbalance). Second, it gives you the full DiD toolkit: you can add multiple waves, test pre-trend balance, and use the event study framework to trace the treatment trajectory over time.


Simulation: information disclosure intervention
We simulate 120 participants (60 per arm) measured at baseline (pre) and 8-week follow-up (post). An information disclosure intervention (gain-framed vs. standard disclosure) is randomized. The disclosure intervention is expected to increase risk_willingness (gain framing increases confidence in recommended investments). True DiD effect = +8 units.


Code
n_per <- 60

df_pp <- expand_grid(
  participant = 1:(n_per * 2),
  wave        = c("pre", "post")
) |>
  mutate(
    condition = ifelse(participant <= n_per, "standard", "gain_frame"),
    time_num  = as.integer(wave == "post"),
    treat_num = as.integer(condition == "gain_frame"),
    u0        = rnorm(n_per * 2, 0, 6)[participant],
    risk_willingness = 45 + u0 + 1.5 * time_num + 8 * time_num * treat_num + rnorm(n(), 0, 5),
    participant = factor(participant),
    wave      = factor(wave, levels = c("pre", "post")),
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("standard", "gain_frame"))
  )




DiD mixed model


Code
m_did_exp <- lmer(risk_willingness ~ wave * condition + (1 | participant),
                  data = df_pp, REML = FALSE)

broom.mixed::tidy(m_did_exp, effects = "fixed") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "DiD mixed model. The wave:condition interaction is the DiD estimate (target: +8).")

Comparison to ANCOVA
ANCOVA on the wide-format outcome, controlling for the pre-test, is a common alternative:


Code
df_wide <- df_pp |>
  select(participant, condition, wave, risk_willingness) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = wave, values_from = risk_willingness,
              names_prefix = "rw_") |>

The two approaches converge when the pre-test is mean-centered and the random-effect variance is estimated well. The DiD mixed model generalizes more naturally to three or more waves and produces an interpretable random-effects structure, making it preferred for longitudinal experimental designs.
Recognizing this equivalence is valuable: the pre-test provides a baseline for the DiD logic, and randomization supports parallel trends in expectation.


Event study visualization


Code
summ_pp <- df_pp |>
  group_by(wave, condition) |>
  summarise(mean_rw = mean(risk_willingness), se_rw = sd(risk_willingness) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")

                     color = condition, group = condition)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_rw - 1.96 * se_rw,
                    ymax = mean_rw + 1.96 * se_rw), width = 0.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("standard" = "#aec6e8", "gain_frame" = "#1e3a5f")) +
  annotate("segment",
           x = 2.05, xend = 2.05, y = 47, yend = 55,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), ends = "both"),
           color = "#c0392b") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.12, y = 51,
           label = "DiD \u2248 +8", color = "#c0392b", hjust = 0, size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title    = "Pre-post risk willingness by condition",
    subtitle = "Parallel pre-period (randomization), divergent post-period (treatment)",
    x        = "Wave",
    y        = "Mean risk willingness (0\u2013100)",
    color    = "Condition"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)











Three-wave extension
With baseline, mid-point, and follow-up, the time × condition interaction becomes a trajectory. Pre-baseline balance checks verify randomization; post-baseline coefficients trace how the treatment effect builds over time. This is the experimental event study:


Code
# Three-wave data with weeks 0, 4, 8
m_3wave <- lmer(risk_willingness ~ factor(week) * condition + (1 | participant),
                data = df_3wave)
# Plot estimated coefficients for each week x condition cell


Pre-period interaction coefficients near zero confirm that randomization produced balanced groups. Post-period coefficients show whether treatment effects are immediate, delayed, or accumulating.

title: Quasi-Experimental Methods for Applied Researchers
text:
Section 3: IPW for Non-Random Attrition

The problem
Even in a fully randomized trial, attrition at follow-up can reintroduce bias. If high-risk-averse control-group participants are more likely to drop out — because the study involves making financial decisions that feel threatening and they disengage — then the observed control-group follow-up average is deflated (it excludes the most risk-averse participants). The treatment appears less effective than it truly is for the full intention-to-treat sample, biasing the naive estimate downward.


Simulation


Code
n_att <- 200
set.seed(42)

treatment_att    <- rep(c(0, 1), each = 100)
baseline_risk_av <- rnorm(n_att, 50, 10)   # baseline risk aversion

# High risk aversion + control group → higher dropout
# (risk-averse participants avoid making financial decisions in the study)
p_remain   <- plogis(2.5 - 0.07 * baseline_risk_av + 0.8 * treatment_att)
remained   <- rbinom(n_att, 1, p_remain)

# True treatment effect = +6 (disclosure increases willingness to take recommended risk)
outcome_att <- 45 + 6 * treatment_att - 0.3 * baseline_risk_av + rnorm(n_att, 0, 6)

df_att <- tibble(treatment = treatment_att, baseline_risk_av, remained, outcome_att)

cat("Retention rate — control:  ", mean(remained[treatment_att == 0]), "\n")


Retention rate — control:   0.26 


Code
cat("Retention rate — treatment:", mean(remained[treatment_att == 1]), "\n")


Retention rate — treatment: 0.48 




IPW correction
We model the probability of remaining in the study as a function of baseline risk aversion and treatment, then weight complete cases by the inverse of their retention probability:


Code
ps_att     <- glm(remained ~ baseline_risk_av + treatment, family = binomial, data = df_att)
df_att$ipw_att <- 1 / fitted(ps_att)

df_complete     <- df_att |> filter(remained == 1)
m_naive_att     <- lm(outcome_att ~ treatment, data = df_complete)
m_ipw_att       <- lm(outcome_att ~ treatment, data = df_complete,
                       weights = df_att$ipw_att[df_att$remained == 1])





Attrition bias: naive vs. IPW-weighted (true treatment effect = +6). High-risk-averse participants in the control group drop out more, biasing the naive estimate downward. IPW is consistent under MAR.

WarningIPW Assumptions for Attrition Correction



IPW corrects for attrition under Missing at Random (MAR): the probability of dropout depends on observed pre-treatment variables (here, baseline risk aversion and treatment condition), but not on the unobserved post-treatment outcome. If dropout is driven by the unmeasured outcome itself — e.g., people drop out because their financial situation has worsened and they do not want to be measured — IPW will not fully correct the bias. Consider collecting data on dropouts via brief follow-up contacts to test the MAR assumption empirically.




Visualization


Code
# Retention probability plot
df_plot_ret <- df_att |>
  mutate(
    p_ret    = fitted(ps_att),
    trt_lab  = ifelse(treatment == 1, "Treatment", "Control")
  )

ggplot(df_plot_ret, aes(x = baseline_risk_av, y = p_ret, color = trt_lab)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#e67e22", "Treatment" = "#1e3a5f"),
                     name = "Group") +
  labs(
    title    = "Retention probability by baseline risk aversion and treatment",
    subtitle = "High-risk-averse controls are most likely to drop out — biasing naive estimate downward",
    x        = "Baseline Risk Aversion",
    y        = "P(Retained at follow-up)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

section: Section 4: PSM for Voluntary Sub-Treatment Participation
text:
Section 4: PSM for Voluntary Sub-Treatment Participation

The within-experiment observational problem
Random assignment creates treatment and control arms, but within the treatment arm, engagement is voluntary. In a financial coaching field experiment, random assignment gives participants access to an AI-powered savings advisor. Actual usage is voluntary — high-usage participants likely differ systematically from low-usage participants in motivation, baseline financial literacy, and financial goals.
Propensity score matching on pre-treatment covariates makes this within-arm comparison more credible by constructing a control group of low-users who resembled high-users at baseline.


Simulation and matching
We work within the treatment arm of the attrition simulation and create a high-use indicator that is related to baseline risk aversion:


Code
df_treat_only <- df_att |>
  filter(treatment == 1) |>
  mutate(
    high_user = rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-0.5 + 0.04 * baseline_risk_av))
  )

# Within the coaching arm: match high-users to low-users
# on pre-randomization covariates
m_sub <- matchit(
  high_user ~ baseline_risk_av,
  data   = df_treat_only,
  method = "nearest",
  ratio  = 1
)

summary(m_sub)$sum.matched |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Covariate balance after 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching on baseline risk aversion.")

WarningWhat PSM Within an Experiment Identifies



Matching on pre-treatment covariates removes observed confounders of the high-use vs. low-use comparison. But unobserved motivation, financial self-efficacy, and expectancy effects remain. The matched estimate is closer to causal than the naive comparison, but it is not an RCT-quality estimate.
Formally, this identifies the Average Treatment effect on the Treated (ATT) for the sub-population of high-users — the effect of high engagement among people with observable characteristics similar to those who actually engaged heavily. This is not a LATE (which is an IV estimand defined by instrument-induced compliers) and is not the ATE for all participants. Interpret as “the effect of high engagement, for people with similar observable characteristics to high engagers,” not “the effect of high engagement for everyone.” Crucially, this rests on a selection-on-observables assumption: all confounders of the usage–outcome relationship are measured and included in the PS model.

title: Quasi-Experimental Methods for Applied Researchers
section: Section 5: Threshold-Based Eligibility (RDD in Applied Research)
text:
Section 5: Threshold-Based Eligibility (RDD in Applied Research)
When access to a program is determined by whether a continuous running variable crosses a threshold, regression discontinuity design (RDD) is the appropriate analysis. The continuity assumption — that potential outcomes vary smoothly across the cutoff — is often more credible in financial-decision settings than the selection-on-observables assumption required by propensity score methods.
A common example: a platform introduces a fee waiver for customers whose account balance exceeds $1,000. Customers just below and just above the threshold are otherwise similar — the threshold creates local quasi-random variation. Similarly, subsidy eligibility cutoffs based on income or credit score thresholds produce the same discontinuity logic.


Code
# Requires rdrobust package
library(rdrobust)

# score_threshold: running variable (e.g., account balance in dollars)
# eligible: indicator for whether balance >= 1000
# outcome_rdd: e.g., monthly savings rate or financial product adoption

rdd_out <- rdrobust(y = df$outcome_rdd, x = df$score_threshold, c = 1000)
summary(rdd_out)
rdplot(y = df$outcome_rdd, x = df$score_threshold, c = 1000,
       title = "RDD: account balance fee-waiver threshold at $1,000")


The rdrobust package implements optimal bandwidth selection, bias-corrected confidence intervals, and the McCrary density test (for manipulation of the running variable). The full treatment of RDD mechanics, bandwidth selection, and robustness checks is in Module 3 Part 4; that framework applies directly here.






TipRDD in Financial and Consumer Behavior Research



RDD is underused in consumer behavior and financial decision research relative to economics, despite being highly credible when a threshold rule genuinely determines assignment. Common examples: credit score thresholds for product access, account balance thresholds for fee waivers or tier upgrades, subsidy eligibility cutoffs based on income, and performance review thresholds that trigger intervention. If your research setting uses a cutoff rule, seriously consider RDD before reaching for PSM.

title: Quasi-Experimental Methods for Applied Researchers
text:
Section 6: Practical Decision Guide






TipChoosing Your Method When Randomization Is Imperfect



Work through this sequence when your experimental data does not satisfy the simple randomization ideal:

Fully randomized, no attrition, full compliance? Standard mixed model (Modules 1–2). No quasi-experimental adjustment needed.
Randomized + differential attrition? IPW for attrition (this chapter, Section 3). Requires MAR assumption.
Randomized + noncompliance? Report ITT (always). If complier effect is of interest, add LATE via IV (Module 5 Part 8).
Eligibility determined by a continuous threshold? Regression discontinuity (Module 3 Part 4). Local to the threshold — do not generalize far from cutoff.
Pre-post design with randomized comparison group? DiD mixed model (this chapter, Section 2). Generalizes to multiple waves as event study.
Self-selection into sub-treatment within an experiment? PSM within treatment arm (this chapter, Section 4). Residual unobserved confounding remains.
Observational study with good observed confounders? PSM or IPW on covariates (Module 3 Part 6). Validity depends entirely on selection-on-observables.
Observational study with a credible instrument? IV or LATE (Module 3 Part 2, Module 5 Part 8). Validity depends on exclusion restriction.

No method is universally best. The right method depends on the data-generating process and which assumption is most defensible given your study design.

title: Quasi-Experimental Methods for Applied Researchers
text:
Section 7: The Full Course Arc
This workshop has built from the ground up.
Module 1 established the mixed-effects framework: how to model data where observations are nested within units, how to decompose variance across levels, and why treating clustered data as independent inflates false positive rates. The random intercept model is not a statistical correction tacked on after the fact — it is a direct translation of the sampling structure into the model.
Module 2 showed that how you enter predictors matters as much as which predictors you include. Within-unit centering decomposes predictors into their between-unit and within-unit components, corresponding to different mechanisms operating at different levels of the hierarchy. Getting the centering wrong means estimating the wrong estimand, even with a correctly specified error structure.
Module 3 showed where the well-specified mixed model can still go wrong: omitted variables (time-invariant and time-varying), endogenous regressors, selection into the sample, regression discontinuities at thresholds, treatment effect heterogeneity, and non-random treatment assignment. Six threats; six identification strategies. Each strategy requires a different source of identifying variation and a different set of untestable assumptions.
Module 4 addressed the practicalities of longitudinal data: handling missing values without complete-case bias, and applying the Module 3 identification strategies to the panel setting where time creates both new threats and new opportunities.
Module 5 closed the loop for applied experimental researchers: what to do when the experiment is imperfect, and how to connect the quasi-experimental toolkit back to the experimental design.
The unifying insight across all five modules:

Understanding your data generating process — who is nested in whom, what varies within units versus across units, what mechanisms connect your predictors to your outcome, and what determines who ends up in each condition — is the prerequisite for every methodological choice covered in this workshop.

The nesting structure is not a nuisance to correct for with a random effect and move on. It is the scientific structure of your data. The causal question is always about a mechanism operating at a particular level of that structure, through a particular pathway, for a particular population. The method is in service of making that mechanism legible.

title: Appendix A — About
text:
Dan Schley is an Associate Professor in the Department of Marketing Management at Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University Rotterdam. His work sits at the intersection of psychology, economics, and statistical methodology, with a particular focus on measurement, experimentation, and causal inference in behavioral research. Contact: schley@rsm.nl

I came to multilevel modeling the way many behavioral researchers do — not as a statistician, but as someone who kept noticing that the standard tools didn’t quite fit the data. My training moved across economics at UC San Diego, quantitative psychology at The Ohio State University, and ultimately marketing research at Erasmus. Each transition brought a different set of methodological assumptions into view.
Repeated-measures experiments. Panel datasets. Longitudinal surveys. Cross-national comparisons. In every case, observations are clustered in ways that basic regression ignores. And in every case, the right question is not just “how do I fit this model?” but “what process generated this data, and how close does my model get to it?”
This workshop grew out of teaching the ERIM doctoral program at RSM, where I found that students’ biggest stumbling block was not the mathematics — it was the conceptual leap from thinking about data as a flat table to thinking about data as a slice through a structured, multi-layered process. The DGP framing — treating your dataset as a snapshot of a larger data-generating process — helped more students than any single equation.
The companion workshop on Measurement, Experimentation, and Causal Inference covers many of the same research design questions from a different angle. Together, these workshops aim to bridge the vocabulary gap between psychology, economics, and quantitative social science.
